The Glad Century and the Stitching Laws

For a hundred years it looked like a miracle. Mothers who would have died in childbed rose and nursed; fishermen swept off the weirs came home with weed in their hair. There were no widows and no orphans, and the reed-towns danced through the long fen evenings. The songs of that century are the only happy songs in Sallowreach, and nobody sings them now. The dancing stopped when the first generation began to come apart: a man who died in the year 3 was by the year 90 something that could not hold a fiddle. By 130 the state recognized what it was. The Stitching Laws made families responsible for keeping their dead in one piece, chartered the Seamers’ Guild, and made it a fineable offence to fall apart in public. The fines are still collected: four lacks for a hand on the boardwalk, twenty for a face.

The War of the Heirs and the Licensing

By 288 no property had changed hands by inheritance in two centuries, and the young rose. The Heirs won every battle, hacked their fathers apart in their own halls, and changed nothing: the fathers were back at their desks within the week, stitched, lacquered and furious, and sent their children to the jar. The Heirs’ banner, a hand cut off at the wrist, still hangs in the Sinks. Thirteen years later, in 301, the Hand-lines announced what some of them had known for decades: their touch could finish a person. They did not give it away. The Court set a price and built the Hall of Closings, and made death scarce on purpose.

The Hushes

In Carving of 633, a ferryman poling past Dunmere at dawn could not hear the village dogs, or his pole in the water, or himself shouting. Everyone in the village was simply, properly dead. When the news reached Lastgate, half the country wept with envy. Seventeen more Hushes have been found since, some no bigger than a room, every one within a day of a Hand-line estate.

The Grey Plague

In the hot Plenty of 512 a Fatlands drover brought a fever up the border road. In the south it killed one in ten. In the south fen of Sallowreach it killed no one, and Kept a third of everyone it touched in a single month: they burned, they sweated, they died in their beds, and they sat up in the morning still burning, still sweating, with the fever going on inside them forever. Brinemoss and the stilt-hamlets around it are still full of the fever-Kept, flushed and shivering under their blankets in the heat, their skin hot to the touch a hundred and twenty-nine years later, their teeth chattering in the dark like a weir-trap knocking. They are the only Kept who are warm. Nobody wants to hold their hands either.

The Restitution of 639

By the spring of 639 there were eleven Hushes and the Court had Provost Sedge’s first maps, and the Leaden party, which wanted the Course-stricken walled in lead, found itself outvoted by a stranger notion. It came from the Confessors of the Theft, whose whole doctrine is that what the north lives in is a bill for a stolen god. If the Hushes were the god coming back for what was taken, said Confessor Ambrose Weal before the Court in Grace of that year, then what was taken might be given back. The hands had been stolen. Return a pair of hands.

The Court debated it for nine days, which is fast for the Court. It settled on Lord Pellam Fallow, of a lesser Hand-line, forty-four, at the Course, the son of the Lady Imber Fallow who had closed her father in 588; and Pellam, who had grown up in that house and knew what his mother’s hands had done, said yes before he was asked twice. The Seamers’ Guild was ordered to take the hands. Thessaly Mort refused to do it herself and sent her senior Master of the Seam, who did it in the Hall of Hands at dawn with a bone-saw, before the whole Court. The witnesses agreed on one detail more than any other: the saw blade went cold and grey where it touched the wrist, and the Master had to change blades three times, because each one the hands touched was finished, and would not cut again.

The hands lived. Everything in Sallowreach lives. Severed, they lay on the cedar tray and opened and closed, slowly, nine joints to a finger, and the clerk who carried the tray found his breath smoking and his ears full of silence. They were sealed in a lead box. A procession of the whole Court, with the Confessors singing the Hymn of the Open Hands, carried the box by punt to the edge of Dunmere Hush. At the grey line Lord Pellam, his stumps bound in lint and pitch, opened the box with his teeth, and the Master of the Seam tipped the hands out over the line.

They fell into the grey and lay palm upward in the ash-coloured reeds, about ten feet from the edge, where everyone could see them. They did not move again. The Confessors sang the seventh verse and sat through the eighth in silence, as is the custom, and the procession poled home.

The next month Dunmere Hush grew forty yards, which was twice its rate in any month before. That season two new Hushes opened, one at the Fallow estate at Wending Mound. The Leaden party has not raised the Restitution since and the Confessors do not preach it. Lord Pellam lives at Wending, handless, in a house where the orchard has gone grey. He does not leave his rooms. His stumps, his servants say, have not healed, because nothing heals on the Kept and in the end not much on the living either, and lately there is something at the end of each of them, small, grey and smooth, like the first buds on a branch, with tiny joints in it, that closes when it is touched.

The hands are still where they fell. On a clear evening you can see them from the Verge with a spyglass, open, among the grey reeds, as if waiting to be given something else.

We thought it wanted its hands back. It never wanted anything. It was only coming home, and we went out to meet it with a present, like children.
Confessor Ambrose Weal, in a letter to the Shut House of the Landing, never sent
Using the Restitution

The Restitution is the north’s present-day worthless sacrifice, and Lord Pellam Fallow is its living monument (see New Faces). Learning that the Restitution quickened the Hushes, rather than merely failing, is a Dread 5 revelation for anyone who took part, and Dread 3 for anyone who believed in it. A PC Confessor, a PC of the Court, or a PC who was paid to row the box, should carry it: it is the kind of knowledge that does not get smaller. The hands can be reached. They lie ten feet inside the line. What a living PC would have to give to fetch them is the whole price.

Rule, Law and Politics

Sallowreach is governed by the Mortuary Court, a council of the Hand-lines seated in the Hall of Hands, under a Regent, Ansel Grue, who has held the post since 341 A.G. The Court makes law, levies the fly-tax and the stitching-tithe, licenses every Closing, and judges every capital crime, of which there is only one penalty that matters.

Property never passes. Owners never die. The oldest Kept, called the Unvacated, hold every title, deed and office in the country. A house built in 150 A.G. belongs to the man who built it. A seat on a guild council is held by whoever first sat in it. A living man of seventy is legally a minor if his father is still upright, and cannot sign a lease, marry without consent, or vote in a guild. The living are tenants, clerks, apprentices and servants of the dead, and will be until they join them.

Death is the only currency of power. A Closing costs more than a house. The Court grants Closings as rewards (to loyal officers, to the parents of useful men), withholds them as punishment, and sells them by license to those who can pay. The Court’s worst sentence is the opposite of death: to be jarred, Kept forever in pieces in the Jar Room. Lesser crimes are punished by fines, by flogging (it heals badly on the Kept and never closes), by unstitching (the removal of the Seamers’ work, a public humiliation), and by refusal, the striking of a name from the Court’s Closing ledger forever.

Courts in Sallowreach hear cases between parties who were wronged three hundred years ago and are still present to give evidence. Statutes of limitation do not exist. Murder, as a crime, is hard to define: the Stitching Laws class it as grievous unmaking and punish it by the cost of repair. The only true murder in Sallowreach is an unlicensed Closing, and it is punished with the jar.

A death-license of the Mortuary Court, as issued. Printed on vellum, black and grey, with blanks filled in a clerk’s hand. The Regent’s signature takes him one minute.

THE MORTUARY COURT OF SALLOWREACH, sitting in the Hall of Hands, by authority of the Licensing of 301 and in the name of the Hand that Closes:

LICENSE No. 18,422. Issued this ninth day of Carving, 641 A.G.

TO THE BEARER, being Margery Ann Tull, of Eighth, Tanner’s Boards, Kept since the year 506, in her one hundred and thirty-fifth year of Keeping:

ONE CLOSING, by a Closer of the Court, at the Hall of Closings, upon the bearer’s own body and no other, the bearer consenting thrice before witness.

FEE PAID: four thousand three hundred lacks, in platters and minutes, by the sale of a weir-share and the pledge of a grandson’s wages to 660. License-levy paid: four hundred and thirty lacks.

THIS LICENSE is not transferable, save by order of the Court; is void if the bearer is found falling apart in public before the date of Closing; is void if the bearer is closed by any other means, whereupon no fee is returned; and may be revoked at the Court’s pleasure, whereupon no fee is returned.

WAITING LIST: Chamber Six, Lady C. Vane presiding. Estimated date: Grace, 644.

Signed, Ansel Grue, Regent. Sealed, the Left Hand.

Example — The Case of the Thirty-Year Debt

A cooper named Wenna Hale borrowed sixty lacks from a moneylender in 589 to pay for her mother’s restitching. She died in a boating accident in 602, came back, and kept working. In 640 the moneylender, who died in 410, sued her for the debt and thirty-eight years’ interest. The court ruled that a dead debtor is the same person as a living one. Wenna’s Kept mother, who lives with her, testified that the money had been well spent. Wenna now works for the moneylender, unpaid, until 731.

The Only Inheritance

There is one family in Sallowreach in which property passes, and everyone knows which, and nobody says why.

The Hand-lines inherit. Not often, and never in public, but over six centuries the great houses of Grue, Vane, Sedge and Hethe, and the dozen lesser lines, have each seen their seats pass from parent to child perhaps four or five times, while in the rest of the country nothing has passed at all. The Court calls these occasions retirements. A Hand-line lord or lady, Kept a century or so, grows tired of the seat, retires to a wing of the estate, and is not seen again; and the heir, who is always at the Course, takes the seat; and the household, for a week afterward, wears grey ribbons and speaks quietly; and the wing is shut up and its windows bricked.

It was put into law in 588. Lady Imber Fallow, then thirty, at the Course, went up to her father’s rooms at Wending Mound in the evening with a basin of warm water and a towel, as she had every evening for twenty years since he had lost the use of his arms; and Lord Odo Fallow, Kept since 471, Unvacated master of Wending and eleven weirs, was found the next morning in his bath, finished, the water cold and grey, his face sunk and peaceful and smelling of nothing at all. Imber said only that he had asked her. There was no license. No one else had been in the room. By the law of 301 it was unlicensed Closing and the sentence was the jar.

The Court sat on it for a year. Then Regent Grue, in a ruling of nine lines that is still read aloud in every Hand-line nursery, held that a Closing performed within the line, upon a member of the line, by one of the line’s own hands was a private matter of the house, licensed by blood, and not a matter for the Court at all. The doctrine is called domestic license. It applies only to the Hand-lines, because only the Hand-lines have hands. Since 588 forty-three Hand-line heads have retired. Every one of them was succeeded by a child or a niece at the Course. Not one of the forty-three is recorded as having asked a Closer of the Court.

Imber Fallow sat in her father’s chair for fifty years, raised her son Pellam in the house where she had done it, and was herself retired in 638, at Pellam’s hands, a year before the Court took them off him. The Heirs’ broadsheet printed the whole case in 640 under the headline THEY DO IT TOO. That issue sold more copies than any other, and the Court jarred the printer’s tongue.

In other families the eldest son waits. In ours, he practises.
attributed to Lord Odo Fallow, Kept, in 560, at his own table, as a joke
Kin-Slaying at the Table

A Hand-line PC who uses the Closing Touch on their own Kept parent or grandparent commits the only murder the Court will not punish, and the oldest sin in the north. It is a Dread 4 act for the one who does it (kin-slaying by your own hand), whatever the parent asked. The PC inherits whatever the parent held: a seat, a house, a weir, a debt, a feud three hundred years long, and a household that will never again speak above a murmur in their presence. The heir’s own children begin, from that day, to watch their parent’s hands.

Culture and Daily Life

Keeping. Families are responsible for their dead. Six or seven generations share a house: the living on the ground floor and in the kitchen, the Kept upstairs in the cool rooms with the shutters closed. Grandmothers are restitched each spring in Restitching Week. Kept relatives sit at table, mind the children, mend nets, complain. The quarrel over whose turn it is to keep great-great-grandfather is the standard subject of comedy; the play Uncle on the Stair, in which three brothers try to lose the old man in Lastgate and he keeps coming back, has run since 340.

A Kept attic has its own climate. The shutters are kept closed for the flies and the stairs are kept closed for the smell, and so the cool rooms at the top of a Lastgate house are dim, still and sweet, hung with drying lavender and fly-paper black with catch, and furnished with the chairs of the dead: high-backed, deep-seated, upholstered in oilcloth that wipes clean. The floorboards under each chair are stained dark in a ring. Under the window there is always a basin of vinegar and a stack of clean cloths, and in a drawer the family keeps the parts that have come away and have not yet been sewn back, each in its labeled twist of paper, Gran’s ear, Plenty 639, so that nothing of anyone is lost.

Three generations to a bed, four to a chair, nine to a stair, and Gran on the landing, telling you to mind your step.
Weir Row housekeeping chant

Smell. Everyone carries perfume, vinegar or smoke. Scent is class. The rich smell of cedar, myrrh and ambergris, burned in braziers at their doors and soaked into their clothes. The middling smell of lavender and vinegar. The poor smell of peat smoke, and when they cannot afford it, of themselves. A pomander is a gift for a betrothal. Sniffing in company is extremely rude.

Dress. High collars, long sleeves, gloves and veils, to cover seams. Linen is preferred because it can be boiled; wool takes the smell and keeps it. The Kept favor wrapping: strips of waxed linen, wound tight, which hold things in. The Hand-lines wear mittens at the Appetite and gloves after, black kid sewn at the wrists. Never offer to shake a Sallowreacher’s hand.

Food. The living eat eel (lively), reed-bread, fen-mushroom, pickled everything, and imported Fatlands meat at feasts. Vinegar is in every dish. Stilled meat, closed by a licensed butcher, is a luxury. A dish of lively eel is eaten quickly, with a strong jaw, and washed down with sour, a peat-smoked beer. The Kept do not need to eat. Many still sit at table and chew, for company, and spit into a dish.

Lively Eel in Sour, the Weir Row way. As written in the receipt-book of the Mallory house, in four hands across two hundred years.

Take your eels from the trap and do not wash them, it only makes them lively. Have the pot boiling hard with sour and vinegar and a fist of dill. Take each eel behind the head with a rag and cut it in four with the big knife, quick, on the block, and put the pieces in the pot straight off, before they find each other. Lid down and a stone on the lid. They knock about a while. (In Gran’s hand:) They always knock. Never mind it.

Boil the length of a hymn. Lift the lid and if a piece has climbed up the side put it back with the spoon. Serve hot on reed-bread with a pickle. Eat it fast and with your back teeth and do not talk while you chew, it gives them a chance.

(In a later hand:) If it is still going in the belly after an hour, drink a cup of sour standing up and walk about. It settles. Do not lie down.

(In the latest hand, Teal’s:) Mam says don’t give it to visitors. I say let them learn.

Marriage. Vows in Sallowreach end with until finished, which once meant something. Widowhood does not exist. A spouse who died is still a spouse, and remarriage is bigamy. Many marriages carry on between the living and the Kept, and what passes between them behind the shutters is a matter the Court does not regulate and no one discusses; the word for it is coldbed, and it is said only by the rude. A living person may petition for a setting-apart, which is not a divorce but a court order permitting them to live in another house from their Kept spouse. It requires the spouse’s consent. Henna Farrow has filed forty-one times.

Children. Living children grow up surrounded by the dead and are fearless about it. They are trained young to hold a lamp for a Seamer, to tie a wrap, and never to stare. Children who die stay the age they died, forever. The Smalls, the child-dead of the Drowned Storeys, have their own society and their own queen. The living do not speak of them at dinner.

A counting game of the Weir Row children, played on the boardwalks with a pebble and a chalk ladder of nine rungs. The one who is “it” hops the rungs while the others chant; whoever lands on the ninth has to touch the eyes of the next child and say “shut.” There is no tenth rung.

One for the eel and two for the pot,

Three for the stitches and four for the rot,

Five on the shelf and six in the sack,

Seven in the Sump and they never come back,

Eight at the table, and who’s in the chair?

Nine, close your eyes, love, nobody’s there.

The children of Lastgate also play Closer, in which one child wears their mother’s mittens and the others line up to be “finished” with a tap on the forehead and lie down in the road very still, and the winner is the one who can lie still the longest while the others tickle. Parents on the Upper Boards forbid it. Parents in the Sinks do not, and the Heirs say the Sinks children are better at it.

Setting Aside. When someone is too far gone to stand, they are wrapped, labeled and shelved in the Lofts, still aware. This is the nearest thing to a funeral. The family gathers and the wrapper winds the linen from the feet up, and the family speaks to the face until it is covered. Families visit on feast days and read aloud: letters, news, the old one’s favorite books. Many do not visit. The Wardens read to those.

Proverbs. May you finish is the polite greeting. Long life is the worst curse. Mind your stitches means be careful. He’ll keep means a problem can wait forever. Fresh as a Glad Century fiddler means hopelessly out of date. The Court has hands means you cannot escape it. Close the book means end an argument by force.

Oaths on the dead. Sallowreachers swear by their dead in the literal sense. The strongest oath is sworn with the right hand placed inside the mouth of a Kept parent, who must consent and must be able to bite. To break such an oath is to invite the parent to close their jaw, and the oldest jaws in Lastgate are wired shut until a promise falls due. Debts sworn this way are the only ones the moneylenders trust.

The jaw-oath has teeth in the most literal sense, and the Court of Wrongs keeps a box of the evidence. When Hamo Rudd of Tanner’s Boards swore in 597 on his Kept mother’s jaw to pay a debt by Carving and did not, his mother, who loved him, closed her mouth in the Court before witnesses as the law required, slowly, with her eyes on his, and he did not take his hand out until the bone gave. She wept afterward, they say, for nine years. She keeps the two fingers in her shut-niche, beside his milk-teeth. That is what an oath on the dead is in the north: not a curse sent from somewhere else but a mother’s mouth, and she is obliged to use it, and she does.

Blasphemy, in a country that ate its god, is a matter of where you put your hands. To clasp them open on your knees, as Ossel sat in the carvings, is the gravest insult a Sallowreacher can offer, and drunk Heirs do it in the doorways of Hand-line houses to start fights. To shut someone’s eyes who is not asleep is a mortal offence. To finish a song that was not written to be finished, by inventing a last verse to one of the old fen-songs, is the commonest blasphemy of the young, and the Finishers have made a liturgy of it.

Never close the book on someone else’s finger.
Lastgate proverb, meaning: do not take a death that was not yours to take

Crime. Theft, fraud and debt are common. Violence is cheap but pointless, since it kills nobody; Sallowreach’s criminals specialize in leverage. The worst crimes are part-theft (see Marrow Jack), unlicensed Closing, and stilling, the illegal sale of closed meat.

Tablenight. On the longest night of Lack, the living cook a banquet for their dead, who cannot taste it, and everyone pretends. The table is laid with the best plates. The Kept are dressed, lacquered and seated. The living serve. Everyone eats, the living swallowing and the Kept chewing and spitting. Speeches are made praising the food. At midnight the eldest present says “May we all finish,” and the room drinks. In the old houses of the Upper Boards one chair at the end of the table is always left empty, and nobody can say for whom. When asked, the Unvacated say only that it was always so, and that it would be rude to sit there.

Bill of fare for Tablenight, as chalked in the kitchen of a modest Needle Street household, 640 A.G.

TO BEGIN — Grace said by the eldest upright (Great-Grandfather, if his jaw holds). Lack keep away.

FIRST — Eel in jelly, stilled (the one luxury; 3 lacks from the Hethe butcher). Served to the living. Served also to the Kept, who will chew it for company.

SECOND — Pie of Fatlands mutton and fen-mushroom, with a crust made to look like a closed eye.

THIRD — The Dish for the Dead: a whole loaf of reed-bread, broken by the youngest child and laid at every Kept place, which no one eats, and which is carried to the Lofts in the morning for the shelved.

FOURTH — Undying cheese, from the Brinemoss decade-wheel opened at Gran’s Setting Aside, still ripening.

SWEET — Burnt honey cakes. The Kept to be helped to spit into the blue dish, not the good one.

AT MIDNIGHT — May we all finish. The chair at the end to be laid with a plate, the way they do it on the Upper Boards, because Gran insists; and no one to sit there; and no one to ask.

The Closing

The only good death in Sallowreach is bought. A licensed Closing follows a rite fixed by the Court in 301 and never altered.

From A Fair Copy of the Proceedings at the Hall of Closings, prepared for the family of Mr. Josiah Rook, deceased 517 A.G., closed 641 A.G. Witnessed by Bram Hollin, mourner.

At the third bell the Closer’s clerk called the name. Mr. Rook was carried into Chamber Four on his board by his two great-grandsons, who are sixty and fifty-eight. He had dressed for it. He had been dead one hundred and twenty-four years and the Guild had done its best for him that morning, but the lacquer was fresh and still soft and under it he was mostly brown and black, and the smell in a small cedar room was very great. The great-grandsons breathed through their mouths. Mr. Rook said, “Do not make faces, boys, it is my day.”

The clerk read the license aloud: the number, the fee paid (four thousand two hundred lacks, in platters, by the sale of the house on Tanner’s Boards), the Regent’s signature, the date. Mr. Rook was asked three times if he wished to finish. He said yes three times, the third time very loudly.

Then the family said what they had to say. The younger great-grandson read out a letter from Mr. Rook’s wife, who is shelved in the Lofts and could not come, saying she would see him soon, which everyone understood was not true. Mr. Rook asked for the letter to be put in his hand. His fingers would not close on it. I closed them for him, and he thanked me.

Lady Corrow Vane came in last. She did not speak. She is tall and very still and smells of nothing at all, which in that room was the most frightening thing. Her gloves are black and sewn on at the wrist. Her clerk unpicked the stitches of the right glove, nine of them, and drew it off, and we saw her hand.

I have been asked to describe it for the family record and I will try. It was grey, as they say, a cold slate grey, and very long. The fingers had too many joints and moved one at a time, like a creature testing a branch. The room got colder. My breath showed. The flies on the window, which had been ticking all morning, stopped.

Mr. Rook was crying. He said, “Is it going to hurt?” Lady Vane did not answer. I said the words of the old rite, which I had from my mother: Hand that closes, close this. What was opened, shut. What was begun, end. Lady Vane laid her hand over his eyes.

It did not take long. There was a sound like a breath going out of a room, though he had not breathed in a century. He went still, and then he went on going still, past any stillness I have seen, and the long rot caught up with him all at once. His face sank. The lacquer cracked. The smell came up out of him in one great wave, all of the hundred and twenty-four years of it, and the younger boy fell to his knees and was sick, and then, all at once, it was gone. There was no smell. There was only a man on a board, properly dead, and grey dust settling in the folds of his good coat.

The great-grandsons sat with him for a long while. Lady Vane’s clerk stitched the glove back on. She did not look at the body. She looked at the floor, and then she went out to Chamber Five, where the next license was waiting.

The Closing in Play

A Closing requires a licensed Closer at the Course or beyond, the subject’s consent (the Court is strict on this, at least in public), and the license. A PC Hand-line at the Course can perform one with a Routine Hand + Rites roll; the Closer gains 1 Hunger. Witnessing a Closing is Dread 2. Performing one without a license is the crime of unlicensed Closing, punished by the jar, and every Heir and every grandmother in the country knows the PC can do it.

Factions

The Mortuary Court

The Hand-lines nobility: Grue, Vane, Sedge, Hethe and a dozen lesser houses. Sellers of death, hoarders of it, and increasingly afraid of their own hands. The Court believes in order: that a country of the undying must be governed by the oldest, that death is too precious to give away, and that the Hand-lines were chosen by the god to ration its mercy. What it wants now is to survive its own success. It knows the Hushes follow its blood. Its factions are split between those who would wall up the Course-stricken in lead (the Leaden party), those who would sell the Hushes as estates (the Quiet Market), and a very few who suspect that being closed like a book might be the god’s kindness to the land.

RankTitleGrants
1GlovebearerA clerk’s post; carries a Closer’s gloves; access to the Hall of Closings
2LicenserDrafts and seals licenses; may bend a waiting list by one name a season
3CloserPerforms Closings; a salary of 40 lacks a day and a house on the Upper Boards
4Hand of the CourtA seat on the Court; may grant one Closing a year without fee
5Left or Right HandCommands the Closers or the Court’s agents; answers only to the Regent

Joining: Hand-line blood is required beyond the second rank. Outsiders serve as Glovebearers, agents, spies and enforcers. Enemies: the Heirs, the Finishers, Reckoners. Allies: the Unvacated; uneasily, the Seamers’ Guild.

The Court has hands.
the commonest saying in Sallowreach, meaning that there is no escaping it; said with a glance at one’s own

The Proving of Hands

The Court licenses every Closing in Sallowreach but one kind, and that kind it does not record. When a Hand-line heir reaches the Course, the house must know that the hand works, and the hand must be taught. This is done in the family chapel at dusk, in a rite older than the Licensing, and the Hand-lines call it the Proving.

A living person is needed: a whole one, unready, with a pulse. Never a servant of the house, because servants talk, and never one of the line. The house’s steward buys a wage-pledge from the debt-rolls of the Sinks, where there is always a laborer or a spinster whose wages are owed to an Unvacated landlord until some year in the next century, and the house pays off the debt, and the debtor is told they have been taken into service. They are brought to the estate by punt. They are washed and dressed in grey linen and given the best supper of their lives, and the household is kind to them all that day, very kind, the way you are kind to the beast before a feast. At dusk they are seated in the single chair in the chapel. The household stands along the walls and sings the first six verses of the Ferrying Song. The heir’s gloves are unpicked.

The first touch is laid flat on the breastbone, and it takes the living person as Ossel took the fen’s dying for a thousand years, gently: the heart stops, the breath goes out, the head drops. Then the household waits, in silence, as long as it takes, usually less than an hour, for what everyone in Sallowreach waits for: the Proof opens its eyes again, Kept, and sees where it is, and understands. The second touch is laid over those eyes. That one finishes. Two deaths in one hour, the Hand-lines say, one to teach the hand to take and one to teach it to end; and the heir who can do the second with the Proof’s eyes open and pleading is judged ready to sit at the Court.

From the household book of Wending Mound, seat of the Fallows; the steward’s entries for Carving, 621 A.G. Recovered by the Heirs in 640 and printed in The Bequest.

To the Sinks debt-roll, for the wage-pledge of one Ebba Corn, spinster, 31, living, owing to 702: 220 lacks.

Punt-hire, two men, there and back: 4 lacks.

Grey linen, a shift and a wrap: 4 lacks. Bath, lye, rosemary: 1 lack.

Supper for the Proof: stilled eel, white bread, a pear from the orchard, a cup of Fatlands red. She asked if she might keep the pear for the morning. Told yes. 6 lacks.

Candles for the chapel, nine (Tallow, the steady kind, so they will not gutter at the wrong moment): 5 lacks 4 crumbs.

To the Licenser, for the record not kept: 400 lacks.

To the Sackman, one sack, no strip, no words: 3 lacks.

Lye and sand for the chapel floor, and a new cushion for the chair.

Note in the Lady’s hand: Master Pellam was sick after. This is as it should be. He did the second very well.

The Court, which knows, has never forbidden it. The Licensers keep a quiet tariff. The sacks go into the Sump without names, and the Sackmen who drop them are paid not to say the words. There are, by the Heirs’ reckoning, some five hundred Proofs under the black water since the Licensing, and not one of them has a strip. Ebba Corn is the only one whose name anyone knows. The Heirs have painted it on the Ferrying Post.

The Hollowe Tree

Every Hand-line keeps its Cut strong by marrying within the Hand-lines; that much is public, and the genealogies on the walls of the Hall of Hands are a thicket of Grue-Vanes and Sedge-Hethes. One line keeps it stronger. The Hollowe-Vanes of Hollowe Mound, a cadet line of the Vanes three hours north of Glovehall, have married no one but Hollowe-Vanes since the Licensing. The Vanes count the night the eldest Vane boy spent with his hand held in the god’s hand as a kind of wedding, and say so at their weddings; the Hollowes say that the line has been married to the hand ever since, and that it would be a kind of faithlessness to marry out. Provost Sedge’s ledgers record the Hollowe family tree on a single page, because it does not branch. It folds.

The house keeps a nursery wing with no windows. Its children are said to be born quiet, not crying, with fingertips already grey, at the Taste in the cradle. More than one Hollowe nurse has left service and gone to the Sinks and would not say why, except that the household was very close, and that in a house where everyone is cousin, aunt, brother and husband to everyone else at once, nobody can be sure which word to use at table, and nobody tries. There are three Hushes within a day of Hollowe Mound, the densest cluster in the north. The young cousin Lord Casimir Hollowe-Vane, who wrote to Osric Vane every month for years, ran south across the Finishing Post in 638 and has not been heard of since. In the Sinks they say he ran to marry somebody, anybody, else.

The Seamers' Guild

Stitchers, embalmers, lacquerers and wire-workers who hold the population together. Every Kept body in Sallowreach owes its shape to the Guild, and every family owes it money. The Guild believes in craft and in continuance: that a well-kept body is a dignity and a duty. What it wants is pay, respect, and to be left alone. A Seamers’ strike would be a national collapse within a month, and the Guild has threatened one only once, in 459, when the Court tried to tax wire. The tax was withdrawn in nine days, by which time the Sinks were knee-deep in what had fallen off people.

RankTitleGrants
1ThreaderApprenticeship; a needle-case; board and a cot on Needle Street
2JourneymanLicensed to restitch; a client list of thirty families
3SeamerWire-work and lacquer; may take apprentices; Stitching training
4Master of the SeamA shop of one’s own; Guild vote; access to the Guild’s stock of spare parts
5Master SeamerHead of the Guild; may call a strike

Joining: any PC with Stitching 1 can be taken on as a Threader. Enemies: Marrow Jack and the back-alley seamers. Allies: everyone, by necessity.

In Restitching Week, at the start of Grace, Needle Street does not sleep for nine days. The queue of the Kept runs down the canal-side boards and over two bridges: grandmothers on boards carried by grandsons, fishermen holding their own forearms like parcels, Smalls led by the hand by their living great-nieces. The smell is the worst of the year, because everything that rotted through the damp of Lack is opened at once, and the Guild burns cedar in braziers every ten yards and the smoke lies on the canal like a second fog. The bellows hiss. The wire-cutters click. The Threaders run between the shops with buckets of what has been cut out, black, for the burning-barge, and every so often someone in the queue laughs, because it is the one week of the year that the dead are made to look like themselves again, and the families come out in their best and walk them home lacquered and shining, like brides.

Brown is still hers. Black is the god’s. And the money is ours.
Seamers’ rhyme, the last line added by Journeymen, not to be said before a Master

The Heirs

The living young, permanently disinherited: everyone in Sallowreach under three hundred who still has a pulse and a parent. Most Heirs are clerks, servants and laborers in their forties and fifties who have never owned a pot. Some want reform: inheritance at the Setting Aside, votes for the living, a cap on Unvacated office. Some want every Unvacated elder dragged to a Hush. Since the Hushes appeared, for the first time in six centuries, the second group has had a method, and the first has had trouble arguing with them.

RankTitleGrants
1MinorMembership; a cut-hand token; a safehouse bed in the Sinks
2PamphleteerAccess to the presses and the Smoking Ground meetings
3BequeatherCommand of a cell of twelve; access to the cell’s weapons and punts
4ExecutorA seat at Jory Welt’s table; knowledge of the Hush map
5The BoyLeader of the Heirs (held by Jory Welt)

Joining: be living and disinherited, or help with something that cannot be undone. Enemies: the Court, the Unvacated. Allies: the Finishers, sometimes; the Purgation, dangerously.

Notice posted by the Court’s Hookmen on the Landing, the Sinks bridges and the Smoking Ground boardwalk. Most copies are torn down within the hour; the rest have the Heirs’ cut hand painted over them.

BY ORDER OF THE MORTUARY COURT. WANTED, for GRIEVOUS UNMAKING and UNLICENSED CLOSING BY HUSH, contrary to the Licensing of 301 and the Ruling on Hushes of 634:

PERSONS UNKNOWN, being living Minors of the Sinks and Tanner’s Boards, who on or about the night of the 4th of Carving last DID bind, sack and carry by punt one Alderman TOBIAS WREN, Unvacated, aged 340, owner of nineteen houses, to the verge of the HUSH at COLDMERE, and DID drag him across it.

The Alderman’s household offers TWO HUNDRED LACKS for names. The Court offers a MINUTE OF CLOSING, to be redeemed by the informant at a date of the Court’s choosing.

The Alderman’s chair, house and rents are held in trust by the Court until the matter is resolved. No heir of the Alderman will be recognized.

Statement of Corlis Mead, aged fifty-three, given to the Court’s examiners in the matter of the late Alderman Hollis Mead. Taken down by a clerk.

He was my father and he was three hundred and two. He was a good alderman. He never once let me sign for anything. I was fifty-three and I still asked him for my wages every Plenty-day and he gave me eight lacks and told me to make them last.

We did it at night. My brother Tobin and my sister and me. We had the punt ready. We had the sack. We didn’t hurt him more than we had to. You can’t hurt them, you know, not in a way that stops anything. That’s the thing. My great-grandfather tried to kill him in the War of the Heirs, with a halberd, in the year 288. Took his head clean off. Father had it sewn on and sat in the same chair the next week and sent great-grandfather to the jar. He’s still in there. Third shelf from the door.

So we didn’t try to kill him. We tied him. He said, Corlis, what is this. He said, I am your father. I said I knew. He said, I will forgive you if you untie me now, and he said it the way he always said it, the way he said it when I was six. And I nearly did.

It took four hours to pole to the edge of the Dunmere Hush. He talked the whole way. He said he had loved our mother. He said he was sorry about the house. He offered me the house. He offered me the boat. Then he stopped offering and started screaming, but there’s a way the Breath takes a scream on open water, it just sort of soaks it up.

At the edge the reeds go grey. You can see the line. The birds go over it and drop. We pulled him out of the punt and he was fighting and he got his teeth into Tobin’s arm, and Tobin was crying, and we dragged him the last ten yards on his back through the reeds. When his head went over the line he went quiet. Not quiet like stopped talking. Quiet like there had never been any sound in him. His mouth was still open. And then the rest of him came across and he just went soft and settled into the reeds like a coat dropped on a chair.

He looked peaceful. I want that written down. He looked like he had never been angry with anybody.

We stood there a long time. My sister said, We should say something. And none of us could think of anything, because none of us had ever been to a funeral. Nobody had, not for six hundred years.

Then I went home and sat in his chair. It’s my chair now. I’m the eldest. You can jar me if you like. I’ll keep.

The Finishers

A death cult in the plainest sense, and the fastest-growing faith in the north. The Finishers believe that the Hushes are Ossel’s mercy returning, that the god never wanted to be eaten and is calling its people home, and that to walk into a Hush is to be closed by the god’s own hand instead of a Court official’s. They make pilgrimage to the Hushes in long, singing processions, mostly of the Kept, carrying candles and the names of the dead, and they walk in. The Court calls it theft of a licensed good and has posted guards at the larger Hushes. The guards are Kept, and some of them have walked in too.

The Finishers’ songs have last verses, which in Sallowreach is a revolutionary act. They are sung at the edge of the grey reeds, and the singers go over the line one by one, and the song gets thinner and thinner as it goes, until there is no one left outside to finish it. Those who remain behind are the worst of it: the living children of Kept parents who went in, the husbands who held their wives’ hands to the edge and could not follow, because the living who enter a Hush die too, and do not come back, and the Finishers do not want them yet. The Court records the number of pilgrims. Nobody records the number of people who stood at the edge and watched someone they loved go quiet.

RankTitleGrants
1WalkerA candle and a pilgrim’s name-strip; the Finishers’ hospitality
2SingerLeads a procession’s song; knows the routes past the Court’s guards
3LampLeads a pilgrimage; may bless; knows the secret Hushes
4Shut EyeA voice in the cult’s councils; is told where new Hushes form
5High Shut EyeHigh priest (held by Sister Lorn)

Joining: carry a candle and a name to the edge, and come back. Enemies: the Court, the Seamers’ Guild (who lose customers). Allies: the Loft-Wardens, quietly; the Heirs, by convenience.

What the Edge Takes: the Coldharrow Carving

The Court’s figures say that fifty-nine of the living of Coldharrow walked into Dunmere Hush between Carving 637 and the end of Lack 638. The Court’s figures are correct. They are a list of names, a list of dates and a bill. This is what they do not record.

Petition of Agathe Rusk, living, aged sixty-one, of Coldharrow, to the Clerk of Fees of the Mortuary Court, contesting a bill of eight hundred lacks for “two deaths not paid for.” Written for her by the Coldharrow schoolmaster.

Sir, I have your bill and I will pay it. I write only to tell you who it is for, because the bill says Rusk, W. and Rusk, B., and they had names.

My husband’s mother went first. Old Mam Rusk, Kept since 519. She had been at the Settling a hundred years and she hurt every day of them, and when the Finishers came through with their candles in the Carving she put on her good shawl and went with them, and I helped her down the ladder into the punt. I am not sorry for that. I would do it again. She kissed me on the forehead and her lips were cold and she said, “You’ve been a good girl to me, Aggie.” I had not been. She said it anyway.

My son Wendel went after her to bring her back. He was thirty-four. He was always the one who went after things. He got to the Verge the next night and she had gone over already, and he stood at the grey line, they told me, from dusk until the morning, and then he came home.

He came home quiet. That is the only word for it. He did his work. He cut reed. He ate what I put in front of him. But he hummed, sir, all the day, under his breath, the same tune, and when I asked him what it was he did not know he had been doing it. It was the last verse of the Finishers’ song, the one that is not written down. I know that now. I did not know it then.

Nine days after, he was gone in the night. His boots were by the door, side by side, the toes pointed south-east, toward Dunmere. He had not taken them. He had cleaned them first.

After Wendel it was Hobb Lister’s girl, who had been sweet on him. Then old Lister. Then the Coopers’ two. By Lack there was humming in every house in Coldharrow. People did not know they did it. You would be pulling reed with a neighbour and she would be humming it and you would find that you were humming it with her, and then the both of you would stop and not look at each other. People started to say they could hear their dead out there in the quiet, waiting, and that it was very kind, the quiet. Children drew grey lines in the hearth-ash. Men left their boots by the door at night pointed south-east, and in the morning they did not remember doing it, and their wives turned the boots round, and the next night they were pointed south-east again.

We tried. You should know that we tried. We put bells on the doors. We slept in pairs. I tied my daughter Bryony’s wrist to mine with a ribbon every night, the blue one from her christening, and she let me, and she said, “I’m not going anywhere, Mam,” and she meant it. She was twenty-nine. She was the cleverest of us.

On the first night of the Shutter Days I fell asleep. I had not slept properly for forty nights. When I woke the ribbon was untied and folded on the pillow, very neat. I went to the Verge. I asked every Lamp and Singer at the edge. Nobody had seen her. Her name was on no strip. But I stood at the line, sir, where the grey starts, and I could feel it, how kind it was, the quiet, and how it would not hurt. I understood her. I want the Court to know that I understood her completely.

I did not go over. Someone has to pay the bill.

I will pay it. I ask only that the Court write their names on the receipt, the whole names, Wendel Amos Rusk and Bryony Agathe Rusk, because nobody else has written them anywhere.

(Endorsed by the Clerk: Fee confirmed. Names noted. Receipt to be issued as requested. No further action.)

Coldharrow is the worst of it, but it is not alone. Wherever the Finishers pass, or a Hush grows near enough to hear its silence, the same thing begins among the living: the humming first, then the boots by the door, then the talk of how kind it is, then one, and then more, and always those who had already lost someone to the edge. The Kept walk in because they have suffered too long. The living go because grief has made the quiet sound like home. The Finishers say they do not want the living yet and turn them back where they can. They cannot always tell, in the dark at the edge, who is breathing.

Running the Contagion

Treat the Verge-hum as madness spreading by the god’s influence, and treat it with care. A PC who spends a season within a day of a Hush, or who stands at the edge while someone they love walks in, makes a Dread 3 check; on failure, beyond the Fray, they find the hum in their mouth. A PC who Breaks within sight of a Hush should take The Pull as their Derangement, and those who witness that Break make the usual Dread 2 check to share it. Never stage the walking-in of a living character as a scene to be watched; cut to the morning, to the boots, to the ribbon on the pillow, to the bill. The horror of Coldharrow belongs to Agathe Rusk. Let the players meet her, and let her offer them tea, and let them hear her not humming.

Handling the Finishers

The Finishers are a portrait of despair in a land that has no exit, and the pull of a god that offers one. Play them as tragedy. Their pilgrims are tired, frightened, often kind, and they have been suffering for longer than any human being was meant to. The horror is not the walking in; it is what it says about a country that this is the only door, and who it leaves behind. Never present a pilgrimage as triumphant or a Hush as an attractive solution for the living. Focus scenes on the people at the edge.

The Loft-Wardens

Keepers of the Set-Aside: quiet, underpaid, and in possession of forty thousand witnesses who hear everything. The shelved Kept cannot move but can listen, and the Lofts are built against the walls of Lastgate’s oldest streets. Every conversation in nine storeys of the north city is overheard by somebody wrapped on a shelf, and the Wardens read to the shelved every night and write down what they whisper back. The Wardens believe in attendance: that no one should be left alone in the dark. What they want is pay, more linen, and for the families to visit. What they have, without much wanting it, is the best intelligence service on the Table.

RankTitleGrants
1Ladder-handA lamp, a key to one hall, and a list of the shelved to read to
2ReaderAccess to the whisper-books of one hall
3Warden of a HallCommand of a hall’s staff; the right to move the shelved
4Senior WardenAccess to all whisper-books; may sell what is in them
5Warden of the LoftsKeeper of the whole (held by Old Bettany Shroud)

Joining: read aloud to the shelved for a season without pay. Enemies: Marrow Jack. Allies: the Seamers, the Finishers.

From whisper-book 112, Hall Four, Third Storey, in the hand of the Reader of Hall Four. Lack, 641 A.G.

Shelf 9, Ma Drabble (Set Aside 488): asked for the end of the almanac. Read it. She said, Company. Asked her whose. She said, Ours.

Shelf 10, Josias Penn (Set Aside 530): asked if the stairs were swept. Told yes. He said, Sweep them again. Someone is coming up them and it would be shameful.

Shelf 11, unnamed (label rotted, Warden to rewrite): whispering the old count, one to eight. Stops at seven. Waits. Starts again.

Shelf 12, Hepzie Moule (Set Aside 602): Tell my daughter there’s a place laid. Asked where. At the end.

Shelves 13 to 40: Company. All of them. All at once, at the ninth bell, and then quiet, and then the drip.

Whispers from the Shelves

Roll when a PC reads to the shelved, sleeps in Loftside, or buys a page of a whisper-book from a Senior Warden. Some whispers are true, some are the long rot talking, and some, increasingly, are the same word.

d20What the shelved whisper back
1Company. Only that, from every shelf in the aisle at once, and then a silence like an intake of breath.
2A recipe, perfect and complete, for a dish nobody has cooked in four hundred years, and at the end: set a place for the one who’s late.
3The true name of a PC’s grandmother, which is not the name the family uses.
4My son took my rings while I slept. I felt him. Tell him I forgive him. Tell him I know which hand.
5Directions, street by sunken street, to a door in the Fifth Storey that has been shut since 300 and that something is knocking on from the inside.
6The Regent asked to be finished. I was his clerk. I heard it through the floor.
7A hymn with eight verses. The whisperer sings seven and then holds the silence so long the Reader gets up to check on them.
8Tell Nell I am coming down. From the fourth floor of Hall Two, as it has been every night for a hundred and thirty-eight years.
9There’s a hand under the Hall of Hands, much bigger than ours. It’s been opening since spring.
10The whole of a love letter written in 402 to someone who never answered, word for word, ending: I am still waiting. I will always be still waiting.
11Who is the tall one at the end of the aisle? There is no one at the end of the aisle.
12The name of a living person in Lastgate who has been taking parts from the shelf below, and what he does with them.
13Don’t read me the end. I can’t bear the end. Read me the middle again.
14A list of every Proof sunk without a strip by one Hand-line house, by name and date, recited by the Kept steward who bought them.
15I can feel the ones in the Sump. They’re all turning over. Like a bed when someone sits on the edge of it.
16A confession of kin-slaying, in the War of the Heirs, by a shelved man whose father is still upright on the Upper Boards and still does not know who did it.
17The quiet is coming up the stairs. It is so polite. It’s wiping its feet.
18The PC’s own name, whispered, by someone who has been shelved since before the PC was born.
19Weeping. Hours of it. In the morning the Warden finds that the whisperer has, against every law of the north, gone dry inside the linen, as if finished; and then, at the ninth bell, starts again.
20Company. Company. Company. Lay the board. Lay the board. Eight chairs. No: lay the board.
Whispers at the Table

Reading to the shelved for a night is an Eye + Search roll (Hard 14) to catch something useful in the whispering; a Helping lets the PC roll twice on the table above. Results 1, 7, 11, 17 and 20 are Dread 2. Result 19 is Dread 3. Nothing the shelved say should be treated as prophecy, and nothing they say should be entirely ignored.

Powers from Abroad

The Cutwrights’ College keeps its northern ledgers in Lastgate under Provost Carrion Sedge, and those ledgers are now the most dangerous documents in the land. The Purgation has a small, fanatical following among the Heirs, who argue that the god can be thrown up if the Hand-lines are emptied of it; their method is the Sump. The Second Table has members on the Mortuary Court and wants Osric Vane’s hands for the second meal (see Lord Absalom Hethe). The Reckoners have raided Sallowreach six times since 402 and learned that their blades are useless here; the last of them, Withhold Pennick, is stranded in Lastgate. The Rim Road Company runs the border inn at the Finishing Post and clears the heap.

Sallowreach Now

Sallowreach has started to end. The Hushes are multiplying, eighteen now, and they appear fastest near Hand-line estates. The Court has realized what that means: the nobility is the god’s way back, and the country will not be freed from undeath so much as closed like a book. Provost Carrion Sedge can prove it. The Court’s answer, so far, is lead mittens, locked wings and silence.

Meanwhile the Vigil’s envoy, Castellan Dray, has taken rooms on the Upper Boards and is offering Regent Grue the oil of a nation for the secret of Keeping. The Finishers have tripled in a year. A Scrapling girl in the Sinks can close things with her hands. The forty thousand in the Lofts have begun, all of them, to whisper the same word. And the Heirs have noticed that, for the first time in six centuries, an elder can be made to die.

Adventure Hooks

  • The Deadwatch. Castellan Dray hires the PCs as guides and bodyguards while he negotiates. The Regent is tempted. The secret of Keeping is not a secret: it is the god in the soil, and the Vigil would have to move to Sallowreach to use it. Dray knows this. His real commission is to find out how many Vigil citizens Sallowreach could house.
  • The Glovehall Garden. The Hush behind Glovehall grew three yards last week. Lady Corrow Vane hires the PCs to measure it secretly, nightly, and to find out whether it is growing from her brother’s wing or from her own bedroom.
  • The Little Closer. The Court, the Finishers, the Cutwrights and Marrow Jack all want Pim Sorrel. Her mother hires the PCs to get her across the border, where the Closing touch might stop. It might not. And the girl does not want to leave.
  • Sack Seventeen. A Sump dredger has hauled up a sack whose occupant claims to be a Regent of Sallowreach older than Ansel Grue, sunk for treason in 340. If true, Grue’s appointment was illegal and every license he ever signed is void.
  • The Last Verse. Bram Hollin has been hired to mourn the first proper funeral in Lastgate in six hundred years, for a living woman closed by accident. The family wants it done right. Halfway through the rite, the corpse begins to whisper the same word as the Lofts.

Rumors of the Fen

d20Rumor
1The Regent has not signed his own Closing because he has already tried, and Corrow Vane’s hand did not work on him. (True.)
2Hushes can be carried. Finishers bring back grey reeds in boxes, and where they plant them, silence grows. (False, but the Finishers believe it.)
3Wick Tallow’s candles are made only from the unclaimed. (False. Some families sell.)
4The word the Lofts are whispering is “company.” (True.)
5Marrow Jack is a Seamer of the Guild. (Half true. He was.)
6Outsiders who die in Sallowreach can leave if they are carried across before sundown. (False, and cruelly so.)
7Captain Morrow’s soldiers are finding parts of him in the barracks. (True.)
8The Court is building a lead-lined vault under the Hall of Hands to hold the Hand-line children. (True.)
9Mother Gall’s brine can cure the Kept of rot. (False. It only halts it, while they stay in the barrel.)
10A Hush opened in the Jar Room last month and closed nine prisoners, and the Court has hidden it. (True; the nine were the oldest jars.)
11Lord Pellam Fallow’s stumps are growing new hands, smaller and greyer, with more joints. (True.)
12The Restitution worked, and the Hushes would be twice as large without it. (False. The Confessors know it.)
13Every Hand-line house keeps an unmarked sack in the Sump for each heir it has raised. (True; see the Proving.)
14The Coldharrow hum can be caught from a letter written by someone who has it. (False, but people burn the letters.)
15Ned Scurl the dredger was not the only one; there are a dozen huts like his on the Sump. (True, though none so tender.)
16The Brack Mound is empty because Ysmay Brack walked away on the First Morning and is somewhere in Lastgate still. (False. Grimmer than that.)
17The Hollowe-Vanes have a child who was born at the Course and has never been seen. (The Hollowes do not deny it.)
18Captain Morrow will arrest Sister Lorn before Tablenight. (False. He cannot bring himself to.)
19Things floating in the fen have been drifting toward Lastgate, all of them, for a season, against the current. (True.)
20Ansel Grue has a son, living, two hundred years old, in a lead room at Gruesholt. (False. Probably.)

More Hooks

  • Two Plates at Grimsey. Ned Scurl’s ledger lists his buyers by initial. One set of initials matches a Master of the Seam; another matches a Hand of the Court. Someone wants the ledger sunk before Scurl’s trial; someone else wants the PCs to find Joan Ottery’s sack again and ask her what Scurl told her about his customers, because he talked to her, all those years, about everything.
  • The Bill for Coldharrow. Agathe Rusk has paid the Court eight hundred lacks by pledging her weir-share to 690. The Heirs want to make her their martyr. The Finishers want her as a Singer. The humming has started again in Coldharrow, three houses down from hers, and she asks the PCs to stay a night and keep the boots turned round.
  • Ebba Corn’s Name. Someone has painted the name of the Fallows’ Proof on the Ferrying Post, and the next night thirty more names in the same hand. The Court wants the painter. The PCs are hired to find them, and discover that the names are correct, every one, and that whoever is painting them can only have learned them from the Sump.
  • The Hands Ten Feet In. A Second Table agent offers a fortune to anyone who can fetch Lord Pellam’s severed hands from inside the edge of Dunmere Hush. The living cannot cross and come back. The Kept cannot cross and come back. Edda Thrush can, and is not saying yes.

The People of Sallowreach

Ansel Grue — the Unvacated Regent
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 3 · Lung 1 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Hand-line) · Regrowth 6 (the Appetite) · Hunger 4
SkillsClause 5, Persuade 4, Resolve 5, Lore 4, Intimidate 3
BodyFlesh 14 · Guard 11 · Armor 2 (lacquer and wire) · Fray 7
Attacksnone worth the name; he has never needed one

SecretHe asked Corrow Vane to close him in 610. Her hand did nothing. He does not know if he is beyond closing or if she held back.

Ansel Grue, the Unvacated Regent. Four hundred and twelve years old, three hundred of them in office. Grue died in 371 of a fall from a horse, and has been mostly wire, lacquer and habit since. He sits in a high chair in the Hall of Hands with his jaw wired shut and his face lacquered to a deep glossy amber, like a violin. Up close he smells of cedar, varnish and, faintly, sweet, like a bowl of fruit forgotten in a warm room. He speaks through a brass tube set into his throat, in a dry clicking voice that makes clerks lean in. He signs every death license personally, by hand, a slow, beautiful signature that takes a minute each. He has never once considered signing his own, or says he has not. What Grue fears is not death. It is the end of order, and the Hushes, which close without license, are disorder in its purest form. PCs meet him if they petition the Court, or if they become a threat to it.

He signs a license the way other men pray: slowly, completely, and without any expectation that it will be answered.
a Licenser of the Court, in his cups
Lady Corrow Vane — the Left Hand of the Court
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Hand-line) · Regrowth 7 (the Course) · Hunger 6

WantsClose; Quiet (cannot bear laughter near her)
Dread2 (to see her gloves come off)
SecretThe Hush at Glovehall is growing from her rooms, not her brother’s. She has measured it.

Lady Corrow Vane, the Left Hand of the Court. The Court’s chief Closer, sixty-one years old and living. She has finished eleven thousand people by touch, at a price. She is tall, pale and composed, with ash-blonde hair worn in a severe coil and a face that rarely moves. She smells of nothing at all, which is the first thing people notice and the thing they remember. Her gloves are black kid, sewn on at the wrist by her clerk, and unpicked nine stitches at a time. She has never held her own children. Her two sons were raised by nurses and taught to keep three paces from her; one is forty and has never touched his mother’s skin. She speaks briefly and with exquisite courtesy. She is afraid of only one thing, and it is herself. PCs meet her at a Closing, or when the Court needs agents it can deny.

I have been in a room with her four hundred times and I could not tell you the colour of her eyes. You do not look at her face. You look at her gloves, the whole time, like a dog watching a stick.
Bram Hollin, the Last Mourner
Osric Vane — the Gloved
AttributesHand 5 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 3 · Tongue 3 · Caul 5

SkillsRites 4, Godsign 5, Instinct 4, Lore 3

SecretHe has been finishing his guards through the door, by stare, one a month, for a year. They are replaced. He keeps count.

Osric Vane, the Gloved. Corrow’s brother, fifty-four, deep in the Course and now at its Brink. His hands are grey, long and have nine joints a finger; they fold like fans and click like abacus beads in a room that has gone too quiet to carry the sound. He is kept in lead mittens, padlocked at the wrist, in a locked wing of Glovehall where no fly lives. His face has gone smooth and soft-featured and faintly smiling. He is gentle, well read and lonely, and he has begun asking politely to be used on the enemy: the Reckoners, the Fast, anyone. I should like to be useful, he says. I should like to be put somewhere I can do good. Lord Absalom Hethe has offered him exactly that.

He asked me, through the hatch, whether I was tired. I said a little, sir. He said, “Only a little?” and he sounded so disappointed.
a Kept guard of Glovehall’s west wing, since reassigned

Thessaly Mort, Master Seamer. Head of the Guild for a hundred and ninety years. She has replaced so much of herself over two centuries that she keeps a ledger of which parts were hers originally. The ledger is short. She is a patchwork of a dozen donors in a dozen skin tones, wired at the joints, seams lacquered in cedar-gold so that she glimmers like a cracked bowl mended in a fine shop. She smells of wax thread, pitch and spirits. Her voice is a borrowed one, deep and pleasant, from a larynx she bought in 498. She is practical, brisk, and the most powerful person in Sallowreach after the Regent, because she could stop the country in a month. She fears that she is no longer anyone. She pays well for odd jobs: recovering stolen parts, shutting down back-alley seamers, finding out what Marrow Jack does with his stock.

She sewed my mother’s face back on in 499 and my daughter’s in 640, and both times she said the same thing: “Hold the lamp higher, love, I’m not a bat.”
Teal Mallory, of Weir Row

SecretHis father, Alderman Rufus Welt, is his son’s most generous anonymous donor, and wants to be the first taken to the Hush. Jory cannot do it.

Jory Welt, the Boy. Seventy-one years old and legally a child, since his father is three hundred and upright. He leads the Heirs. He is stooped, white-whiskered and arthritic, and his voice still cracks with anger like a youth’s. He lives in two rooms over a tannery in the Sinks, smelling of oak bark and old dogs, and he has a map of every Hush pinned to his wall, measured weekly, with pins for the Hand-line estates. He has dragged elders to the edge. He has watched them go soft. He is tired, and very gentle with children, and he has begun to wonder whether the Heirs have won or merely discovered a new way to bury their parents without mourning them.

Old Bettany Shroud, Loft-Warden. Keeper of forty thousand shelved dead, eighty-eight and living. She is small and bent and wrapped in shawls that smell of camphor, and her fingers are stained with ink to the second knuckle. She reads to the shelved every night, a hall at a time, and writes down what they whisper back, in a hundred and twelve whisper-books going back fifty years. She knows every secret in north Lastgate, and has never sold one. Lately they all whisper the same word: company. They whisper it as if someone is coming up the stairs. Bettany does not know what it means. She has been sleeping in the Lofts, on a cot between the shelves, so that they will not be alone when it arrives.

Old Bettany Shroud Threat 3 · Flesh 9 · Guard 11 · Attack +1 (fist 1) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Pim Sorrel, the Scrap Finisher. A Scrapling girl of twelve from the Sinks, thin, freckled, quick, smelling of peat smoke and eel. Her touch ends things, which should be impossible for her blood. It began a year ago with a cat that had been crushed by a cart and could not stop crying; she picked it up and it was quiet. Since then she has closed a neighbor’s grandfather, two Smalls who asked her to, and a candle she did not mean to. Her hands are not grey. They are ordinary, warm, a child’s hands, with bitten nails. The Court wants her dissected. The Finishers want her crowned. She wants to go to school. GM options for her secret: she is a Vane bastard’s granddaughter (Sedge’s ledgers say so); or Ossel, growing back, is reaching through the least of its eaters first; or the face the Scraplings ate is waking.

Justice Ever Lathe, the Honorable Maggot. A judge of the Court of Wrongs, Kept since 389, rotted down to bone, a few black tendons and a resident colony. He sits in a robe of office that seethes. The colony has worked its way through every soft part of him and taken up residence in the skull, and his rulings are delivered in the buzzing: a thick drone that rises and falls in cadences like speech. His clerk, Absalom Pike, translates. Lathe’s judgments are famously fair. Nobody is sure any longer which of them is deciding, Lathe, the flies or Pike, and nobody wants to find out, because the conviction rate has never been better.

Justice Ever Lathe Threat 4 · Flesh 6 · Guard 9 · Attack +3 (swarm 1, blinds on a Helping) · Armor 0 · Dread 2

Dr. Halloran Quease. A physician in a land where no illness is fatal. He has made pain his whole study, since it is the one ailment left, and he has catalogued four hundred kinds, from the long bell (the pain of a seam pulling through) to the attic (the pain of being shelved and forgotten). He is living, fifty, plump, scrupulously clean, smelling of carbolic and lemon. He keeps meticulous notes and Kept volunteers in his surgery, who allow him to test on them in return for opiates. He is kind to them. He wants to end pain. He fears that he enjoys measuring it. He pays PCs to bring him new kinds.

Wick Tallow, the Chandler. He renders the unclaimed dead into candles that feel themselves burn. His shop on Wick Lane smells of hot fat, smoke and something like singed hair, and the candles on his shelves are yellow, smooth and very slightly warm. They give a very steady light; they do not gutter, because they are trying not to. Half of Lastgate reads by people it used to know. If you hold a Tallow candle close, you can hear it, very faintly, a thin high sound like a kettle a long way off. Wick is a cheerful, practical man with burn-scarred forearms who sees nothing wrong with any of this. The dead are unclaimed; the light is needed. He has begun to take commissions from families.

Wick Tallow Threat 3 · Flesh 12 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (rendering hook 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Sister Lorn of the Shut Eye — High Shut Eye of the Finishers
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 2 · Lung 3 · Eye 3 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 3 (the Taste) · Hunger 3
SkillsPersuade 5, Rites 4, Resolve 3, Wayfaring 3, Lore 2
BodyFlesh 10 · Guard 13 · Armor 0 · Fray 9
Attacksnone
GiftsKept; the Last Verse (her singing grants all who hear it +2 to resist Dread for a scene)
WantsLead
Dread1
SecretShe has stood at the edge nine hundred times and walked in once, in the night, alone. She stopped one step from the line. She cannot forgive herself either way.

Sister Lorn of the Shut Eye. High priest of the Finishers, Kept since 590, slender and wrapped in grey linen, one eye stitched shut in the old fashion of mourning. She smells of beeswax and fen-mint, which she chews constantly. Her singing voice is extraordinary, low and kind. She has led nine hundred pilgrims into the Hushes and has stayed outside every time, saying someone must. Her flock has started asking why. She does not know the answer. She tells herself it is duty. She fears it is cowardice, or worse, that she enjoys the walking back. PCs meet her at the edge of a Hush, or when a family hires them to bring someone home before the singing stops.

Captain Dace Morrow — the Sixty-Times Slain
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 5 · Lung 2 · Eye 3 · Tongue 3 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 1 · Hunger 0
SkillsBlades 5, Endure 6, Intimidate 4, Wayfaring 3, Reckoning 2
BodyFlesh 19 · Guard 16 · Armor 3 (bone lamellar over wire) · Fray 6
Attackssword +9 (4); he does not stop
GiftsKept; Thread-Bound (ignores the first Ruin each scene)
WantsHold the Line
Dread2
SecretThe pieces he leaves in the barracks are deliberate. He is trying to get a little of himself across the border without dying, a finger at a time. None of it has survived.

Captain Dace Morrow, the Sixty-Times Slain. Commander of the Fen Guard, an army that cannot lose a man and cannot cross a border. He has been killed sixty times, by Reckoners, smugglers, Heirs and once by his own horse, and stitched back after each. He is more thread than soldier now: a tall figure bound in grey cord, wire and leather, his face held on by a lattice of brass. He smells of oil and old blood and wet rope. He is laconic, decent and very tired, and he has started deserting in small pieces. A finger is found on the parade ground. An ear in the mess. His sergeants gather them in a box and do not report it.

Henna Farrow, the Widow Unmade. Her husband Amos died ninety years ago, of a fever, and still comes home each evening from a job at the weir that was abolished in 570. He opens the door, says “Something smells good, Hen,” and sits down. He does not know. He has never known. His face has long since gone, and the Guild keeps a lacquered mask on him with a painted smile. Henna is a hundred and twelve, living, bent double, smelling of lye and lavender. She has petitioned for his Closing forty-one times. The Court refuses because Amos must consent, and to consent he would have to be told. She sets his place anyway, every night, and cooks his favorite, and scrapes it into the eel barrel. She would like the PCs to tell him.

Grandfather Peat. A bog body hauled from the Sump in 611, who drowned the week of the Gorging. He is leather-brown, flattened, shining wet, with a fringe of red hair and a rope still knotted at his throat, and he smells of peat, tannin and old rainwater. He speaks a dead dialect that only a few Cutwrights can follow. He is the last witness to the Night of Seven Tables, and he repeats one thing: the god was smiling. Asked more, he holds up his fingers and counts, slowly, to eight, then folds one down very carefully as if it might bite. The College keeps him in a tank in Sedge’s offices. He would like to go back in the water.

Grandfather Peat Threat 1 · Flesh 8 · Guard 8 · Attack +0 · Armor 1 · Dread 2

Tam Ruddock, the Lastgate Ferryman. He poles a long black punt from the border road across the Landing, and for a heavy fee he smuggles the dying of other lands across the border so they will not die: Fatlanders with wasting sickness, Brinehollowers Called too far, Vigil sleepers on stretchers. They do not die. He has never told a single one of them what happens next, and he sleeps badly. He is forty, heavy, with a broken nose and a soft voice, and he smells of tar and rum. He keeps a list of every passenger, and on his days off he visits them. Idony Pask was one. She has never forgiven him, and he visits her most.

Marrow Jack — the Part-Thief
AttributesHand 5 · Gut 2 · Lung 4 · Eye 3 · Tongue 3 · Caul 2
Cut & RegrowthCut 1 (Scrapling) · Regrowth 0 · Hunger 0
SkillsStitching 4, Filch 5, Stealth 5, Blades 3, Haggle 4
BodyFlesh 11 · Guard 16 · Armor 1 · Fray 3
Attacksbone-saw +8 (3, takes a limb from a Kept target on a Helping); knife +8 (2)
Giftsnone; skill only
Wantsnone
Dread2 (his stock room)
SecretHe was a Guild Journeyman under Thessaly Mort, and he supplies her. A third of the parts in the Guild’s stores came from him.

Marrow Jack. A part-thief, thin as wire, with a pleasant freckled face and hands that never stop moving. He smells of clove oil, which he uses to cover his trade. He takes limbs from the Kept while they shelve in the Lofts or lie in the slow stupor some of them call sleep, and sells them to back-alley seamers in the Sinks: an arm to a woman whose own has rotted through, a jaw to a Kept singer, a whole pair of hands to buyers who will not say why. He works the Lofts, the Sump (dredging sacks for usable stock) and the potter’s corners where the unclaimed are left. His victims wake able to feel what their missing hands are being used for. Some of them have tracked him by it. One of them is in his stock room now, in eleven pieces, and he does not know what to do with her.

Little Nell Ash, Queen of the Smalls. She died of a fever at seven, in 441, and has been seven since. She rules the child-dead of Lastgate’s Drowned Storeys from a throne of a waterlogged armchair in a flooded schoolroom, crowned with a ring of tarnished spoons. She is small, grey-green, very carefully stitched by Smalls who taught themselves, and she smells of canal water and the violet sweets she cannot eat but likes to hold. She has a two-century-old mind and a seven-year-old’s sense of fairness: absolute, unforgiving and sometimes very funny. The Smalls do not grow up, ever; she has kept them safe, mostly, from the Court and from Marrow Jack. She wants Pim Sorrel for herself. Several of the Smalls have asked to be closed, and Nell has not decided whether to let them.

Provost Carrion Sedge. Head of the Cutwrights’ College in the north, Hand-line by birth, Kept since 598. Gaunt, ink-stained, lacquered in a dull brown that smells of old paper and the glue of bindings. His ledgers prove that the Hushes follow Hand-line blood exactly; plotted on a map, every Hush is a family tree. He has not decided which is worse: publishing it, which would bring the Heirs to every Hand-line nursery, or selling it, to the Court, the Second Table, or the Vigil’s envoy, who has asked. He is also Hand-line, at the Taste, and has found himself closing his ledgers too firmly, and sometimes being unable to open them again.

Mother Gall. A fen witch who pickles. She is enormous, red-handed, cheerful, and smells overwhelmingly of brine, dill and garlic. In the right brine, a recipe she will not share, she can keep a body sound for a century: no rot, no flies, no further decay, so long as it stays submerged. Her cellar under Brinemoss holds four hundred customers in barrels, paid up in advance, all wide awake, all blinking up through the green. Some have been in for ninety years. They cannot speak; they knock. She charges for visiting. She is the closest thing to a cure in the north, and she knows it is not one.

Edda Thrush, the Hushwalker. A Court surveyor who walked into Dunmere Hush with a chain and a theodolite in 638 and walked out again three hours later. Nobody else has. She cannot hear anything now, and insists that this is not deafness: something is listening in her place. She is forty, living, with a cropped head and grey-streaked eyebrows, and she smells of nothing at all. She speaks too loudly, then too softly, and sometimes stops mid-sentence and tilts her head, as though someone just behind her has cleared their throat. She has drawn the inside of Dunmere from memory. In the center of her drawing is something she has not drawn, only left blank, very carefully.

Bram Hollin, the Last Mourner. His family were professional mourners, a trade six centuries extinct. He alone, by an unbroken line of fathers teaching sons for a job none of them could do, knows the full funeral rite by heart: the keening, the washing, the coin on the tongue, the six last songs. Now that people are dying again, everyone wants him. He is sixty, small, tidy, in a black coat green with age, and smells of rosemary. He weeps easily and professionally and, lately, privately. He did not know until this year what the songs were for.

Idony Pask, the Tourist. A Fatlands woman who came north with a wasting sickness so she would not die of it. She did not die of it. She died in 627 and kept going, and the sickness has not stopped. She is now very thin, then thinner: a creature of skin and bone wrapped in a Fatlands shawl, still hungry with her land’s bottomless hunger and unable to eat. She smells of sour milk and decay. She can never leave. She has written to her family in the south every week for fourteen years. They stopped replying. She is bright, bitter and good company, and she would like someone to take her letters south and tell her what they find.

Everyone in the north is somebody’s ancestor. In Lastgate, they are all still in the house.
Idony Pask, in a letter to her sister in the Fatlands, unanswered

New Faces

Fenwick Lisp, Interpreter of Jaw-Clicks. Kept since 501, gaunt and courteous, with a lacquered jaw of his own he clicks as he thinks. He interprets for the jawless and tongueless of Lastgate, most famously in the Long Argument, and is the only person who understands either party. He has not translated accurately since 560. He has been running the argument himself, out of loneliness, and he is afraid both men know.

Merrit Cask, Keeper of the Jar Room. A living woman of forty-four who inherited the post from her Kept mother, who inherited it from hers. She dusts the jars, oils the lead seals, reads the labels aloud each morning and sweeps the drains. She smells of lamp oil and lye. Since nine of the oldest jars went silent last month, at once, she has heard the shelf whispering about who will be next, and has begun moving her chair further down the vault each night.

Merrit Cask Threat 2 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +3 (cudgel 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Withhold Pennick, the Stranded Reckoner. A wiry Unfed woman of thirty from the Fast who crossed in 639 to kill a Hand-line lord and did: she cut his throat in his bed. He sat up and called the guard. She has been hiding in the Sinks ever since, unable to complete her oath and unwilling to go home. She has learned the Hushes exist. She has begun to wonder whether she could drag a lord into one. She is clean-smelling, ascetic, appalled by everything, and slowly starving on food she will not eat.

Lord Absalom Hethe — Hand of the Court, Second Table
