It seemed obscene to put good meat in the ground when the ground was already so full. The last burial ground on the plain, at the old chapel of Saint Ember outside Sated, was opened by order of the Board in 133, and the dead of the Long Lack were lifted out, salted, and served at a public feast in the Weighhouse yard, as a gesture of national unity. The chronicle records that they were “tough, but well received,” and that the diggers who opened the oldest graves found some of the dead lying face-down, with soil in their mouths, as though they had been hungry even there.

Tough, but well received.
the Board’s minute on the Saint Ember feast, 133 A.G.; the phrase is still used in Sated of a bad sermon

The Weighing and the Rising

By 260 A.G. the largest Gut-lines could no longer travel to the Board, and the Board came to them; the Weighing simply made their bulk a formal measure of power. The poor accepted it, because the poor were eating well. Two centuries later, they were not. Export had swallowed the surplus, the Reaping had grown, and a preacher named Hester Gaunt began teaching in the Orchards that the god was in the hunger, and that if the people stopped feeding it, it would starve back down into the soil. The Thin Rising of 455 A.G. was not an army. It was eleven thousand people in Low Tilth sitting down in the roads and refusing to eat. The Board sent the Bailiffs with funnels. Within a month most of the Thin were fat, and the rest were dead, and Hester Gaunt had been fed in the Weighhouse before the whole Board for nine days until she burst. Fasting has been treason since.

The Board’s minute of the ninth day survives, and is read aloud to new Members as part of their oath, so that they understand what the Board is.

MINUTES OF THE BOARD OF PLENTY, SITTING IN FULL, THE NINTH DAY OF THE FEEDING OF H. GAUNT, GRACE 455.

Present: one hundred and eighty-four Members, aggregate weight one hundred and ninety-one thousand pounds.

Item: the Feeder reported the prisoner had taken eleven gallons since the last sitting, and had ceased to resist on the seventh day, and had on the eighth day asked for more, which was given. Laughter.

Item: the Physician reported the prisoner’s belly “past the capacity of any human vessel he had seen or read of,” and that the skin had begun to shine and to go thin at the navel. He asked leave to stop. Leave was refused, by weight.

Item: at the fourth hour the prisoner spoke, and said, “It is in here with me. It is so glad.” The Chairman asked that this be struck. It was struck.

Item: at the fifth hour the prisoner was fed the last ladle, and the matter was concluded. The Members, being in some distress, adjourned to Supper. It was noted that no Member left food on his plate.

Item: the prisoner’s remains to be thrown in the Brawn, uneaten, as a Thin. Carried.

— Board archive; the struck line is still legible, and new Members are shown it

The Gammon Twins

The Weighing of 619 is remembered in the Fold as a scandal and in the Leanings as a joke, and in the Gammon House as nothing at all, because nobody there speaks of it.

The Gammons are an old Gut-line of the Fold, and in 619 the family’s Board seat was contested between twin brothers, Lard and Cress Gammon, then thirty-one, then each of about nine hundred pounds, then so alike that their own Washers told them apart by the shoots in their elbow-folds. The seat went by custom to the heavier. For a year the brothers ate against each other: at the same table, plate for plate, their mother’s Dowager hill having advised them both, when asked, Eat. Three days before the Weighing, Cress Gammon was the heavier by six pounds.

On the night before the Weighing he died. The Gammon House said his heart had stopped at table, which is how a great many Gut-lines die. The wake was held at once, by special licence, the next morning, at dawn, so that it might be finished in time for the Weighing at noon; and at the wake Lard Gammon took the heart, as the elder by a quarter-hour, and the liver, and the belly fat, and both hands in their pie, and sat at the head of the board and ate his twin, alone, steadily, for six hours, while the family watched and the house was silent except for the sound of his jaws. When a cousin asked aloud whether Cress’s heart had really stopped on its own, Lard Gammon took a morsel of his brother’s cheek on his tongue, held it there, and swore: By my brother’s meat, which is in me, I did him no harm.

At noon he was carried to the Scales and outweighed his brother’s last recorded weight by eleven pounds, and took the seat. He sits it still.

The Gammons’ cook, who had been in the kitchen that night, was found in the Great Gravy a month later, and the Washers who washed Cress for his wake were pensioned off to a village on the coast and have not been heard of. But the Washers talked first, as Washers do, and what they said in the Leanings was this: that there were marks on Cress’s throat, deep in the folds, in the shape of a large soft hand pressed down for a long time; and that the hand had been the left one, and Lard Gammon is left-handed, and Cress was not.

To eat your brother is no crime in the Fatlands. To kill him is murder. To swear falsely on his meat is, to every Fatlander, the vilest act there is, worse than either. Nobody has ever proved it. Nobody has needed to. In the Leanings, a man who wins an argument unfairly is said to have weighed in Gammon. And in the Gammon House the great dining room has been locked since the morning of the wake, because Lard Gammon says that when he sits in it he can hear, inside his own body, from somewhere under the ribs, his brother’s voice asking him to pass the salt.

By my brother’s meat, which is in me.
the oath of Lard Gammon, 619; in the Leanings, said with a wink, it means I am lying and you cannot touch me

The Long Count

In 629, Pell Hogget of Kettle Furrow noticed that his village had been one smaller each autumn for as long as he could remember, and scratched it on his barn wall. He started asking neighbouring villages. Then they started sending him their numbers. The Long Count is now copied in two hundred villages, by people who share no organization but a habit, and it shows something the Board has spent three centuries calling wolves: the Reaping has doubled in ten years, and it is still accelerating.

The Count is not a book. It is a habit, a wall, a set of tally-sticks, a column of knife-cuts on a hundred barn doors, and a slow, patient correspondence by carter and drover and child, carried folded in a shoe. Its marks are simple: a stroke for each Reaped, a stroke with a cross-bar for each dusk-shifted who did not come back, a circle for each Seated, and, since 638, a new mark that nobody agreed on but everyone uses, a stroke with a small open curve at the top like a hand held out, for taken by a hill. A copy of the Kettle Furrow wall, as transcribed by a Cutwright surveyor in Plenty 640, runs:

KETTLE FURROW — HOGGET’S BARN — EAST WALL, LOWER COURSE (as found)

629: IIII — Abner Thrush · Polly Thrush · old Mag · the Breen lad.

630: IIII I — & Tam Breen, who went looking for the lad.

631: IIII II — names on the beam, too high to read; Pell says they are there.

632: IIII IIII — & a bowl on the wall for each.

633: IIII IIII I

634: IIII IIII IIII

635: IIII IIII IIII I — & ½, for the Pennick baby, who was only half-way out of the furrow when they got her. She lived a week.

636: IIII IIII IIII IIII

637: IIII IIII IIII IIII II — in chalk, under, in a child’s hand: WOLVES WOLVES WOLVES

638: IIII IIII IIII IIII IIII

639: IIII IIII IIII IIII IIII IIII — & one stroke scored out so deep the knife has gone through the plank.

640: (wall not yet marked; the Count is kept on the barn door this year, “in case the wall is full”)

At the foot of the course, in paint, in a large slow hand: NELL — and nothing after it.

— the surveyor’s note: “Hogget states that the deep stroke in 639 is ’a mistake.’ He says ’Nell’ is the name of the barn. It is not.”

Pell’s arithmetic is simple and his neighbours can follow it. The Reaping in a Low Tilth village doubles every eight or nine years. Kettle Furrow had two hundred and six souls in 629. At the present rate, the year’s Reaping will equal the village in 660 A.G., and the whole of Low Tilth will have gone into the wheat before 680. The Board’s own figures, in the root-choked cellar under the Weighhouse, say the same thing to the head, and the Board has known it longer. The difference is that Pell Hogget wrote it on a wall where people could see.

I don’t say what it means. I only say what it is. Mark, mark, mark. You can see the shape of it from the door.
Pell Hogget

The First Furrow at Dimble

Dimble, under its old carving, has always been a strange village. Since 636 it has become a frightening one.

Every village in the Fatlands keeps the rite of First Furrow in Grace: the year’s first ploughing, pulled by the heaviest man of the parish in harness, the furrow fed a loaf. In Dimble, the oldest families say, the rite was once different, before the Gorging, when Ummer walked ahead of the plough; there are marks on the granary carving that show it, a plough and a figure lying in the furrow before the share. In 636, after a Reaping that took a fifth of the village in one Carving, Dimble went back to the old way. The Board heard of it in 640 and sent a Bailiff, Ambrose Tull, to inquire. His report was filed and sealed. A copy of the interrogation is held, against the Board’s wishes, in the Long Count’s collection at Kettle Furrow.

EXAMINATION OF GAMMET RAKE, GRANARY-KEEPER OF DIMBLE, BEFORE BAILIFF A. TULL, LACK 640. HELD AT TABLE, BOTH PARTIES EATING.

Q. You know why I am here.

A. The plough. Have some of this, it’s the good ham.

Q. Who was put in the furrow last Grace?

A. Jory Pask. He was on the list for the Dusk Acres anyway, for his debt. We asked him would he rather go in our field for us than in the Board’s field for nobody. He said yes. He was a good lad.

Q. Describe the rite.

A. You’ve a stomach for it? Good. We fed him three days. Best of everything, the way the Cullmasters do, you know, so he’d be heavy and glad. Then at dawn we washed him in warm milk and bound him to the beam of the plough, face down, along it, so his face was over the share, and the heaviest of us took the harness, and we all of us pulled. The share opens the soil. Then the share opens him. Not quick. You walk slow on First Furrow. The furrow takes him in a long red line, the whole length of the Long Strip, and we walk behind it singing and we lay our hands in it as we go. By the end of the strip there is not much of him on the beam. What there is we bury, standing, at the head of the furrow. Upright, so he can see.

Q. Did he cry out?

A. At first. Then he said it was warm. Then he asked us to pull faster. You’ll not have heard that, but that’s what it sounds like when they’re in the soil, they want you to hurry. Then he was quiet. You’re not eating.

Q. How many have you put in the furrow?

A. Four Graces now. Four lads.

Q. And has it lessened the Reaping?

A. (The witness put down his fork.) The first year we lost nine instead of eleven. The second, eleven. The third, fourteen. Last Carving we lost twenty. We’d have done better to keep the lads. I know. I know that. But you’ve to do something, haven’t you? You can’t just sit and eat and wait. Can you? Can you?

Q. Who chose Jory Pask?

A. His mam. She put his name in. She said it was better than the Board’s field, and at least she’d know which strip. She eats the bread off it. She says it’s the best bread she ever had. She says he was always a sweet boy.

[Note in the Bailiff’s hand: I have recommended no action. There is no statute against ploughing. I could not finish the ham.]

— the “Tull Examination,” Long Count collection; Ambrose Tull was named on the Cullmasters’ list for Carving 641, as “a troublemaker”

The Bargain at Hask's End

Of all the stories the Long Count keeps, the one the Thin tell most often, and the one that ends most arguments about whether the god can be bargained with, is the story of Hask’s End.

Mother Furlong was the hill over the common pot: the Seated body of Bette Furlong, Harvest Mother of the parish in her life, a woman of six hundred pounds and great kindness, who rooted in 590 at the edge of the village yard where she had cooked the parish supper for forty years. She kept a mouth. She was much loved. Children slept against her warm flank on Sweating Night; couples courted on her. She was consulted on everything and was always right.

In Carving 638 Hask’s End lost seven to the Reaping, its worst year in memory. At Harvest Home the Reeve, Amos Tallis, a broad, careful, decent man, went to Mother Furlong with the best cut of the last wake and asked her what the village should do. She chewed for a day and a night. Then she said, through the turf, in the voice everybody remembered from the supper-hatch: Give me Linnet, and I will speak to the field, and the field will pass you by for seven years.

Linnet Tallis was the Reeve’s daughter. She was nineteen, plump and freckled and quick to laugh, betrothed to a miller’s son, and she had been fed by Mother Furlong’s own hands at every parish supper of her childhood.

The village argued all Lack. The Reeve said no, and then said nothing, and then stopped eating at table, which frightened everyone more than anything else. It was Linnet who decided. She said, in the yard at Tablenight, that seven was seven, and that she would rather be in Mother Furlong than in the wheat, and that if it was her or seven of them every year then there was no sum to do. She was fed for nine days by every household in turn, the best of everything, and she laughed and cried and grew round and pink, and her betrothed fed her last, at dusk on the ninth day, and kissed her greasy mouth. Then her father walked her to the hill himself, in her white smock, through the whole village standing in silence with their plates in their hands. Mother Furlong’s mouth opened wide in the turf, wider than anyone had seen it, and Linnet lay down in it, as a child lies down in a warm bed. The Reeve knelt and held her hand while it closed. It took the whole night. He did not let go until there was no hand.

The next Carving, 639, Hask’s End lost nine to the Reaping. In 640, eleven. Mother Furlong, asked what had gone wrong, chewed on the question for three days and then said, quite calmly: I was hungry, Amos.

That was all. A hill has no say over a field. A hill is not a god’s counsellor or a god’s priest; it is a piece of the god with a mouth, and it said what a mouth says to be fed. There was no bargain. There had never been a bargain. Linnet Tallis was eaten for nothing, by a kind old woman who had loved her, and the village had paid her with its own hands.

Amos Tallis walked into the Long Strip at dusk in Carving 640, and stood there, and waited, and was not Reaped; the field passed over him that night, as if out of spite, or as if it were simply not hungry for him. He came back at full dark and sat by Mother Furlong until morning and did not speak. In the spring he went out again, out of season, when the fields do not take, and lay down in the furrow in the cold, and did not get up. They found him a week later. He had not been Reaped. He had simply stopped. His bowl is on the yard wall. His name is not in the Long Count, because Pell Hogget does not count those the god did not take, and the people of Hask’s End have argued about that ever since, and some of them have stopped sending their tally.

Linnet’s betrothed still brings Mother Furlong meat. He cannot stop himself. She thanks him warmly, every time, and calls him son.

Running the Bargain

The story of Hask’s End is the Fatlands’ answer to every PC who asks can we make a deal with it? Hills will offer bargains; Dowagers, Old Mother Rind, the Seated of any family. They are always sincere when they offer and always hungry when they eat. A GM who wants to stage a worthless sacrifice of this kind should let the bargain be struck and paid with real cost (an NPC the players love, a PC’s own Flesh or Regrowth), and let it fail quietly, with no villain to blame. The Dread is not in the eating. It is in the next Carving’s tally. Witnessing a Hask’s End-style giving is Dread 3; learning, afterward, that it bought nothing is a second Dread 2 check, because grief that was for nothing warps the mind more than grief that bought something.

I was hungry, Amos.
Mother Furlong of Hask’s End, Carving 640; the only explanation she ever gave

Rule, Law and Politics

The Fatlands are governed by the Board of Plenty, seated in the Weighhouse at Sated. The Board has about two hundred members, drawn from the Gut-lines, the Renderers, the great granaries and a handful of elected district deacons. Each member’s vote counts in proportion to their weight, taken publicly once a year at the Weighing. A Gut-lines matriarch of fourteen hundred pounds outvotes nine farmers’ deacons together. The Chairman, Obb Tullow, at nineteen hundred pounds, holds more votes alone than the whole of Low Tilth. He has not walked in thirty years.

The Gut-lines are the nobility. They are the largest, the hungriest, and the furthest along the Regrowth, and their estates are run from beds, then from drays, then from the ground. Succession disputes turn on whether a rooted, mouthless hill can still be said to hold title. The courts have ruled that it can, which is why the Dowager Hills still own a third of the country and why their consultations carry the force of law.

Law in the Fatlands is mostly about eating. The Feasting Laws set five meals a day; leaving food on the plate is a fine of one lack per crumb-weight, assessed by the Bailiff’s scale; refusing a meal is sedition, punishable by the Gavage. Theft of food is barely a crime, since the thief will eat it and the court considers the matter closed. Theft of weight, by contrast, is grave: to starve a person, to keep a child thin, to purge, to bleed for the purpose of lightness, is treason against the Weighing. The worst crime of all is waste. A man who let a barrel of meat rot in 602 A.G. was rendered for tallow by order of the Board, and the tallow was used to light the courtroom for the next trial.

Punishment is by feeding (the Gavage), by fine, by the dusk-shift, or by the table. A convicted murderer in the Fatlands is executed in the Renderers’ yards, and the family of the victim has first cut. This is called making good. It is done in public, at noon, on a scrubbed board under an awning, by a Union jointer, and the killing is quick, a single stroke at the throat over a copper basin, because the Union will not spoil meat with fear. The jointing is slow. The victim’s kin stand at the board’s head with their plates and are served first, by the jointer’s own hand, the cut of their choosing, and they eat it there, standing, while the crowd watches; and it is said in Sated that a widow who has made good on her husband’s killer goes home lighter in her heart and heavier in her belly, and that both are the point.

Abroad, the Fatlands’ power is food. They feed half the Table by way of the Rim Road, and every other land depends on that meat while trying not to think about it. The Vigil eats Fatland salt-beef to keep its strength through sleepless decades. Oathen buys toothed flour by the shipload. Sallowreach, which needs little food, buys Fatland tallow for its Seamers. The Board knows exactly how much the world would starve without it, and charges accordingly.

Your Honour, the accused ate the evidence. — Then the matter is closed. Pass the gravy.
a Plate-Justice’s court in Gristmoot, as reported

Culture and Daily Life

Meals. Five meals a day are mandatory: Firstbite at dawn, Elevenses, Midday, Fourth Plate, and Supper, with whatever the purse allows in between. Every meal begins with the grace, which thanks the field by name (“Thank you, Long Acre. Thank you, Hessop’s Rise.”) and ends with the plate wiped clean with bread. Strangers add the common “Lack keep away.” Fatland cooking is lavish, rich and brown: pies and puddings, roasts and dripping, sausages fat as a forearm, gravy on everything. The poor eat potatoes and fat bacon and are not, by any outside measure, poor eaters.

Dress. Fatlanders dress in loose layered smocks, laced at the side so they can be let out as the wearer grows. Belts are a mark of ill-omen and worn only by the Thin. The rich wear silk in field-colours, red and gold and green, cut wide, and pin their folds with brooches of polished bone. Teeth from the toothed wheat are threaded into necklaces for children.

Marriage and the body. Weight is beauty, and courtship is conducted over food. A suitor feeds the beloved with his own hands at the betrothal supper, and the beloved’s family watches to see that the feeding is generous. Wedding vows are sworn over a shared plate. Couples speak of “growing together,” and Gut-lines marriages sometimes end with both partners rooted side by side in a single hill. What happens in a Fatland marriage bed is, in the Fatland view, simply another kind of appetite and is spoken of in the same breath as supper, with a knowing look. Outsiders are discomfited by how readily lovers there speak of wanting to eat each other, and by how literally some of them mean it. The love-tokens of the south are bites: a crescent of tooth-marks on the soft of the shoulder, worn proudly above a low smock; and widows of the Leanings keep, in a little bone box, a strip of their husband’s wake-meat dried hard as leather, to put on the tongue at night when they cannot sleep.

The Hessops

Every household in the south that thanks Granny Hessop’s Rise at table is, in a sense, a Hessop household; the grain is sold everywhere. The Hessops themselves are another matter. They have lived on and around their matriarch’s slope for five hundred years in a warren of low old houses joined by covered ways, and in all that time, according to the Cutwrights’ registry, no Hessop has married outside the family. Their marriages are arranged by the Rise. The bride and groom (always cousins, the registry says; sometimes closer, the registry does not say) spend their wedding night not in a bed but out on the slope, on the warm breathing grass, alone with the hill, and come down at dawn silent and flushed and smelling of loam, and the children of those marriages are born with a soft brown seam of loam-flesh down the spine, and their feet already threaded with fine pale roots. Hessops are famously, almost unbearably beautiful: fair, full, sweet-faced, with the same wide grey eyes and the same small even teeth in every generation, so that a portrait of a Hessop girl of 300 A.G. hangs in the Fold and visitors take it for one of the girls now living. Hessops do not grow old in the face. They grow heavy very young, root before forty, and Seat on the slope beside their foremothers, so that the Rise grows a little longer every generation. Nobody in Low Tilth will say what they think the Rise is to the Hessops, or the Hessops to the Rise. They only say that Hessop flour is the sweetest in the world; that it is unlucky to marry a Hessop, and impossible; and that on Sweating Night, when the Rise breathes hardest, the windows of the Hessop houses are all left open, and nobody in the covered ways is asleep. Granny Cracknel strings Hessop teeth on a wire of their own, and will tell you, chuckling, that she cannot tell them apart.

Children. Fatland children are fed from the moment they are born and weighed every week. A child who fails to gain is a scandal for its parents and a matter for the Bailiff. Children glean behind the harvesters, turn spits, and are put to sleep with a strip of fat to suck. They are warned never to go into the fields alone at dusk in Carving, and they all do, once, on a dare.

One for the pot and two for the plate,

three for the Bailiff who comes round late,

four for the field and five for the wheat,

six for the Cullmaster, white on his feet,

seven for Granny who’s under the hill,

eight for the Scarecrow, standing so still,

nine for the furrow, ten for the bone,

and you’re the one that walks out alone.

— counting-out rhyme, Low Tilth; the child the rhyme ends on must stand at the field’s edge until the others count a hundred. The Board has forbidden it twice. It is sung everywhere.

Death rites. There are no graves. The dead are served at the wake, by the family, on the best plates. To be buried uneaten would be the deepest insult to a life; it is reserved for traitors and the Thin, whose lean bodies are thrown in the Brawn. A wake begins at noon on the day after death. A jointer is hired if the family can afford one; the deceased’s fat is rendered first, the heart goes to the eldest, the hands into a pie, the marrow to the most beloved. Neighbours bring bread and are fed in return. The bones are cracked, boiled for stock, and then returned to the family’s field, ground fine, so that the person goes back to the god and comes up again as crop. A good wake is talked about for years. “He ate well” is said of the dead, meaning he tasted good.

A wake requires a licence from the parish Bailiff, issued on the morning of death for a fee of two crumbs, which certifies that the deceased died of something other than a crime, a contagion, or the Thin, and is fit for table. It is pinned to the door of the house through the wake, and then burned in the rendering fire, so that the dead go to the table with their papers in order. The great families print bills of fare, in the manner of a banquet, and the bills are kept, and passed down, and collected; the College holds four thousand of them.

THE WAKE OF MISTRESS ADELINE FENN OF THE FOLD, THIRTEEN HUNDRED AND TWELVE POUNDS, WHO WENT ON THE TRENCHER IN HER SLEEP. GIVEN AT FENN HOUSE, CARVING 637, BY HER LOVING CHILDREN. COOKED BY WAKEMOTHER P. HESK. JOINTED BY H. GRISTLE.

FIRST REMOVE: A clear broth of Mistress’s marrowbones, with toothed-wheat dumplings. Crackling of the shoulder, salted, served in a cone.

SECOND REMOVE: Mistress’s cheeks, braised in Orchard cider until they may be cut with a spoon. A terrine of her tongue, pressed with her own aspic, garnished with the pickled shoots from her elbows, which she grew with such pride.

THE GREAT REMOVE: The haunch, roasted whole on the Fenn spit over applewood, basted nine hours in her dripping and Sapwell honey. The heart, for Master Rowan, seared. The Hands of a Lady in a Pie, with turnips from Hessop’s Rise.

FOURTH REMOVE: Her famous belly, rolled and stuffed with sage and her own sweetbreads, and roasted until the rind shatters.

SWEETS: A pudding of her blood, with Bleeding Orchard pears and cream. Marrow on toast for the grandchildren, sprinkled with sugar.

TO FINISH: Her fingers, candied in the old way, one for each of her ten best friends, in a ribboned box to take home.

Mistress Fenn’s bones will return to Fenn Long Field on the first day of Lack. The family thanks you. Lack keep away.

— a printed wake-bill, Fenn family papers; at the foot, in pencil, in a child’s hand: “I had a finger. It was nice. I miss Gran.”

Wake Dishes

When the party sits down at a wake (and sooner or later it will), roll or choose from the following for what comes to their plate. Every dish is the best thing they have ever tasted.

d20Wake DishWhat it is
1Hands in a Piethe custom for a worker; the knuckles stand up through the crust like a little fence
2Heart Seared Thinfor the eldest; laid out in overlapping slices like scales on the blue plate
3Crackling Coneshoulder skin, scored and blistered, sold at the gate to passers-by for a crumb
4Widow’s Drippingthe first rendering, on hot bread; the widow skims it herself and weeps into it
5Marrow on Toastfor the most beloved; sweet and grey, on toasted name-loaf
6Cheek Braiseslow-cooked in cider until it falls; it keeps the shape of a smile in the pan
7Tongue Terrinepressed in the deceased’s own aspic; the custom is to say a kind thing before eating it
8Black Pudding of the Deadblood, fat, oats and Orchard sap, coiled in their own casing
9Belly Rollstuffed with sage and sweetbreads; the rind shatters like sugar-glass
10Brawn of the Headthe head boiled, picked and set in a mould; turned out, it looks very like them
11Liver and Onionsfor the Gut-lines, who claim the liver by right; the onions flinch in the pan
12Ear-Crispsfried in dripping and salted; children fight over them
13Toe-Picklein vinegar, in a jar, to be eaten through the winter, one each Sunday
14Candied Fingersone to each best friend, in a ribboned box
15Bone Broththe last dish, from the cracked bones; served at dawn to those who sat up
16Name-Loafbaked from flour milled with their ground bones; eaten in silence
17Eyes in Jellya Gut-line delicacy; they are said to see the eater, once, at the moment of swallowing
18Fat-Candlesnot a dish; rendered from what is left, and lit at the board; they smell of the dead for a year
19Sweetbread Frittersin toothed-wheat batter; a jointer’s perquisite, shared with whoever helped
20The Unasked Coursea covered dish nobody ordered; the cook says it was on the bill; it is someone else

Festivals. The Weighing in Grace is a festival of three days, with pie-stalls the length of Sated and the Board brought to the scales on drays before a roaring crowd. Marbling morning is a children’s holiday. Harvest Home at the end of Carving is a week of feasting that the Long Count has made very quiet in recent years. And on Tablenight the whole country attempts a one-day fast in penance for the Meal. Pantries are locked, keys are given to the priest, and everyone sits in silence. Nobody has ever recorded a village that made it to sundown. By noon children are screaming; by mid-afternoon someone has broken the pantry door; by dusk there is a riot of eating, shameful and joyful, in every village on the plain, and the year begins again.

Crime and punishment. Fatland justice is fast and fed. Petty offenders are fined in meals owed. Brawlers are made to sit and eat together until they reconcile. Debtors are sent to the dusk-shift, from which they return, mostly, with the debt worked off. Mostly.

Proverbs. A thin man has a secret. Eat while it’s warm; it won’t be. The field remembers who fed it. Never trust a cook who isn’t heavy. Nobody’s full, but some are fuller. What the wheat took, the bread gives back. Love is wanting to feed someone; hate is wanting to eat them; marriage is both. Don’t make bread of your friends. A hill never says no. Every pot has a granny in it.

Oaths on the dead. The binding oath of the Fatlands is sworn with a mouthful of a dead relative’s flesh held on the tongue: By my mother’s meat, which is in me. To break it is to have eaten your mother for nothing, and Fatlanders consider this the vilest thing a person can do. Wakes are often delayed so that the family can settle disputes by such oaths while the meat is fresh. Families keep a little dried meat of their elders in a salt-box for the purpose, against the day they must swear; the salt-box is the most private object in a Fatland house, kept under the marriage bed, and to open another family’s salt-box is a crime the courts treat as a kind of rape of the dead. An oath-breaker, when found out, is not punished by the law. Their family simply stops serving them at table. They are set a place and an empty plate, five times a day, for the rest of their lives, and nobody looks at them while the others eat.

Remember, she was soft. Remember, she was sweet. Pass the plate along, along; there’s not a bit to waste.

Remember, she was heavy, love. Remember, she was kind. Lick the bowl and crack the bone, there’s marrow yet to find.

And when you’re in the furrow, love, and when you’re in the wheat, we’ll sit at board and say your name, and you’ll be what we eat.

— wake-song, sung across the plains while the copper boils
Wakes and the Outsider

A PC from another land will be invited to a wake sooner or later. It is the highest courtesy a Fatland family can offer a guest. Refusing to eat is not merely rude; it is sedition, and a Bailiff may be called. Eating counts as cannibalism for any Dread or Rites purpose the GM’s table cares about (Dread 2 the first time for a non-Fatlander; Dread 1 thereafter; Dread 0 for a native). It is also, without exception, the most delicious thing the character has ever tasted, and a non-Fatlander of Cut 1+ who eats at a wake gains 1 Hunger, because the meat is looking for somewhere to be hungry from.

I’ve jointed nine hundred and four. You stop seeing faces after the first fifty. Then about the eight hundredth you start again, and it’s all faces.
a jointer of Wakeside

Factions

The Board of Plenty

The government: two hundred members, vast, slow, and aware of the Reaping in more detail than it admits. The Board believes in continuity, export, and the Weighing. It knows the “wolves” are the fields; it has known for three hundred years; it has records, in the root-choked cellars of the Weighhouse, of every Reaping by district and year, and its private projections match Pell Hogget’s to the head. What the Board wants is to keep the Fatlands eating and the Table buying until the god arrives, and then, if possible, to be the god’s favoured guests. Its enemies are the Thin and the Long Count; its allies are the Renderers (uneasily) and the Rim Road Company (expensively). A PC joins by service: as a clerk, a Bailiff, a Weigher’s assistant, or a member’s Carrier.

RankTitleGrants
1LadleA Bailiff’s or clerk’s badge; right to enforce the Feasting Laws; free Supper at any inn.
2DeaconA district seat; one vote per hundred pounds; the ear of the Wolf-Warden.
3MemberA Board vote by weight; immunity from the dusk-shift; a Carrier retinue.
4Great MemberCommittee seat; access to the Weighhouse cellars and the real Reaping figures.
5ChairmanThe heaviest vote. Rule of the Fatlands, from a cart, then from the ground.

MINUTES OF THE INNER COMMITTEE (NOT FOR THE FULL BOARD), SITTING IN THE CELLARS, CARVING 640.

Present: the Chairman (rooted); seven Great Members; the Cullmaster-General; the Physician, by invitation, who was asked to leave after item two.

Item one: the Cullmaster-General reported the season’s yield. Dusk-shift taken: one thousand one hundred and four. Reaped (general): four thousand nine hundred and ninety. Ratio of the dusk-shift to the whole: worse. The Cullmaster-General asked that this be minuted. It was minuted.

Item two: the Physician reported on the Vigil buyer. The Committee resolved that the Vigil buyer had eaten something disagreeable on the Rim Road.

Item three: the Long Count. Resolved, that it is to be ignored, as a thing that encourages itself by notice.

Item four: the Chairman asked, through his Washer, that the Reaping figures be read aloud to him slowly by district. They were read. During the reading the floor of the cellar was observed to rise and fall. The Chairman thanked the Committee and said he was “very nearly full.” It was noted that this has not been said in the Weighhouse before. Members were asked not to repeat it.

Item five: the wolves. Carried, nem. con.

— copied secretly by the Chairman’s Washer and sent to Kettle Furrow folded in a shoe

The Thin

Outlawed fasters who believe starving the body starves the god. They are gaunt, hunted, and the only people in the south who seem clear-headed. The Thin eat once every three days, in secret, a handful of ash-bread and water; they bind their bellies with cord, live in barns and ditches, and meet in the Orchards where the deafened keepers will not hear. Their faith is Purgation-adjacent, and the cross-border Purgation sends them money, but the Thin are stranger and gentler than their foreign cousins: they do not kill nobles. They simply refuse. They want the Fatlands to stop feeding the god for one whole season, and believe that if it did, the Reaping would end. Their allies are the Purgation and, secretly, a few Orchard-keepers; their enemies are every Bailiff on the plain. A PC joins by fasting in their company for nine days and being seen to suffer.

To be Thin in the Fatlands is to live as a ghost. You stuff your cheeks with bread at your mother’s table and spit it into your apron. You lie in a ditch at night with the cord pulled tight across your belly, and hear, across the warm dark fields, every house on the plain eating. Ash-bread is grey and gritty and tastes of a cold hearth; the Thin eat it slowly, in a circle, passing the loaf along, and it is the only bread in the Fatlands that is not delicious, and they love it for that.

RankTitleGrants
1HollowA cord for the belly; a hiding place; the Thin’s hand-signs.
2LeanKnowledge of the safe barns; a share of the ash-bread.
3GauntLeads a cell; may rescue prisoners from the Gavage.
4BoneSpeaks for a district; carries messages to the Purgation.
5The Thin ManCorder Lank. Unopposed.

The Gavage. Captured Thin are not executed. They are fed. A prisoner is strapped into an oak chair, head locked back in a padded iron frame, jaw held open with a boxwood wedge. A funnel of polished horn is seated in the throat. The feeders are kindly, plump, singing women in white aprons, and they pour: warm lard-porridge first, then gravy thick with marrow, then a puree of pork and bread and dripping, slowly, a ladle every few breaths, while the prisoner chokes and heaves and the feeder strokes the throat downward with a buttered thumb to help it along, murmuring there, there, love, there’s a good belly. A Gavage session lasts three hours and comes five times a day. The prisoner’s body, after nine years of hunger, does not want to fight. It wants. That is the true torture of the Gavage: the Thin weep because it is wonderful, because the gravy is the best thing they have tasted in years, because their bellies stretch and gurgle and rejoice, and with every ladle they can feel the god in them waking up and growing fat and grateful. Most leave the Gavage in a season, heavy and silent and eating. Some come back to the Thin anyway, and weigh the cord around them, and begin again.

The Coldharbour Lack

In Lack 640, Corder Lank brought the Fasting Girl, Wren Hollowell, to Coldharbour Barn and fasted beside her for nine days, and on the ninth night something went wrong that only he understands. The nineteen Thin sheltering in the barn felt their hunger, in the space of an hour, double. They did not know why. They thought it was their own weakness. Over the next season, the hunger in them did not lessen; it gnawed and talked, and what it said, in the cold barn, in the long nights, was that the field was warm. Nan Tidy, a Lean of twenty, was the first to go out to the Dusk Acres in the snow, and lie down in a furrow, and not come back; out of season, when the fields do not take, so that what took her was only the cold and her own wish to be gone. She left her cord folded on her pallet. Within a fortnight two more had gone the same way, and left their cords the same way. Then it spread like a sentence passed round a table, and seven of the nineteen were gone by Grace, all to the same frozen strip, all leaving their cords neatly folded, and a boy called Tobin Ash, the youngest, wrote on the barn beam in charcoal: it is not hungry if you are in it. The survivors scattered and will not use the barn. Corder Lank went there alone at the end of Grace and gathered up the seven cords and has worn them, knotted together, under his own ever since. He has not told the Thin what he did on the ninth night. He has told them, gently, that the seven were weak, and that the Thin must be strong, and he hates himself for it more than he has hated anything. GM’s note: treat this as tragedy, never spectacle. Any PC who knew one of the seven, or who learns the truth of Lank’s hunger, faces a Dread 3 check; a Thin PC who fails must check against the Want Stillness (Hard 14) the next time they stand in a field at dusk, whatever their Regrowth, because the sentence from the barn has found them too. The way out is people: a PC who spends a scene with another who asks them plainly to stay may reroll that check.

It is not hungry if you are in it.
charcoal on the beam at Coldharbour Barn; the Thin sand it off, and it comes back

The Renderers' Union

The slaughter, salting, and shipping trades: butchers, renderers, coopers, drovers, salters, jointers and the dock-gangs of the Chute. They control what leaves the country and know what is in it. The Union’s members are broad, red-armed, practical people who smell of brine and tallow and talk frankly about anything. They believe in work and in the barrel. They want their wages, their monopoly, and the Board’s continued need of them; they also want, more and more, someone else to be blamed when the world finds out what has been in the barrels. Their allies are the Rim Road Company; their enemies, the Board when it tries to tax them. A PC joins by apprenticeship, or by doing a job in the Chute and keeping quiet.

A rendering-house at full work is a particular hell, and the Union is proud of it: rows of coppers the height of a man, a hot brown greasy fog thick enough to taste, floors like skating-rinks of tallow and sawdust, and a ceaseless seething like a crowd whispering. The Hooks eat the cracklings by the fistful as they work. What sinks to the bottom of the copper, the grounds, is scraped out at the end of each day and is the Union’s secret: a dark sweet paste sold, very quietly, as a flavouring, which is what the Vigil buyer was eating.

RankTitleGrants
1HookWork in the yards; Union protection; a cleaver.
2JointerRight to carve at wakes for a fee; the trade’s secret cuts.
3YardmasterCommand of a rendering-house; a share of export profits.
4StamperControl of a barrel-mark; knows what is in each consignment.
5Mistress of the UnionBrisket Annalow. Can stop the Rim Road with a word.

The Cullmasters

A quiet office of the Board which holds that the Reaping can be steered. If the fields must take, the Cullmasters reason, better that they take vagrants, debtors and troublemakers than good farmers and children. They draw up the lists. They assign the dusk shift. They think of it as agriculture.

The dusk-shift is a ritual, though no Cullmaster would use the word. On Carving afternoons, a Cullmaster’s clerk reads the list in the village square: names, debts, and a plot-number in the Dusk Acres. The named are fed a large and excellent supper at the Board’s expense, a real feast with roast and pie and hot bread and as much as they can hold, because the Cullmasters have found that the fields take the well-fed more gently, and because, they say, it is only decent. Then the named are dressed in clean white field-smocks and walked out along the furrows in a line, each carrying a sickle with a ribboned handle, to their numbered stones. The Cullmaster walks behind them with a lantern. At each stone he stops, bows to the worker, and says the words: Work well. The field is grateful. You are paid in full. Then he unrolls a strip of red cloth across the end of the row, so that the worker will know which side of it to stay on, and walks back to the road, and stands with his clerk and his lantern to watch the light go. The workers who try to leave the row are turned back by Bailiffs. The ones who stay bent over their work, cutting and binding, see the wheat begin to lean. A good Cullmaster records each Reaping in his ledger with the plot-number, the time, and the weight of the following year’s yield. A great Cullmaster can tell you, to the pound, how much bread one debtor makes.

Not all of the dusk-shift are taken. Perhaps one in three walk back at full dark, shaking, their debts paid. That fraction, the Cullmasters insist, proves it is labour and not execution. The Long Count suggests the fraction is falling.

Hear the list for the parish of Bramble Furrow, Carving, the year six hundred and forty.

Item: Josiah Pell, labourer, debt of sixty-one lacks to the Board stores. Plot LT-209.

Item: Widow Marn, no debt, a troublemaker, for teaching the Count. Plot LT-210.

Item: Hennet Hollowell, rush-weaver, for harbouring a person wanted by the Board. Plot LT-211.

Item: a vagrant, name not given, found sleeping in the common house. Plot LT-212.

Supper is at Fourth Plate in the yard, and there is pork. The Board thanks you. Work well.

— a dusk-list as read, preserved on a tally-stick at Kettle Furrow; a fifth name has been scraped off with a knife
RankTitleGrants
1LanternbearerWalks the line; carries the light; a stipend.
2Listing ClerkDrafts the dusk-shift lists; may strike or add one name a season.
3CullmasterOwns a plot-ledger; command of Bailiffs on Carving evenings.
4Senior CullmasterChooses which districts are spared; reports to the Board’s inner committee.
5Cullmaster-GeneralVarn Sweetbread. Steers the Reaping, he believes.

The Second Helping

A joyous cult of the Bait doctrine. The god starved us so we would eat it, they say; it wanted to be inside us, and now it wants to be fed and to feed, and the holiest thing a person can do is join in. Eat, and be eaten, and be glad. The Second Helping meets at Gladbelly and in a hundred kitchens across the plain, and they are the happiest people in the south: fat, laughing, singing hymns about gravy, embracing strangers. They want the Seating, and they want it soon, and they intend to hurry it along by giving the god as much of themselves as it will take. Their allies are the Second Table, which finds them useful and gullible; their enemies are the Thin, who pity them, and the Board, which finds them embarrassing and quietly very convenient. A PC joins by sharing a meal at Gladbelly and accepting a second helping. Everyone is offered one.

The cult’s highest sacrament is the Offering. A member who has decided to go to the god announces it at table, and everyone cheers. There is a week of feasting in the Offered’s honour, in which they are fed by every hand in the commune. On the last evening they are bathed in warm dripping and garlanded with toothed wheat and carried in procession to the pavilion, singing. Their family walks beside them. Their family, too, is singing, and it is only afterward, on the long benches, with the plates going round, that the singing becomes something else: a widower holding a fork he cannot lift, a daughter who keeps saying but she was happy, she was happy, she said she was happy, a small boy asking where his mother has gone while a sweet brown smell drifts out of the kitchens. The Second Helping does not talk about the ones left behind. They are expected to rejoice, and to eat, and to offer themselves in their turn. Many do. That is how the cult grows: by grief that has nowhere else to go.

Lay me in the dripping, love, and lay me on the board;

garland me in toothy wheat and give me to the Lord.

Take a slice and pass it down, and take a slice and smile;

I’ll be in you, I’ll be in you, I’ll be in you for a while.

— Gladbelly hymn, sung in procession to the pavilion; the last line repeats until the pavilion door is shut
RankTitleGrants
1GuestA seat at the long tables; the hymns; never to eat alone again.
2ServerFeeds newcomers; may speak at table.
3PlateholderLeads a household kitchen; tends the Offered in their last week.
4GarlandHas given part of themselves (a finger, an ear) and is honoured.
5The ProphetBrother Glut, who is being served one piece at a time.
Cross-Border Powers in the South

The Second Table is strong in the Fatlands, because the Gut-lines are its natural members: who better to eat a god twice than a family already eating everything? Its southern chapter meets in Marrable Hall under cover of the Unending Dinner. The Cutwrights’ College keeps a southern registry in Sated and knows, from three centuries of weighing records, exactly which families will Seat next. The Purgation funds the Thin. The Reckoners find the Fatlands hard going: a high-Cut Gut-line, rooted on its estate, is almost impossible to kill, and the hills do not die when stabbed. The Rim Road Company owns a third of the Chute’s wagons and does not inspect the barrels.

The Fatlands Now

The Reaping has doubled in ten years, and the fields are turning up things with faces: a turnip with a nose and two shut lids, a squash with the profile of a missing child, an ear of wheat that, when split, held a single human molar with a silver filling. The Board’s answer is the Cullmasters, and the dusk-shift lists grow longer every Carving. The Thin are growing, recruiting among the families of the culled. A girl has appeared who feels no hunger at all, and the Board has put a price on her that does not specify alive. And for the first time, an exile from the Fast has sat down at a Fatlands table and eaten. What is happening to him has no name yet.

The field-faces have frightened the ordinary people of the plain more than any tally. A woman of Millsop lifted a swede in Carving 638 and found on its underside a small, closed, perfectly human face, warm, with the brown mole her lost husband had on his cheek. She did what a Fatlander does with everything: she cooked it, with butter, and ate it with her children, and said his name. That night all three dreamed of him, standing at the end of a long table in a field, laying one more place than there were chairs. The markets of Sated have quietly begun to sell root-crops already peeled.

Underneath all of it is the arithmetic the Board will not publish. The Reaping doubles; the hills multiply; the Dowagers creep toward one another. Ummer is gathering itself up out of ten thousand graves and ten thousand bellies, and it is hungry, and it has the whole of the Fatlands for a body. Many Fatlanders have started, without saying why, to dream of walking in procession.

I cooked him with butter. What else would I do? He liked butter.
a widow of Millsop, 638

Adventure Hooks

  • The Notched Barrels. Quartermaster Ivo Stockpot sends a sealed list to a PC he trusts: the export barrels he has notched. A Vigil buyer has fallen ill in a way that sounds very like the Appetite. The PCs must trace a consignment from the Chute to the Rim Road, against the Renderers, the Company, and the Board, and decide who on the Table should know what they have been eating.
  • The Dusk List. A PC, or someone they love, is named on a Cullmaster’s list. Varn Sweetbread is courteous and immovable. The PCs have until Carving dusk to bribe a Listing Clerk, find a substitute (Fatlanders will suggest one), break the Gavage open for a Thin rescue as distraction, or walk the row themselves and survive.
  • Wren for Weight. Wren Hollowell is hidden in a Thin barn in the Orchards. The Board will pay her weight in bone coin; the Second Table will pay more for her organs; the Thin will die for her. The Fasting Girl wants none of it. She wants to see the sea.
  • The Hill That Walked. Mercy Sowerby, the Hill-Speaker, reports that two Dowager Hills have moved close enough to touch, and that their mouths are talking to each other in a language no one living speaks. The Gut-lines want it hushed. The College wants measurements. The hills want visitors.
  • The Scarecrow Turns. In Low Tilth, the Scarecrow has turned around, and it is facing Pell Hogget’s barn. The villagers want it burned. Nobody who has tried to light it has come back from the far field.
  • Plot LT-211. A Thin courier brings Wren Hollowell a tally-stick with her mother’s name on it, from the Bramble Furrow list of 640. Did Hennet Hollowell walk back at full dark? The Cullmaster’s ledger knows; so does the strip, and the bread from it, which is in a Board granary waiting for export. Wren wants to know. She does not want to be told by anyone who would sell her.
  • A Place at Hask’s End. Mother Furlong of Hask’s End has offered the village another bargain: one more, and this time she means it. The village is split; the new Reeve has sent for outsiders to “advise,” meaning to choose. Linnet’s betrothed has volunteered. The PCs may find a way to show the village the truth, or may find that a village that has already paid once cannot bear to have paid for nothing, and will pay again to prove it was not.
  • Weighed in Gammon. A Washer pensioned off to the coast in 619 has died, and her daughter has found among her things a sworn account of what was found in Cress Gammon’s folds, and a scrap of something in a salt-box. Lard Gammon votes with the Chairman on the dusk-lists. The Thin would give a great deal to unseat him. Lard Gammon would give more to have the salt-box back, and he has never once been refused a dish by Jem Crackle.

Rumors of the Fatlands

d10Rumor
1The Chairman’s roots have reached the Weighhouse cellars and are drinking from the Gravy. (True.)
2There are wolves after all; a pack was seen near Kettle Furrow. (False; it was a Cullmaster’s line in white.)
3Dame Marrable’s Dinner has a second table in the cellar where only nobles sit, and the meat there is different. (True: it is the Second Table.)
4Eat a Blank’s heart and you’ll be full forever. (False, but it is why Wren is hunted.)
5The Fast’s god is walking the Rim Road, and if you follow it you’ll find a meal that fills. (Half-true.)
6The Board fasts in secret and only pretends to eat. (False. They eat more than anyone.)
7The Thin Man drinks something from the Orchards that kills the hunger. (False. See Corder Lank.)
8Granny Cracknel can tell who’s next for the Reaping by the teeth in the flour. (True.)
9Low Tilth was once twice the size, and half of it is under the wheat. (True.)
10The Brother Glut who preaches now is the third man to bear that name. (False; it has always been the same man, less each year.)

The People of the Fatlands

Chairman Obb Tullow, the Heaviest Vote. Head of the Board at nineteen hundred pounds, he is moved by dray and eight oxen through streets cleared by Bailiffs. Up close he is a landscape: rolls of cool, brown, loam-soft flesh draped over the dray’s iron bed like a slumped haystack, crusted with the green shoots his Washers never quite get off, and at the summit a small, pink, clever face that looks out of the folds like a man peering from a cellar. His voice is reedy and precise. He is still the shrewdest mind on the Board. His feet rooted through the cart’s iron floor last spring, through a seam the smiths had missed, and the Board has agreed not to notice; the dray has not moved since, and the Board now meets around it. He wants to die Chairman. He fears the moment his mouth closes and the hill keeps voting. His secret is that the roots go all the way down to the Weighhouse cellars, and he can feel the Reaping through them, every one, as a warm full mouthful. Close to, he smells of a cellar full of apples, of warm hay and of the inside of a cow, and the air around the dray is close and humid as a glasshouse. His Washer, Nell Haslet, feeds him by hand from a silver spoon, and when the Reaping figures are read he closes his small eyes and his lips move with the numbers, and the floor of the Weighhouse rises and falls.

Obb Tullow — Chairman of the Board of Plenty
AttributesHand 1 · Gut 6 · Lung 1 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 10 (the Brink) · Hunger 8
SkillsFeast 5, Endure 4, Clause 3, Persuade 3, Intimidate 3, Reckoning 3
BodyFlesh 18 · Guard 12 · Armor 1 (loam-flesh) · Fray 5
Attacksrolling crush +2 (4); cannot pursue
GiftsField-Body (feels every footstep in the Weighhouse and on the Weighing Road); the Board’s grain bends toward him when he speaks; regains 1d6 Flesh per meal
Wantsto eat whatever is placed within reach; never to be moved; to be told the Reaping figures, aloud, slowly
Dread3 (to watch him eat, or to see what grows under the dray)
SecretTullow has arranged for the Cullmasters to list the families of every Deacon who votes against him.
Read them again, slowly. Low Tilth first. Ah. Ah, yes. That one was a big lad.
Chairman Obb Tullow, in committee, 640

Dame Suet Marrable. Gut-lines matriarch, mistress of Marrable Hall, and hostess of the Unending Dinner, in continuous service for eighty-one years. She sits at the head of the three-hundred-foot table on a reinforced throne that is slowly sinking into the floorboards, swathed in gold silk, her face powdered white and her many chins hung with pearls like dew on a hedge. She smells of rosewater over roast pork. Her voice is warm and husky and she calls everyone duck. Guests have been born at her table and several have been served at it, when they died there; the custom is that no one leaves, and some have not. She wants the Dinner to outlast her and fears that it will not, because her feet have begun to grow down through the floor. She is the Second Table’s southern chair, and the cellar beneath her dining hall holds a smaller table where the guests are older and the meat is something rarer. Her guests’ plates are nicked at the rim, so that with the first cut of meat their own blood is on her knife, and she licks it, smiling, and calls them by their grandmothers’ names. The Dinner has its own smell, which visitors carry home in their clothes for a week: eighty-one years of gravy soaked into the floorboards, rose-water, beeswax, and under it, faintly, the sweet heavy reek of the cellar.

Dame Suet Marrable — Hostess of the Unending Dinner
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsPersuade 4, Feast 5, Clause 3, Endure 3, Search 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 16 · Guard 12 · Armor 1 · Fray 3
Attackscarving knife +3 (2)
GiftsTaste the Name (one bite of a guest’s blood tells her their family, Cut and one secret); her hall’s food compels (Caul + Resolve, Hard 14, to rise from her table)
Wantsthat no guest leave hungry; that no guest leave
Dread2 (to see a guest served)
SecretShe has Tobias Wether’s name on a place card, and a seat waiting for him in the cellar.

Pell Hogget, the Counter. A farmer from Kettle Furrow in Low Tilth: short, broad, sunburnt, with a wheat-coloured beard and a stub of chalk always behind one ear. He speaks slowly and carefully and gives numbers instead of opinions. He noticed his village was one smaller each autumn and wrote it down, and now two hundred villages send him their tallies and his barn wall is a ledger of the dead. He eats less than he should and the Bailiff has begun to look at him. He wishes he had never learned to count. He fears that the numbers have a shape: his projection crosses his own village’s population in nineteen years, and the whole country’s soon after. His secret is that his wife was culled four years ago, and he has never put her mark on the wall. He keeps a tally-stick of his own in his boot with no notch on it, and touches it before every meal, and his neighbours have learned not to ask whose it is.

Don’t ask me if it’s the god. Ask me how many. I know how many.
Pell Hogget, to a Cutwright surveyor

Corder Lank, the Thin Man. Leader of the Thin. He has eaten nothing but water and ash for six years and can be counted bone by bone: a long, brown, tendon-strung figure in a rope belt, his skin tight as a drumhead over ribs and hips and knuckles, his eyes huge and calm and very clear. He smells of woodsmoke and nothing else. He speaks quietly and always first asks whether you are hungry. He is the only man in the south who does not feel the hunger, and he will not say how. The truth is that the hunger did not leave him: it went out of him, piece by piece, into those who fast beside him. Every Thin cell carries a share of Corder Lank’s gnawing on top of its own. He worked this out three years ago. He has not told them. He cannot stop leading, because it is the only thing that keeps him clear. Since the Coldharbour Lack he wears seven belly-cords knotted together under his own, and when the Thin ask him why he is heavier in the cord than he was, he says it is penance, which is true.

Corder Lank — the Thin Man
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 1 · Lung 3 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 3 (the Taste, dormant) · Hunger 0
SkillsResolve 5, Endure 4, Persuade 3, Stealth 3, Athletics 2, Rites 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 15 · Armor 0 · Fray 6
Attacksknife +3 (2)
GiftsPassing the Plate: anyone who fasts a day in his company loses 1 Hunger and he loses none; they gain it back, doubled, the day they leave him
Wantsto be needed; never to be fed
Dread1
SecretHis hunger lives in his followers. If he dies, it goes back to the god all at once, and the Thin will feel it go.

Mistress Brisket Annalow. Boss of the Renderers’ Union: a vast, red-armed woman in a leather apron stiff with salt, her grey hair cropped short, a cleaver on a chain at her hip and a pencil behind her ear. She talks like a drover and laughs like a kettle. She can stop every barrel on the Rim Road with one word, and she knows precisely which of them should never have been filled, because she has kept a second ledger for twenty-two years. She wants the Union paid and her people safe. She fears the day the Table stops buying. She would sell the Board out in an afternoon to keep the Chute open. She knows the grounds at the bottom of the coppers are what the Vigil buyer ate. She knows where Sal Trotter’s calves come from. Her hands are cracked from the brine to the elbow and she rubs them with tallow at night, and does not ask herself whose.

Brisket Annalow Threat 5 · Flesh 15 · Guard 12 · Attack +6 (cleaver 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Hob Gristle, the Honest Butcher. A big, mild, sorrowful man with forearms like hams and a bald head beaded with sweat. He can tell by taste what a cut used to be, down to the name: a mouthful of sausage tells him the pig, the field it ate from, and the name of anyone Reaped into that field. It has ruined him for the trade. He still works, because jointing at wakes is the only honest money left, and he apologizes to every joint, quietly, by name. He wants one barrel from the Chute that tastes of nothing but beef. He fears the day he tastes someone he loves. He has already tasted his brother, in a pie in Sated, and has told no one. He knows from the taste that his brother was not taken by any field: the meat in the pie tasted of a kitchen knife and of fear, and no field has ever made meat taste of fear.

Sorry, old lad. Sorry. Sorry.
Hob Gristle, at every joint, under his breath

Cullmaster Varn Sweetbread. The Board’s quiet hand: a neat, plump, pink man in grey broadcloth, with soft white fingers, rimless spectacles and a ledger chained to his belt. He smells faintly of lavender, which he uses to cover the field. His voice is gentle and his manners perfect. He decides which vagrants, debtors and troublemakers are assigned the dusk shift, and he thinks of it as agriculture, in the most literal sense: he weighs the next year’s yields and has proved, to his own satisfaction, that a culled vagrant makes better bread than a Reaped farmer. He walks every line himself and bows at every stone. He is not cruel. That is the worst thing about him. It was his ink that struck out the Hask’s End Wolf-Warden’s last two lines, out of kindness, because he thought the man would be listed for them. He was right; the man was listed anyway.

Varn Sweetbread — Cullmaster-General
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 3 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 3 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 · Regrowth 5 (the Appetite) · Hunger 4
SkillsReckoning 4, Clause 3, Intimidate 3, Resolve 3, Rites 2, Endure 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 13 · Armor 0 · Fray 2
Attacksribboned sickle +3 (3)
GiftsField-Reading: he knows, on any Carving evening, which plot will Reap first
Wantsto see the line through to the end; to taste the bread of each plot he culled
Dread2 (to watch his dusk-shift)
SecretHis own name is on next year’s list, in the Chairman’s hand.

Tansy Lard, the Gleaner. A girl of ten who gleans behind the harvesters in Low Tilth: skinny for a Fatlander, with tangled straw hair and a smock too short in the arms, and dirt permanently under her nails. She dug up a root with her mother’s birthmark on it, a brown splash shaped like a running hare, and has replanted it behind the house and waters it every day. It has grown. It has leaves like hands. Last week, at dusk, it said her name. Her father has noticed she has stopped eating at table and goes out after dark with the bowl. She wants her mother back. She is the reason the PCs may first learn what a Fatland root can become. The root is warm when she touches it and turns its hand-leaves toward her when she comes out of the back door, the way a sunflower turns, and the soil around it has begun, very slightly, to breathe.

Brother Glut. Prophet of the Second Helping: enormous, radiant, and happy, a mountain of pink flesh in a garland of wheat, his face shining with sweat and tears of joy, his voice a deep golden bell that fills a meadow without trying. He preaches that being eaten is the highest form of being loved, and he has volunteered parts of himself to prove it: his left hand, both ears, three toes, a long strip from the flank. The wounds are bound with clean linen and he shows them off like medals. He embraces every stranger. He believes every word. What he does not see is the widows at the back of each meeting, holding their plates. He smells of hot dripping and lavender and a faint sweet sourness from under the linen where the wounds are. When he embraces a stranger the stranger is held a long time, against the soft enormous warmth of him, and many weep without knowing why.

Brother Glut — Prophet of the Second Helping
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 2 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 5
SkillsPersuade 5, Rites 4, Feast 4, Endure 4, Godsign 3
BodyFlesh 17 · Guard 11 · Armor 1 · Fray 0
Attackscrushing embrace +2 (1, held)
GiftsThe Shared Plate: anyone who eats his flesh loses 1d6 Hunger and must pass Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) or come back for more
Wantsto give; to see others give
Dread2 (to see him carve himself, smiling)
SecretHe has not felt the hunger since his hand was eaten. He thinks this is grace. It is the god, moving out.
I gave them my hand, and do you know, I have never felt so held.
Brother Glut, at Gladbelly

Old Mother Rind. A Laden woman who rooted forty years ago and is now a small orchard hill outside the village of Kettle Furrow, with nine pear trees growing from her back and a working mouth half-hidden in the clover at her foot. Her lips are brown and cracked like bark and her teeth are wheat-teeth, many rows. Her voice is a dry old woman’s, amused and sharp. Her village asks her advice on marriages; she is always right, and always hungry, and her fee is meat. Lately she has asked for particular people. The names she asks for are always ones the far field wants this Carving. She says that if they are fed to her, they will be hers and not the Scarecrow’s, and that she is quick and the field is slow, and that this is mercy. Hask’s End once believed something very like it of Mother Furlong.

Dr. Emmerich Paunch. The Board’s physician: a stooped, heavy, myopic man with ink-stained cuffs and a voice like a dry quill. He opened a Gut-lines stomach, under licence, to measure its capacity, and lowered a plumb line into it. He ran out of line at two hundred feet. He has since obtained longer line. He has not been able to bring himself to use it, because when he drew the first one up, the lead weight had been chewed. He wants to publish. He fears the Board, and what he heard echoing up the line. He will pay adventurers very well to hold the rope.

The stomach of a Gut-line lady is not an organ. It is a door. I should like very much to know what it opens on, and I should like very much not to.
Dr. Emmerich Paunch, private notebook

Sal Trotter, the Drover. A lean, weathered woman in a dung-crusted oilskin, with a crook, a whip she never uses, and a pipe she never lights. She walks herds to market at the Chute that the buyers call cattle. They walk on two legs when no one is watching the road. She has stopped naming them, because they started answering. She speaks little, mostly to the herd, in a low, even croon. She wants to finish one drive without looking back. She fears the day one of them asks her where they are going. It will be soon; the lead steer has begun to hum her songs. The lead steer’s flank bears a scar where a brand would be, and she has never looked at it closely.

Sal Trotter’s Herd (each) Threat 2 · Flesh 16 · Guard 10 · Attack +4 (trample 3) · Armor 1 · Dread 2 (to see them stand)

Wren Hollowell, the Fasting Girl. A Blank of fifteen from Bramble Furrow who has never once felt hungry. She is small and narrow and pale, with a long plain face and grey eyes that rest on things without wanting them, and in a land of the vast she looks like a drawing of a girl rather than a girl. She eats when reminded, without interest. The Thin kneel to her, which she hates. The Board has offered her weight in bone coin to whoever brings her in, and has not specified alive; the Second Table has a surgeon waiting. She wants to see the sea, and to be left alone. She is beginning to notice that fields go quiet when she walks through them, as though they cannot smell her at all. She does not yet know that her mother’s name was read on the Bramble Furrow list in Carving 640, or which strip it was given.

Wren Hollowell Threat 2 · Flesh 10 · Guard 14 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0 · cannot be Reaped; no Cut, no Hunger

Garrick Tripe, the Weigher. Keeper of the official scales at the annual Weighing: a jovial, oily man in a brass-buttoned coat, with a waxed moustache and a dozen rings. For the right fee your pockets fill with lead, and for a better one your rival’s empty. He has personally elected three governments. He wants to retire rich. He fears that the Chairman knows exactly how much of his vote is lead; Tullow does, and is waiting for the right moment.

Lady Aspic Dellamore. A noble chef whose speciality is preservation: tall for a Gut-line, sleek and plump, in a white silk apron, with lacquered nails and a cold, musical laugh. Her rivals are displayed in her gallery, set in clear golden jelly, garnished with herbs and quail’s eggs, and blinking. The jelly keeps them; the Gut-line blood keeps them hungry. They watch visitors eat at her table. She wants to be the greatest cook on the Table. She fears blandness. She is working on a new piece for the gallery, and has been measuring Dame Marrable. The Gallery smells of cold gelatine and tarragon, and of something under it like a larder in which a mouse has died; the jelly sweats a little in Plenty, and her servants wipe it down each morning with linen cloths while the faces inside follow the cloths with their eyes.

Jem Crackle, the Cook’s Knife. A former spit-boy and now the most reliable assassin in Sated: wiry, quick, red-knuckled, with burn scars to the elbow and the cheerful, sweaty face of a kitchen lad. He smells of onions and hot iron. He kills only in kitchens, and what he kills is on the table by evening, jointed, dressed and served so beautifully that the families often do not complain. He is proud of his work and owes nothing to anyone. He fears only being bored. He takes contracts from the Board, the Union and the Second Table impartially.

Jem Crackle — the Cook’s Knife
AttributesHand 5 · Gut 2 · Lung 4 · Eye 3 · Tongue 2 · Caul 2
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 3 (the Taste) · Hunger 3
SkillsBlades 5, Stealth 4, Athletics 3, Feast 3, Craft 3, Filch 2, Endure 2
BodyFlesh 12 · Guard 19 · Armor 0 · Fray 1
Attacksboning knife +10 (2); cleaver +10 (3)
GiftsIn any kitchen he gains a free Helping on his first attack; he can joint a body in the time it takes to boil a kettle
Wantsto cook what he kills
Dread2 (to find a missing friend on his table)
SecretHe has a list of every person he has served, and who ate them. He sells it.

Bailiff Dunmow Fatt. Enforcer of the Feasting Laws in Sated: a huge, slow, pink-cheeked man with a gentle lisp, a blue sash, and a funnel and ladle of office worn like a sword and sceptre. He is, by every account, gentle about it. He kneels to feed the stubborn, strokes their throats, sings to them. He has wept over every Thin prisoner he has ever taken. He wants everyone to be well. He does not understand why anyone would refuse. He fears, a little, the quiet in Corder Lank’s eyes.

Dunmow Fatt Threat 3 · Flesh 16 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (ladle 3, Grappling) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Marigold Chine. Keeper of the oldest grove in the Bleeding Orchards: a slender, freckled woman of fifty with a strong alto and a straw hat. She refused the deafening and sings to her trees through the pruning. They have begun to sing back, in tune, in her voice, a thousand trees at once, and the other keepers, who cannot hear it, feel it in their teeth. She wants to learn what the trees are trying to say. She fears she already knows: the last verse is the wake-song, and it is about her. Her mother’s mother was a Strake.

Tobias Wether, the First to Eat. A runaway from the Fast, twenty-four, raised on six centuries of refusal, who crossed the Rim Road and ate. He was thin as a rake when he came; he is filling out now, and his skin has taken on a warm brown loam-tint. He carries no god in his blood. The meat seems to be looking for one. He feels the hunger now, a borrowed hunger with no lineage, and it is worse than any Fatlander’s, because it has nowhere to settle. He is ashamed, delighted, and terrified. The Second Table wants him; the Reckoners want him dead; Dame Marrable wants him at dinner. He has taken, without knowing why, to setting one more place at every table than there are diners, and he is upset if anybody sits in it.

The Scarecrow of Low Tilth. Nobody put it up. It stands in the far field of Kettle Furrow with its back to the village: a tall, thin shape of sacking and straw on a pole, in a farmer’s smock and a wide hat, its arms spread. The straw is toothed wheat. The sacking is warm. Each Carving it is a few furrows closer. Last year someone saw it turn around. Its face, they say, is a mouth, and the mouth is full of the names on Pell Hogget’s wall.

The Scarecrow — the Far Field
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 6 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 0 · Caul 7
Cut & Regrowthnone; it is a piece of Ummer standing up
SkillsStealth 5, Instinct 5, Brawl 3, Endure 4
BodyFlesh 30 · Guard 15 · Armor 2 · Fray —
Attacksstraw fingers +6 (3, and the target’s feet begin to root: Gut + Endure, Hard 14, or held)
Giftsmoves only when unobserved; any field it stands in Reaps at dusk; fire will not take on it
Wantsto reach the village
Dread4 (to see it face you)
SecretIt is walking toward the Weighhouse, by way of every village that has stopped counting.

Quartermaster Ivo Stockpot. He feeds the army and stamps the export barrels at the Chute: a portly, fussy, honest man with a bald freckled head, a stamp on a cord and a tremor in his left hand. He has started marking a small notch on the ones he would not eat from himself. There are a great many notches. He wants someone outside the Fatlands to know. He fears that if they knew, they would keep buying.

Granny Cracknel, the Tooth-Miller. She mills the toothed wheat at the old water-mill on the Little Gravy and keeps the teeth. Her mill is decorated with eleven hundred sets, sorted by village and strung on wires like rattling wind-chimes. She is tiny, ancient, floury, toothless herself, and chuckles constantly. She says some of the sets match people she knew. She is right; and she has started to find, in each new harvest’s sieve, the teeth of people who are still alive. Hessop teeth she keeps on a wire of their own, because she says she cannot tell one generation from the next.

New Faces

Wakemother Pudding Hesk. The most sought-after wake-cook in Sated: a round, brisk, broad-faced woman with forearms scarred by spatter and a laugh that rattles crockery. Families wait months for her. She bastes the dead with their own dripping and a little honey, roasts them slow over applewood, and sends them to the table glazed and crackling, and she weeps every time, openly, while she carves. She knows everyone’s secrets, because the dead taste of them. She wants to cook the Chairman. She has been asked to. She fears she will be too greedy to share him.

Feeder Callow Pudge. Head feeder at the Gavage: a soft-voiced, motherly woman in a starched white apron, with plump dimpled hands and a funnel she has polished for thirty years. She hums lullabies as she pours. She sincerely believes she saves lives. She keeps a book of the Thin she has fed, with their weights in and their weights out, and letters from their grateful families. She fears the ones who come back to the Thin, and she has begun, secretly, to leave one cell door unbarred each Lack.

Callow Pudge and Gavage Feeders Threat 3 · Flesh 12 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (grapple, then funnel: Gut + Endure, Hard 14, or helpless) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Mercy Sowerby, the Hill-Speaker. A young widow employed by the Gut-lines to interpret the Dowager Hills: thin-lipped, careful, dressed in field-brown with soil always on her knees, because she must lie face-down on the turf to hear. She translates the Dowagers’ slow speech and lays their offerings. She has noticed that two hills are moving together, that their mouths are talking, and that the language is older than Table-speech. She wants someone to tell. She fears the Dowagers have noticed her noticing; last week one of them used her name.

Lord Chastain Loin. Heir to a Gut-line that Seated last generation: a young, enormous, beautiful man of eight hundred pounds, with oiled ringlets, perfect teeth, and a voice like warm cream. He is Dame Marrable’s protégé in the Second Table, charged with acquiring Blanks for the cellar table. He eats elegantly and constantly, and his manners never slip. He wants to be at the table when Ummer stands up, with a knife in his hand. He fears that his own mother, the hill behind his house, will stand up first, and that she has never forgiven him for the wake.

Lord Lard Gammon, the Twin Who Weighed In. Head of the Gammons of the Fold and a Member of the Board since 619: fifty-three now, near thirteen hundred pounds, moved on a dray and sitting always to the Chairman’s left, with a soft, mild, slightly bewildered face like a large baby’s, and pale lashes, and small damp hands that he folds over his belly as if keeping something in. He votes with the Chairman on every dusk-list, and adds no names of his own, and has never been known to raise his voice. He eats in his kitchen, among the servants, because the dining room is locked. At table he sometimes stops, with the spoon half-raised, and listens to something inside himself, and says, to nobody, “Yes, all right,” and passes the salt along the board to an empty place. He wants to be forgiven and does not know by whom. He fears the salt-box: a small one, of his brother’s meat, that the Washers took with them in 619, and that would let anyone in the Fatlands put him to the oath again. The Gammon Dowager, when he last consulted her, said only: There are two of you in there, son. Which one of you is asking?

Lard Gammon — Member of the Board, Kin-Slayer
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 2 · Tongue 3 · Caul 2
Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsFeast 4, Endure 4, Deceive 3, Clause 2, Brawl 2, Intimidate 2
BodyFlesh 17 · Guard 11 · Armor 1 (loam-flesh) · Fray 8
Attackssmothering press +4 (3, Grappling; the target must pass Gut + Endure, Hard 14, each round or lose 1d6 Flesh)
