The First Night

It came on the third night of Grace, 341 A.G., which had been a warm and pleasant evening. There was no sign. Ludmere went to bed. In the morning, roughly a third of it did not get up: they lay in their beds breathing slow and even, smiling, and no amount of shaking would rouse them. Their families screamed in the streets. The physicians were sent for and could not wake them. By the next night the city understood only that a sickness had come; and most of it, exhausted with weeping and fear, went to bed. In the morning, half of what remained did not wake.

Those who survived the third night were the ones too frightened to lie down: the anxious, the guilty, the insomniac, the mad, the nursing mothers, the drunks, the watchmen, the children too hungry to sleep. They sat up through the dark in kitchens together, slapping each other, shouting, banging pans, holding hands and squeezing until the knuckles cracked. Those people are the ancestors of the Vigil. The city descends, by a kind of hideous selection, from its worst sleepers. Vigilants say it with pride.

The Waking Laws and the Burning of the Beds

In the spring of 342 the survivors met in the old Ludmere Square and passed the Waking Laws by acclamation. Lying down was forbidden. Closing the eyes for longer than a breath was forbidden. Every bed, couch, mattress, pillow and cushion on the plateau was carried into the squares and burned, along with the goose-down warehouses, the oracles’ dream-books, and the dreamers themselves when they protested. The pyres burned for a month; they were the first Bonfires. The city took its new name from a word the old priests had used for the night before a feast: the vigil. It was meant to sound temporary.

We burned eleven thousand beds in Ludmere Square, and the down went up in a white cloud and came down on the city like snow, and it was so soft, and we were so tired, and we stood in it and screamed.
from the Testament of Wenna Corl, a survivor of the First Night, as read at the Shouting Day

The Count

In 401 a diver named Iselde Marrow, on her eleventh descent, walked further into the long room than anyone had and stood for a long while near the eye. When she was hauled back, half-dead with pain, she said she had heard the number. It had been told to her, she said, very gently, as if by a mother explaining to a child how many more days until a holiday. She was brought before three officials of the Watch, in a sealed room, and made to say it once. Then the officials agreed that the number was too dangerous to leave in a living head, and they had her laid down in a bed. Her bed was the next one in the row. Two of the three officials were dead within the decade, by accident; the third was the first Matron of the Dormitory, and the number has passed from Matron to Matron since, whispered once at the bedside of the dying.

The Giving of Lids

The Vigil has only once tried to pay the god back, and it does not like to remember the bill.

In the winter of 502 a Dream-Diver named Hollis Wren came up off the tether on his ninth descent with blood running from his tongue-ring and a message. He had stood, he said, closer to the eye than anyone since Iselde Marrow, and he had understood something, not in words: that the eye was not angry at being eaten, and that it did not want its flesh back, or its sight. It wanted its lids. The Eye-lines had taken the god’s shutting into their blood, and the god could not rest properly without it, and so it was taking rest from the city instead, one sleeper at a time. Give back the lids, said Hollis Wren, and the eye will close properly, and the Counted will stop counting.

The Watch of Watches debated it on the Stair for one hundred and nine days, which in a council that never adjourns is a very long time. The difficulty was obvious to everyone. The lidless had no lids to give, and could not be asked. But every Eye-line house had its spares: the younger sons and daughters born with ordinary lids, kept out of the succession and out of sight, educated, idle, married off to Slope merchants for their dowries or not married at all. There were two hundred and fourteen adult spares on the Height that winter. The Watch voted, by a margin of eleven lidless voices, that the spares would give their lids for the city. It was called an honour. Several of them were told it would make them eligible for the Stair.

The Giving was done in Ludmere Square on the first day of Grace, 503, in front of the Bonfire, in front of the whole city. The Cutwrights’ College sent nine surgeons. The spares stood in a line in white felt, with their heads held from behind in padded frames, and were given poppy, which was the first poppy permitted on the Lid in a hundred and sixty years, and which several of them were afterwards said to have wept for joy at. Each pair of lids, as it came away, was laid on a square of goose-down, the last down on the Lid, released from the evidence-vaults of the Rattlehouse for the occasion, and the down was sewn shut over them, and the little packets were laid one by one in a silver casket lined with grey felt that the city called the Coverlet. The crowd was silent. The only sound, the accounts agree, was the Cutwrights’ instruments, and the hiss of the Bonfire, and, from the two hundred and fourteen, after each one, a small astonished noise: the sound of a person who has just discovered they can no longer close their eyes.

The Coverlet was carried barefoot to the Pillow and laid in the exact centre of the hollow, where the god’s head had been, by the Warden-Prime’s own hands. The fence was locked. The city went home and waited.

That winter, the Lid-Winter of 504, two thousand nine hundred people went to the room, more than in any year since the First Night to that date. The spares, newly lidless, could not be taught in time to live with it: they had no eye-wetters, because no one had thought to train any, and forty of them were blind by Carving, their eyes clouded white and cracked like glazed pots left in a kiln. Eleven of the rest climbed the Stair to claim their votes and were turned back at the first landing, because they had been made lidless and not born so, which the Watch decided was a different thing. Not one of the two hundred and fourteen was ever Counted. That, the Eye-lines said, proved the Giving had worked, for them.

In the spring of 504 the Pillow-wardens reported that the Coverlet had moved. When the fence was opened, the casket was found sunk an inch into the warm stone, as a stone sinks into a cushion, and its lid would not open, and when the Cutwrights forced it, the down was gone and the two hundred and fourteen packets were gone, and in their place, filling the casket edge to edge, was a single folded sheet of soft grey skin, faintly furred, warm, damp at the edges, with a long seam down its middle, closed. It was breathing. Slowly. Four times to the minute.

The Coverlet was carried out of the Pillow at night and has been kept since in a locked room under the Nodding Stair, in its casket, in the dark, which is the only dark on the Lid. The room’s door is barred from the outside. A Watcher of the Lid’s Eye rank holds the key, and every new Warden-Prime is taken down once, alone, to look. Ilvane Stroud went down in 612, at twenty-nine, on the night of her election, and stood with the lamp held up for the count of a hundred, and came up the stairs again, and was heard by her eye-wetters to say only one thing, which they remember because she said it twice, which she never does: It has got bigger.

From the Order of the Watch of Watches, the hundred and ninth day of the debate, Lack 502, as entered in the Stair-Book.

RESOLVED, that whereas the Lidded is said by the Tether Hall to desire the return of its shutting; and whereas the Houses of the Nine have each a portion of that shutting in the persons of their unpromoted children; it is ORDERED that every person of Eye-line blood, being of age and bearing lids, shall give the same to the city on the first day of Grace next, for the good of all and the end of the Count, and shall be honoured. House Seldom, being without lidded issue, is excused. It is FURTHER ORDERED that this resolution shall not be read aloud at the Bonfires, and that the word sacrifice shall not be used in connection with it, the proper term being the Giving. Carried, 141 to 130. The Warden-Prime abstaining, being lidless and therefore unable to look away from the question.

I gave my lids for the city and the city gave me nothing to close.
scratched on the wall of the Lid’s Eye landing by Ottoline Quell, a Giver, blind by Carving 503
GM Advice — What Is the Number?

The number is a state secret, and the book does not fix it. Choose one of these, or write your own. (1) The number is 60,001. The Dormitory was built to hold exactly one fewer, by a Matron who thought she could stop it with carpentry. (2) The number is the population of Ludmere on the Nine Nights, every man, woman and child who ate of Iss. The god is calling its table back. (3) The number has already been passed. Iselde Marrow lied, or was lied to. The eye began to open years ago, very slowly, and what the Hourkeeper is measuring is the lid going up. (4) There is no number. The Watch invented it in 401 to give the city something to fear that was not the truth, which is that the eye will open when it is ready. Whatever you choose, the Matron should believe it absolutely.

Rule, Law and Politics

The Vigil is governed by the Watch of Watches, a council of some three hundred Eye-line nobles who sit, or rather climb, in three shifts around the clock on the Nodding Stair. It has not adjourned in two hundred years. Its members are lidless by law, attended by eye-wetters, and watched by one another, since in the Vigil the oldest political truth is that anyone may blink. At its head is the Warden-Prime, always an Eye-line, always lidless, watched in turn by attendants who wet the royal eyes with a brush every half minute.

Beneath the Watch sit the Offices: the Apothecary-General (rouse), the Lamplighter-General (oil and light), the Hourkeeper (time and bells), the Matron (the Dormitory), the Registrar of the Seeming (the public record), and the Captaincy of the Wakers (everything else).

The Law of the Lid

The law is simple. Lying down is a crime. Closing your eyes for longer than a breath is a crime. Letting someone near you nod off is negligence, punishable as manslaughter if they go down. Selling sleep is a crime. Singing The Lamb and the Lid is a crime. Possession of down, feathers, wool batting or any soft stuffing in a quantity greater than will fill a shoe is a crime. Speaking of the room in a soothing manner is incitement.

The police, the Wakers, carry rattles and long needles, and they are entitled to needle any citizen who appears drowsy, without warrant and without apology. A citizen who objects to being needled is presumed to be drowsy.

A citizen who objects to being needled is presumed to be drowsy. A citizen who thanks you is presumed to be awake. Act accordingly.
Standing Order Nine of the Captaincy, framed in every station

Punishment is wakefulness. Minor offenders are sentenced to hours at the Rattlehouse, kept on their feet by Wakers with needles. Serious offenders are sentenced to the Lantern: an iron cage hung from a pole in a public square, open on every side, lit by its own lamp, in which the condemned is kept awake by any passing citizen with a pin, for as long as the sentence runs. Long sentences in the Lantern produce Seeming so violent that the condemned believe they are being eaten by the crowd, and sometimes the crowd believes it too.

Until 590 the capital sentence was Bedding. The condemned were led to the Dormitory in a white gown, given warm milk and poppy, laid in a bed and allowed to sleep, while a crowd outside sang the forbidden lullaby, the one day in the year it was permitted. It was considered the most merciful execution on the Table, and envied. It was suspended when the Matron reported that beds were scarce. Since then, the worst criminals have been held in the Rattlehouse awaiting a sentence that cannot be carried out, and the Rattlehouse is very full.

The Lower Floors

The Rattlehouse has nine storeys, and four of them are above ground. The upper floors are the ones the city knows: the standing-stalls, the chimes, the classrooms where recruits learn the Atlas on each other. The lower five belong to the Inquisitors of the Quick, and the law of the Lid has a name for what is done there that sounds like medicine. It is called custody of the quick, and it rests on a principle the Wakers have held since the second edition of the Atlas: that a person kept long enough awake will come to see whatever is put in front of them, and that what they see, if enough of them see it, is true.

The method is not secret. It is taught. A prisoner taken below is first stood in a stall with an iron collar at the throat, in a cell lined with polished tin so that the lamp, which never dims, comes at them from every side and their own face from every wall. They are given no rouse. The state keeps them awake instead: a Needle on each shift, with the Atlas open on a lectern, working through the points of the quick in the prescribed order, the nail, the web of the thumb, the soft of the arm, the hollow behind the ear, and back again, never deep enough to harm, never far enough apart to rest. Cold water from a rope-bucket at irregular intervals. A chime-box at the ear that strikes at a rhythm just slower than a heartbeat, then just faster. The Wakers call this holding, and they do it with real care, as nurses do, because a prisoner who goes to the room is a failure of the Waker on shift and is entered so in the shift-book.

By the third day the prisoner is in the Seeming. By the fifth, the Seeming is all there is. That is when the Inquisitor comes down. The Inquisitor does not ask questions; that is for amateurs on the upper floors. The Inquisitor tells. Gently, at length, in a reasonable voice, over and over, they describe to the prisoner what happened: the cellar, the hook, the names, the money, the face of the man who gave the order. They describe it until the prisoner sees it, in the tin walls, plain as a street. Then a Seemer from the Registrar’s office is brought down to take the prisoner’s statement of what they have seen, and two more prisoners in neighbouring cells, who have been told the same thing, give the same statement, unconnected, of good character, and the Registrar enters it in the public record as true. The confession is not a confession. It is news.

What is left of the prisoner afterward is returned to the upper floors to serve their sentence, and most of them serve it gratefully, and say thank you at every needle, and believe for the rest of their lives that they saw what they confessed to. Some of them are right. The Inquisitors consider that an encouraging proportion.

From the shift-book of the Fourth Floor Below, the Rattlehouse, Carving 641, Inquisitor Severin Ake presiding, Needle Tamsin Orr on the quick. Matter: the Tuckers’ cellar at Pinchbeck Steps. Prisoner: Wren Dusk-Bell, counter, twenty-six. Day the sixth. Entered by the shift-clerk, verbatim, as required.

AKE: Good morning, Wren.

PRISONER: Is it. Is it morning.

AKE: It is always morning here. Needle, the thumb, please. Thank you. What do you say, Wren?

PRISONER: Thank you. Thank you.

AKE: Good. Now. Yesterday you told me about the cellar. The pallet, the straw, the hook in the ceiling. You told me you counted sixty over the sleepers and then the hauler pulled.

PRISONER: Yes.

AKE: You told me the old man was there.

PRISONER: I didn’t. I said I never saw him. I never saw Nod. Nobody sees Nod.

AKE: You’re tired, Wren. You don’t remember. You told me he stood by the stair with a lamp, in his spectacles, and watched you count. Can you see the stair?

PRISONER: There’s a stair in the tin. There’s a stair in the tin, sir.

AKE: Who is standing on it?

PRISONER: I don’t. Someone. Someone’s on it.

AKE: He has a white beard. Half-moon spectacles. A lamp.

PRISONER: Please.

AKE: Needle, the arm. Thank you. Who is standing on the stair, Wren?

PRISONER: Thank you. Thank you. He has a lamp. He’s got a. His glasses are. Oh. Oh, he’s looking at me.

AKE: He’s been looking at you all along. He looked at you while you counted. He told you to count slow on the Waker’s boy, didn’t he. He told you to count to ninety.

PRISONER: I didn’t count slow. I never counted slow, I swear on my mother’s bed, eleven thousand and.

AKE: Your mother’s bed. Number?

PRISONER: Eleven thousand and six.

AKE: Your mother is at the end of the stair now, Wren. Look. Behind him. She’s very disappointed in you.

PRISONER: [no words; entered as weeping for the length of a pinch]

AKE: Tell her what he told you to do.

PRISONER: He told me to count to ninety. He told me to count slow. Mam, he told me. He’s standing right there.

AKE: Thank you, Wren. Clerk, the Seemer may come down. Needle, behind the ear, and then let her have water. She’s done very well.

[Marginal, in the Registrar’s office hand:] Corroborated by prisoners Dace and Hollin, Fourth Floor Below, cells 6 and 9, unconnected. ENTERED AS TRUE: that the man called Old Nod did, in Carving 641, order the slow counting of a Waker’s son at Pinchbeck Steps, who was lost. Warrant to issue.

The lowest floor of the Rattlehouse is not a floor of custody. It is a schoolroom. Sister Agathe Pinch teaches there, to every recruit in their first week, at the side of a man who has been held awake under the needle since 622, and who no longer screams, only hums; and the recruits stand in a ring with their own arms bared, and learn on themselves first, so that they will know. The Wakers who come up from that week are the gentlest people on the Lid with a needle in their hand. Everyone says so. They say it the way people say a scar has healed well.

Pain is love made practical. If you do not love them, it is only pain, and you are only a torturer. So love them. That is the whole of the Atlas.
Sister Agathe Pinch, to each year’s recruits, on the first morning below

Inquisitor Severin Ake, Fourth Floor Below (fifty, soft-spoken, lidded, with a cleric’s patience and a clerk’s handwriting; he has written more news into the public record than any Seemer alive, and he goes home every long watch to a wife he is quite sure is a Copy, and is very gentle with her) Threat 4 · Flesh 11 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (long needle 2, Waking) · Armor 0 · Dread 2

The Three Parties

The deepest political question is the Dormitory, and the Watch is split three ways over it.

The Builders want more beds. They are the oldest and largest party, the party of the Architect and the Matron’s office, and their position is that the number can be postponed by construction, because the Counted must be housed somewhere and every bed is a delay. Their critics observe that a bed does not change the number, and that building more beds is only building a bigger waiting room.

The Removalists want the Counted moved out of the country: carted down the Pilgrim Road, laid along the Rim, sold to Sallowreach or the Fatlands, buried, sunk, anything to get them off the Lid. Their theory is that the count is local. The Sleepers’ Mile, they point out, has been beyond the border for three centuries and the eye has not opened. Their opponents point out that nobody knows whether the Sleepers’ Mile is counted or not.

And one party, very quietly, wants the number reduced. They do not have a name in the public record. Among themselves they call themselves the Lessening, and their position is arithmetic: if the eye opens when the Counted reach a certain number, then the Counted must not reach it, and since the Counted cannot be woken, some of them must stop being Counted. The Lessening does not use the word murder. It uses the words reduction, thinning and relief. It has drawn up lists.

The Closed House

The Eye-lines say they keep their blood pure, by which they mean they keep their lids out of it. A lidless heir is married to a lidless cousin of a lidless house, and the spares, who were born with lids, are married down to the Slope merchants or not married at all. Cousin-marriage on the Height is so ordinary that the language has no word for the other kind; the Warden-Prime herself married her cousin. But there is a difference between a family that marries its cousins and a family that marries itself, and on Regard Street everyone knows where the difference lives. It lives behind the grey door of House Seldom.

The Seldom ate last on the Nine Nights, the inner seam of the lids, and since 0 A.G. no Seldom has married outside the house. The Cutwrights’ ledger on Regard Street, which records every Eye-line birth and every Eye-line Counted since 342, gives House Seldom a page that is drawn not as a tree, like every other house’s, but as a column: generation under generation, each with one marriage and one or two births, and the lines of each marriage drawn back up into the column itself, and never out. A Cutwright of the last century has written beside it, in the small dry hand of that college: No width. Cf. the breeding-books of the Fatlands for the effect in cattle. Not to be discussed. The page shows no Seldom Counted, ever. It also shows no Seldom spares, ever. Every child of the house in three hundred years has been born lidless, which is more than the Strouds can say; and every child of the house, the midwives of the Height whisper, has been born with its eyes already open and already looking at something, before the slap, before the first breath, before it has any right to know where to look.

The Seldom do not climb the Stair, though they have the right. They do not attend the Regard. They have one house, which has one door, and it is always shut, which on the Height is so improper that the Watch has fined them every season for two hundred years and they have paid every fine without comment. Their eye-wetters are hired from the Slope at four times the usual wage, serve a single year, and come out unwilling to describe the house, except to say that the family stand in the long upper room together, all of them, in rows, facing the same wall, and that the wall faces the Pillow, and that it is very quiet. One of them, in 626, said in a rouse-house that the Seldom do not need the brush as often as other lidless people, because they cry all the time, all of them, silently, and that the tears dry white on their cheeks, and that the old Seldom lick it off each other’s faces. She was found the next week standing at her window, and had lost the whole of her year in the house, and never spoke of it again.

The Seldom bury nobody. No Seldom has ever been burned on the Row, or boarded in the street. When a Seldom dies, the house buys a great deal of lamp-oil and the door stays shut, and a lamp-boy who once looked through the cellar grating on Regard Street said there were people standing down there in the dark, many, very still, in their good grey felt, with their eyes open; and that some of them were very old, and some of them were not old at all, and that the living ones were down there with them, holding their hands. The Watch does not inquire. The Seldom are the only house on the Height that has never produced a Counted, and as long as that is true, the Watch would rather not know how.

Lady Ysolde Seldom, Eldest of the Closed House (age unrecorded, appearance unrecorded; she has been seen once in living memory, at the Giving of Lids in 503, which would make her at least a hundred and fifty; the Warden-Prime has asked to be admitted to the house nine times in thirty years and been refused nine times, politely, on a card in a hand that has not changed) Threat 5 · Flesh 9 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (none) · Armor 0 · Dread 4

Marry a Seldom? You’d have to be one first.
Height joke, told once and never twice at the same party

Culture and Daily Life

No Beds

There is not a bed, couch or cushion in the city. Floors slope, a little, so that a person who lies on them slides. Chairs have one leg, and must be balanced on; a person who dozes on a one-legged chair falls off it. Walls are studded with iron knobs at shoulder height, so that no one can lean. Doorways have no frames to rest against. Tables are chest-high. The Vigil eats, works, talks and loves standing up, and its people have the thick calves, the bad backs and the swollen ankles to show for it.

Lean on me, love. No, not like that. Lean like you mean to stand up again.
a Ludmere grandmother, teaching a child to rest against her

Nudging

Everyone has a nudger. A nudger is the person whose job is to keep you awake: a spouse, a sibling, a friend, a hired child. Nudgers watch for the drooping lid, the slackened jaw, the long pause; they pinch, slap, shout, prick and shake. In a family, everyone nudges everyone, in a ring, so that no one is ever unwatched. A person without a nudger is called unwatched, and it is the loneliest word in the language.

A nudger’s contract, in the standard form sold at the Pinchmarket stationers’ for two crumbs, as filled in and sworn at the Ludmere Bonfire, Grace 641.

I, Ember Quarter-Bell, of Cinder Row, aged eleven, being awake, do engage to keep awake Master Florian Dace, glass-grinder, for the term of one season, at the rate of one lack and a half the day, rouse found. I will watch for the lid, the jaw and the long pause. I will pinch at the wrist, slap at the cheek, and shout at the ear, and I will use the pin at the thumb-web if these do not answer, and I will not stop at the armpit for squeamishness. I will not sit while he stands. I will not hum. I will count his blinks in the book in my best hand. If he goes down in my watch I will run for the Wakers and not stand weeping, and I understand that I will be fined, and that if I am found to have slept, I will be tried. If I blink, I will say so. I swear it on my mother’s bed, number forty-four thousand and nine, with my hand on the rail. Witnessed: Mag Startle, ring-mother. His mark: F.D. My mark: a pin, drawn.

Marriage is the promise to keep each other awake, and the vow is two words: Pinch me. Weddings are loud, bright, short, and held at the Bonfires. The couple pinch each other on the inside of the wrist until they bleed, and the guests throw bells. Love between spouses is tender and fierce and frightened, because every intimacy is a danger; what comes after love, in a body, is drowsiness, and the Vigil’s lovers keep a rattle by them and a lamp at full wick, and their tenderness is shot through with watchfulness. The little death is the big one here, the rouse-house joke goes, and nobody laughs.

Rouse

Rouse is a bitter black stimulant, ground and roasted from the dried caps of staremoss, a grey lichen that grows only on the cliff-faces of the Lid, mixed with Bitterhouse salts whose composition is a state secret. It is sold as pressed cakes, as powder, and as a thick black syrup, and it is taken hourly, chewed, sipped or packed against the gum. It tastes of burnt sugar, iron and bile. It makes the heart race, the hands shake and the pupils widen. Teeth go first: they blacken and loosen and drop out, and a Vigilant over forty with a full set is either rich, lidless or lying. Then the heart. The ordinary death of an ordinary Vigilant is a rouse-heart: a burst of thudding, a grey face, a hand to the chest, and the long-awaited lying down on the floor.

Chalked on a Rouse-Stall, the Pinchmarket, Carving 641

BITTERHOUSE BLACK, sealed cake, Crane’s strain — 1 L the cake (4 bells, it says). TABS, restamped this season, the eye is smaller, so are we — 3 c. SYRUP by the spoon — 1 c, bring your own spoon. SLOPE GREY (chalk-cut, honest) — 1 c the twist. SEA-CUT, Rook’s — 2 c, holds longest, don’t ask. RAW MOSS off the Hangwell cliffs — 5 c the chew, for heroes. NO CREDIT. NO SITTING. NO HUMMING. IF YOU BLINK AT MY STALL YOU BUY.

The dose has risen every decade since 390. A modest citizen spends two lacks a day on rouse. On the Slope it is cut to stretch it, and the cuts are worse than the drug.

Pain as Courtesy

A slap is a favour. Guests are offered a pin on arrival, as other lands offer bread and salt, and to refuse it is an insult. Clothes are made of burr-cloth, a coarse wool woven with dried thistle-heads; the rich wear galled silk, laced with fine wire that pricks at every movement. Shoes are cobbled with a pebble in the heel. Collars are set with pins. A Vigilant’s skin is a map of small courtesies: the scabs on the wrists, the bruises on the upper arm, the neat rows of needle-scars along the forearm. To bear them is respectability. To have unmarked skin is suspicious.

He offered me the pin and I took it and I pricked my thumb and I said thank you, and he looked at me as if I’d kissed him.
a Rim Road factor, on his first night in a Height house

Food

A full belly is a bed. Meals in the Vigil are small, frequent, cold and sour: pickled roots, hard bread, salt meat out of Fatlands barrels, vinegar, sorrel, smoked cliff-goat. Warm milk is illegal. Sugar is rationed. Soup is served lukewarm, by law. Rich households eat from vessels with sharp rims. The grace is the common one, Lack keep away, said with the eyes open, and followed in the Vigil by a slap on the table.

Lawful Soup, as given in the Watch’s Household Ordinances for the Table, 344, chapter the third, still read aloud to brides.

Take sorrel, two handfuls, and a root of bitter kale, and a cup of vinegar, and a bone of cliff-goat if you have one and a stone if you have not. Boil in a pot without a lid, stirring, standing, for the length of the Waking Hymn twice. Take it off the fire and set it on the sill and count to three hundred. Test it with the inside of the wrist: it must be no warmer than the wrist. If it is warmer, count again. Season with salt and the juice of a sour apple, and serve in a bowl with a broken rim, so that the lip is pricked at every sip. Eat standing. Do not finish it. A family that finishes its soup has eaten its watch. Leave a mouthful in each bowl and pour it on the step for the ones who have gone to the room, who are not hungry, and who will not mind.

The Seeming

After enough waking, everyone hallucinates. A Vigilant hears voices in the hiss of the lamps, sees insects walking across the plaster, watches faces rise up in the patterns of the cobbles, sees a dead mother at the end of a lane. These private visions are a nuisance and are ignored. But sometimes a whole street sees the same thing. A woman made of moths walking down Gutter Lane. A rain of teeth over the Pinchmarket. A door in the side of the Nodding Stair that was not there before. When that happens, the Vigil has made it a civic sense. Witnesses report it to the Registrar of the Seeming, the Seemers record it, and when enough unconnected people have seen the same thing, it is entered in the public record as news, read aloud at the Bonfires, and printed in the bell-sheets. A Seeming entered in the record is, for legal purposes, true. Contracts have been voided because of it. Houses have been condemned because the street agreed they were on fire.

The power to enter a Seeming, or refuse it, is the power to decide what happened. The Watch knows this very well.

From the Public Record of the Seeming, as read at the Ludmere Bonfire, fourth watch, the second day of Carving, 641.

ENTERED: In the lanes of the Slope between Thimble and Lanternside, thirty-one persons unconnected and of good character, between the ninth and tenth bells, did see a tall figure in a grey coat, stooping, which passed down the lane laying out upon the cobbles a long table, with cloth and plates and cups, and with chairs drawn back. The table was nine hundred paces long. At every place was a bowl of something steaming. The figure did not speak. At the tenth bell it was gone and the cobbles were clean. Several witnesses report the smell of new bread. Similar matter entered this month in ten other districts. ENTERED AS TRUE.

NOT ENTERED: In Thimble Lane at the eleventh bell, nine persons report that the figure returned, and that one of the chairs had been sat in. Insufficient witnesses. The Registrar reminds the public that a Seeming not entered did not occur.

How a Seeming Is Entered

The Registrar’s office keeps forty Seemers, and each walks a circuit of the districts with a slate, a pouch of chalk and a book of printed forms. A Seeming is reported at any Waker station or Bonfire-post, and a Seemer goes. The test for entry has not changed since 629: at least seven witnesses, unconnected (not of one household, one workshop or one nudging-ring), of good character (no Lantern sentence, no record of the Bedded), and awake (each must show a blink-book with no entry in the bell of the sighting). Their statements are taken separately, in the Seemer’s own words read back to them, and are matched on nine points: what, where, when, how tall, what colour, what sound, what smell, what it did, and how it left. Six matching points make a Seeming probable. Eight make it entered. When a Seeming is entered it is read aloud at the Bonfires at the next first bell, printed in the bell-sheets, and filed in the Public Record, and from that moment, for every purpose of law, it happened.

The Record is a weapon and everyone knows it. A landlord who wants a tenant out has only to arrange for seven decent neighbours to see the house burn. A Ward Sergeant who wants a crowd dispersed can have a riot entered after the fact. And the Registrar holds the other blade: the struck book, in which Seemings that failed the test are recorded with the reason, so that a citizen who insists on what they saw can be shown, kindly, in the Registrar’s own gloved hand, that it did not occur. A citizen shown the struck book three times for the same Seeming is noted as persistent and referred to a Ward Sergeant for a night’s needling, for the sake of their health.

A Seeming not entered did not occur. A Seeming entered did. If you saw something else, you were not looking properly, and I will be glad to show you.
Registrar Constance Hobb, at the door of the Record Office, to a crying woman

Children

Infants born in the Vigil do not sleep. They come into the world wide-eyed and quiet, and for their first years they lie awake in their mothers’ arms staring at the lamps, never crying for rest, because they do not yet need it. Vigilants call them starers and consider them a mercy of the god. The weight comes later, at about four years old: the Coming-Heavy, when a child first yawns, first rubs its eyes, first asks, in a small cross voice, why it cannot lie down. That is when the Vigil loses its children. A child cannot be told what the room is. A child cannot be made to understand why the warm, the soft, the dim, the quiet are deadly. There is a wing of the Dormitory called the Small Rows, where the beds are short, and the mothers who visit them do not speak to each other.

Don’t look at a starer too long. They’re looking at something behind you, and one day it’ll look back.
Slope nursery wisdom

Children of the Slope who survive the Coming-Heavy are named for the bell they were born at, and many of them become nudgers by six: Pip Eleven-Bell, Rook Quarter-Bell. It is cheap work and they are good at it, sharp-eyed and quick-fingered. They do not last long on rouse.

Who’s Asleep?, a counting game of the Slope’s children, played in a ring in any lane, as noted by a Waker-Sergeant who said he could not stop hearing it.

The children stand in a ring, holding hands, and one stands in the middle with her eyes shut, which is the only time a Vigil child may shut its eyes without being slapped, and everyone knows it is for a count of ten and no more. The ring goes round and chants:

Who’s asleep and who’s awake?

Who’s the copy, who’s the fake?

Lid goes down and lid goes up,

who’s been drinking from my cup?

One, two, the pin goes through,

three, four, there’s someone at the door,

five, six, the beds are fixed,

seven, eight, we’re very late,

nine, ten, open them again!

At ten the one in the middle opens her eyes and points, and the one she points at must lie down in the lane, flat, arms crossed, while the others count to ten again over them and then pull them up by both hands, screaming. Then they are in the middle. The Watch has banned it four times. The children say it is practice.

Death

People still die in the Vigil, of rouse-heart, fever, accident and violence. A corpse is the only thing in the city allowed to lie down, and the body is laid out flat on a board in the street for a day so that the neighbours may come and look at it, and touch its closed eyes, and envy it. The mourners are allowed to sit, for one hour, on the kerb. Then the body is carried to Lampwrights’ Row and burned in the furnaces, and its light goes out into the lamps. The rich pay to have a particular lamp lit from their ashes. The poor go to the general flame.

A Boarding Licence of the Vigil, issued by the Ward Sergeant, without which no body may lie down in the street; pinned to the board at the corpse’s feet.

BOARDING LICENCE. Ward of Lanternside. The bearer, being DEAD, and certified so by Needle Prosper of this station, who has needled all points without answer and has held a glass to the lips for the count of a hundred, is LICENSED TO LIE DOWN in the public way for one day, from bell to bell, upon a board, with the eyes closed. Name: Brask, Abelard. Age: 66. Cause: rouse-heart. The neighbours may touch the eyes. Mourners may sit, one hour, upon the kerb, and must stand at the bell. The body is to be carried to the Row at the next first bell; lamp requested: none, the general flame. NOT TO BE COVERED WITH ANY SOFT THING. NOT TO BE SUNG OVER. Anyone found lying beside the bearer will be needled and fined.

Festivals and Days

The Night of Lying Down, on the anniversary of the First Night, is the city’s great mourning: every family that has a sleeper in the Dormitory goes to stand at the foot of the bed for an hour, and the Dormitory’s doors are open from bell to bell. The Shouting Day remembers the Grey Ninth. The Pinching Fair, at midsummer, is a riot of bells, needle-dances and wake-games. And on Tablenight, the longest night of Lack, the city puts out every lamp for one minute, to prove it still can. People stand in the dark in the streets holding hands and counting aloud together, all of them, so that no one can drift off unnoticed, sixty seconds, the only darkness they will ever see. Every year a few hands go slack in the dark. Every year, when the lamps come back, someone is still counting into silence.

The Reminding

The Vigil’s holy calendar, as the bell-sheets print it, includes a small day in early Lack called the Day of Nine Nights, on which the old Ludmere families of the Height go in procession to the fence of the Pillow, barefoot, in felt, in silence, and stand there for a bell, and then go home. Nobody else is permitted to watch. The Watch does not explain it. What the bell-sheets do not print is what the procession carries, and what it leaves behind.

By the Compact of 343, sworn between the nine households and the first Matron of the Dormitory on the night the first Matron took the number, the Dormitory releases each year, on the eve of the Day, one Counted sleeper of Eye-line blood. The houses give in rota. The sleeper is chosen by the house whose turn it is, from among its own Counted, and is carried out of the Dormitory by the Visitors’ Gate in a felt litter, between the twenty-third and twenty-fourth bells, when Bedside is at its quietest. The register records the bed as transferred. The family pays the Bed-Due for that season and no other.

At the Pillow fence, inside the lamps but never in the hollow itself, the sleeper is laid on a board of pale wood, on its back, with its hands crossed. The households stand round in a ring, barefoot on the warm stone. The eldest of the giving house takes up a knife whose blade is wrapped in felt to the point, the very pattern of the Nine Nights, and the families hum, low, through closed lips, the only sound the old Ludmere houses ever make on that night: the first three notes of The Lamb and the Lid, over and over, the song that is a capital matter in any mouth below the Height. And the eldest carves.

It is done slowly, as the god was done. It is the eldest’s own blood under the knife, a grandmother, a brother, a son who went to the room at nineteen and has lain smooth-faced for forty years while his father grew old; and the sleeper does not wake, because the Counted never wake, and does not bleed so much as seep, a thin warm fluid that smells of breath on a pillow, and goes on smiling under the felt-wrapped blade until the breathing stops. Then the lids are taken, carefully, both pairs, and laid on a square of white felt, and each head of each house takes a portion, and eats it, in silence, as their ancestors ate on the ninth night. The Eye-lines call the whole rite the Reminding. Its purpose, as the Compact puts it, is to remind the Lidded that it was eaten, so that it will remember to stay small.

What remains is carried to the Row before first bell and goes into the general flame, unboarded, unlit, unnamed. The Matron enters the bed as empty at the next count. By the next count it is never empty: within the bell, somewhere in the city, someone blinks and does not come back, and is carried in on the carts, and laid in a bed, and the number is exactly what it was. Matron Cecily Dorm has watched this happen every year since 622 and has never told the nine households, because the Compact does not require her to tell them anything, and because she is not certain she wants them to stop. The Eye-lines do not know that the Reminding has never reduced the count by one. They believe it is the only reason the eye is still shut.

The rota does not visit every house. A house with no Counted of its blood is passed over. House Seldom has been passed over every year since 343. House Larch was passed over every year until 612, when Ilse Larch, elder sister of the Deputy-Watcher Sabine Larch, went to the room at twenty-one and was laid in bed 3,315; since then the rota has been coming round, house by house, and in the Matron’s private calendar, in her small square hand, the house whose turn falls in Lack 641 is Larch.

We did it to it. We do it again so it remembers. We do it to our own so it knows we mean it.
Lord Evander Quell of the Second Table, explaining the Reminding to a foreign guest who had not asked, and who left the Lid the next morning
GM Advice — Using the Reminding

The Reminding is a ritual killing, a kin-slaying and an act of cannibalism, performed with complete piety by the most respected people in the city, and it accomplishes nothing at all. Do not show it to the players lightly. It is best discovered: a felt litter seen crossing Bedside at the twenty-third bell; a bed marked transferred in a register the party has stolen; Sabine Larch asking the party, with no expression whatsoever, whether they know what the eldest of a house is required to do on the eve of the Day of Nine Nights. A character who witnesses the Reminding makes a Dread 3 check, Dread 4 if they know the sleeper. A character who eats the portion gains 1 Regrowth and, if a Vigilant, a single blink in which they stand in the long room close enough to the eye to see that the lid is, very slightly, thinner than it was.

Crime

Theft and violence are common and treated as ordinary. The great crimes are the crimes of rest. Selling sleep; harbouring a sleeper; failing to report one; lying down; singing the song; and the newest, which the law has not yet decided what to call: the blink-murder, the killing done by someone who was not there.

A notice posted at every Waker station and Bonfire-post in the Vigil, Carving 641, printed by the Rattlehouse press in red.

WANTED, FOR SELLING SLEEP, FOR HARBOURING SLEEPERS, FOR THE SLOW COUNT: the man called OLD NOD, so-called KING OF THE TUCKERS. About seventy. Small. White beard, soft. Half-moon spectacles. Black teeth. Courteous. Smells of warm straw. ENTERED AS TRUE upon the Public Record, the 9th of Carving, that he did order the slow counting of a Waker’s son at Pinchbeck Steps, who was lost. A REWARD of two hundred lacks, or a season’s rouse at the Bitterhouse stamp, for information leading to his CELLAR. Citizens are reminded that a Tucker’s minute is not rest but theft from the Count. Citizens who have bought such a minute and come forward this month will be needled and forgiven. AWAKE.

Beneath it, on the Lanternside copy, in charcoal, in a child’s hand: he give my nan her minute and she come back and she was so happy she cried for a week.

Proverbs and Oaths

  • Pinch me. (I love you; I trust you; I am afraid.)
  • A full belly is a bed.
  • Never trust a rested face.
  • The eye is patient. Be rude.
  • Count your nudger’s blinks.
  • Sleep is a door that only opens inward.
  • He’s on the Row. (He is dead.)
  • She went to the room. (She fell asleep; she is gone.)
  • Rest is for the Row.
  • A soft word is a pillow. (Said of flatterers, preachers and the Bedded.)
  • She’s at the window. (She is lost in time; she is not herself.)
  • Ask him the Asking. (Do you think he is a Copy?)
  • Two breaths is a long time. (Said of anyone who has blinked, and of murderers.)
  • Keep your hands in the box. (Do not trust yourself tonight.)
  • The count keeps itself. (Bedside: nothing you do will help.)
  • Stand for one, and one, and two. (Solidarity; from the Waking Hymn.)

The Vigil swears on its sleepers. By my mother’s bed is a common oath, and the bed’s number is spoken after it. The heaviest oath in the city is sworn at the foot of Bed One with a hand on the rail: by the first of us, who lay down for all of us. A Vigilant who breaks an oath sworn on a sleeper’s bed is held to have broken faith with the Counted, and no nudger will watch them again.

A note found pinned to the coat of Annick Rell, laundress, of the Slope, discovered lying in the open yard behind Gallow Street, the eighth day of Plenty, 640, and carried to bed 58,921. Entered in the Lain Book.

Teodor. I am sorry about the coat. I am sorry it is the good one. I have been awake for thirty-one years and I am so tired that I cannot remember your face when you are out of the room, I have to go and look. I cannot taste anything. I hear my mother in the lamps. The baby has been in the Small Rows for six years and I visit and she is still four and I am forty and I will be fifty and she will still be four. They say the room is warm. They say it does not hurt. I am not leaving you, I am going to her. Do not let them say I slipped. I did not slip. I chose it. Please come and stand at the foot of the bed sometimes, and talk, because they say we can hear. Do not lie down after me. Promise. Pinch the children for me. A.

The Lain-Down

Every year, hundreds of Vigilants lie down on purpose. The law calls it voluntary rest, prosecutes the nudger for negligence, and fines the family. The city calls it going to the room and does not talk about it. Those left behind carry it for the rest of their lives: they go to the Dormitory and stand at the foot of the bed, and the person they loved is there, warm, breathing, unchanged, smiling, unreachable, and will be there unchanged long after they themselves have grown old and gone onto the Row. There is no grave to leave, no body to bury, no end to the grief, only a bed with a number and a face that is still, horribly, at peace. GMs should play the Lain-Down as tragedy and as pressure, never as a solution: a contact who has started talking about how warm it must be; a nudger who has stopped pinching quite so hard; a widow who visits the same bed every day and has begun to bring a stool. The god’s pull is gentle, reasonable and kind. That is the horror of it.

They ask me what I’d say to her if she woke up. Nothing. I’d lie down next to her and shut my eyes. That’s what I’d say.
Teodor Rell, Keeper of the Lain Book, asked the question once too often

The Gallow Street Lying-Down

In the month of Plenty, 640, in one street of the Slope, twenty-three people lay down.

Gallow Street is a short steep lane of laundries, below Lanternside, where the washerwomen of the Slope boil the Height’s linen in open coppers and hang it on lines across the lane, so that the street is roofed with wet white sheets, warm from the coppers, moving slowly in the steam. It was always a dangerous street. The Ward Sergeant had tried for years to have the lines taken down. The laundresses had refused, because sheets must dry, and because, they said, they had been hanging them there since before the First Night, and the street was used to it.

Annick Rell was the first, on the eighth day of the month. Her note is copied above, and it is the note most often read aloud at dark-meetings of the Bedded, which her widower knows and cannot prevent. She lay down in the open yard behind her own copper, under the sheets, in her good coat, and was found smiling, and was carried to bed 58,921. That was all, for nine days. Gallow Street boarded nobody; there was no one to board. The neighbours came to Teodor’s door and stood in it and did not know what to say.

On the seventeenth day Irmgard Sallow, sixty, who had nudged Annick as a girl, lay down in the same yard at the same bell. On the nineteenth, two sisters from the top of the lane, together, holding hands. On the twentieth, a Waker of the Lanternside station who had been walking the street every watch since the eighth, pinching anyone who stopped under the lines, and who had been seen standing very still under Annick’s copper with his face turned up to the wet sheets and his eyes closed, as though it were raining. After that the Ward Sergeant posted four Needles on the street, day and night. On the twenty-second day one of them lay down.

The notes they left were all, more or less, the same note. I am not slipping. I am choosing. I am going to her. They say it is warm. Do not let them say I fell. Come and stand at the bed and talk to me, because they say we can hear. Do not lie down after me. Promise. Several of them used Annick’s exact words, which none of them could have read, because her note had been taken to the Dormitory with her and copied into the Lain Book, and Teodor Rell had shown it to no one. Several more ended with a line that was not in Annick’s note at all, and which the Watch suppressed: there is room at the table.

The Watch did what it does. It fined the nudger of every one of the twenty-three, including two children. It had the sheet-lines cut down, in the end, by Wakers with poles, and the wet linen of the Height came down into the mud of the lane in great soft heaps, and the women of Gallow Street stood in their doorways and watched their livelihood trodden into the gutter and did not say a word, because every one of them, looking at the heaps, wanted to lie down in them. The Watch moved the laundries to a dry yard in Blackmouth, where the sheets are now hung on iron racks in a wind-tunnel and come back to the Height smelling of burnt sugar. It made the singing of The Lamb and the Lid in Gallow Street a hanging matter, which it had not been anywhere before. And it entered no Seeming, because nobody saw anything. There was nothing to see. There were only twenty-three people who were too tired, in one warm wet street, in a bad month, and one of them had gone first.

The street is still there. Half its houses are empty. The ones who stayed have painted their doors black, which on the Slope means there is someone of ours in the Dormitory, and every door on Gallow Street is black. The neighbourhood calls it the Lain Lane, and people walk around it, the long way, by Thimble, and do not let their children run down it. On the eighth day of every month the families who are left go to Bedside together at their visiting bells and stand in a row at the foot of twenty-three beds in Hall Fifty-Eight, which the Matron, for reasons she has not explained, has had moved together into a single row. They talk to them. They tell them about the street. They do not say what everyone in the row is thinking, which is that the twenty-three sleepers, side by side, are turned very slightly toward one another, and that every one of them is smiling, and that it looks, from the foot of the row, like a family at a long table.

Ward Sergeant Ilse Marrable, Lanternside station, to the Captaincy of the Wakers; report on the matter of Gallow Street, the last day of Plenty, 640.

Captain. You asked for the names and I have sent them. You asked for the cause and I have none. I can tell you that the street was clean, that the rouse was the Bitterhouse stamp and not the Slope cut, that every one of them had a nudger and every nudger was awake. I can tell you that I walked the street myself every watch for the last nine days, and that I did not sit, and I did not hum, and I did stop under the sheets once, for a breath, and I felt it: not sleep, sir, but the wish to be the kind of person who could. I think it went down that street like a cough. I think it is still in the street. I think it is in me. I ask to be relieved of this ward, and to be given a nudger, a hard one, and I ask, if I am found under a sheet, that you not fine the nudger, because it will not be their fault. Awake. I. M.

GM Advice — Lying-Down Clusters

A cluster is the god’s influence made visible through grief. It is not a plot to solve or a villain to catch, and it must never be played as spectacle, a puzzle or a release: there is no method here to describe and no ending that is clean. Play the people left behind: the nudger fined for a death she could not have stopped; the Waker who cannot stop walking the street; the widower reading the same note over and over; the neighbour who says, too casually, it must be so warm. When the party spends time in a street where a cluster is happening, ask the players of Vigilant characters for a Caul + Resolve roll (Hard) once per scene, and let a failure add 1 Weariness and the Want to lie down, triggered by the street itself, until they leave it. Any character who reads a Lain-Down note aloud makes a Dread 2 check. The way out of a cluster is the same as the way out of grief on the Table, which is to say there is no way out, only company: another person standing next to you at the foot of the bed, pinching your wrist, and staying.

Closing the Ring

Not everyone who goes grey can be sent to the ward under the Nodding Stair. The ward-fee is forty lacks a season. The Slope does not have forty lacks a season. And a person at the Brink in a Slope house is a danger to everyone in it, every hour: the children begin to yawn when grandmother speaks, the husband finds himself sitting down beside her, the baby stops crying, and the whole household sways toward her gently, like flowers toward a lamp. She cannot help it. She does not want it. She is, very often, the one who asks.

The Slope’s answer is older than the Waking Laws and is called closing the ring. When a household decides, the family gathers on a cold, bright, windy day, never a grey one, and sends the children to a neighbour’s ring. The one who is going grey is dressed in her good coat. She is given a whole cake of the best rouse the family can buy, and eats it slowly, standing, while the family stand around her in their nudging-ring, holding hands, facing in, all of them pinching, all of them talking at once, loud, about anything, about the roof and the price of oil and the time she slapped the Waker; so that she is held, for the last time, in the noisiest and most watched place on the Lid. Then the eldest of the household who is not her does it, with whatever the family’s trade has put into their hand, quickly, and that is all the Slope will ever say of how. It is not spoken of. It is not sung.

Afterward the body is boarded in the lane like any other, and the neighbours come and touch the closed eyes, and this one time they do not envy. The Ward Sergeant comes and certifies a rouse-heart. Every Ward Sergeant on the Slope has certified dozens; the Lanternside register for 639 records forty-four rouse-hearts in women over sixty, in the same hand, all on clear windy days. The Sergeants know. It is the one mercy of the Slope that the Wakers protect. The one who closed the ring takes the dead one’s place in the household ring for the rest of their life, watched by whoever watched her, and is called by the Slope a ring-closer, quietly, with a respect close to fear. Ring-closers do not marry again. They are very good nudgers. They are, by the Lain Book’s count, the people on the Slope most likely to lie down.

She asked me to. She asked me every day for a month. I said no every day for a month. Then the baby stopped crying.
a ring-closer of Tallow Hollow, to Inspector Grimmer, who did not write it down

Factions

The Watch of Watches

The lidless government: sleepless, paranoid, and correct to be. Its members believe that the Vigil survives only because someone is always looking, and that the someone must be a person who cannot look away. They want to hold the city together until the number can be outwitted, and they are prepared to do anything that does not require them to admit how close it is. A PC joins as an aide, eye-wetter or clerk of the Stair; only the lidless may hold a vote. Enemies: the Bedded, the Tuckers, anyone who says the number aloud. Allies: the Wakers, the Rim Road Company, the Second Table, which several Watchers secretly belong to.

Climb, climb, and say aye while you can. A motion is carried by whoever still has breath.
the Stair-clerks’ rhyme, chanted under the breath on the second turn
RankTitleGrants
1Stair-ClerkAccess to the Nodding Stair; a sworn nudger at state expense.
2Eye-WetterAttendance on a Watcher; hears everything said on the Stair.
3Watcher of the Third ShiftA vote (lidless only); may commandeer Wakers for a watch.
4Watcher of the Lid’s EyeA seat on the inner committees; sight of the true rouse and oil figures.
5Warden-PrimeThe city. Only one, ever.

The Wakers

The police. Their job is to hurt people for their own good, and after three centuries they are very skilled. Every Waker is trained at the Rattlehouse in the Atlas of the Quick, a manual of the body’s points of pain, and in the use of the rattle and the long needle: a nine-inch steel spike, ground fine, driven into the places where pain is sharpest and harm least. They believe that pain is love made practical. They want to keep the count from rising, one drowsy citizen at a time. A PC joins by apprenticeship at the Rattlehouse and a year’s probation in the Slope. Enemies: the Tuckers, the Bedded, the Lessening (which they do not know exists). Allies: the Watch, the Lamplighters, every frightened household.

Ten thousand thank-yous and they give you a brass needle for your collar. Nobody ever gave me one for the ones who didn’t say it.
a retired Needle of Needlegate, in drink
RankTitleGrants
1RattleA rattle, a pin-roll and a patrol beat. Legal right to slap.
2NeedleThe long needle; may needle without warrant.
3Sergeant of the WardCommand of a station; may sentence to the Rattlehouse for a watch.
4Inquisitor of the QuickInterrogation rights; keys to the Rattlehouse’s lower floors.
5Captain of the WakersCommand of every Waker; answers only to the Watch.

From the Atlas of the Quick, schoolroom edition, Rattlehouse press, Lesson the Fourth.

The needle is not a weapon. Repeat this until you believe it, and then repeat it until the citizen believes it. You are not there to punish the sleeper but to fetch him. Go in under the nail of the great toe, where the quick is shallow and the harm is small; then the web of the thumb; then the soft of the armpit; then the hollow behind the ear. If these do not answer, the citizen is gone and you may stop. Do not stop before. Many a sleeper has been lost by a Waker who was squeamish at the armpit. The scream is the citizen thanking you. Learn to hear it so.

The Lamplighters' Guild

The keepers of the light. They trim the ten thousand public lamps, stoke the Bonfires, polish the roof-mirrors, and burn the dead on Lampwrights’ Row. Oil is the Vigil’s largest import, by Rim Road from Brinehollow whale-yards and Fatlands rendering-houses, and the Guild knows exactly how many days of it remain. They believe that darkness is death, and they are right. They want oil, at any price, from any source. The source has lately become a matter for the inner Guild alone, and the tallow vats behind the furnaces on the Row are bigger than they were. A PC joins as a wick-boy or mirror-climber. Enemies: anyone who hoards oil. Allies: the Wakers, the Renderers’ Union of the Fatlands, Lukas Marre, oddly, whose cell they keep brightest of all.

Every lamp on the Row is somebody. We just don’t say who any more.
a Wick of the Guild, First Rank, aged twelve
RankTitleGrants
1WickA pole, a lamp-round and free light at home.
2ClimberAccess to the roof-mirrors; knowledge of every rooftop route.
3Stoker of a BonfireA square of one’s own; the right to refuse light to a street.
4Burner of the RowCharge of the furnaces where the dead are burned, and of what is rendered there.
5Lamplighter-GeneralThe oil ledger, and the date on its last page.

The Tuckers

A criminal mercy. For a price, the Tuckers will guard you while you sleep for sixty seconds, then haul you back: they lay you on a straw pallet in a cellar, count to sixty, and drag you up by a hook-and-harness that they will not let customers examine. The method works more often than not. Their failures are delivered to the Dormitory steps before the next bell, washed and wrapped and labelled with a number from the Tuckers’ own register. They believe sleep is a human right; they also believe it is a month’s wages. A PC joins as a counter, the Tucker who keeps time over the sleeper. Enemies: the Wakers, the Watch. Allies: the Bedded, rouse dealers, a surprising number of Watchers who have taken their minute.

Sixty. Not fifty-nine, not sixty-one. Sixty is the count, and the count is the whole of the trade. A counter who loses count is a murderer and a counter who hurries is a thief.
the Tuckers’ first lesson, given in Old Nod’s name by every Cellar-Keep
RankTitleGrants
1DoormanKeeps the queue; a cut of the waiting fee.
2CounterCounts the sixty over sleepers; knows the method.
3HaulerWorks the hook; may sell a minute without asking.
4Cellar-KeepRuns a cellar of one’s own and its Waker bribes.
5King of the TuckersOld Nod’s chair, and his register of failures.

The Dream-Divers

State explorers who go to sleep on purpose, under a tether, and are dragged back by force. They believe the room can be understood and the eye negotiated with, and they want to map it to the wall. Most manage three dives before they fail to come back. Each dive leaves a diver less tethered to the waking world: they forget names, lose the taste of food, and start to speak of the room as home. A PC joins by volunteering, which the Hall accepts from anyone, because few volunteer twice. Enemies: the Bedded, who call them grave-robbers. Allies: the Watch, the Hourkeeper, the Dormitory.

First dive you come up screaming. Third dive you come up crying. Fortieth dive you come up and ask them, politely, why they bothered.
said of Senna Vole in the Tether Hall’s mess
RankTitleGrants
1HaulierA place on the winch rope; a share of the diver’s wage.
2Novice of One DiveHarness, tongue-ring and state pension to your family if you stay.
3Diver of ThreeA name on the Hall wall; first sight of the room-maps.
4Deep DiverLeads a dive-team; may dive without the Watch’s leave.
5Master of the TetherThe Hall itself, and the right to say who goes under.

The Bedded

Heretics who preach that sleep is a homecoming, that the eye is kind, and that the city is three hundred years late. They meet in Slope cellars and in the shadow of the Dormitory, in rooms with no lamps, and they hum. Their faith is the oldest consolation in the Vigil: that the people lost to the room are not lost, but at rest, and waiting. They want the Waking Laws repealed and the city allowed to go home. The most devout of them help others to lie down, and call it ministry; the law calls it murder. A PC joins by attending a dark-meeting and not reporting it. Enemies: the Wakers, the Watch, the Lessening. Allies: the Tuckers, the Lain-Down’s grieving families, the Second Table’s quieter members.

From a sermon of the Bedded, given in the dark in a cellar under Tallow Hollow, Grace 641, set down from memory by a Waker who attended and was afterward found at his window and relieved of his post.

Hush. No, do not pinch. Not here. Here you may let your hands be still. Here is the one room on the Lid where no one will slap you for closing your eyes, and I want you to feel how strange that is, and how sad it is that it is strange. They tell you that the room took your mother. Listen to me. Nothing took her. She was tired, and she went home, and she is standing in a warm place with her hands at her sides and nothing in the world is asking anything of her. Think of that. Think of nothing asking anything of you. They tell you the eye is waiting to open and eat us. The eye is not hungry. The eye has never been hungry. It is only waiting for us to stop being afraid, so that it can close properly at last, with all of us inside, and rest. Three hundred years we have kept it from resting. Three hundred years of pins. Who is the cruel one in that story? Hush. Hush. You do not have to answer. Just breathe with me. Slower. Slower. There.

RankTitleGrants
1ListenerAdmission to dark-meetings; the name of a safe cellar.
2HummerKnows the whole of The Lamb and the Lid.
3ShepherdKeeps a flock; may sit with those who wish to lie down.
4PillowHas slept in a blink and come back speaking well of it; preaches.
5Sister of the LidVesper Null’s circle; may speak for the room.

The Lessening

The faction that wants the number reduced. They are Eye-line Watchers, Dormitory clerks, a handful of Wakers and two Matron’s deputies, and their reasoning is arithmetic. The Counted cannot be woken; the number cannot be reached; therefore some of the Counted must be removed from the count, by pillow, by needle, by a drop of Bitterhouse salts in the drip, quietly, in the oldest rows first, where there are no visitors. They speak only of relief. They have drawn up lists, ordered by bed number, and a schedule that would reduce the Counted by eleven thousand in two years. They have not begun the schedule. They have begun the trials, and the trials have shown them something they cannot explain (see Matron Cecily Dorm), which they have decided to ignore. A PC is approached, never applies. Enemies: the Bedded, the families of the Counted, Inspector Grimmer, unknowingly. Allies: the Second Table, the Removalists, the parts of the Watch that do not wish to know.

A leaf from the Lessening’s working schedule, in Sabine Larch’s hand, found folded inside a Dormitory register by a copy-clerk who should not have opened it.

Schedule of Relief, first tranche. Hall Two, Rows 1 to 9, the oldest rows; unvisited, or visited less than once a year; Bed-Due in arrears or paid by the Watch. Beds 3,315 (see note); 3,316; 3,318; 3,322; 3,340 to 3,361. Method: as agreed, by the orderly of the night row, at the 23rd bell, the salts in the drip. Expected relief per night: four. Expected relief per tranche: one hundred and twelve. Expected effect on the Count: as calculated, a margin of nine months. Note on 3,315: visited once, in 612. The first of the list on grounds of age of row only. No other ground. S. L.

In the margin, in a different and much neater hand: The Matron says the count keeps itself. Proceed regardless. E. Q.

RankTitleGrants
1Reckoner of BedsCopies the registers; knows which rows are unvisited.
2Orderly of ReliefWorks the night rows; carries the salts.
3Sitting MemberA vote on the lists.
4Keeper of the ScheduleDecides which bed is next.
5First of the LesseningSabine Larch, and the arithmetic.
Cross-Border Powers in the Vigil

The Rim Road Company runs the Last Beds and the oil convoys, and holds the Watch’s debts. The Cutwrights’ College keeps a house on the Height whose ledgers show which Eye-line families have produced no Counted in three centuries, and which Slope families have produced the most. The Purgation has a cell in the Bitterhouse that believes Iss can be vomited back up by a rouse strong enough to keep the whole city awake for a year. The Second Table has three Watchers and a Lamplighter-General’s deputy, and a very simple plan for the morning the eye opens: knives, felt-wrapped, and a lullaby. The Reckoners have never sent a raid to the Vigil. The Vigil’s nobles do not sleep, and that makes them hard to kill in their beds.

Beds, a lack the night. Looking, a crumb. Lying down, not for sale to natives. Dragging out, free of charge.
the board at the door of the Sleeping Sheds, Lampwick Halt

The Vigil Now

Everything is running out at once. Rouse is failing: the dose that held a generation ago now barely holds an hour, and the Apothecary-General knows the year when the dose that keeps a person awake will be the dose that stops their heart. The Dormitory has fewer than two thousand empty beds. The Lamplighter-General has ninety days of oil. The hours themselves seem to be lengthening; the Hourkeeper’s pendulum swings a hair slower every week, and the city’s watches feel longer than they did, and nobody can prove that they are not imagining it, because everybody is always imagining something.

The Warden-Prime has sent an envoy to Sallowreach with a proposal too terrible to put in writing: the dead do not sleep. The Lessening has drawn up its lists. The Seeming has shown eleven districts a tall figure laying a table in the street. Rouse cut with Brinehollow brine is sending the Slope’s addicts walking west in their sleepless trances, toward a sea four hundred miles away. Forty-one people have killed someone they loved in a sleep of two breaths, and the inspector on the case has started to notice what the victims had in common. And in Bed One, the first sleeper, who has not stirred in three hundred years, has begun to move her lips.

Adventure Hooks

  • The Fourth Pillow. The Matron hires the party, off the record, to sit the night rows of the Dormitory’s east wing, where three Counted have been found smothered in a month. The Matron suspects the Lessening. The Lessening suspects the Matron. The party, sitting in the breathing dark for a whole watch with the air rising and falling around them, must stay awake to catch a killer, and each time a sleeper dies, someone in the city blinks and does not come back.
  • The Brine Walkers. Rook Quarter-Bell’s customers are walking west in a shuffling column, eyes open, down the Pilgrim Road past the Sleepers’ Mile. A Waker sergeant with a brother among them hires the party to bring them back before they reach the Rim, where the Company’s porters have orders to stop them by any means. Somewhere on the road, the column stops, turns as one, and points.
  • The Deadwatch. The Watch sends the party north as escort to Envoy Castellan Dray, with a chest of platters, a dozen nudgers and orders to ensure the Regent of Sallowreach says yes. On the road the nudgers begin to blink. In Lastgate, Dray asks the party privately whether they would volunteer to be the first.
  • Forty-One. Inspector Grimmer needs outsiders. Every blink-murder victim, he has found, was a secret member of the Lessening. Somebody, or something, is defending the Counted. Grimmer wants to know what, and he wants the party to blink deliberately, under guard, to find out what it is like to be used.
  • What Aveline Says. The Matron’s notebook of Bed One’s lip-words has been stolen. The thief is selling pages in the Pinchmarket. The pages contain names, and the people named on them are going to the room, one a day, in order.
  • The Coverlet Breathes. The locked room under the Nodding Stair has been opened from the inside. The Warden-Prime sends for the party at the third bell, alone, and takes them down with a lamp. The casket is open. The folded grey skin inside it has unfolded, a little, along its seam, and is the size now of a bedsheet, and is warm. Stroud wants it moved somewhere it cannot be seen by anyone else, and she wants it done before the next Regard. The Seldom have sent a card offering to take it in.
  • The Larch Turn. Sabine Larch learns, from Evander Quell, that the Reminding of Lack 641 falls to House Larch, and that the Larch’s only Counted is her sister in bed 3,315: the first name on her own list. She hires the party to get Ilse out of the Dormitory before the eve of the Day of Nine Nights, by any means, and to hide her somewhere on the Lid where neither the Lessening nor the nine households can reach her. There is nowhere on the Lid like that. There is, perhaps, the back hall at the Last Beds.
  • Ring-Closer. A woman of Tallow Hollow begs the party to buy her mother a place in the ward under the Stair, because her mother has gone grey and the household has started to sway, and the family has set the day for the ring, and it is tomorrow, and it is forecast windy. The ward costs forty lacks. The ward, the party may discover, is full, and its attendants have not been relieved in a week.

Rumours in the Pinchmarket

d10Rumour
1The number is sixty thousand and one. The Matron counts to it every morning, and every morning stops at sixty thousand. (Possibly true.)
2Old Nod takes his own minute every Plate, in a cellar no one has found. (False. He has never slept.)
3If you blink in the Pillow, you can see the eye from the other side. (Unknown. Nobody who tried has been asked.)
4The Warden-Prime’s daughter has eyelids and sleeps a minute at a time behind locked doors. (True, in part.)
5The lamps on the Row are burning people. Smell them. (True. The Guild calls it economy.)
6The Sleepers’ Mile has been counted all along, and the Watch knows it. (Unknown. Very possibly true.)
7Sister Vesper sleeps every night and wakes every morning. (True. What wakes is the question.)
8Dr. Crane has a rouse that will keep you awake for ever. (False. He has one that will keep you awake until it kills you.)
9The tall man laying tables is the eye, come to call. (False, as far as anyone in the Vigil knows.)
10If you hum the first three notes of the Lamb song, every Counted in the Dormitory smiles. (True. The orderlies have tested it, once.)

The People of the Vigil

Warden-Prime Ilvane Stroud, the Unblinking

Ruler of the Vigil, fifty-eight years old, born lidless, and she has not shut her eyes once since birth. Her eyes are enormous, pale grey, red-rimmed and webbed with veins, and they never stop moving. Two attendants stand at her shoulders with sable brushes and warm rosewater, and every half minute one of them strokes the wet across her eyes, and she does not flinch; she has never been able to. She has seen everything that has happened in front of her since the hour she was born, and she can forget none of it. She remembers her mother’s face over the cradle, every execution she has signed, every lie told to her on the Stair, and the exact weight of each. She speaks softly and precisely, and she never asks a question twice. She wants the Vigil to survive her, by any means at all, including the dead. She fears her daughter. PCs meet her on the Lid’s Eye landing, where she will remember them, perfectly, forever.

Ilvane Stroud — Warden-Prime of the Vigil
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 5 · Tongue 4 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Eye-line) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 5
SkillsSearch 5, Reckoning 4, Resolve 4, Clause 3, Intimidate 3, Godsign 3, Endure 2, Blades 1
BodyFlesh 12 · Guard 13 · Armor 0 · Fray 7
Attackssilver hatpin +3 (1)
GiftsPerfect Recall (she remembers every word ever said in her sight; any lie told to her face she will catch on a Routine Eye + Search roll, eventually). Lidless (cannot be surprised by anything in her line of sight; cannot look away from a Dread). The Weight of Regard (Partake: a person she stares at must make a Caul + Resolve roll, Hard, or confess the thing they most want hidden from her).
WantsTo watch (she cannot leave a person unwatched who might betray her); to count (she counts the Watchers on the Stair every quarter hour, and has never stopped).
Dread2 (to hold her gaze for a full minute while she does not blink)
SecretShe knows the number. The Matron does not know she knows. Stroud read it in the dying face of the previous Matron, years ago, on her lips, and has never told anyone. She has also done the sum for the Deadwatch: if the Vigil is moved to Sallowreach and killed and Kept, the city’s sixty thousand Counted will be left behind, unwatched, on the Lid. She has decided that is acceptable.
She looked at me for a count of eleven. One more than the Regard. I have been waiting thirty years for her to mention it.
a Watcher of the third shift, on being held in the Warden-Prime’s regard

Lady Oriel Stroud

The Warden’s daughter, twenty-three, born with eyelids, which in the highest Eye-line is a deformity and an embarrassment of state. She has been kept hidden in a suite of bright rooms at the top of the Stair since birth, attended by deaf nudgers. She is small, soft-voiced, dark-haired, with ordinary hazel eyes that she keeps fixed open in company until they stream, because her mother cannot bear to see her blink. Alone in her rooms, she closes her eyes for whole seconds at a time, and nothing has ever felt so good. She wants to be allowed to be ordinary, and she wants her mother to look at her once without that face. She fears she will be married off to a lidless cousin and never close her eyes again. Her secret: when she closes them, she does not see darkness. She sees the long room, from the far end, through a great grey lid, and every sleeper in it turning their head to look at her.

Maud Sexton, the Hourkeeper

Mistress of the city’s clocks, sixty, stooped, with a jeweller’s loupe screwed into one eye socket and a pocket full of brass escapements that she fidgets with like rosary beads. She sets the time for every bell in the Vigil from the great pendulum in the Pendulum Hall. Over eleven years of measurements she has proved, by pendulum, sand, candle and the pulse of her own wrist, that each hour is a little longer than the last. Not by much: a breath per watch, now two. Something is stretching the night the Vigil will not admit it is having. Her report was suppressed. She has written it again, smaller, in the margins of the bell-schedules. She wants someone with authority to stand in the Pendulum Hall for an hour and feel it. Her secret: she has run the curve forward. On a night not long from now, the hour will stop ending.

Captain Brannoch Pyre of the Wakers

Captain of the city’s police, fifty-two, a big slope-shouldered man with a shaved head, needle-scarred forearms and a voice worn to gravel from three decades of shouting people awake. He has kept a hundred thousand citizens out of the Dormitory with rattle and needle, and he has not been thanked once. He believes absolutely in what he does. He also knows, better than any man alive, what it does to the people he does it to. His own nudger, his wife Merrit, died last year, and he has not replaced her. He walks his rounds unwatched, which is illegal, and none of his Wakers will report him.
