The Captain walks his rounds alone. We know. We walk behind him at a distance, two of us, every watch, and we don’t let him see.
a Needle of the Felt House

Old Nod, King of the Tuckers

He sells one minute of guarded sleep for a month’s wage, and people queue around the block. He is seventy, small, quick and courteous, with a soft white beard, half-moon spectacles and the black stumps of a lifetime of rouse, and he receives customers in a warm cellar off the Slope under a sign that says only Rest. He has never tried his own product. He says a man should not get high on his own supply. He keeps a register, in his own hand, of every customer the hook failed to bring back: one in eleven, these days, up from one in thirty. He wants a better hook. He fears the Bedded, who say his failures are the lucky ones. His secret: he was a Dream-Diver once, three dives, and he knows what sixty seconds in the room feels like from the inside. It feels like a lifetime. That is what he is really selling.

Tucker Hauler Threat 3 · Flesh 13 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (hook-and-harness 3, Hooking) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Rest. That’s all it says on the door. Rest. You’d think it’d say price.
a rope-twister, in the queue outside Old Nod’s cellar

Senna Vole, Dream-Diver

Forty descents, where three is the usual career. She is thirty-four and looks fifty: grey-haired, gaunt, her wrists and throat ridged with harness-scars, a silver ring through her tongue where the Hall’s hook goes. She speaks slowly and seldom, as if words came from a long way off. She has mapped the long room to within thirty paces of the eye: the soft floor, the warm air, the sleepers standing in their silent ranks, and the place near the wall where the floor begins to slope downward, toward the lid. On her last dive, something behind the lid said her name. She wants to go back. She tells the Hall she wants to finish the map.

WantsTo lie down (she must resist on a Grim roll whenever she passes the Tether Hall’s bed).
Dread3 (to hear her say what she heard)
SecretThe voice behind the lid did not sound like a god. It sounded like her own voice, asleep. She believes that the eye is not Iss’s at all but all of theirs: everyone who ever went to the room, dreaming one enormous dream with one eye, and that when it opens, it will be the Counted waking up together, as one thing. She has not told the Hall, because she thinks they would stop her diving.

Dr. Aldous Crane, Apothecary-General

Inventor of the current strain of rouse, sixty-one, thin as a heron, with the steady hands of a man who has never in his life taken his own product and the yellow fingertips of a man who handles it all day. He speaks to people as though reading them a dosage. He knows the dose curve and where it ends: there is a point at which the amount of rouse needed to stay awake is the amount that stops the heart, and it is eleven years off, for an average adult; three or four for the Slope, where the cut is worse; less than one for children. He wants a new compound, and has tested nine hundred in the Proving Rooms on prisoners lent by the Rattlehouse. His secret: the Watch has ordered one more compound, the nine hundred and first, finished and warehoused, for the day the beds are full. It is a rouse that does not wake you. It stops you, gently, standing up, and you do not go to the room. He calls it the Last Cake.

Eleven years for an adult. Four for the Slope. Less than one for a child. I give you these figures because you asked, and because nobody else will.
Dr. Aldous Crane, to the Watch, in a session struck from the Stair-Book

Matron Cecily Dorm

Keeper of the Dormitory, fifty, broad and soft-spoken, in a starched grey gown and felt slippers, with a heavy ring of bed-keys at her belt that she holds still with one hand as she walks so it will not jingle. She is the only living person who knows the number, and she walks the rows every day, counting, under her breath, from one. She has been seen removing a pillow and standing over a bed for a long time. She loves the Counted. She knows their faces as a mother knows her children’s. She hates them, sometimes, with a hatred she confesses to no one.

Cecily Dorm — Matron of the Dormitory

SecretShe has smothered four of the Counted, in the oldest rows, testing the Lessening’s arithmetic. Each time, within the bell, someone somewhere in the city blinked and did not come back, and was carried in, and the number was exactly what it had been. The count keeps itself. The Lessening’s schedule would not reduce the number by a single bed; it would only change who is in them. She has told the Lessening. They have decided not to believe her. She has started to wonder whether she was the one who decided who went down.

Garron Ashlock, Lamplighter-General

He keeps ten thousand lamps burning. He is forty-eight, red-faced, burn-scarred to the elbow, with no eyebrows and a cheerful bellow that he has cultivated to hide the fact that he cannot sleep, of course, and cannot rest either, ever, because he can count. He has ninety days of oil, a Brinehollow supplier who has doubled the price and a Fatlands one who has stopped answering, and a standing order from the Watch to tell no one. He wants a miracle and will settle for tallow. His secret: he has already found it. The furnaces on the Row do not burn the dead to ash any more. They render them. A quarter of the city’s lamps now burn on the people who used to read by them, and the Guild has begun to look, with a professional eye, at the Dormitory.

The lamps on the Row smell like Sunday dinner now. My ma says don’t think about it. So I don’t. So I don’t.
a lamp-boy of Lampwrights’ Row

Pip Eleven-Bell

A street nudger of nine, born at the eleventh bell on the Slope, paid by the hour to pinch strangers in the Pinchmarket. Pip is fast, sharp, thin as a pin, all elbows and grubby knuckles, with a voice like a gull and a laugh like a rattle, and the best pinch-fingers in the market. Pip has been unpaid for two weeks by a client who has gone to the room and has been taking rouse from the cheapest dealers to keep working. Children do not last on rouse, and Pip has begun to blink. Pip wants a proper client, a hot meal and a nudger of their own. Pip fears nothing out loud. Pip’s secret: in the blinks, there is a kind lady in the room, in a baker’s apron, who holds out her hand and says it is all right to stay. Pip has started to hold on longer each time.

Lukas Marre, the Yawning Man

His yawns are catching beyond all reason: one gape of his jaw and a room goes down, a street sways, and once, at nineteen, before he knew, a whole market square. He is thirty-one now and has lived twelve years in a cell in the Glass House, masked in a leather muzzle that holds his jaw half shut, alone, in the coldest corner of the city. He is gentle, bookish and painfully polite, and he apologises through the pane to everyone who visits, and to the guards, and to the Matron, whom he writes to every Plate asking after the people from the square. He wants to be forgiven. His secret: the muzzle does not stop it any more. Lately he only has to feel the yawn rising in himself, and the people on the far side of the glass sway.

Sister Vesper Null, Prophet of the Bedded

She preaches that the eye is kind, the room is home, and the Counted are the only citizens of the Vigil at peace. She is about forty, with smooth unlined skin, clear bright eyes and a calm low voice, and she looks more rested than anyone in the city, and nobody can explain it. Her sermons in the Slope cellars are given in the dark, in a murmur, and her listeners sway. She is not cruel. She holds the hands of the grieving and tells them their dead are waiting, and they weep with relief.

Vesper Null — Sister of the Lid, Prophet of the Bedded

What gets up in her body every morning is something the room sends back, a little less like Vesper each time: an emissary, practising. She is the first restless sleeper outside the Dormitory. Her body is the god’s rehearsal for walking.
She held my hand in the dark and told me my Davey was waiting, and I believed her, and I have never been so happy, and I hate her for it.
a Slope mother, of Sister Vesper Null

Corwin Half-Bell, the Man Who Woke

The only sleeper who ever came back without a tether, after half an hour under, twelve years ago, when a cart-horse kicked him in the ribs where he lay in the street. He is forty, gaunt and grey, and he has not blinked since: his lids have gone stiff and fixed half open from disuse. He flinches whenever a door opens. He will not describe the room. He works as a rope-walker at the Rattlehouse, where the noise comforts him. He wants never to be asked again. His secret, which he will tell only to someone who has been in the room themselves: he heard knocking. Far behind him, at the other end of the long room, at a door none of the sleepers face, someone was knocking, slow and patient and polite, the way a guest knocks. And the eye, he swears, was not sleeping. It was holding still, the way a mouse holds still. It was hiding.

Thaddeus Knell, Chief Bell-Ringer

The city’s bells sound every quarter hour to keep it awake, and they deafened him years ago. He is sixty-four, bull-necked, with forearms like hawsers and ears that ooze, and he rings from the great tower over Ludmere Square by the clock and by the shaking in his teeth. He speaks too loud and reads lips badly. He is the most rested-looking man on the Height, because he hears no lullaby, no rain, no hush; the silence inside him is total and it does not soothe him at all. He wants an apprentice who will not go deaf. His secret: lately the bells do not shake his teeth on the quarter. They shake them a little after, a little later each day, and he has begun ringing by his teeth instead of the Hourkeeper’s clock.

Mirela Sconce, the Seemer

She reads the Seeming for the public record. Forty, sharp-chinned, ink-stained, with a habit of narrating what she sees under her breath, she spends her watches walking the districts with a slate, taking statements, cross-matching witnesses. This month eleven districts, separately, hallucinated the same thing: a tall figure laying a table in the street. She has interviewed two hundred witnesses. Their descriptions match down to the stoop under the doorways and the warmth on the cobbles afterward. She wants to know what it is. She fears the Registrar, who has started striking her entries. Her secret: she saw it too, on Thimble Lane, and it looked up at her, and there was a card on the nearest plate, and her name was on it.

Jack Tenterhook, Wake-Valet

Keeper-awake to the rich, an artist of the precisely tolerable pain. He is forty-five, elegant, soft-handed, with a velvet roll of silver pins and a voice like warm oil. He arrives at a client’s house at the first bell and leaves at the last, and between them he keeps his client awake with an exquisite programme of pinches, pricks, ice and pressure, never too much, never too little. His clients swear by him and recommend him to their friends. He was a torturer before, for the Rattlehouse’s lower floors, and says the only difference is the tipping.

Jack Tenterhook — Wake-Valet to the Height

Two of those six have blink-murdered.

Inspector Hale Grimmer

He investigates blink-murders, killings done by ordinary people during a two-second sleep, with no memory after. He has forty-one cases. The method is the same in each: the victim laid flat on the floor, a folded cloth beneath the head, hands crossed on the chest, eyes closed under the killer’s thumbs, and the killer’s palms laid gently over mouth and nose until the breathing stops. Every killer comes back with no memory and the victim’s teeth in their palm. Grimmer is fifty, ragged, chain-chewing rouse, with a mind that goes on working long after his body has stopped wanting to. He wants to know who is doing it. He fears that he will be next, in one direction or the other. His secret is what he found last week: all forty-one victims were members of the Lessening, down to Tobin Coyle, the Slope rope-twister, who copied Dormitory registers for them at night for beer money. Something is defending the Counted.

Forty-one. Same hands, same pillow, same thumbs. Same thing in common, too, and I’ve only just seen it. Something is keeping house.
Inspector Hale Grimmer, to his own case-book

Odile Farthing

Her son, Marten, fell asleep at four, eleven years ago, in her arms, on a grey afternoon, while she was counting out loud to him. She visits bed 40,112 daily, and stands at its foot for an hour, and talks. She is thirty-eight, rouse-thin and quiet, with the scabbed wrists of a woman who has had no nudger but herself. The Counted do not age, but her boy has grown. He is the size of a man now, long and broad under the sheet, with a man’s hands and a man’s jaw and a beard coming in, and he is smiling. She wants him back. She fears what will come back. Her secret: when she leans close, he smells of bread, and his lips move along with hers when she counts.

Benedikt Lour, the Architect

He designed the modern city: the sloped floors, the one-legged chairs, the studded walls, the endless Stair. He is seventy, frail, bent, with the elegant scrawl of a man whose hands shake for everything but a pen, and he is proud of every discomfort he has ever invented. He is now drawing a Second Dormitory. He has been told to plan for the whole population. He has drafted it on the Pillow, the only open ground left, and the drawings show four hundred thousand beds, in rows, radiating outward from the hollow like the rays of an eye. He wants to finish before he dies. He fears that the Watch will not wait. His secret: the Second Dormitory has no doors that lock from the inside, and its ventilation is designed to carry warm air.

Rook Quarter-Bell

A rouse dealer on the Slope, twenty-two, lean, quick, wolfish, his teeth already gone, gums packed black with his own product. He cuts what he sells with bottled Brinehollow brine, bought by the cask from Dry Jonah’s agents, because it is cheap and it works. His customers stay awake longer than anyone else’s. They have also started bailing salt water every dawn and dusk, and walking west. There are two hundred of them now, in a slow eyes-open column. Rook wants to stop selling it and cannot, because nothing else holds. His secret: he has been taking it himself. He tastes salt every morning, and he has started standing at windows facing west.

Envoy Castellan Dray

The Warden’s ambassador to Sallowreach, fifty-five, a tall immaculate Eye-line courtier with a lidless stare and a chest of documents he never lets out of sight, travelling with twelve paid nudgers and a cask of Bitterhouse rouse. His commission is to buy the secret of Keeping, so that the Vigil’s citizens can be killed and kept upright: a city of the dead, who never need to sleep. He has been in Lastgate for two months, negotiating with the Regent. He wants to save his city. He fears that the price will be paid in its people. His secret: he has learned that the Kept cannot leave Sallowreach, and that the Vigil would have to move there, all of it, to die; and he has not yet told the Warden, because he thinks she will say yes.

I tell him about the weather. I tell him about the roof. Last week he told me something back. His lips did. I won’t tell you what.
Odile Farthing, at the foot of bed 40,112

Aveline Morne, the Sleeper in Bed One

A baker’s daughter, nineteen years old forever, who lay down on the First Night in 341 and was the first not to rise. She has lain unmoving for three hundred years under a white sheet in a bed with a brass rail, a plump fair girl with flour still in the creases of her knuckles, cheeks pink, lips slightly parted, breathing with the rows. Last month her lips began to shape words. The Matron has started writing them down. Most of them are names, one a day, and each person named has gone to the room the next day. One, last week, was a sentence: There is someone at the door who has not been fed. Set another place.

There is someone at the door who has not been fed. Set another place.
Bed One, as written down by the Matron, Carving 641

New Characters

Deputy-Watcher Sabine Larch, First of the Lessening

An Eye-line Watcher of the second shift, forty-four, lidless, soft-voiced, with a mathematician’s courtesy and the kind of face people forget while it is in front of them. She sits on the Matron’s oversight committee and has read every register in the Dormitory. Her lists are in her own hand.

Registrar Constance Hobb

Keeper of the Public Record of the Seeming, sixty, white-gloved, iron-haired. She decides which Seemings are entered and which are struck. A Seeming not entered, she says, did not occur. She has struck forty Seemings of the tall figure this year, and every report of blink-murders, and she has entered, on Watch instruction, three Seemings that nobody saw: a fire that justified condemning a Bedded cellar, a riot that justified the doubled needle-patrols, and the death of Corwin Half-Bell, who is still alive. When citizens come to her to insist on what they saw, she shows them the record, kindly, until they doubt it. She sleeps, she believes, not at all. Her secret: her own clerk tells her she has blinked eleven times today, and she has entered none of them.

Sister Agathe Pinch, Mistress of the Needle

Head instructor at the Rattlehouse and author of the current edition of the Atlas of the Quick, sixty-eight, tiny, bright-eyed and grandmotherly, with a cap of white lace and a lap-tray of needles laid out like embroidery tools. She has trained every Waker alive. She believes that pain is a teacher and that the city’s Wakers must learn it first on their own bodies, and every recruit spends their first week strapped in a standing-stall under her needles, so they will know. She is loved by her students the way a scar is loved. Her secret: on the Rattlehouse’s lowest floor she keeps a man who has been awake under the needle for nineteen years. She uses him to teach. He has stopped screaming. He hums.

Teodor Rell, Keeper of the Lain Book

A laundress’s widower, forty, from Gallow Street on the Slope, who found his wife’s note pinned to her good coat and has not been able to stop reading it. He took a clerk’s post at the Dormitory so that he could see her every day, and the Matron gave him the Lain Book: the register of those who went to the room by choice, with their notes copied out, two hundred to four hundred a year. He reads every note. He answers some of them aloud, at the foot of the bed. He is gentle, tired beyond tiredness, and very dangerous to himself. He has kept his promise not to lie down after her. His secret: he has begun writing a note of his own, a line a day, so that it will be ready.

Lord Evander Quell of the Second Table

An Eye-line Watcher of the first shift, fifty, handsome, lidless, beautifully mannered, and the Second Table’s senior hand in the Vigil. He believes the eye’s opening is the best news in six centuries: the god of sleep, whole again, in one place, awake and blinking and catchable. He has a set of felt-wrapped knives in a case on his wall, a choir of twelve trained in The Lamb and the Lid, and the Matron’s spare keys. He wants the number reached. Not exceeded, not prevented: reached, cleanly, on a date he can plan for. His secret: he has been feeding Sabine Larch’s lists to Jack Tenterhook’s clients, and he knows exactly what the blink-murders are, and he finds them encouraging.

Factor Joss Mallory of the Last Beds

The Rim Road Company’s innkeeper at the foot of the Pilgrim Road, fifty, big-bellied, foreign, comfortable, with the only soft voice and the only soft bed within thirty miles of the Vigil. Every Company caravan stops at his inn so its drivers can sleep before the climb, and every Vigilant coming down on business stops at his sleeping-hall doorway and looks at the beds. He keeps a book of the ones his porters could not stop. He sells passes across the border, maps of the Sleepers’ Mile, rouse, nudgers and gossip. He is the first friendly face most PCs see before the Lid, and the last one some see before the room. His secret: the Watch pays him a bounty for every Vigilant his porters drag back from the beds. The Lessening pays him a larger one for every Vigilant they don’t.

Playing a Vigilant

You will never rest. Not once, not for a breath, not until you are on the Row. Now go and do something with it.
— what Slope mothers say to a child on the morning of the Coming-Heavy

A Vigilant has been awake since the age of four. Every hour of every day of their life is still behind their eyes. They are sharp-sighted, suspicious, quick to see a lie and quicker to see a yawn, and they are carrying a weight that no one from any other land can imagine. They have a nudger, or they had one. They know someone in the Dormitory. They do not trust their own memory, and they are right not to.

Attribute bonus: +1 EYE.

You will never rest. You will never rest. Say it back to me. Good. Now you are one of us.
the words of the Coming-Heavy, as said in Needlegate

Questions for a Vigilant

Answer these when you make a Vigilant, and tell the table at least three of the answers. The GM will use the rest.

  • Who is your nudger? Name them. Do you love them? Do you trust them? Are they a Copy?
  • Whose bed do you visit? Give the number. Every Vigilant has one. When did you last go, and what did you tell them?
  • What is in your blink-book that you have not read? Your nudger wrote it. You have never asked.
  • Which bell were you born at, and what does your family say about children of that bell?
  • What is the worst thing you have done in a blink that you know about? What does the person you did it to think happened?
  • Have you ever lain down? For a breath, on purpose, in a Tucker’s cellar, under a sheet, in a doorway, on a grey afternoon? Who fetched you back, and do you thank them?
  • What do you see in the lamps? Every Vigilant has a private Seeming they have had since the Bright Years. Name it.

Weariness

Every character in the Vigil, native or foreign, tracks Weariness from 0 to 10. A foreigner who has slept well arrives at 0. A Vigilant has never slept and can never fall below 2: that is the floor, the silt of a lifetime.

Gaining Weariness. +1 for each watch (eight hours) spent without a dose of rouse. +1 for each scene of comfort: warmth, softness, a full meal, rain on a roof, quiet, a long dull wait, a lullaby, a sermon. Yawn days double all gains. A contagious yawn in earshot calls for a Caul + Resolve roll (Routine, or Hard from a Glass House yawner); failure adds +1. A Tooth that bites back (see below) adds +1.

Shedding Weariness. A dose of rouse removes 2 Weariness and prevents gains from the watch’s passing for that watch; a day’s rouse costs 2 lacks on the Height and half that, cut, on the Slope. A second dose in the same watch requires a Gut + Endure roll (Hard; Grim for a third); failure costs 2 Flesh, and a Lack is a rouse-heart: the character suffers Ruin. A pin, slap or pinch from a nudger removes 1 Weariness, once a scene. A Waker’s long needle removes 2 and costs 1 Flesh. Foreigners sleeping outside the Vigil’s borders clear Weariness to 0. Vigilants have nowhere to sleep.

WearinessStateEffect
0–2FreshAs fresh as anyone on the Lid.
3–4Heavy−1 on all Eye and Lung rolls.
5–6Drifting−2 on Eye and Lung rolls. The Seeming begins. Blink checks on triggers.
7–8Grey−2 on all rolls. Blink check every scene, and on triggers. Dread checks one step harder.
9Going UnderBlink check every few minutes of play.
10AsleepThe character falls asleep (see below).

Falling asleep. At Weariness 10 the character sleeps, and goes to the room. A nudger has one breath to fetch them: a Hand + Stitching or Tongue + Intimidate roll at Hard (a Waker’s needle succeeds automatically if it is already drawn). If that fails, the nudger may try once more, at Grim, in the next breath. After that the character is Counted. There is no further roll. Foreigners and Vigilants alike are carried to the Dormitory and given a number.

Blinks

A blink check is Caul + Resolve against a Difficulty set by Weariness: Routine at 5–6, Hard at 7–8, Grim at 9. Characters in the Appetite or beyond (Regrowth 4+) make blink checks on triggers even below Weariness 5, at Routine. Triggers are anything that would make a tired person drift: warmth, softness, silence, monotony, a yawn, lying down, a voice that murmurs, watching the Dormitory breathe.

On a failure the character blinks, and the GM rolls on the table below. Each blink also adds 1 Fray, for the lost time, whether or not the character learns what happened. On a Lack, the GM rolls twice and uses both results, and if the character sees what they did, they make a Dread check at the rating the GM judges right (usually 2 or 3).

d10The Blink
1–4A second gone. You lose the last thing said, and drop what you were holding.
5–6Moved. You are up to ten paces from where you stood, facing another way.
7You said something. The GM speaks one line in your voice, often a true thing you wanted kept.
8Your hands did something small: a lamp put out, a door unbarred, a word written.
9The room held you longer: d6 minutes, standing. You remember the warmth and nothing else.
10Tucked. The most vulnerable person near you is lying down, eyes closed, and your hands are on them. Roll d6: on 1–4 you came back in time.

What You Did in the Blink

When a blink lasts longer than a breath (a result of 9 on the table above, a Lack on a blink check, the Lost Seconds Gift, or any time the GM judges the room held the character longer), roll d20 instead of, or as well as, the d10. The character does not remember any of it. They find out the way the Vigil always finds out: from the evidence, from the faces of the people around them, and from their blink-book, in someone else’s handwriting. A character who learns what they did makes a Dread check at the rating the GM judges right; results marked † are always at least Dread 2.

d20What you did
1Wrote a name in lamp-black on the nearest surface. It is your own name, in a hand you do not know.
2Took off your shoes and set them side by side, toes to the door, the way the Lain-Down leave them. †
3Unbarred the nearest door or shutter and opened it a hand’s width. Warm air is coming in.
4Put out the nearest lamp with your fingers. The tips are blistered and smell of clean linen.
5Told the person nearest you, very gently, that they look tired. They have begun to yawn and cannot stop.
6Crossed your own hands on your chest. They are still crossed when you come back, and it is hard to uncross them.
7Hummed the first three notes of The Lamb and the Lid. Someone heard. Somebody is already running for a Waker.
8Gave something away (your purse, your rouse, your knife). The one who has it says you insisted, and you were so kind about it.
9Walked 2d6 × 10 paces toward the Dormitory or the Pillow, whichever is nearer, and you are standing facing it.
10Laid out a table on the nearest flat surface: cups, plates, whatever was to hand, one place for each person present, and one more. †
11Answered a question nobody asked, aloud. The GM tells another player privately what you said. It was true.
12Wrote a bed number in your own blink-book, in your own hand. You do not recognise it. It is occupied.
13Pinched the nearest person so hard you drew blood. They thanked you. They are looking at you strangely now.
14Pressed your face against something warm (a stove, a wall, a horse’s flank) and stood there nuzzling. Someone respectable saw.
15Took the rouse out of a companion’s pouch and ate it. They gain 2 Weariness when they next reach for it.
16Folded a coat or cloth into a neat pillow and laid it on the floor. No one is lying on it. Yet. †
17Lied to your nudger, perfectly: told them you had not blinked. There is no entry in your book. Only you know, now.
18Spoke to the room in the voice of one of your dead. Everyone who heard knows whose voice it was. †
19Stroked the hair of the most frightened person present and told them it was all right to rest. They gain 3 Weariness and make a blink check. †
20Tucked. Someone is lying on the floor, hands crossed, a cloth under their head, and your palms are on their face. Dread 3. Roll d6: on 1–3 you came back in time; on 4–5 they are breathing slow and even and will not wake; on 6 they have stopped, and their teeth are in your hand. †
GM Advice — Did I Blink?

Blinks are a tool for gaslighting the players, gently and fairly. Once a character is Drifting or worse, the GM may tell a player that something has changed, a door now open, a companion now across the room, a cup now empty, and decline to say whether it is a blink or a Seeming or the truth. A character may make an Eye + Reckoning roll (Routine at Drifting, Hard at Grey) to trust a memory; on a failure, they cannot be sure, and NPCs who say otherwise are as likely to be right. Never use this to cheat players out of earned success. Use it to make them look at one another and ask, quietly, did you see me move?

Watched and Unwatched

A Vigilant’s nudger is not a convenience. It is half of a life. A character whose sworn nudger is present in a scene gains +2 on blink checks, and the nudger, not the character, rolls to fetch them if they fall asleep. A character who is unwatched, with no one in the scene who has undertaken to keep them awake, makes every blink check one step harder when alone, and gains 1 Fray at the end of any scene in which nobody noticed they had blinked. Player characters may nudge each other, and are encouraged to swear it; a party that pinches each other’s wrists and says pinch me before a dangerous scene gains the bonus for that scene. Breaking a sworn nudging, by walking away from a drowsing companion, by failing to slap, by being the one who sat down first, is a Dread 2 matter for the one who broke it, and the Vigil never quite forgives it.

The Seeming

At Weariness 5 and above, the GM gives characters private hallucinations: voices in the lamps, insects in the plaster, the dead in the lane. Shared Seemings, which a whole street sees, are real enough for law in the Vigil whether or not they are real at all. An Eye + Search roll at Hard tells a character whether a Seeming leaves traces (warm cobbles, a crumb, a place card). A character who Breaks in the Vigil most often takes a Derangement of the Seeming: that a loved one has been replaced by a sleeper’s dream of them; that they themselves are asleep in a bed and dreaming all of this; that the room is real and the city is the dream.

Seemings at the Table

When a character at Weariness 5 or more is in a quiet moment, a grey afternoon, a long wait, a crowd, or anywhere near the Dormitory, the GM may roll d20 for a Seeming, or choose. If only one character is Drifting or worse, it is private, and the GM should tell that player alone. If two or more characters present are at Weariness 5 or more, roll d6: on a 1–2 they share it, and may disagree about the details for the rest of the campaign. Any Seeming may be real. An Eye + Search roll at Hard finds traces, if there are any.

d20The Seeming
1A rain of teeth over the street, small and white, clicking on the tin roofs. They are milk teeth. They melt like hail.
2A woman made of moths walks down the lane. Every lamp she passes gutters and dims. She stops in front of you, and you smell flour.
3Every face in the crowd turns toward you at once, eyes closed; then, all together, opens them.
4Someone you lost, at the end of the lane, in their good coat, holding out a hand. When you blink they are a step closer.
5The bells strike, but the bell-ropes in the tower you can see are hanging perfectly still. They strike one more than they should.
6Snow falls out of the lamp-smoke. It is warm. It is not snow. It is down, soft and white, settling on your sleeves.
7A door in a wall that has no door. Warm light under it. The smell of clean linen. Someone on your side of it is reaching for the latch.
8The brown smoke-ceiling over the city rises and falls, slowly, four times to the minute, and you are breathing with it.
9A tall stooping figure in a grey coat, laying a table down the lane. A card at the nearest plate. The GM decides whose name is on it.
10A procession of the Counted, in their sheets, eyes shut, walking in step up the lane toward the Pillow. One of them is someone you know.
11Your own body, laid out on a board in the street, the neighbours queueing to touch its eyes. They look envious.
12Insects under the plaster crawl into the shape of numbers. It is a bed number. It changes when you look away.
13Every lamp flame in sight leans the same way, toward the centre of the Lid, as if something there were drawing breath.
14A child’s voice in every speaking-tube, drain and chimney, counting, slowly, somewhere past fifty-nine thousand.
15The cobbles go soft and warm under your feet, like the Pillow. When you step off them your footprints stay, pressed and shallow.
16A young man’s face in every window you pass, gentle, apologetic, yawning. Lukas Marre is in the Glass House, on the far side of the Lid.
17The sky closes: a vast grey lid, downy and slow, comes down across the lamp-glow from the east, and everything goes dim and kind.
18Everyone you know is, for the rest of the scene, very slightly wrong. Kinder. Patient. They answer the Asking perfectly.
19Knocking: slow, polite, three times, at every door in the street at once. Nobody is standing at any of them.
20It leaves something behind: warm crumbs on the cobbles, a felt slipper, a place card with a player character’s name, written in a fine old hand.

The Sop: the Lull

Iss is quieted by rest, and in the Vigil rest is a crime. The Lull is the act of closing your eyes on purpose for a count of ten while a nudger holds your hand. It removes 1d6 Hunger. It feeds the Want to lie down. The character must immediately make a blink check at Hard, whatever their Weariness; on a failure they are in the room for the count, and their nudger must fetch them back as if they had fallen asleep. Every Vigilant knows someone who took the Lull once too often.

The Long Waking in Play

When a character Breaks in the Vigil, they may take one of the Derangements below in place of one from the core rules. Each is resisted, when triggered, with Caul + Resolve at Hard, like any Derangement. They are not exotic in the Vigil. Half the people on any street have one.

d6DerangementTrigger and effect
1The CopyChoose a loved one: they have been replaced. Triggered by their kindness. You cannot accept help from them, and you perform the Asking whenever you can. They always answer correctly.
2Already CountedYou are asleep in a bed and dreaming all this. Triggered by pain or by the Dormitory. You ignore Weariness penalties for the scene and refuse rouse; at the end of the scene gain 2 Weariness.
3Borrowed HandsYour hands are not yours. Triggered by a blink. −2 on Hand rolls until someone you trust holds them and says your name.
4The Watch-SelfYou have a second self (see below). Triggered by the change of watch or by a Lack.
5At the WindowYou lose hours standing still. Triggered by a grey afternoon or Fray 5+. The GM may skip you forward up to a long watch; you gain 1 Weariness and smell of linen.
6The Lamp-FriendThe voice you heard in the lamps as a child has come back, and it is reasonable, and it knows things. Triggered by Partaking. It gives you one true fact a session, and one lie, and you cannot tell them apart.

The Watch-Self. A character with this Derangement shares their body with another person. The player and GM create that self together: a name, an age they believe they are, one thing they love that the character does not, one Want from the Vigil’s list, and one secret. The other self has the same Attributes and Skills, and no memory of the character’s hours. When triggered and not mastered, the other self takes the next scene, played by the player with the GM’s guidance, and the character comes back with lost time, a changed purse, and very often a note. Over a campaign the two may come to an arrangement. They may not. A Watch-Self can be ended only by the treatment of Derangements in the core rules, which in the Vigil means months of patient nudging by someone who will learn both names, and which, the Slope says, always leaves one of the two feeling as though they have been lain down.

The Tooth

When a Vigilant Partakes, their pupils blow wide and black, the world slows and softens at its edges, sounds come as if through a wall, and for a heartbeat they see the scene as if from very high up and very far away, every detail at once. Everyone nearby yawns. The air smells of clean linen. When a Tooth shows a 1 and the god bites back, the character takes the extra Hunger and +1 Weariness as well, and their next blink check is one step harder.

Gifts

The Taste (Regrowth 1–3). Choose one. The Catching Yawn: Partake and yawn deliberately; everyone in earshot with Weariness 3+ makes a Caul + Resolve roll at Hard or gains 2 Weariness and loses their next action to drowsiness. You gain 1 Weariness yourself. Heavy-Eyed: you always know when someone in sight is about to blink, gaining +2 to Instinct and Search against blinkers, and you know when someone lies about having blinked.

The Appetite (Regrowth 4–6). Choose one. Lost Seconds: Partake and blink on purpose; for 1d6 seconds you are gone, and you reappear up to ten paces away anywhere you could have walked. Nobody present remembers seeing you move. Roll on the Blink table afterwards, rerolling results of 1–6. The Long Look: blink under a nudger’s guard and ask the GM one question about a Counted sleeper or anyone currently blinking in the city; gain 2 Weariness and 1 Fray.

The Course (Regrowth 7–9). Lidless. Your lids shrink and are gone. You gain +2 to Search and can never be surprised by anything in your line of sight. You remember everything you have seen. Dread checks against anything before your eyes are one step harder, because you cannot look away. Your eyes must be wetted every half minute; without it you lose 1 Flesh an hour and are blind within a day. And the great privilege of the Eye-lines is yours: a lidless character who reaches Weariness 10 does not sleep. Instead they Break, at once, and their Weariness drops to 7. This is not mercy. It is how the Eye-lines rule.

The Brink (Regrowth 10–11). Lay Them Down. Partake and speak softly to one person with Weariness 5+ who can hear you; they make a Caul + Resolve roll at Grim or fall asleep, and go to the room. Each use forces a Dread 3 check on you. While you are at the Brink, everyone who spends a scene in the same room as you gains 1 Weariness, and restless sleepers turn their faces toward you.

The Wants

  • To lie down. Triggered by beds, softness, warmth, a body lying peacefully, the Pillow. Resist with Caul + Resolve at Hard; on a failure, the character presses against the comfort for a minute and makes a blink check.
  • To count. Triggered by rows, crowds, sleepers and fear. Resist at Routine; on a failure, the character must count the thing aloud to the end before acting.
  • To watch. Triggered by a sleeping or drowsing person. Resist at Hard; on a failure, the character cannot leave that person unwatched for the scene.
  • To tuck in (the Brink only). Triggered by a weeping, wounded or frightened person. Resist at Grim; on a failure, the character tries to make them lie down and rest.

The Seating

At Regrowth 12 the character falls asleep, one last time, smiling, and no nudger on the Table can fetch them. They are carried to the Dormitory and given a number. Their player should take a moment with that. Later, perhaps much later, the GM may tell the surviving characters that a sleeper in a certain bed has become restless. Lips first. The god has been furnishing the character from the inside, and when it speaks, it will use their voice, and it will know their friends’ names, and it will be very glad to see them.

Background Concepts

  • Slope Nudger. Born at a bell, pinching strangers for crumbs by six, you know every rouse-cut on the Slope and every face that is about to go down. You have outlived three clients.
  • Washed-Out Waker. You did your week in Sister Pinch’s standing-stall, and your year on the beat, and then you put the needle down one night and could not pick it up. You still know the Atlas. You still hear the screams as thanks.
  • Eye-line Spare. A younger child of a lidless house, born with eyelids, or born lidless and too far down the line to matter. You have been educated, watched, and kept out of sight, and you have never once been allowed to look away.
  • Bedside Visitor. Somebody you love is in the Dormitory, and you have stood at the foot of their bed every day for years at your visiting bell. You know the orderlies, the clerks, the hymn of the halls and the way the breathing changes. You suspect, lately, that the one in the bed knows you are there.
  • Lantern Survivor. You did three days in a Lantern in a public square, years ago, for lying down on a grey afternoon, and you came out believing the crowd had eaten part of you. You are still not sure they did not. You have no fear of crowds at all, now, which frightens them.
  • Hangwell Gatherer. You grew up on the ropes of the north cliffs, chewing raw staremoss, and you have heard the whole cliff call your name as someone fell. You are the most awake person in any room, and you see a great grey lid in every rock face.
  • Tucker’s Counter. You counted sixty over sleepers in a warm cellar, for money, and hauled most of them back. You know the count to the breath. You know exactly how long a minute is from the outside, and that is the only thing you are sure you know.
  • Lessening Copyist. You copied Dormitory registers at night for beer money and never asked what for. Then you saw a list. Now you count the blink-murders in the bell-sheets, and every one of them is a name you knew from the copying-room.
  • Burner’s Apprentice. You worked the vats behind the Row for a season before you understood what came in on the carts. You kept the wage. You still cannot be in a room with a lamp without knowing, by the smell, that it is someone.

A Vigilant Abroad

The rule follows the blood, and a Vigilant who leaves the Lid takes the room with them. There is no bed on the Table they can lie in. On the Rim Road they travel with paid nudgers and chests of rouse, and in Sallowreach or Oathen they are the strangers who stand at the back of every inn all night, pinching their own wrists, watching the locals sleep with an expression the locals find hard to bear. The rest of the Table thinks them mad, rude, morbid and frightening. They are right on every count. A Vigilant abroad keeps tracking Weariness exactly as on the Lid, but every scene of comfort counts double, because the rest of the world is so soft, and a Vigilant who sees another person asleep for the first time must make a Dread 1 check, because the sight is obscene and holy and they cannot look away. Foreign party members who sleep near a Vigilant should know that the Vigilant is watching them do it, every night, and counting their breaths, and that it is the most intimate thing a Vigilant can do for another person.

Playing the Weight

Play a Vigilant as someone carrying something. They do not complain about tiredness; nobody on the Lid does. They are rude, because rudeness keeps people awake. They argue for the sake of it, and they mean it as friendship. They touch people more than other Tablefolk, briskly, a pinch, a slap, a hand on the wrist, and they think of it as tenderness. They distrust anyone who looks rested. They count things. They suspect the people they love of being copies and love them anyway. They have done something terrible in a blink and they know it and they cannot remember it. And underneath all of it, every minute of every watch, they want to lie down, and they are not going to, and that refusal, repeated forever, is the bravest thing on the Table.

The eye is patient. Be rude.
Vigil proverb, and the whole of its advice to strangers

Names

Feminine: Aveline, Cecily, Iselde, Ilvane, Maud, Mirela, Odile, Oriel, Senna, Vesper, Constance, Agathe, Sabine, Hesper, Annick, Merrit, Lisbet, Wenna.

Masculine: Aldous, Benedikt, Brannoch, Castellan, Corwin, Evander, Garron, Hale, Lukas, Marten, Teodor, Thaddeus, Tobin, Ansgar, Pell, Florian.

Neutral and bell-names (the Slope): Pip, Rook, Wick, Ember, Nod, Rue, Quill; with a bell for a surname: Eleven-Bell, Quarter-Bell, Half-Bell, First-Bell, Dusk-Bell.

Surnames: Stroud, Sexton, Pyre, Vole, Crane, Dorm, Ashlock, Marre, Null, Knell, Sconce, Tenterhook, Grimmer, Farthing, Lour, Dray, Morne, Larch, Hobb, Rell, Quell, Coyle, Lantern, Wakely, Pinchbeck, Startle.

Horrors of the Vigil

GM Advice — Using the Horrors

Roll d10, or choose, when the city needs to remind the party where they are. Most of these scenes call for a Dread check (Dread 1 or 2; Dread 3 where someone the party knows is involved), and most of them happen on a grey, quiet afternoon. Several are good moments to ask everyone at Weariness 5 or above for a blink check.

d10Horror
1A whole rouse-house yawns in a wave, bench by bench, jaws cracking, eyes streaming, and at the far end of it a man sits down on the floor, smiling, and does not get up. Everyone looks at the party.
2A Dormitory cart passes down the Slope piled with the day’s sleepers, warm, breathing in time. The crowd counts them aloud. At the last body the counting stops: it is someone the party spoke to this morning.
3A Waker needles a drowsing girl at a street corner, under the nail, the armpit, behind the ear. She screams and thanks him. Her mother pays him. He moves on to the next.
4A Seeming: every lamp in the lane flickers in rhythm, slow, four beats to the minute, and the party’s own breathing has already matched it.
5A woman runs up, wet-faced, asking whether the party saw her blink, because her nudger is lying on the floor with his eyes closed and her hands smell of his breath.
6A child of four is crying in a doorway that she is so tired, she is so tired, why can’t she lie down. Her mother is slapping her, sobbing, again and again, harder each time.
7The Lantern in the square holds a man in his fifth day. He thinks the crowd is eating him. Some of the crowd have started to agree, and one has a knife.
8Someone in a window is humming the first three notes of The Lamb and the Lid. Every head on the street turns. A Waker begins to run.
9Lain-Down: a neat pair of shoes on a doorstep, a folded coat on top, a note pinned to it, and the open door of a dark, warm room.
10A Brine Walker column shuffles past, eyes open, coughing salt water, all of them facing west. One of them is someone a PC loves, who does not know them.

The Lamb and the Lid, as recorded in the Rattlehouse register of forbidden matter, the only copy permitted to exist.

Hush now, lamb, the lid is low,

the long room’s warm and the lamps burn slow;

lie you down where the sleepers keep,

and the eye won’t open while the lambs still sleep.

Hush now, lamb, and count to three,

there’s a bed for you and a bed for me;

and when the beds are full, my sweet,

the eye will open, and we’ll all go to eat.

Chapter 7

Cradlewrack

The Land in Labor
First we ask what it is. Then we ask whether it stays.
— the Midwife’s Two Questions
Knock before you open. Whatever is on the other side has a right to be warned, and so do you.
— Cradlewrack proverb, taught before the alphabet

Set down by Wenna Thrale, apprentice of the Attendance, third year of her apron, for the Lying-In’s own book and not for the Tally. Rudge parish, the fourth night after a pang, Carving 641.

They sent for us at the second bell because the father had begun. Not the mother: she had been delivered of a girl in Grace and sat by the hearth with the girl at her breast and her face to the wall. It was the father on the floor, a shepherd’s son named Corran with hands like spades, curled on the red clay in a shirt soaked black. The room smelled the way every highland room smells when something is coming: iron, wet wool, and under it the warm salt of the springs, as if the ground had broken its waters under the house.

Mother Sabeth went to him first. I went to the door, as I was taught, because the door had opened on its own when we came in and would not stay shut. I put my back to it. I could feel it pushing, very gently, the way a hand pushes from the inside of a belly. I have stood against a hundred doors and that is the only way I can describe it.

Corran’s belly was not large. That was the worst of it. It was a man’s flat belly, but the skin of it was moving in a long slow roll from the ribs to the groin, and each time it rolled he made a sound I have heard cattle make and never a man. Sabeth laid her palm on him and counted under her breath. Then she opened her case and laid out the things in the order we lay them out: the cord-thread, the basin, the clean linen, the bone hook, and last, wrapped in its own oiled cloth, the knife.

It took until the fourth bell. I will write only that he did not open where a woman opens, because he has nowhere to, and that he opened at an old scar on his flank from a ram’s horn, twenty years shut and white, which parted now like a mouth deciding to speak. Sabeth had her arm in him to the elbow and her face was calm. The mother at the hearth did not turn around once. The baby at her breast did not cry once, but watched.

What came out was the size of a lamb and the color of the clay floor. It had a great many fingers. It drew breath. That is the thing nobody tells you before your apron, that they all draw breath, that the first sound out of the worst of them is the same small wet gasp as out of the best. Sabeth held it up in the lamplight and turned it, slowly, the way you turn a pot to look for cracks, and she asked the First Question aloud, because it must be asked aloud.

What is it.

Nobody answered. Nobody ever answers. She answered it herself, quietly, in the words of the Book, and then she was quiet for a long time. Corran had stopped making his sound. The door had stopped pushing against my back. The only noise in the room was the thing breathing and the clay ticking as it cooled. I counted eleven breaths. I have been told since that Sabeth Thorne never takes more than three. She looked at it for eleven.

Then she asked the Second Question, and she answered it, and she unwrapped the oiled cloth.

I am meant to write what I saw, for the Lying-In’s book. I saw her turn her back to the hearth so the mother would not see. I saw her shoulder move once. I saw her wrap the linen and tie the knot we tie, the one that cannot come undone, and hand the bundle to me without looking at it, and I held it, and it was warm, and it stayed warm against my chest the whole cold walk back to the Lying-In, longer than it should have. I did not look either. I want that written down. I did not look.

Corran lived. We closed his flank with eight stitches, and he will have them redone at every pang for the rest of his life, because in Cradlewrack a wound opened once remembers how. In the morning the mother turned from the wall and asked what it had been. I said, as I am taught, that nothing had been born, that the Tally would show a son of the household entered and struck through. She nodded. Then she held up her girl, six months old and unnamed, and asked whether I thought this one would stay.

The girl looked at me. She has her father’s eyes, very dark. She opened her mouth as if to answer.

I said that the naming waits a year. I said it the way I was taught. I put the knife-case back in Sabeth’s bag myself because Sabeth’s hands were busy at the basin, scrubbing, long after there was anything left on them to scrub.

Nine days. Count them on your fingers, love, and then count them again, because next year it will take fewer fingers.
a Rudge grandmother, to a child learning the interval

The Meal

Vey, the Opening, was the smallest of the Providers. The highland songs agree on that and on almost nothing else. It was no taller than a woman of middle height, and in the old carvings at Kest it is shown standing in a doorway with its arms spread to either jamb, so that the eye cannot tell whether it is holding the door open or holding something back. It had no face that anyone could keep in mind afterward. Those who saw it remembered only the feeling of being about to begin something: a breath drawn in and not yet let out, the half-second before a first word. Mothers in labor reached for it. It came. For three thousand years, the highlands say, no child in Vey’s country was born without the god standing at the foot of the bed, its hands spread, its faceless attention fixed on the opening.

In the ninth winter of the Long Lack, Vey stood at the foot of every bed and nothing came. The wombs of the highlands had closed. Ewes stood dry and staring. Seeds lay in the red clay like teeth in a dead jaw. The god went from house to house with its hands spread, and the doorways it stood in were empty, and at last the midwives stopped calling it, because it was unbearable to watch it wait.

They took it in the birthing-house at Kest, the round red building that still stands at the heart of the city and is now called the Old Lying-In. They did not need to chase it. It came when the midwives called, the way it always came, and stood in the doorway of the birthing-room with its arms spread, and they shut the door on it. It was the first time anything had ever been shut against Vey. The songs say the god looked at the closed door for a long time, as if it had never seen one from that side.

Then they killed it, and it would not stay killed.

This is the part the highlands remember in their bodies. Vey was the hardest of the Providers to kill because it kept starting again. They opened its throat with a shearing knife and from the wound came, wet and blinking, a smaller Vey, whole, its arms already spread. They killed that one and it began again from its own wound, and again, each new god crawling up out of the opened body of the last like a child crowning. By dawn the floor was a drift of gods the size of hares, of mice, of fingernails, each still trying to begin, and the clay was ankle-deep in caul and cord and a clear warm fluid that smelled of iron and the inside of a mouth. The last was no larger than a barleycorn. The midwife who crushed it between her thumbnails, Hollan Kest, ancestor of every Midwife-Paramount since, is said to have wept and said, “There. Now nothing begins.”

The songs do not spare the room. They say the smell was the smell of a lambing-shed in a hot spring, if the shed had been shut for a week: iron, milk, wet straw, and under it the sweet, flat, faintly fecal stink of things newly come out of a body. They say the floor of the birthing-room had been laid with fresh rushes that afternoon and that by midnight the rushes floated. They say the little gods made a sound as they crawled, a soft continuous clicking of tiny joints opening for the first time, and that the midwives who survived the night heard it in every hearth fire for the rest of their lives. They say that the smaller the god became, the harder it was to look at, because the smaller ones had faces, finally, and every face was the face of a child the woman looking at it had lost.

There were nine women in the room. The songs name them all, and the five great Caul-line houses and the House of Aubrey are each descended from one of them or from the households that stood at their backs. Hollan Kest held the knife. Grizel Aubrey held the door shut with her shoulders and was the first person in the history of the world to feel Vey push against a door from the other side; her granddaughter wore the first highland crown. Mab Morwen tended the copper and skimmed it. Ottilie Seele carried the bowls. Two Calloway sisters and a Danner cousin held the god down, again and again, each new god smaller than the last, until their aprons were stiff to the waist. The ninth woman is not named in any song, only called the one who counted, and the songs say she counted every Vey as it was killed, aloud, and that the number she reached is the number the Attendance still will not write down.

Then they ate it, because the Lack had to end. They ate it the way the highlands eat a lambing’s afterbirth: stewed with clay salt in the great copper and ladled out by the senior midwife into bowls brought from home. The boldest households, pressed closest to the copper, came away with the choicest part, which was not flesh but the membrane that had sheathed the god’s thousand rebirths, a grey-pink translucent skin the cooks skimmed off the pot like the skin on milk. These families ate the caul. They became the Caul-lines.

The famine ended in the morning. By midday the first ewes were dropping lambs in the snow. By the end of Grace every woman in the highlands who could carry was carrying, and by the end of Plenty every one of them had been delivered, easily, without blood, without death. The midwives who had done the killing were made the guardians of the cradles. They were thanked. Nobody asked why the doors of the old birthing-house had all swung open on their own at the moment the last god died, or why no one has managed to close them since.

The Barleycorn, as it is sung in the Rudge ravines at the end of lambing, slow, by women only:

Out of the big one came the small one, and we cut the small one through,

out of the small one came the smaller, with its arms out, like the first one, like you.

Hollan, Hollan, put down the knife, there’s nothing left that’s growing,

and Hollan held it on her nail, a barleycorn, still going.

She pressed. We heard it. Like a seed between your teeth.

And all the doors came open, love, above us and beneath.

The Old Lying-In keeps, under glass in the Book-room, a list in Mab Morwen’s hand: the inventory of the bowls ladled out from the copper on the morning of the Meal, by household, with the share each took. It is the oldest document in the highlands and every Caul-line genealogy begins from it. Scholars of the Cutwrights’ College who have been allowed to read it note three things. The Morwens took the first and deepest bowl. The caul went, by Mab’s own hand, to the five households nearest her elbow and to no others. And the bowl-count at the foot of the page does not match the households listed above it: one more bowl was returned to the copper than was ever ladled out, and it came back, the inventory says in a smaller, shakier hand, licked clean, and no household would own it.

We ate the caul so we would see forward. Nobody told us it would be a door we’d be looking at.
Duchess Ottoline Morwen, in her last foretelling, 609 A.G.
The Carving Above the Old Lying-In

Over the round door of the Old Lying-In in Kest is a frieze older than the Gorging: eight figures standing in eight doorways, each in its own arch, each with its arms spread. Seven have been worn by six centuries of hands touched to them for luck. The eighth arch is empty. Its figure has been chiselled out so deeply that the stone behind it has gone through to the hollow of the wall, and the hole breathes warm air on cold days. Midwives touch the seven arches on the way in. Nobody touches the eighth. The apprentices say that if you put your ear to the hole you can hear someone on the other side laying a table. The apprentices say a great many things.

The Rule of the Land

Nothing here is born right, and too much is born.

That is the whole of it, and it has been the whole of it for six centuries. Vey was the god of things coming into the world, and Vey is in the blood of the highlands now, and things will not stop coming. The births began wrong in 94 A.G. and have never gone right since. Every highland family has a story about what came out of whom, and every story is told the same way, flat and practical, the way other peoples talk about weather.

Children arrive speaking. Not babbling: speaking, in full sentences, in the voices of adults, with opinions. The first, in Kest in 94 A.G., opened its eyes and said, “Not yet,” and died within the hour, and nobody has ever agreed on what it meant. Children arrive old, white-haired and arthritic, with failing hearts and worn teeth, and either grow younger year by year toward the cradle or simply die of age at three. Children arrive full-grown, tearing their way out into a world they are already too big for: men and women of thirty, of fifty, born mid-stride or mid-sentence, slick with blood and cord, who must be taught to use a spoon although their hands already know how to use a sword. These are the born-grown, and the country has found uses for them.

And some arrive as Parts. A single living hand, warm, clenching. An ear that turns toward sound. A length of spine that crawls by flexing, like a caterpillar. A heart in its own little caul, kept in a covered dish in Cleave for nineteen years before it stopped. The Parts are healthy. They feed through the skin or through mouths that open in unlikely places. They grow. They are also drawn toward each other: a hand left on a table will, overnight, drag itself to the edge nearest the nearest other Part, however far away, and two Parts in one room will strain together and, if allowed, seal along a seam that heals in a night. Since 500 A.G. it has been known that Parts from unrelated families fit, a hand born in Rudge sitting perfectly on a wrist born in Kest a century apart, as if they were born to go together.

Parts

Outsiders imagine the Parts as something out of a butcher’s window: lumps, scraps, wet and dying. They are not. A born Part is finished, the way a good stitch is finished. A hand arrives with its nails grown and its creases deep, the skin of the wrist closed over in a smooth pink dome like the end of a sausage-casing, faintly translucent, through which on a warm day you can see the bones of the wrist moving as it clenches. An ear arrives with a ridge of soft gristle behind it that it uses to drag itself along a table, a fraction of an inch at a time. A length of spine arrives sheathed in a thin wet skin the color of a peeled grape and crawls, as the highlands say, like a caterpillar that has decided where it is going. Every Part is warm. Every Part has a pulse, though nobody has found a heart in a hand, and the pulse of a Part is always, always, the pulse of whoever bore it. Mothers who sit up with their Parts at night say that the hardest thing is not the look of it but the sound, in a quiet room, of two hearts keeping time.

They feed. A Part laid in a dish of warm milk will take the milk in through its skin over a night, so that the dish is dry by morning and the skin smells of curd. Some Parts grow mouths: a small lipless slit opening in the palm of a hand, in the lobe of an ear, at the end of a finger, which makes a wet clicking noise when it is hungry and must be fed with a spoon. They grow. A hand born the size of a baby’s fist will be the size of a grown woman’s hand in four years, and nobody has learned to stop it at any size in between. They sleep; they wake; they have moods. A foot will curl and uncurl its toes for hours when it is unhappy. An eye will weep. And they are drawn, every one of them, to the others, the way a sleeper turns toward warmth.

The Parts that are hardest to speak of are the ones that are not born free. In the Course, and sometimes earlier, a body may bear a Part that does not come away: a second hand, small and perfect, growing from the inside of an elbow; a cluster of fingers at the base of a spine; an ear opening in the side of a neck, which hears, and which the bearer hears with. These are called keepings, and the Book of Questions has three hundred pages of cases about them. The Attendance may cut a keeping free, and it then becomes a Part like any other, crawling, hungry, drawn to the others; and the place it was cut from remembers, in the way of the highlands, and on a pang night opens, and begins again. Most bearers learn to live with their keepings bandaged under their clothes. A few come to love them. A few take a knife to them alone at night in a bricked room, and are found in the morning, and the Tally enters the keeping and the bearer both.

It holds my finger when I sleep. Tell me what else in this world has ever held my finger when I sleep.
a Tarnbrow shepherd, to the Attendance, refusing to surrender a hand
Rules — Keeping a Part

A character who keeps a Part (born to them, bought, found or stolen) must feed it daily: a horn of milk, or a few drops of the keeper’s own blood, which a Part prefers. Each day it goes unfed, it loses heart and the keeper gains 1 Hunger, because it is the god’s piece and the god notices. A kept Part is warm, smells faintly of curd and the springs, and is detectable by anyone with the Taste or higher within ten paces (Caul + Instinct vs Hard 14). Each night, roll a d10: on a 1 it has moved toward the nearest other Part, and on a double-1 week (two 1s in a row) it has reached it, or tried to. A keeper who has slept beside a Part for a full season gains the Knack-like benefit of always knowing where it is, and suffers a Dread 3 check if it is taken, destroyed, or joined to another. Parts used in play take stats from the Crawling Part quick line in this chapter.

What Is Found: Parts

Roll when the characters search a hidden crock, a Part-hunter’s crate, a midden, a ravine after the waters, or the bed of someone who has died in the Course. Every Part found is warm.

d20The Part
1A left hand, a man’s, with a wedding band grown into the flesh of the finger. The band is engraved with a name nobody in the parish has.
2An ear in a bread-crock, wrapped in a child’s shawl. It turns toward whichever character is speaking, and keeps turning after they stop.
3A coil of gut, alive, in a jar of milk. It has tied itself into the knot that cannot come undone, and it is pulling tighter.
4Two eyes, joined at the back by a stalk of pink nerve, in a pewter dish. One sleeps while the other watches.
5A foot of a child of about three. It has never stood on anything. Its sole is as soft as a cheek, and it flinches at the floor.
6A tongue in a covered cup. When the cup is lifted it says one word, the name of whoever bore it, and then is silent for nine days.
7A heart in its own little caul, beating slowly. Laid against a character’s chest, it falls into their rhythm, and they cannot afterward get it out.
8A pair of lips sewn shut by someone who loved them, nine stitches, the knot that cannot come undone. Behind the stitches something is humming the counting-song.
9A length of spine, nine vertebrae, curled around a spindle like a sleeping cat. It wakes and tries to fit itself to the nearest back.
10A breast, small, in milk, wrapped in linen at the bottom of a Part-hunter’s crate. The linen is soaked. The crate is labelled with a parish nobody has heard of.
11A hand of seven fingers, all of them thumbs. It holds things very carefully, as if it has been told it is clumsy.
12A scalp of thick red hair with no skull beneath, which breathes, slowly, through its skin. It smells of the hearth of the house it was born in.
13Twelve teeth in a wooden box, each in its own nest of gum. They chatter when a pang is near, a full day before anyone feels it.
14A forearm and hand, already joined to a second forearm and hand at the elbow, so that the thing has a hand at each end. It walks on them.
15A navel, only a navel, in a disc of belly-skin the size of a lack. A thin pale cord grows from it and goes out under the door.
16A face, without a head behind it, in a hatbox. It is the face of one of the characters, perhaps twenty years older. It is asleep.
17A womb, in a lidded crock, the size of a fist. It is, unmistakably, carrying something of its own.
18A finger of nine joints, grey as old wax, which does not belong to any body born in the highlands. It is cold, the only cold Part anyone has ever found.
19A small left hand with a midwife’s callus on the inside of the ring finger, where the hook of the knife rests. It reaches for any blade in the room.
20Nothing in the crock. The lid is off, the straw is warm, and there is a trail of small damp prints across the floor toward the east and the Barn. (The Gathering it joins may come back.)

Birth is not limited to mothers. Men have borne, through scars, through the navel, through the mouth. A widow of eighty-seven in Tarnbrow was delivered of twins older than she was. A ewe may drop eleven lambs, or one lamb with eleven heads. And things that are not alive bear. A well in Rudge gave birth in 403 A.G. to something that climbed up the rope and was not seen again. A locked chest in the Morwen strong-room was found open with a damp, curled thing inside and the lock still turned. A hillside above Cleave dilated for a month and delivered a warm boulder with a pulse. A woman four days dead in the Stillyard went into labor on her bier, and the Attendance attended, because it must, and the Tally records what came as “one, living, struck through.”

The Tally is the evidence of the land’s condition. Every birth in Cradlewrack is entered in a public ledger, by law, and the Tally of births has outrun the count of conceptions every year for two centuries. Last year, by the figures of Rufus Ochre the Tallyman, eleven hundred more people were born in the highlands than were carried by any woman, man, beast, well, chest, or hillside. The country is making people out of nothing, and nobody knows where they are.

The Tally

The Tally is not a book but a building, a habit and a voice. Each parish keeps a Tally-board, a long slate under an awning, on which the parish Attendant chalks the day’s births at dusk; a crier reads the board aloud; a runner copies it on oiled paper and carries it to the Tally-house in Kest, where Rufus Ochre’s scriveners enter it in the great ledger that has been kept, without a missed day, since 131 A.G. The ledger is public. Anyone may climb Tally Hill and ask to see any page, and many do, because in Cradlewrack the Tally is the only proof that you were born, that you were permitted, and that you are who you say you are. A highlander with no line in the Tally does not legally exist; a highlander whose line is struck through does not legally exist either, and there are more of the second kind walking about than the Attendance would like.

Every entry has five parts: the number, the household, the bearer, what, and stays. The fourth column is the First Question, answered in the Attendant’s own words; the fifth is the Second, and it has only three possible entries: stays, surrendered (for Parts), and a single ruled line, which is what struck through means on the page. The Tally has its own shorthand, learned by every child who learns letters: sp. for speaking-born, o.b. for old-born, g. for born-grown, pt. for a Part, w.b. for without bearer. What follows is a true copy of a part of one evening’s page.

Four thousand four hundred and eighteen. Carried by somebody: four thousand two hundred and nine. Rufus, where are the rest sleeping tonight?
marginal note in a scrivener’s hand, the Tally of Carving 641, crossed out and initialled R.O.

The evening reading is a rite in itself. The crier stands on the Tally-house steps with a lamp, reads each line, and pauses after the fifth column; at stays the crowd murmurs “and let it stay,” the highland half of the common grace; at surrendered it says nothing; at the ruled line it turns its face away from the steps for a count of three, the time an Opinion is meant to take, and then turns back. Mothers who have not yet been read stand at the front. Those who have been read and struck through stand at the back, and nobody speaks to them on the way home, and they are not expected to answer if anybody does.

Doors

Vey was also the god of doors, of openings, of thresholds and first steps over them. In Cradlewrack nothing stays shut.

Doors drift open in the night. Not violently: they are found at dawn a hand’s width ajar, latches lifted, bars slid back, as if someone very patient had worked at them for hours. Locks undo. Lids rise off jars. Knots slip. Coffins open. A sealed letter is found unsealed. And wounds reopen.

That last is the one that wears a body down. A cut that has knitted, a scar twenty years white, a surgical seam neatly closed: in Cradlewrack all of them remember how to open, and on pang nights many of them do. Old soldiers of the Foundling Companies bleed from every wound they have ever taken, all at once, every nine days. A woman who was cut for a stone in her youth wakes in a wet bed with her side yawning. The Attendance employs whole wards of stitchers whose only work is to close, each morning, what the night opened. There is no cure. There is only thread.

Every threshold is something waiting to be crossed. The highlanders knock before they open anything, door, cupboard, box or letter, because you knock to warn whatever is on the other side. They brick up rooms they never want opened again, and brick themselves into rooms at night, and break out in the morning.

Knock, and wait. If it knocks back, you were right to knock. If it doesn’t, you were right to wait.
a Kest mother’s rule, taught at the lintel
Rules — Wounds That Reopen

Any character who has spent at least one night in Cradlewrack is subject to the land. Each pang (every nine days at present), roll a d10 for each healed Injury from the Mangling table the character carries, and for each surgical seam closed by Stitching in the last year. On a 1–3 it reopens during the night: the character loses 2 Flesh per reopened wound and wakes bleeding (Dread 1 for anyone unused to it). Closing it again is a Stitching roll at Hard 14. A Lack on that roll means the wound has learned the stitch: the next reopening is automatic. Natives of Cradlewrack carry their stitching kit the way other peoples carry a knife, and most have a Stitching of at least 1.

Doors and locks fare no better. Any lock in Cradlewrack must be checked each night; a lock that matters holds only on a Craft or Filch roll at Grim 18 by whoever set it, and even then not past the next pang. Bricking in always holds. That is why they brick.

The Body Is a Door

In the rest of the Table a body is a house a person lives in. In Cradlewrack a body is a doorway, and everybody knows it, and nobody is allowed to forget it, least of all by the law.

Every highland body belongs, a little, to the Attendance. An Attendant may lay her palm on any belly in the country, at any hour, without asking, and it is a crime to step back from her hand. Every woman of bearing age, every man in the Course, every child old enough to be returned, is examined at every Unbricking: stripped to the waist in the parish birthing-room, palpated, listened to with an ear on the navel, asked the date of their last cramp, their last waters, their last dream of a door. The examinations are brisk, cold-handed and not unkind, and they are hated more quietly and more completely than anything else the Attendance does. At Breech’s Gate the examination is done to foreigners too, and the Rim Road Company’s own guidance to its drivers warns that “the highlanders will put their hands on you, and you will let them, and you will not discuss it afterward among yourselves, which is the only part of the experience that will help.”

Breathe out, sir. No, all the way out. I need to feel what’s breathing in there besides you.
Examiner at Breech’s Gate, to a Fatlands wool-buyer

What the Examination finds is worse than the Examination. The land does not ask before it begins in someone. A drover of forty, a grandmother, a Purgation zealot who has never touched another living soul, a girl of fifteen who has never been out of her mother’s sight: any of them may wake with the low slow roll in the belly and the warm flood between the legs and know, in the flat highland way, what it means. The god does not need an act, a partner, a season or a consent. It needs an opening, and it makes them. Men in the Course feel their pelvis loosen and spread over a season with a deep grinding ache like a joint being slowly levered apart, until they walk with the rolling gait of the heavily pregnant and cannot remember how they used to walk. Breasts fill in old men and leak, and the milk is warm and salt and pink at the edges. Old scars soften, pucker, gain lips. A navel deepens, month by month, until a finger can be laid in it to the second knuckle and feel something on the other side lean against the fingertip.

The highlands have no word for this that is not a midwife’s word, and so it is spoken of in a midwife’s voice: she’s begun, he’s carrying, she’s open, he’s near. People are kind to the carrying. They give up seats. They do not ask by whom. But the kindness has the edge of the Examination in it, because a carrying neighbor is a neighbor the Attendance will come for, and a neighbor who has stopped looking like herself, and every highlander knows the madness that goes with it, which the Lying-In’s book calls tenancy and the parishes call the lodger: the certainty, in the carrying, that the thing inside is awake and listening and has opinions about what they eat and whom they speak to; the certainty, in their families, that the person they love has been moved out of their own face by whatever moved in. Husbands sit up at night watching wives who sleep with their arms spread to the bed-frame. Wives refuse to eat at table with husbands whose voices have begun, they swear, to come from a little lower than their mouths. Most of them are wrong. Some of them are not, and the Book of Questions has a section on how to tell, and it is not long, and it does not end with a reassurance.

Rules — Carrying

A character with Regrowth 1 or more may begin to carry in Cradlewrack without any act, at any age, of any sex. The Carver may impose it as the consequence of a Lack on a Tooth (when Partaking in the highlands, a Tooth showing 1 on a pang day), of a Regrowth rise to the Appetite or the Course, or of sleeping a night in an unhinged house, a pang-house, or within a mile of the Dilation. Carrying is never a punishment the Carver springs for a laugh; it is the land taking a body that was not offered, and it should be played with the weight of that.

  • Signs. The character feels the roll at each pang and loses 1 Flesh to the cramp. Anyone who examines them (Hand + Stitching vs Routine 10, or a Midwife’s talent) knows.
  • Term. Carrying lasts 1d10 days in the Course, or until the next pang otherwise. Each day of it, the character gains 1 Hunger and must make a Dread 1 check on waking.
  • Delivery. At term the character labors for 1d6 hours and must roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or suffer Ruin from the Mangling table; an attending Midwife or any character with Stitching 2+ adds +2 and may roll in their place. What comes is rolled on the Parts table above, or, at the Brink, on the crowning table below. Witnesses check Dread 2.
  • The Questions. In Cradlewrack, a birth without an Attendant is concealment, and the Attendance will come. Abroad, nobody knows what to do, which is worse.
  • Refusal. A character may try to end a carrying early by going to an Opinion; the Opinion will do it, without comment, and the character checks Dread 2 and keeps the scar, which opens at every pang thereafter. There is no other way that works, and the Carver should make sure no player is ever told there is.

The Regrowth in Cradlewrack

Vey is growing back, and what grows back is beginning.
