The house wants the characters to find out who its new twin is before the Council does, and the Cutwrights’ College wants its locked volume back from whoever stole it from the Kest chapter last week.

Rumors of the Highlands

d10Rumor
1The pangs will stop if the Queen Dowager is delivered. (False. The King Within would not agree to it, by kick, anyway.)
2The figure in the Barn wept last week, from forty-one eyes. (True. It has more than two of several things.)
3The Dilation is a mouth, not a womb, and something is coming up to eat. (False, says the Attendance. Madder Rudge is less sure.)
4The Midwife-Paramount has a struck-through sibling of her own. (True, and she was the one who held the door.)
5The Barren Order is buying grey stone by the shipload from the Fast to fill the Dilation. (True. It would take four centuries of shipping.)
6Agnes Latch has built a door that held for a year. (False. It held for nineteen days. The customer died on the twentieth.)
7The Sill opened a full hand’s width this Grace. (True. Old Hinge has not told the Attendance.)
8The eleven hundred unaccounted births are walking toward the Dilation by night. (Partly true. Some are.)
9A Caul-line duchess can be killed only by cutting her veil, and the veil grows back. (False. But the veil does grow back.)
10The Uncut’s oldest Root is joined to something under the ground that is not dead and is not their mother. (True.)

The People of Cradlewrack

What is it. Does it stay. Every one of us was asked both, and not one of us was let answer.
[ chalked on the Tally-house steps, Kest, the morning after a pang ]

Midwife-Paramount Orla Kest

Head of the Attendance, sixty-eight, descended in the female line from Hollan Kest, who crushed the last god. She is small, square, and grey, with forearms like a laundress’s and a voice she has never once in her life raised. She smells of lye and lavender. She has attended nine thousand births and permitted six thousand. She remembers the other three thousand individually, by parish and date and the color of the mother’s eyes, and can tell you why, in each case, without raising her voice. She has never asked to be forgiven for any of them. What she fears is not the knife but its failure: that the Late-faction is right, that she has spent her life answering small questions while the large one dilated under her feet. She meets the characters when one of them is carrying, or when one of them is close to Sabeth Thorne. Secret: Orla’s mother bore a second child when Orla was nine, and Orla held the door. She has asked herself the Second Question about the country, and answered it, and is waiting only for the room.

Sabeth Thorne, the Second Opinion

The Attendance’s most trusted knife, forty, long-boned and quiet, with cropped black hair and hands she scrubs until they crack. For eighteen years she was the Opinion the other Opinions sent for: the one who could look for the count of three and decide. Last winter, at a farmhouse in Tarnbrow, she hesitated. She counted eleven breaths. The thing lived. She paid the shepherd’s widow a year’s wages to keep it in her loft, and has been watching it grow ever since, and has not reported it. It is now the size of a child of six, after ten months; it has her eyes, though it cannot have; it calls her Mother and asks to be taken to see the Sill. Sabeth knows exactly what she must do. She has walked to Tarnbrow eleven times with the knife-case. She wants someone else to make her choose. She is Wenna Thrale’s master, and the likeliest way a party meets her is in the room.

Ambrose, the Eldest Infant

Born twelve years ago in a Kest weaver’s house with a white beard to his chest and a full vocabulary, Ambrose was eighty at birth by the look of him, and is now perhaps sixty: his beard is iron-grey, his back has straightened, and his voice has lost its quaver. He is courteous, learned, faintly amused, and smells of camphor and warm milk. He claims to remember being Vey’s left eye, and describes the Meal from inside the pot: the heat, the ladle, the caul lifting off above him like a sky. He is getting younger, and he says that when he reaches the cradle it will be time. He tutors Caul-line children and receives visitors who want to know what the god saw. His fear is that he will forget, at the end, what he was born to say.

Hester Lowe

A clay-digger’s widow of Rudge, thirty-four, broad, sunburned, with a cleft chin and a laugh like a crow. Three years ago she bore a hand: only a hand, left, healthy, warm, the size of a grown woman’s, with a ring-finger callus nobody can explain. She did not call the Attendance. She hides it from the Lying-In and the Assemblers both, in a lined bread-crock under the hearthstone, and she feeds it warm milk through the skin of the palm, and talks to it while she works. It holds her finger at night. It strains, always, toward the east, toward Kest and the Barn, and she wakes to find it at the crock’s lip, fingers hooked over. Her fear is the morning she will find it gone. She will kill anyone who comes for it, and keeps a clay-spade sharpened for the purpose. Her secret: twice now, the hand has written, in flour, a word she cannot read.

Hester Lowe Threat 3 · Flesh 14 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (clay-spade 4) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Dov Marrin, Assembler-Prime

A former shepherd-surgeon, fifty-five, mild, balding, bespectacled, smelling of tallow and catgut, with a gentle voice for frightened mothers and very clean nails. He has fitted together four hundred Parts from four hundred families into one figure, eleven feet long, lying on a bed of warm straw at the far end of the Barn. It breathes. It is missing a left hand and a voice. Dov is devout, patient, and absolutely certain; he speaks of the figure as “Herself” and of each Part by the name of its bearer. He wants the hand, the voice, and the god’s easy birth. His fear is that the figure’s head has turned toward the Sill without him.

Brother Callum Stillwater

Abbot of the Barren Order, fifty, grey-robed, gaunt and gentle, with a soft tenor voice and the careful gait of a man whose sutures are renewed every nine days. He was cut at twenty, by choice, after watching his sister deliver three things in one winter. He preaches that the kindest thing a person can do is start nothing, and he has never had so many listeners; on the rim of the Dilation, at each pang, he stands and reads the names of the struck-through. He is kind to everyone he meets and he is not lying when he says he loves them. His fear is that his old wounds are opening differently now: this month, at the pang, his long-closed scar opened and something on the other side of it said his name in his sister’s voice.

Brother Callum Stillwater Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 12 · Attack +3 (staff 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

General Tibb

Commander of the Foundling Companies, born six years ago in a Cleave lambing-shed as a grown man of thirty, mid-stride, already reaching for a sword that was not there. He is tall, red-bearded, scarred from wounds nobody gave him, with a voice that fills a drill-yard and a brilliant tactical mind that seems to have been born ready. He has no childhood, and he is a better father to his two thousand born-grown than any of them will have. He speaks plainly and laughs often. His private terror is the day he turns seven, the age at which three of his best captains went home, overnight, to the cradle.

Lark Ninedays, the Counter

She times the pangs for the state with a water clock and a bell from a bare room atop the Tally-house in Kest. Fifty-two, wiry, chapped-lipped, with a ring of red notches tattooed around her left wrist, one for each name. She was named Lark Thirtydays at birth. She has changed her name every time the interval shortened and has been Lark Twentydays, Lark Fourteendays, Lark Elevendays; her friends no longer know what to call her. She sleeps beside the clock. She fears the day she will have to take the name Lark Oneday, and has sworn on her mother’s brick that she will not take the name after that.

Oneday. Then nothing. I’ll not take a name with no number in it.
Lark Ninedays, to her mother’s brick

Madder Rudge

An old clay-digger of sixty-nine and head of the watch at the Dilation, a stumpy woman with hands stained permanently red to the elbow and a pipe she smokes upside down against the steam. She has sat at the rim for twenty years. She lies on her belly at its lip each night with her ear to the clay and says the hole has a pulse, and that lately there is a second one under it, faster and smaller. She is blunt, profane, and kind to pilgrims. Her secret is that she has been down. Ninety feet on a rope, in 629, and she touched something warm and smooth that moved under her hand, and she has never told anyone that it moved toward her.

Josiah Fenn, the Man Who Bore

A shepherd of fifty-one, rangy, sun-black, with a pucker of scar over his navel that he keeps wrapped. Eight years ago he labored for three days in a hill bothy and delivered something that stood up, looked at him with great tenderness, and walked out of the door. He has been following its tracks ever since. They are getting larger; the last set he measured was the length of a cart. He talks about it the way a father talks about a son who went to sea. He fears that when he catches it, it will not remember him. He fears more that it will.

Agnes Latch, the Doorwright

She builds doors meant to stay shut in a country where none do. Forty-five, deaf in one ear from her forge, sawdust in her braids, she works in iron-bound bog oak with locks of nine wards and hinges set in poured lead, and knocks on each one for a full day before she sells it. Her best work held for nineteen days. Customers travel from Kest to buy even one quiet night. She is proud, rude and expensive. Her secret is that she has studied the Sill, measuring it from a distance through a glass, and that every one of her best doors was built to its pattern.

Duchess Iphigene Morwen

Head of the highest Caul-line house, fifty, she has lived her whole life inside the membrane she was born in. It has grown with her: a grey-pink veil, glistening, that covers her head and shoulders and moves when she breathes, through which her features are visible only as a pale blur and a darker mouth. She sees the future through it, blurred, and it has lately gone red. She speaks slowly, in a voice wet and muffled, and her prophecies are listened to by the Veiled Council in silence. She is in the Course; she carries almost continuously, and the house’s nurses take away what she delivers before she can ask. She fears the red. Her consort is Lord Casimir Morwen.

Dolour Pym, the Wet-Nurse

A huge, slow, soft-spoken woman of fifty-eight who has been in milk without pause for thirty years. She feeds what no one else will. The Attendance sends her the births it permits but cannot look at, and she takes them into her cottage behind the Lying-In wall, a warm dim place full of cradles and baskets and a smell of milk and wet wool. She loves all of them. Several have never let go: there are small mouths on her that have not left her in years, and she moves about the cottage carefully, singing. She meets the characters when something they rescued needs a home. She fears nothing for herself; she fears the Lying-In will one day want her children back.

Ede and Ada Crewe

Sisters of nineteen and twenty, born a year apart, who are by every test the same child born twice: one memory, one set of scars (both have the burn on the left palm that Ede got at four, a year before Ada was born), one mind in two bodies. They finish each other’s sentences because there is only one sentence. They work as scriveners for the Tally, copying in tandem, each writing half a line. They are charming, quick, and eerie. Their fear is that one of them will die first. Their secret is that, lately, a third girl in Cleave has started finishing their sentences too.

Rufus Ochre, the Tallyman

Keeper of the public ledger, sixty, ink-stained, myopic, a man of columns who loves the Tally like a garden. By his figures, eleven hundred more people were born last year than were carried by anyone or anything. He would like to know where they are. He has started following the unaccounted at night, by their entries, and has found three of them so far, born-grown, walking north in a line, who would not answer questions. He wants the arithmetic to close. He fears it will.

Sister Maeve Cord of the Uncut

Mother of Cords, forty-one, tall, broad-hipped and deep-voiced, still joined to her mother by thirty yards of living cord that loops behind her on a wicker carriage pushed by two Grafted acolytes. Her mother has been dead for six years. The cord has not noticed. It still pulses, still warm, and her mother’s body, bricked in a long low tomb in Cordway with a slot left for the cord, has not decayed. Maeve leads the Uncut with great warmth and great stubbornness. She feels, through the cord, things she will not name.

Marshal Gideon Breech

Commander of the border, fifty-six, iron-grey, a former Foundling drill-mother turned soldier, with a face like an old saddle and a stillness people mistake for patience. His men check every traveler leaving for signs of carrying. He has turned back two thousand, and once let one through. He has never said why. Secret: she was his daughter, carrying, and the Tally of that year shows a birth at Breech’s Gate to a woman in the Fatlands. He has never asked what was born.

Petra Quick

A smuggler of thirty-eight, lean and freckled, quick-tongued, Rim Road-born, who runs expectant mothers across the border so they can deliver somewhere the rule does not hold. It does hold, she has found. The country goes with them: across the Rim, in a Fatlands barn or an Oathen cave, the ground under the birthing woman turns warm and red. Petra keeps running them anyway, because they ask, and because once, in Brinehollow, it worked, and she would like very much to know why.

Petra Quick Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 15 · Attack +6 (knife 2, crossbow 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Queen Dowager Sibyl Aubrey, and the King Within

She has been carrying the heir for forty-four years. She is ninety, hugely swollen, very tired, borne on a padded litter by eight women, and gracious in the vague way of the long-exhausted. The King Within, Aldous the Ninth, rules by kicks: one for yes. The Chamberlain reads the questions. She is the only person who knows that he has recently begun to answer questions nobody asked: three kicks, then one, then three, at night, over and over. She thinks he is counting the interval. She thinks he is counting down.

One kick, yes. Three, then one, then three, at night, and nobody asked him anything.
a bearer of the Queen Dowager’s litter, drunk, in the Coppers

Dr. Lazar Voss

A visiting anatomist from the Vigil, sleepless and precise, forty-four, with bloodshot lidless-trained eyes, a rattle of rouse-pills in his pocket, and impeccable manners. He has examined two hundred Parts and drawn the figure they would make. It has more than two of several things. His drawings show something that is not human and is not the Assemblers’ Herself either: a shape with hands at the end of every limb, doors in its chest, and a head that is mostly mouth. He is selling copies to the Second Table. He has begun to dream, which a man of the Vigil should not survive.

Juniper Dell, called Firstword

A girl of eight from Tarnbrow, small and solemn, who was born saying half a sentence and has never said anything else: “When it opens, tell them that the...” She says it in the morning, and when frightened, and when asked her name. Somewhere in the highlands, she is sure, there is someone born with the other half. She writes and draws normally; what she draws is always doors. She is cared for by her mother and closely watched, without her mother’s knowledge, by the Assemblers.

Old Hinge, Keeper of the Sill

He tends the standing door on the hill, oils it, and measures the gap. He is perhaps eighty, bent and bald, with knuckles like walnuts, and he lives in a turf hut a hundred paces downhill with his back to the door. He has never looked through it. He says he does not need to, because most nights something on the other side describes the view: a long room, warm, with a table laid, and a great many chairs, and one of them pulled out. He tells it to visitors in a pleasant dry voice. He fears the night it stops describing and asks him to come and see.

It’s a long room, it says, and warm, and the table’s laid. One chair’s out. I said who’s that for. It said, no hurry.
Old Hinge, to visitors at the Sill

New Characters

Wenna Thrale, the Apprentice

Twenty, freckled, red-knuckled from the laundries, apprentice to Sabeth Thorne in her third year of the apron. She wrote the testimony that opens this chapter. She keeps, against all rule, a list of the struck-through she has carried, with a name she gave each one on the walk to the Low Wall. There are thirty-one. She wants to be an Opinion. She is afraid that she will be good at it.

Lord Casimir Morwen, the Consort

Husband of the Duchess Iphigene, forty-seven, veiled like her, slender, soft-spoken, with exquisite manners and a perfume of orris and something sour beneath. He is a Morwen born; the Cutwrights’ locked volume records his parentage in shorthand beside hers, and nobody at Morwen Hall would dream of asking what it says. He is deep in the Course and carries more than his wife does. He wants an heir with a thicker veil than any before. He fears he has already borne it, and that the nurses did not take it away.

Absalom Gage, the Bricklayer

The chief mason of the Stillyard, sixty, white with lime-dust, deaf in both ears, with a trowel worn to a sliver. For forty years he has bricked the dead and the condemned and, nightly, the cautious of Kest into their rooms; he knows who sleeps where better than the Tally does. He has begun to hear knocking from inside walls he laid, which, being deaf, he should not. He knocks back. He does not tell anyone what the knocks say.

Tamsin Gorse, the Stitch-Mender

A surgeon of thirty-six who runs the Reopening Ward at Kest, where old soldiers, cut-for-stone widows and Barren brothers come each morning after a pang to be sewn up. Brisk, cheerful, gallows-witted, smelling of spirit and catgut. Last month her own childhood scar, from a fall on a hay-hook, opened during a pang, and in the mirror she saw an eye looking out of it. She closed it with nine stitches. She checks it hourly.

Factor Merriam Toll of the Rim Road Company

The Company’s buyer at Breech’s Gate, fifty, stout, owlish and courteous, from Oathen originally, conditional in all her speech. She buys highland cauls by the crate for export to Brinehollow, where one sewn into a sailor’s coat is believed to stop the Calling; she pays well and asks nothing. Lately the Caul-lines have been selling her their own. She has noticed that the cauls arriving now are warm when they are packed, and warmer when they arrive.

Grisel Ashe, Mother of the Lip

Fifty-two, tall, cropped grey hair, a long bony face weathered red by twenty years of walking the Rudge ravines as a parish Attendant. In 637 she asked the First Question of something in a clay-digger’s house and it asked her back, in her dead mother’s voice, what are you? She put her knife-case down on the table and walked to the Dilation, and has been there since. She smells of warm clay and birth-water and speaks to everyone in the cadence of the birthing-room, there now, nearly done. She believes, with an Opinion’s terrible clarity, that the land is a mother in an obstructed labor and that the Attendance has been too cowardly in six centuries to help it. She weeps through every Unknotting, and thinks this proves she is right. She fears the god will be born and she will not have been in the room.

Grisel Ashe — Mother of the Lip
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 3 · Lung 2 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 6
SkillsStitching 4, Blades 4, Persuade 4, Rites 3, Resolve 3, Instinct 3, Endure 2
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 15 · Armor 0 · Fray 6
Attacksbirthing-knife +8 (2); a precise cut to an opening ignores Armor
GiftsThe First Question (as Orla Kest’s Question, once per scene); What Is Opened Once (with a touch and a Partake, reopens every healed wound a target has had: 1 Flesh per Injury plus 1d6, ignoring Armor; her own scars open in sympathy, 2 Flesh); Midwife’s Voice (anyone in false labor or carrying who hears her speak must roll Caul + Resolve vs Hard 14 or do as she bids for a round)
WantsAttend (Hard 14); Begin (Hard 14; she cannot let a labor, of a body or a land, stall in her presence)
Dread3 (to watch her at work at the rim; she is kind the whole time)
SecretShe is carrying, at the Brink, and the voice in her crowning is the one that asked her what she was. When it tells her to unknot herself at the rim, she will, and the Daughters will sing.

Daughter of the Lip Threat 2 · Flesh 11 · Guard 12 · Attack +5 (little knives 2, attack in pairs) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 · they hum the counting-song while they fight and never stop at sixty

Lady Ysolde Calloway of the Veiled Council

The present head of House Calloway, sixty-one, carried in a litter of black wicker, veiled in a membrane so thick it creaks. In lamplight, from the left, you can make out two faces in it: hers, and the small, still, wet-eyed one the Attendant answered at her birth, which stayed in the veil anyway and has grown with her. For sixty years it was silent. Since the veils went red it speaks in Council, in a high clear voice, always after Ysolde and always disagreeing, and it has been right four times. Ysolde is dry, sardonic, a superb reader of spring-rents, and the only veiled head who speaks of her house’s history with open disgust. She has refused three cousins the Council chose for her, and she is paying someone to steal and burn the Cutwrights’ locked volume.

Lady Ysolde Calloway Threat 4 · Flesh 9 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (none; her wardens carry poleaxes) · Armor 0 · Dread 3 (to hear the second voice answer the first)

Hobb Marl, Slot Four Hundred and Nine

A mason of Mortar Rise, forty-seven, whose testimony is given under Crime and Punishment above. He will talk to anyone who brings bread to the slot, and after eight years of listening he is the best source in Kest on what happens inside the walls after a pang.

Hobb Marl Threat 3 · Flesh 8 (starved) · Guard 8 · Attack none (bricked) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (to see the eye at the slot)

Sister Avis Fallow, Keeper of the Lamps

The Grey Sister of Greystead, fifty-eight, who lived through the Grey Winter and wrote its register. Small, quiet, touching the wall as she walks as if counting stones, she trims thirty-two lamps in thirty-two empty cells every night and speaks to each by name. She is not in despair, she tells visitors; only very tired. Her secret is that she began to carry this Grace, through her sutures, and is counting.

Sister Avis Fallow Threat 3 · Flesh 10 · Guard 11 · Attack +2 (staff 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Joss Tanner, Carrier of the Barn

An Assembler Seamster of thirty from Cleave, freckled, eager and painfully thin, who bears on the inside of his left forearm a born right hand sewn there by Dov Marrin in Plenty. It is warm, its pulse a half-beat behind his, and it reaches for things he has not looked at: knife-handles, latches, the sleeves of pretty strangers. He dreams of its bearer, a Rudge widow he has never met, and knows things about her kitchen. He does not yet know that when the hand is cut away, the place on his arm will begin to bear.

Joss Tanner Threat 2 · Flesh 12 · Guard 13 · Attack +5 (shearing-knife 2; the borne hand grapples at +4) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 (to see the hand reach on its own)

Attendance Opinion Threat 3 · Flesh 12 · Guard 14 · Attack +7 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Border Marshal Threat 2 · Flesh 13 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (spear 4) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Assembler Gatherer Threat 2 · Flesh 11 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (hook 2) · Armor 1 · Dread 0
