The Honest Age

For two centuries after the Supper, Oathen was the conscience of the Table. Other lands discovered they had swallowed monstrous gifts; Oathen discovered it had swallowed honesty, and sold it. A treaty sworn in Tacit could not be broken without the signatories’ bodies breaking too; a merchant house that swore its weights at the Ledger could be trusted to the crumb. Oathen grew rich on notarizing the world. The canyon cities filled with foreign envoys learning to keep quiet.

It was not a kind age. Children broke constantly on promises they did not understand, and the cemeteries of the period are full of small, oddly shaped bones. In 215 A.G. the Bench passed the Muzzling, and the canyons have been quiet in a new way since: the silence of the nursery.

The bones in the children’s galleries of the old Vaults are not arranged by family. They are arranged by what broke. Nobody alive remembers why. Everybody who sees it understands.
Old Sabra Wends, Eldest Keener

The Mute Succession

The old kings spoke, and every word bound them. By 330 A.G. King Orrel the Fourth had sworn so many coronation oaths and treaty-clauses that he ruled his last years from a litter, his body folded into what his physicians called an exact map of his reign’s contradictions. Thereafter the crown passed only to children who had never spoken. Nine such kings have reigned, and all died with their silence intact.

The Vanthe Oath

The Vanthes ate the tip of Tolm’s tongue, the part that touches the teeth, and they have always been the quickest-spoken and the soonest-broken of the high houses. In 312 A.G., when a Vanthe daughter married into the Esks and the Cutwrights reported that her children had the stronger godsign of the two houses, the Vanthe matriarch, Lady Orsa, went down to the Witnessing Vaults with her whole house behind her, laid her hand on the bones of her husband, and swore, at Weight 5, on the dead: The tongue shall not leave this house.

The Bench has argued ever since about whether a living woman can bind her unborn descendants. The Vanthes do not argue. Every Vanthe who has tried to marry outside the house since 312 has broken at the mouth on the wedding morning, the tongue splitting to its root, and the Testimony of Lady Orsa’s husband has been heard from his niche in the Vaults eleven times, each time saying the oath in a dead man’s voice, loud enough to be heard on the Sunward Wall. So the Vanthes marry Vanthes. They have married cousins, and then the children of cousins, and then, the Ledger’s register of marriages implies in a column nobody reads aloud, nearer than cousins. One entry, for 589, records the marriage of Lady Ammet Vanthe to Corvel Vanthe, and beside it, in the Cutwrights’ small grey marginal hand, pressed so hard the nib went through the page, two words: same mother.

The Vanthes are beautiful in the same way, all of them: narrow, very pale, with the house’s grey eyes and the house’s habit of tilting the head when listening. Their children reach the Taste in the cradle. Many are born with their mouths sealed over with a membrane of skin and must be cut open before they can feed, and the house physician does it in silence with a silver knife and stitches nothing, because the god’s tongue must have its door. Some of the sealed ones do not take the knife well. The Vanthe children’s gallery in the Vaults is long. The house does not receive guests for supper, and its servants are hired from Sheathmouth, where people are used to not saying what they have seen.

You never ask a Vanthe who their father is. Not because it’s rude. Because they’d have to think about it.
overheard on the Tenth Bridge, in handtalk, and the hands were broken a month later; nobody knows if it was the god or the house

The Oath in Sworn Gorge

In the drought summer of 419 A.G., something was shouted in a narrow ravine east of Tacit, and the ravine has never stopped saying it. The records of that year are incomplete: a page is cut from the Bench’s minutes and a stretch of the Ledger has been chiselled smooth, very carefully, in a way that took weeks. What is known is that the people of the hamlet of Sowe, at the gorge’s mouth, were all found broken the following spring, every one of them, in the same way, and that the shape of the Breaking was so terrible that the Echo-Wardens’ charter forbids its description. The gorge was walled. The murmur goes on.

The Forsworn Riots

By 506 the Breakdowns held forty thousand broken people, and the Bench passed the Ruling of Visible Marks, requiring every Forsworn to bare their broken part above the third tier. The broken came up the stairs on crutches and wheeled boards, swearing on broken ground that they would burn the Galleries, and the Watch could swear nothing back. Then they cut nine of the lowest bridges, with people on them. The Bench rescinded the Ruling by noon, and no Bench collector has gone down into the Breakdowns since.

Wending Pass

In 627 A.G. Reckoners out of the Fast came through the eastern canyons, and the four hundred soldiers of the Fourth Regiment of the Canyon Watch swore, in the old form, to hold Wending Pass to the death. Captain Renn Hold looked at the raiders and at his men, most of them nineteen, and ordered them to fall back. He kept his own oath by staying. They broke theirs by obeying. The sound came down the road like a rockfall, four hundred Breakings in a breath, each soldier opening at every joint by which he had bound himself to the place. They did not die of it, not at once. The Reckoners found the captain alone at the top with his sword drawn, looked at the road below him, and went back the way they had come.

I ordered them down because I loved them. I have had fourteen years to work out whether that was an oath.
[ Captain Renn Hold, to a drover, at the top of Wending Pass ]

Rule, Law and Politics

Oathen is ruled by the Mute Kings, chosen in infancy, bitted for life, and raised to rule by gesture. The present king, Ket the Ninth, has never made a sound. Beneath him sits the Bench of Clauses, forty-one lawyer-priests called Clausewrights, whose art is the drafting of promises that can survive contact with reality. In theory the Bench interprets the king. In practice the king nods, and the Bench spends a month in forty-page conditionals deciding what the nod meant, and then does what it would have done anyway.

There are no prisons. There is no need. A convicted person is made to swear the terms of their own sentence: “I will not leave the district of Low Dray for nine years.” “I will pay the widow one lack a day until my death.” “I will not speak again.” Breach the sentence and the body enforces it. The Bench’s chief tool of government is therefore not the sword but the clause, and its great fear is the sentence badly drafted, which leaves a convict free, or the sentence too well drafted, which kills him in a way the court did not intend. For the gravest crimes there is the Breaker, Jude Crake, who carries out death sentences with nothing but conversation.

SWORN SENTENCE, Question Court of the Shadeward, Carving 640. To be read aloud by the convict, Merrin Hask, water-thief and slayer, in its entirety, before the Court and a Keener, with a hand laid upon the bones of the slain, Doria Hask, her sister. Weight raised to 5 by the witness of the dead. Drafted by Under-Drafter Lise Amberd, reviewed by Clausewright Ennis Sarrow. Fee, 15 L, paid from the estate of the slain.

I, Merrin Hask, who took water from my sister’s share and struck her when she found me at it, and did not mean her to die of it, and she died of it,

swear on the bones of my sister Doria, under my hand,

that from the setting of this Plate I will not drink from any cistern of Tacit, nor any share sworn at the Rain Shrine, nor any water drawn by another for my sake, for the term of nine years;

that I will drink only from the river, as the Forsworn drink;

that I will carry, each day of the term, barring illness so grave that a Keener attests it, eleven buckets from the river to my sister’s widower’s door, which was the number of her share;

that I will not ask him for anything, nor speak to him unless he speak first;

that I will not leave the Breakdowns save to carry;

and that if I fail in any of this, I will hear my sister say so.

Barring death, which ends it. Barring the ruling of the Bench, which may lighten it. And for no other cause.

I have read it. It is what I mean.

(Marginal note, in the Keener’s hand: Read clean. No Exits taken but the two allowed. The widower, Joss Hask, attended, and did not speak, and at the last line put his hand on the convict’s shoulder, which the Court did not see, because it was not looking.)

Trials are simple. In a Breaking trial, presided over by Judge Thane Urrow, there is no evidence and no testimony. The accused repeats the promise they are alleged to have broken, aloud, in its original words, and the court watches. If they kept it, nothing happens. If they broke it, it breaks them again, now, in front of everyone. For crimes that are not oaths (theft, murder, arson), the accused is asked a single question: “Did you do it?” and must answer. A Forsworn who has nothing left to break in the mouth is a problem the Bench has never solved, which is why the Breakdowns are, to Tacit’s lasting horror, the one place in Oathen where a person can lie.

Oathen’s power abroad is trust. Every other government sends its treaties east to be made real, and the Rim Road Company swears every contract before its notary, Jessamy Quill. Oathen charges a tithe on every sworn page, and has never needed an army larger than its notaries. It has one anyway, the Canyon Watch, small and very well disciplined, because a soldier who has sworn to obey cannot do otherwise. Since Wending Pass, the Watch’s oath has been redrafted. It now runs to eleven pages, and the phrase “to the death” has been removed.

The Ninefold

In the upper gorges, where the ear-eating clans live and the Bench’s writ runs thin, there is an older justice, and it is a ritual killing. The Bench outlawed it in 377. The gorges did not notice.

When a kinsman kills a kinsman in the upper gorges and will not answer the question, the clan takes him to a narrows that throws back nine (every upper-gorge clan has one, and knows its count) and stands him in the place where the echo is cleanest. The dead one’s nearest kin stand above, on the rim. They call down to him the question, did you do it, and he must answer, and whatever he answers comes back nine times. If he says yes, the clan lets him live, sworn to exile on the bones. If he says no, and it is a lie, his mouth breaks, and then breaks again, and again, nine times, each Breaking landing on the last, and by the ninth there is no jaw, no tongue, no lips, and the throat has split down to the breastbone, and the clan on the rim watches in silence until the canyon is quiet. Then they go down and bring him up and lay him in the dead one’s niche, facing in. If he says nothing, they wait. The longest anyone has ever stood silent in a Ninefold narrows is four days. The clan stood on the rim for all of them.

The Ninefold is not cruel by the gorges’ reckoning. Nobody lays a hand on the accused. The god does everything. That is what the clans say, and the Bench, whose own Breaker sits down with the condemned and talks until they promise something, has never found a reply that it could make without hearing itself.

Down here we don’t kill a man. We ask him a question, and let the walls ask it again.
an elder of the Tallow-clan, upper Gullet, to a Bench inspector who did not return to Tacit with his tongue
Politics in a Sentence
  • The Bench wants the Kept Rain explained before the Tablenight silence ends, and has three drafts of a Sayer’s sentence ready.
  • The Forsworn want the Breakdowns made a free city, with its own Bench of the broken, and they have the numbers to cut Tacit’s bridges again.
  • The Rim Road Company wants Jessamy Quill kept whole at any cost, because if she breaks, half the trade of the Table comes unbound.
  • The Tongue-lines want an heir with a voice, and some of them want a Sayer of their own.
  • Highwell wants a stone carved with a girl’s name and the words “she brought the rain”. Its Rainwarden will not carve it, and will not say why.
  • The king wants to say something. He has wanted to for thirty-one years.

Culture and Daily Life

Speech and Silence

  • Handtalk. A sign language used for everything that matters little: prices, directions, the weather, gossip, jokes, flirtation. It is held not to bind. That belief is being tested, and fingers have started breaking. Oatheners sign with the left hand where they can, because it is the hand they can spare.
  • The bit. Children wear a soft leather muzzle until twelve, decorated by their parents with beads, ribbons and family marks. Having it removed is the coming of age, the Unbitting, and the first words spoken afterward are chosen with a Clausewright present. They are usually a family motto, or “I am here,” which is safe.
  • Conditional speech. “If able.” “As I now intend.” “Barring death, illness, or weather.” A polite sentence is mostly exits.
  • Insults. The worst thing you can call someone is “talkative.” The second worst is “certain.”
  • Proverbs. Oathen proverbs are short and verbless where possible: “Fewer words, more fingers.” “A full mouth, an empty hand.” “The canyon keeps the change.” “Listen twice.” “Say it to the dead, pay it to the living.” “Better bitted than broken.”

Food, Drink and Dress

Oatheners eat goat, canyon lizard, flatbread baked on hot stones, dried figs, and a sour green cheese aged in the river caves. Water is life and law: every household’s cistern-share is sworn yearly at the Rain Shrine, and stealing water is the only theft the Bench treats as a crime against the god. Meals are eaten in silence; the grace “Lack keep away” is signed, not said, unless there are foreigners at the table, in which case it is said very slowly with three exits attached. Wine is rare and feared, because drunkenness makes promises.

Dress is plain and close-fitting, in dust-red and ochre wool, with long sleeves to hide what broke. The Tongue-lines wear high collars and veils across the mouth, white for the unwed, black for those whose vows are many. Rings are worn on the thumbs as reminders of oaths outstanding: a ring per vow, so that a man’s hands tell you how much he owes. The Forsworn go bare where they broke, as a point of pride.

FIGS, DRIED, A CRUMB THE HANDFUL. FRESH THIS MORNING, I AM TOLD.
chalked on a stall-board in the Felt Market; the “I am told” is in a different hand, added after the bread-woman’s finger

Marriage and Kin

Marriage vows are negotiated for months and run to forty pages, covering fidelity, property, illness, absence, the care of each other’s dead, and what counts as “cherishing.” Divorce does not exist: a marriage vow cannot be unsworn, only broken, and its Breaking is the chest opened to the air. What the faithless do, and what the vows forbid in their thicket of clauses, the canyon decently does not discuss aloud. The Tongue-lines marry cousin to cousin to keep the god’s tongue in the family, and some old houses have married so close for so long that their children are born with mouths sealed over with skin, and must be cut open before they can feed.

FROM THE MARRIAGE CONTRACT OF TAMSIN ORLE, felt-maker of the Galleries, and BRANNOCK DELL, lift-hauler of the same, sworn at the Bench Terrace in the Plenty of 636. Forty-one pages. Drafted by Under-Drafter Wilm Esse at 5 L the page, the families sharing the cost. Extract, pages 17 to 19, read aloud by both parties on the wedding morning in the felted marrying-room of the Hall.

Article the Ninth: Of Cherishing.

9.1. Each party, as they now intend, shall cherish the other.

9.2. “Cherish” shall be read, for the purposes of this contract, as follows: to wish the other well; to act, where able and where it does not endanger the party’s children, kin or share, for the other’s good; to speak no ill of the other before a third person save in a court, a sickroom, or the Vaults.

9.3. “Cherish” shall not be read to require any feeling at any particular hour. The parties acknowledge that feeling is weather.

9.4. Should either party cease to wish the other well, they shall not be held to have broken this article for a period of one season, during which they shall be held to be “in Lack” and shall attempt, in good faith, a recovery of the wish.

9.5. Attempt is an oath of effort, and is kept by attempting.

Article the Tenth: Of the Bed.

10.1. Each party shall share a bed with no other living adult, barring the nursing of kin in fever, the sharing of warmth in a snowed pass, and any ruling of the Bench.

10.2. The word “living” in 10.1 is deliberate and was argued for nine days. See the annexed opinion of the Under-Drafter, page 38, which the parties have read and which neither shall be required to read aloud.

10.3. On the death of either party this article ends, and the survivor is free of it, and shall not be held to it by any reading, nor by any Testimony of the dead, and the dead party so agrees, here, now, aloud.

Article the Eleventh: Of Absence.

11.1. Neither party shall promise the other to be home by any hour.

11.2. Each party shall instead say, on leaving, “If able,” and the other shall answer “Go on,” and this exchange shall bind neither.

11.3. Should either party fail to come home for nine nights without word, the other may go to the Vaults and ask.

(Annexed note, in the Under-Drafter’s hand, page 38: Article 10.2 is included at the request of the bride’s mother, who was a Keener of the Vaults for thirty years, and who stated to the drafter, in handtalk, with her hands shaking, that she had found what she had found in the widowers’ galleries, and would not have her daughter’s husband find a reading of the word “bed” that the god would allow. The drafter has followed her instruction. The drafter has not asked what she found.)

Children

Children are bitted from the first tooth until twelve. They grow up in handtalk, which they speak faster and more inventively than adults, with a whole private slang of nursery signs. The bit is soft and does not hurt, but it shapes the face: Oathen adults have a groove worn at the corners of the mouth, and some of the old bits, family heirlooms, have been worn by six generations of children and taste of all of them. Every parent in the country carries one fear above all others: that their child will say something before twelve, in the instant the bit is off for cleaning. Some do. The Bench records the Breakings of children only by number. The number this year is higher than last.

The bitted have games of their own: the counting game of the ear and the knife; a game called Closed Hand in which the loser is the first to answer a question; and a cruel one, played in the lanes of the Galleries, in which one child signs a promise very slowly to another, and everyone watches to see if the fingers will break. It used to be a game about nothing. This year it is a game of courage, and mothers are beating it out of their children with the flat of their hands, silently, in doorways.

Careless Promises

It’s never the oaths that get you. It’s the little things you say on the stairs.
a gag-nurse of the Murmuring Tier

Most Breakings in Oathen are not crimes. They are accidents of speech: the small binding sentences that escape tired, frightened, loving or angry people, and that the god, which weighs meaning, does not forgive. When a character speaks carelessly, or when you want to show the country breaking around the PCs, roll on this table. The Weight given is the usual reading; the Breaking is what the Bench’s physicians most often record.

d20The careless promiseHow it usually breaks
1“I’ll be back before dark.” (said leaving for a day’s haul)Weight 1. The heels split on the doorstep at dusk, a hundred yards from home.
2“I could sleep for a week.”Weight 1 at the Course. The speaker does. Nobody can wake them until the seventh day.
3“Over my dead body.”Weight 3. The Bench has a whole file. Do not let a PC say it.
4“I’ll never speak to you again.” (in a quarrel between sisters)Weight 2. Broken at the reconciliation; the lips split as she says “I’m sorry”.
5“I’ll just be a minute.”Weight 1. A minute later the ankles crack, wherever the speaker is standing.
6“Cross my heart.” (a child, the bit off for washing)Weight 2. The breastbone cracks. The mother does not cry out.
7“I’d give anything for a drink.”Weight 2. The god takes the reading literally. Something is gone by morning; the speaker has to find out what.
8“I’ll take care of it.”Weight 2. Breaks if it is not taken care of; the palms split.
9“I’m fine.” (said to a worried husband, by a woman who is not)Weight 1, a lie. The lips split at the corners, a thin line. He sees it and says nothing.
10“I’ll love you forever.” (a foreigner at an inn)Weight 3. The foreigner did not know. The chest cracks at dawn. He leaves Oathen on a litter.
11“I won’t tell anyone.”Weight 2. The ears ring and bleed at the first telling; at Weight 3, the throat opens.
12“You’ll be the death of me.” (to a child)Weight 1, at the Course Weight 4. Do not let a PC say it.
13“I’ll pay you back tomorrow.”Weight 2. Fingers snap backward at the next dawn, one per lack still owed.
14“I’ll eat my own hat if...”Weight 1. He does. He cannot stop himself. It takes all night.
15“I’d die for you.” (a lover’s exaggeration)Weight 2–3. The breath stops for a minute when the chance comes and is not taken.
16“I’ll always be here.” (a mother at a sickbed)Weight 3. When she leaves the room at last to sleep, her tendons draw up and she cannot pass the door.
17“I’ll keep an eye on him.”Weight 2. When he comes to harm out of sight, the eyes bleed. At Weight 3 one eye goes.
18“I’ll never drink again.” (the morning after)Weight 2. The stomach cramps and the speaker vomits blood at the first cup.
19“I won’t let you fall.” (on a lift-rope or bridge)Weight 3. If the other falls, the arms snap at the elbows, still reaching.
20“Nothing could make me leave this city.”Weight 3. Binding until something does. Then the feet turn fully about, facing Tacit.

Death and the Dead

The dead are entombed upright in the Witnessing Vaults, faces outward, so that they may witness the oaths of the living. Before a body is set in its niche, the family gathers and speaks every promise they made to the dead person in life, and the Keener asks the corpse, formally, whether each was kept. The dead do not answer. Usually. A death in Oathen also releases the dead person’s oaths, which is why heirs sometimes wait at a bedside very patiently, and why the Bench has drafted a clause, standard in all wills, binding the heirs to have hoped for recovery.

Oaths sworn on the dead are the heaviest in the land: a hand on the bones, the dead one’s name, the vow said into the niche. They are used for blood feuds, for marriages across feuding families, for debts too large for any Surety. When such an oath breaks, the dead person answers for Tolm, and what the dead do then is the stuff of every Oathen ghost story, and all of them are true.

The Desecrators

Where there is an oath on the dead, there is someone who wants the dead gone. The trade is old and the Keeners hate it above all others: bone-lifting, the theft of a witness from its niche, by an oathbreaker who hopes that a dead one who is no longer in the Vaults can no longer Testify. It does not work. Bones lifted from the Vaults Testify from wherever they are taken: from the bottom of the Hushwater, from a lime-pit in Knot Canyon, from under a hearthstone in the Galleries, where in 602 a family sat at supper above the grandmother they had sworn on and heard her say their oath up through the floor. The Keeners know this. The desperate do not, or will not believe it.

The worst of the desperate go further. There is a belief, old in the upper gorges and spreading in the Breakdowns, that a witness swallowed cannot speak: that an oathbreaker who grinds the bones of the dead they swore on into flour and bakes it into bread and eats it, alone, at night, in silence, has taken the witness inside, where the god cannot hear it. The Keeners call the practice eating the witness. They know of nineteen cases since 500. In every one, the dead Testified anyway, from inside: their voice coming up out of the oathbreaker’s own belly, muffled and wet, speaking the oath aloud in a crowded place, while the oathbreaker clutched at their stomach and the people around them backed away.

We tell the families, the dead will speak from wherever you put them. If you put them in your mouth, that is where they will speak from.
a Keener of the Witnessing Vaults

The Keeners also guard the widowers’ galleries, where the dead of marriages are set facing each other across a narrow aisle, and where, once in a generation, a niche is found empty, and the empty niche belongs to a wife whose husband swore her a vow of the bed, and was a very literal man. The Keeners go up to the house with lamps. What they find there is never entered in any record, and the Bench’s ruling of 503, that a vow of the bed ends at death, was drafted in a single afternoon after one such visit, and is read aloud now at every Tongue-line wedding.

Festivals

  • The Kept Rain (first day of Grace). The whole country stands in the open, faces up, mouths bitted, and the rain comes. Children take their first swim. Lovers make the year’s vows in the downpour, when the noise of it hides the words from the canyon. This year, for three days, the whole country stood and waited, and the sky stayed white.
  • The Unbitting (Plenty). Twelve-year-olds have their bits removed in public, in the Hall of Conditions, and speak their first chosen words. Families weep, silently.
  • The Carving of the Year (Carving). The new vows of public record are cut into the Ledger. Carvers work through the night by lamplight, and the town watches from the canyon floor.
  • The Night of Ears (the eve of Tablenight). Pilgrims walk the Gullet barefoot and lay their ears to the warm sand.
  • Tablenight (longest night of Lack). Twenty-four hours in which no one in the country makes a sound. Shops close. Bells are tied. Babies are nursed constantly. It is the only day Oatheners feel safe, and the happiest day of the year. Couples who have not touched in years hold hands in the street. Enemies sit at one table. Nothing can be promised, so nothing can be broken, and for one day, the canyons say, everybody is whole.

Crime and Punishment

Every crime in Oathen is either an oath broken or a question waiting to be asked: a convict swears a sentence, a debtor a schedule, and a murderer, if the crime is grave, receives Jude Crake. Blasphemy, the cursing of Tolm aloud, is not punished by the Bench at all; it is merely recorded, as Tolm will see to it. Of forty-one blasphemers entered in the record since the Muzzling, thirty-nine were found the next morning with their tongues gone, not cut but missing, as if never grown, and their mouths full of fine red sand. The other two were Sayers. No one has entered their sentences in the record.

Factions

The Bench of Clauses

The Clausewrights: rulers in practice, and the finest contract lawyers who have ever lived. They train for twenty years in the drafting of vows, in the reading of Tolm’s past judgments on the Ledger, and in the art of speaking a whole day without committing to anything. They believe that the Rule is law and that law can be perfected: that somewhere there is a sentence so well drafted that it binds exactly what is intended and nothing more. They want order, the Rain explained, the Sayers kept, and their own power left untouched. They fear the Forsworn, the widening of what counts, and their own Tongue-line blood, which is the most advanced in the land.

RankTitleGrants
1Slate-ClerkCopies drafts; access to the Bench’s lower archives.
2Under-DrafterDrafts minor contracts; a fee of 5 lacks per sworn page.
3ClausewrightSpeaks before the Bench; may witness oaths in the king’s name.
4BencherA vote; a seat in the Hall of Conditions; access to the Ledger’s sealed rooms.
5Chief ClausewrightInterprets the king; drafts the Sayers’ sentences.

A PC joins by passing the Examination of Exits (Tongue + Clause vs Grim, under a Clausewright’s hostile questioning for a full day without a binding misstep). Enemies: the Forsworn, the Second Table’s agents among the Tongue-lines. Allies: the Rim Road Company, the Cutwrights’ College.

Q: Is the sky white? A: It appears so, from where I am seated, at this hour, to these eyes. Q: Good. Next question.
from the Examination of Exits, first hour

The Forsworn

The broken. They live in the Breakdowns, organized, angry, and with very little left to lose. A Forsworn who broke their hands cannot be broken in the hands again; a Forsworn with an opened mouth can lie without further cost. The Breakdowns have made a politics of this. Led by Brakk, the Forsworn swear loudly and freely on what is already broken, take jobs no whole Oathener can, and run the canyon’s smuggling, lying and loud-mouthed trades. They want the Breakdowns made a free city, the end of public shaming, and a share of the Rim Road tithe. Some want much worse: they want everyone in Tacit broken, so that no one is better than anyone.

RankTitleGrants
1CrackedShelter in the Breakdowns; a meal a day from the common pot.
2Broken-inA trade: liar-for-hire, loud-crier, smuggler.
3Open-HandCommand of a lane; a vote at the Gathering of the Broken.
4SplintOne of Brakk’s council; access to the Breakdowns’ arms.
5VoiceSpeaks for the Breakdowns to the Bench.

A PC joins by breaking an oath in public, or by already being broken. Enemies: the Bench, the Echo-Wardens. Allies: the Purgation, which preaches that breaking is a step toward vomiting up the god.

The Sureties

Professionals who take on other people’s oaths for a fee and carry the risk in their own bodies. A Surety swears, before the principal’s oath is made, to stand behind it: if the principal breaks, the Surety breaks in their place. Sureties are licensed by the Compact of 148, tattooed with the oaths they carry in a dense fine script, and among the richest commoners in the land. They are also, inevitably, ruins. A Surety in the trade for twenty years has usually paid on a dozen defaults and carries them all. They believe in the arithmetic of risk; they want fees, fair principals, and a quiet death before the next default. They fear one bad season.

RankTitleGrants
1BondlingCarries Weight 1–2 oaths; fees of 2–10 lacks.
2UnderwriterCarries Weight 3 oaths; a seat in the Surety House.
3BondsmanCarries Weight 4 oaths, including marriages; a private physician.
4Great SuretyCarries treaties and Company contracts; a house on the Sunward Wall.
5Master of the CompactSets fees and refuses principals for the whole trade.

A PC joins by carrying a first oath (see Sureties, below) and surviving the year. Enemies: Grandam Cess, defaulters. Allies: the Rim Road Company, the Bench.

When a Surety dies, the Compact flays the script from her and binds it into a book, and the book goes on the shelf of the Surety House with the others. It is the only library on the Table written entirely in other people’s debts.
Envoy Dorian Sayce, in a letter he did not send

The Quiet

An ascetic order that has given up speech entirely, some by vow and some by knife. Founded in 240 A.G. by Abbess Hollin Mure, the Quiet live in cliff-cells along the upper Gullet and teach, in writing, that speech is the god’s fishing line, and every word a hook. They want silence: first for themselves, then for Oathen, and in their secret texts, for the whole Table. Sister Verity Amn has brought a terrible new teaching: that for the highest bloodlines, even thought now binds, and that the knife is not enough.

RankTitleGrants
1HushedShelter; a slate and chalk; the Quiet’s protection.
2SealedHas taken the vow of speech; may teach handtalk novices.
3TonguelessHas taken the knife; immune to Breakings of the tongue.
4StillmindLearns the disciplines of empty thought.
5Abbess of the QuietWrites the order’s teachings.

A PC joins by a vow of silence (Weight 4) or by the knife. Enemies: the Forsworn, who mock them. Allies: the Echo-Wardens.

The Echo-Wardens

Rangers who police the silent gorges and hunt down old sworn words still bouncing in the deep rock. An oath can live in a canyon for decades, flying from wall to wall, binding everyone who walks through it; the Wardens track such echoes by ear, map them, and kill them with felt baffles, wool dams, sand-falls and, for the worst, controlled rockfall. They are deaf in one ear by tradition (the right, cut at their initiation) and listen with the other like hunting dogs. They want the canyons clean of old words. They fear Sworn Gorge.

RankTitleGrants
1BafflerCarries felt and wool; a Warden’s ration.
2ListenerLicensed to enter posted gorges; the half-deafening.
3TrackerLeads echo-hunts; a horn of signal-silence.
4Gorge-WardenCommands a district; may seal a canyon by order.
5Warden of the WallKeeps the post at Sworn Gorge.

A PC joins by apprenticeship and the cutting of the right ear. Enemies: smugglers who use echoes to bind pursuers. Allies: the Quiet, the Bench.

Powers from Abroad

The Rim Road Company is the great foreign power in Oathen, operating from Quillhouse under Jessamy Quill. The Cutwrights’ College keeps a small, sharp-eyed office in Tacit and knows exactly which Tongue-lines are nearest the Brink. The Purgation preaches among the Forsworn that a broken body is a body vomiting up the god. The Second Table has agents in at least three Tongue-line houses, and an interest in Sayers that needs no explaining. The Reckoners have not come through the canyons since Wending Pass; they know Renn Hold is still at the top.

Oathen Now

The rain was late, which means a god’s promise has slipped, which should not be possible. Handtalkers are starting to break. A scribe has found evidence that written words now bind. If the Regrowth is widening what counts as speech, soon there will be nothing an Oathener can safely say, sign, write, or perhaps think. And the Bench is debating, in forty-page conditionals, whether to take the bit out of a Sayer and have her fix it.

Meanwhile the Forsworn are counting. The Breakdowns have doubled in five years, swollen by handtalkers with broken fingers and scribes with split palms, and Brakk now speaks for a fifth of the capital. The Company has tripled the guard on Quillhouse. Lady Imre Dath, in her gold, is writing, and no one is quite sure on what.

The Girl at the Stone

On the first day of Grace in 641, the high basin of Highwell stood bitted and faced the sky, and the sky stayed white. On the second day it stayed white. An old man died on his feet and his sons held him upright. On the second night, in the Rain Shrine, by lamplight, the elders of the eleven Rain-keeper lines met without their Rainwarden, because Yusra Thole had stopped speaking and would not sign to them about anything but the cisterns. They talked. They had a Lack-era rite in the oldest of the Tally-books, from before the Gorging, when the canyon had tried everything to make the god’s ears open again: the Heart’s Due. When the rain will not come, the rite says, the god’s heart wants a heart.

Before the lot was drawn, every unwed Heart-line adult of the basin between eighteen and thirty, forty-one of them, was made to swear at the Shrine, at Weight 4, before the elders: If the lot is mine, I will go to the stone. It was the old form. Nobody refused, because refusing in front of the whole basin, with the cisterns cracking, was a thing nobody there could do. The lot fell to Hallie Corr, twenty-two, a shepherd, Heart-line on her mother’s side, whose pulse was so slow that her friends used to lay their fingers on her throat as a game, to count how long they had to wait.

She went to the stone at dawn on the third day because she had sworn to. The elders did it with the bronze knife of the Shrine, in silence, as the rite required, and laid her heart in the dry bed of Hollow Cistern, and stood back. Yusra Thole stood at the edge of the ring through all of it, and watched, and did not move, and did not sign. Six hours later, the first cloud came over the basin rim. By noon it was raining as it had always rained, warm and heavy, the canyons roaring, the cisterns filling, the water running red and then clear out of Hollow Cistern, and the whole of Highwell knelt in the flood and wept with relief and gratitude, and the elders said to each other in handtalk, she brought it.

She did not. Yusra Thole knows, from the Tally and from her own slowing pulse, that the rain was never late; that Tolm’s year has grown three days longer; that the rain was coming on that third day whether a girl went to the stone or not, and to the hour. The sacrifice was demanded and given, and it bought nothing. And Yusra cannot say so, because to say so is to say what the god’s longer year means, and she has not been able to make herself say that to anyone. So she says nothing, and the basin has raised a new uncarved stone outside the ring, the height of a young woman, and wants it carved Hallie Corr, who brought the rain, and the elders have begun, quietly, drafting the oath for next year’s lot. The Heart’s Due is in the Tally again, after six hundred and forty years. If nobody tells Highwell the truth, it will be in it every year the rain is late, and the rain will be late every year from now on, a little later each time.

Her mother has gone up to sit by the stone every day since. She doesn’t say anything. Nobody up there says anything now. You’d think they’d be happy. They got their rain.
Ash Merrow, Rain-Deputy of Highwell, to a stranger

The Stilling of Corder's Gallery

It wasn’t a curse. That’s what I want you to understand. Nobody did anything to them. They just stopped.
Dacey Furl, night-sister of the Murmuring House

Corder’s Gallery was forty doors on the eleventh tier of the Shadeward, rope-makers and their families, poor and close and kind. In the Grace of 640, a rope-maker named Isk Corder, at the Course, woke in the night and said to his wife, in the dark, half asleep: “I can’t say anything any more without it being true.” It was true. It had been true for a month; the Taste and the Appetite had run through him fast that year, as they were running fast through everyone. But now he had said it, at the Course, and it was more true than before, and in the morning he found that he could not say anything at all, about anything, that did not immediately happen.

He stopped speaking. That was sensible. His wife stopped speaking too, to keep him company, and because she was afraid that whatever was in him was in her. Their neighbours, who loved them, began to keep a silence around their door, and then in the gallery outside it, and then, because the god was widening that year and everyone in Tacit could feel it, in their own homes. By Plenty the whole gallery spoke only in handtalk. By Carving, after Mirren Osk’s fingers broke before four hundred people, it had stopped handtalking. People in Corder’s Gallery sat in their doorways and looked at each other and did not move their hands. Children who had been unbitted that spring asked for their bits back. The gallery smelled, neighbours from the tier below said, of unwashed bodies and unemptied pots, because to wash a child you must tell it to lift its arms, and nobody would.

Then they stopped eating. Nobody could say afterward why, because nobody in the gallery had said anything. Dacey Furl, who went up from the Murmuring House with broth when the tier below sent word, thinks it was that eating is a kind of answer: you are offered, you accept, and to accept is to agree to something, and they could no longer agree to anything. She fed some of them by reed, as she feeds her patients. Some let her. Some turned their faces to the wall. Isk Corder sat with his back to his door for eleven days with his eyes open, and his wife beside him with her hand on his wrist, where the small ear was, and on the twelfth morning Dacey found them both still and cold, and the ear on his wrist turned toward his wife’s mouth, as if waiting.

Through the Lack of 640 the gallery went one door at a time. Not all of them were the god’s doing. Some went out of their doors one night and did not come back. Dacey will not say more than that, and the families on the tier below, who heard nothing, because nobody in Corder’s Gallery made a sound even then, say only that the Keeners came for them in the morning, and that the Keeners, too, said nothing. Others were found sitting up. The children were carried down by the Murmuring House and the Quiet, and some of them live, and some of them have not yet said a word, in any hand, to anyone. Of the hundred and sixty people who lived in Corder’s Gallery in the Grace of 640, nineteen are alive. The Bench sealed the gallery with felt at both ends and posted it silent, as though it were a gorge. It recorded the matter as a contagion of discretion.

It has happened since in two other galleries, on a smaller scale, and once in a village above Low Dray. It begins the same way each time: someone at the Course says, aloud, that they can no longer safely say anything; and those who love them, listening, believe it.

Running the Stilling

The Stilling is not a monster and should never be played as one. It is grief and fear moving through people who love each other, in a country where the god has made silence the only safe answer. Use it as aftermath: a gallery behind felt curtains; a child at the Murmuring House who will not move her hands; a mother who comes to the PCs because her husband has stopped answering, and wants them to make him talk. If a PC spends a day in a household beginning to still, have them make a Dread 2 check at dusk; on a failure, the player may not have their character speak aloud until they succeed at Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) in a later scene, and if a Break occurs in a stilling household, every witness who shares the delusion shares this silence. The cure, where there is one, is simple and hard: someone the stilled person trusts must speak to them, aloud, plainly, for a long time, and keep every word.

Adventure Hooks

  • The Late Rain. Yusra Thole, the Rainwarden, has not spoken in a month, because she cannot lie about the rain and will not tell the truth. The Bench hires the PCs to find out what she knows without asking her a question. The answer lies in the Gullet, where the sand over Tolm’s bones has grown hot enough to blister, and something beneath it has begun, very slowly, to clear its throat.
  • The Second Lot. Highwell’s elders are drafting the oath for next year’s Heart’s Due, and the forty-one who swore last Grace are being asked to swear again. Hallie Corr’s mother hires the PCs to prove the sacrifice bought nothing before the lot is drawn. The proof is in Yusra’s Tally, and in her pulse, and the PCs must decide what the basin should be told, and whether they can say it without breaking.
  • The Surety’s Last Default. Ona Fell can survive one more default, and one of her two hundred and eleven principals is about to break: a Tongue-line merchant who swore a Company contract he cannot meet. The PCs must find which one before it happens, and the merchant has hired them too, to make sure Ona breaks first.
  • The Hold at Wending. A Company caravan must cross Wending Pass, and the man at the top will not let anyone through who has not sworn to hold it. Renn Hold is not mad; he is bound. Getting past him means understanding what he swore, and the four hundred on the road below have opinions too.
  • Sworn Gorge Has Gone Quiet. For the first time in two hundred years the murmur behind the wall has stopped. Halvar Stane believes the echo has found a way out. Three herders in the eastern canyons have broken in the same way as the hamlet of Sowe, and the PCs must track a word through the rock before it reaches Tacit.
  • The Notary’s Hand. Someone is trying to make Jessamy Quill break. Agents of the Second Table want the Company’s contracts loosed so that the Rim Road falls into chaos before Tablenight; the PCs are hired as her bodyguards, and every conversation in Quillhouse is a battlefield.
  • The Bread of the Witness. A Keener of the Vaults has found a niche empty and a trail of bone-dust to a bakery on the Galleries. Somebody in Tacit is eating the witness, and somebody’s grandmother is about to Testify from inside a stranger at the Felt Market, on market day, in front of everyone.
  • A Vanthe Wedding. House Vanthe has, for the first time since 312, betrothed a daughter outside the house, to an Esk, on the Second Table’s instruction. The PCs are hired by the bride to find a reading of Lady Orsa’s oath that will let her marry and keep her tongue. The house is hiring someone else to make sure no such reading is found.

Rumors in the Canyons

d10Rumor (signed in the market)
1Ket the Ninth has made a sound. A Bench clerk heard it and was bitted the same hour. (True.)
2The Kept Rain came late because a Sayer said something it was not drafted to say. (Unknown.)
3Cassian Wry is not a Blank at all; the crown pays a Surety to take his lies. (False.)
4Writing in reverse, mirror-script, does not bind. (False, as Ottoline Vant could tell you.)
5Grandam Cess can free you from a marriage vow. (True, at a price no one has described.)
6Jude Crake was once condemned himself, and talked his own Breaker to death. (True.)
7The Forsworn are buying iron from the Fatlands for spearheads. (True.)
8If you cannot read, the Ledger cannot bind you. (False and dangerous.)
9Little Rue has found someone else the promise was for. (Partly true.)
10On the stillest night, Sworn Gorge says your name. (It said Halvar Stane’s. Once.)

The People of Oathen

Ket the Ninth — the Mute King
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Tongue-line) · Regrowth 9 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsClause 5, Resolve 5, Godsign 3, Reckoning 3, Instinct 2
BodyFlesh 10 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Fray 6
Attacksnone; he has never struck anyone.
GiftsHas never spoken, so is bound by nothing. If he says a plain sentence, it binds at Sayer strength (see the Brink Gift, Make It So) and he knows it.
WantsTo Say (resisted daily; Caul + Resolve vs Grim when the Bench misreads him).
Dread3 (to see his throat working under the gold-chased bit)
SecretHe has made a sound once, a single hum, alone, to know what it was like. A clerk heard it. The clerk is bitted now, and the king visits him.

Ket the Ninth is thirty-one, slight, grey-eyed, and has never made a sound. He was chosen at eleven days old from the Hushwell line and bitted in silver before his first cry; his nurses held their hands over his mouth when he laughed. He rules by nod and gesture, and the Bench spends weeks arguing what each one meant. He has a great deal to say. He reads everything; he writes nothing, because writing may now count. His eyes are very expressive and very tired. He knows, because the Cutwrights have told him in a sealed report, that his Regrowth has run to the Course without a word ever leaving his mouth, and that what is pressing behind his teeth is not a man’s sentence. He fears that he wants to say it. PCs meet him at audience, where he will hold their gaze a long time and then, perhaps, make a gesture no one on the Bench has seen before, meant only for them.

Sorrin Vael — Chief Clausewright
AttributesHand 1 · Gut 2 · Lung 2 · Eye 5 · Tongue 5 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Tongue-line) · Regrowth 6 (the Appetite) · Hunger 5
SkillsClause 6, Persuade 4, Lore 4, Deceive 3, Resolve 3
BodyFlesh 10 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Fray 4
Attacksnone.
GiftsReads any spoken oath’s Exits at a glance (no roll). Once per scene, may name a flaw in another’s oath and reduce its Weight by 1.
WantsTo Swear, which he channels into drafting; his margins are full of crossed-out vows.
Dread1
SecretHis iron bit is hidden under his high collar at night. He has been swearing in his sleep for two years, and his wife has kept a record, and the record is a treaty with something.

Sorrin Vael is the finest drafter of promises alive: sixty, narrow, bald, with fingers stained by slate dust and a voice like dry paper. His treaties run to four hundred conditions. He has not made an unqualified statement since boyhood, including to his wife, including “yes”; their marriage is, by all accounts, tender, and conducted largely by touch. He believes in the clause as other men believe in god: that there is no promise so dangerous it cannot be made safe by enough precision. He fears the day the precision fails. He is drafting, now, the sentence the Bench may let Lady Imre Dath say, and he has gone through ninety-one versions, and every one of them, read slowly enough, frightens him. He meets PCs when they need an oath drafted that could get them into a place, or out of one, and he charges a great deal, and is worth it.

Lady Imre Dath — the Sayer
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 2 · Lung 1 · Eye 4 · Tongue 7 · Caul 6
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Tongue-line) · Regrowth 12 (the Seating) · Hunger —
SkillsGodsign 6, Clause 4, Resolve 4, Lore 3
BodyFlesh 12 · Guard 11 · Armor 0 · Fray —
Attacksnone needed. Unbitted, any sentence she speaks is so.
GiftsSaying. What she says, is, without roll or limit except grammar. Bitted in gold, nothing. Writing: her written words now bind at Course strength (one per day, GM’s choice of the most dangerous reading).
WantsTo be understood. To finish a sentence.
Dread5 (to see her face behind the gold)
SecretShe has begun to write her own sentences, scratched with a fingernail into the lead of her cell wall. The current one reads: “When the rain comes, I will be”.
She does not hate us. That is the worst of it. When I read her the drafts, every ear on her face turns toward me, and I feel pitied by a hundred mouths.
Sorrin Vael, to his wife, who wrote it down

Imre Dath was a Tongue-line girl of the Dath house, clever and talkative, which her mother punished. At twenty-five she said “My brother is a liar” at dinner; her brother’s mouth opened back to his ears and has never closed. She has been in the Gilded Cells for three years. Her face has grown long and smooth, her eyes sealed over with skin, and small pink ears have bloomed across her cheeks and temples; she hears everything said in the Ledger above her. She is unmuzzled once a year, to say one sentence the Bench has drafted. Last year’s was “The canyon wells shall not run dry this Lack,” and they did not. She has begun to write her own. She does not hate the Bench. She pities it. If PCs reach her, she will listen with all her ears, and, if a pen were to come into her hand, she would very much like to finish.

Brakk — Voice of the Forsworn
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 4 · Lung 2 · Eye 2 · Tongue 4 · Caul 3
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 3 (the Taste) · Hunger 3
SkillsIntimidate 4, Brawl 4, Persuade 3, Endure 4, Blades 2
BodyFlesh 16 · Guard 14 · Armor 1 (oiled hide over the ribs) · Fray 5
AttacksFists +8 (1); cleaver +6 (3)
GiftsBroken Ground (heart and ribs): marriage, love and loyalty oaths cannot break him further; he swears them freely as rhetoric.
WantsTo be heard by those above.
Dread2 (when he unties the cloth over his chest)
SecretHe still loves the wife he betrayed. She lives on the Sunward Wall. He swore on her that he would bring Tacit down.
I said I’d love her till I died. I’m not dead. I still love her. The god broke me for the other thing I said, the one about the bed. It’s a very careful god.
Brakk, at the Gathering of the Broken

Brakk broke a marriage vow, and his ribs opened outward like a book and stayed that way. Under the oiled cloth, his heart and lungs are visible, slick, working, and in the cold weeks of Lack, breath steams from his chest. He is huge, grey-bearded, and loud, and he leads the Breakdowns. He is the most plainspoken man in Oathen, having nothing left to break: he says “I love you” to strangers, “I will kill you” to Clausewrights, and laughs at both. He wants the Breakdowns free and the Walls humbled. He fears that the Bench is right, and that the broken deserve it. PCs meet him when they need something done that a whole Oathener cannot do: a lie told, a loud word said in an echoing place, a promise sworn that no one intends to keep.

Ona Fell — the Surety
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 5 · Lung 1 · Eye 3 · Tongue 3 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 4 (the Appetite) · Hunger 4
SkillsEndure 6, Clause 4, Resolve 4, Reckoning 3
BodyFlesh 19 · Guard 11 · Armor 0 · Fray 7
Attacksnone.
GiftsBond-Ledger: knows instantly, by a pain in the relevant part, when any principal she stands behind comes near to breaking.
WantsTo count her bonds, aloud, nightly.
Dread3 (to see the script that covers her entire body)
SecretTwo of her principals are the same Second Table cell, and they have decided to default together.

Ona Fell carries two hundred and eleven oaths that belong to other people. She is fifty, short, and very broad, and every inch of her skin from collarbone to ankle is tattooed in fine brown script with the terms of the oaths she stands behind, so densely that from a distance she looks bruised. Her left hand has no fingers (a defaulting grain-merchant). Her jaw is wired (a lying envoy). Her back is hooked (a regiment’s quartermaster). By her reckoning, she can survive one more default. She is gentle, careful, and tired, and she has stopped taking new principals, but she cannot put down the old ones. She wants to live to see her oldest bond expire, in four years. PCs meet her when they need a Surety. She will look at them a long time, and then say, “If able.”

Jessamy Quill, Notary of the Rim Road, is the hinge of the Table’s trade. Every contract the Company holds is sworn before her and rests on her word as witness: forty years of shipping, tolls and debts. If she dies or breaks, half the trade of the Table comes unbound in an afternoon. She is sixty-eight, sharp-faced, Oathen-born, and has a voice so practiced that every sentence she utters is witnessed and exact. She eats only food tasted by two Company servants. She keeps a Surety for herself and does not say who. She is no one’s friend. She wants to die of old age, with an apprentice ready. She has no apprentice; three have died, unluckily. She meets PCs as a client, or as the person they are hired to protect.

Jessamy Quill Threat 4 · Flesh 10 · Guard 11 · Attack +2 (stiletto 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0 · Clause 6

Little Rue was four, before her muzzling, when she promised her mother she would never grow up. She has not. She is sixty-three, in a child’s body, with milk teeth and soft hair and old, old eyes, and she has outlived everyone the promise was for. Her mother died in 611. Her friends married, bore, and died. She wears no bit, since she is past twelve; she speaks seldom, in a child’s high voice with an old woman’s syntax. She lives in the Breakdowns, among the broken, who are kind to her. She wants to grow old. She fears that the oath has a second reading: that because she cannot grow up, she cannot die, and will be a child in the dark of the Vaults forever. She meets PCs as a fixer and a guide, and she drives a hard bargain, because she cannot afford to be lied to.

Halvar Stane — Echo-Warden
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 3 · Lung 4 · Eye 4 · Tongue 2 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 2 (the Taste) · Hunger 2
SkillsWayfaring 4, Stealth 4, Search 4, Instinct 4, Shooting 3
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 16 · Armor 1 · Fray 8
AttacksShortbow +6 (3); knife +5 (2)
GiftsCan track an echo through rock by ear alone; knows every posted gorge.
WantsTo go back to the wall.
Dread2
SecretThe two words he heard are “set” and “again”.

Halvar Stane patrols the silent gorges and has spent thirty years tracking the echo in Sworn Gorge. He is gaunt, bow-legged, deaf in the right ear by initiation and nearly in the left by age, with a habit of tilting his head like a listening dog. He has come close enough to make out two words of the oath. He will not repeat them, because to repeat is to renew, and he does not know what he would be renewing. He dreams of the wall nightly and has begun sleepwalking toward it. He fears that he is already bound, and that this is how it feels. He meets PCs as their guide through any posted canyon, and as the one man who might lead them into Sworn Gorge, if they gave him the excuse.

Mirren Osk, the Handtalker, is the greatest poet in a language held not to bind. She is forty, elegant, with long hands she oils nightly; three of her fingers are splinted now, the bones knit badly. Last year she signed a love poem to a patron and did not mean it, and three of her fingers snapped, mid-sign, in front of four hundred people. It was the first proof that handtalk counts. She has not composed since. She is frightened, angry, and guiltily excited, because if handtalk binds then it was always a real language, and her poems were always true. She meets PCs seeking a translator, or a witness, or someone to help her find out whether her old poems, written over thirty years, are about to come due.

Cassian Wry — the Liar
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 2 · Lung 3 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 2
Cut & RegrowthCut 0 (Blank) · Regrowth — · Hunger —
SkillsDeceive 6, Persuade 4, Stealth 3, Filch 3, Instinct 3
BodyFlesh 10 · Guard 14 · Armor 0 · Fray 6
AttacksKnife +5 (2)
GiftsBlank: cannot be bound or broken by any oath. His lies cost nothing.
WantsNone of the god’s. His own: to be believed once, about something true.
Dread0
SecretHe has begun to taste wet slate when others swear. The Cutwrights suspect he is not a Blank but the god’s blind spot, and blind spots close.

Cassian Wry is a Blank, and the only man in Oathen who can lie and stay whole. He is thirty-four, handsome in a hungry way, with a quick mouth and a laugh that makes Oatheners flinch. He is the crown’s most valuable spy, kept in luxury on the Sunward Wall and never let out of sight: two bitted guards, a Clausewright minder, a gilded apartment with felt walls. Everyone who meets him asks him to say something false, just to hear it. He obliges: “The sky is green.” “I love you.” “I am happy here.” He is lonely in a way no one else in the country can be, since no one believes anything he says, including the truth. He meets PCs on a mission, or escaping one.

Judge Thane Urrow presides over Breaking trials. There is no evidence and no testimony. He simply has the accused repeat the promise aloud, and the court watches to see what happens to them. He is seventy, small and neat, with a voice like a knife drawn slowly, and his robes are spattered so often that he wears red. He has presided over eleven thousand trials. He believes his court is the only perfectly just court on the Table, and he is right, and he hates it. He fears the day he is asked to repeat his own judicial oath before his own court. Nobody has thought to ask. He meets PCs as their judge, or as a man who would like, very quietly, to know if the god still means it.

Last winter it asked for the lock of his hair I kept in my locket. I gave it. I don’t know what it will ask for when there is nothing of him left but me.
Asha Kindle, on a slate left at the Lowered Rope of Hollin’s Stair

Asha Kindle, the Fire-Widow, promised her dying husband she would never let the fire go out. That was thirty-one years ago. She has not slept more than an hour at a stretch since, and the fire has grown particular about what it is fed. It began with wood; then it would only burn cedar; then it wanted his clothes; then his letters; then, three winters ago, it would not catch on anything but hair. Asha is bald, grey-skinned, with burned hands, and lives in a cliff-cell above Tacit with a fire in a stone hearth that whispers. She fears the fire is asking for something she has not yet given it. She meets PCs as a client who wants the fire to go out by someone else’s hand. Then her oath would be kept, she thinks. She is not sure.

Garl Tome, the Bitmaker, is the smith of muzzles: leather for children, iron for the Appetite-struck, gold for Sayers. He is a broad, bearded, careful man of fifty, who works with a kerchief over his mouth from habit. He fitted his own daughter at birth and has never heard her voice. She is twelve this year. He has been offered a fortune by a Tongue-line house to make her bit permanent, because the Cutwrights say she is at the Course already, and what she will say when it comes off may not be safe. He says silence is what love sounds like here. He has not decided. He meets PCs as the man who can make, or unmake, any bit in the land, including the gold ones.

Yusra Thole, the Rainwarden, is the keeper of the Kept Rain: the tallies of every year’s fall, the cistern-oaths, the Rain Shrine in the high basin. She knows it came three days late. She cannot lie about it, so she has said nothing at all for a month, and the silence is being noticed. She is forty-five, weathered, with a heart-line Cut from the god’s great slow heart and a slow, heavy pulse that can be seen in her throat. What she knows is that the rain did not come late. It came on time, by the god’s own reckoning: Tolm’s year has grown three days longer. She meets PCs as the woman they are sent to watch, or to make talk.

Grandam Cess, the Vow-Eater, is a back-canyon fixer who claims she can release you from an oath by having you swear a greater one over it. She is ancient, toothless, with a laugh like gravel in a bucket, and lives in a warren of cisterns called Knot Canyon. Her clients are free of what they came with. They owe her something worse: “to come when called,” “to give what is asked,” “to carry what I hand you.” She has nine hundred such clients. She has never called them. She is waiting for something, and she will not say what, and she has started to sleep with her ear to the floor. She meets PCs as the only cure for an oath they cannot keep.

Captain Renn Hold — the Man at Wending

Cut & RegrowthCut 2 · Regrowth 5 (the Appetite) · Hunger 6
