Spare Tolland of the Hostwatch

Sixty, wiry, slow-moving, with a face weathered into deep pleated folds and bright, unblinking grey eyes. He wears a Hostwatch compass on a thong and a coat sewn all over with pockets for pins. He has spent thirty years following Orrum at a mile’s distance, mapping the warm ground, and he knows its gait, its pauses, the places it likes to stand at dusk. He has never seen its face. He has seen it stop and wait for him to catch up, and he has come to think it is lonely. He speaks of it the way an old farmer speaks of a neighbour’s dog that has been chained too long. He is afraid of nothing in the Fast but his own urge to close the mile. Meeting the PCs: he needs someone to hold the far end of his rope, because the gap has been shrinking, and he is not sure, any more, which of them is closing it.

Wont Bellamy, Heretic Elder

A plump man, by Unfed standards, which is to say his ribs cannot be counted through his shirt, and the Abstinent never forget it. Fifty-five, soft-voiced, beautifully mannered, with clever dark eyes and a Rim-cut coat. He sits on the council by right of blood, the Bellamys having stood on the hill, and argues that the Refusal was only a postponement: the Unfed should do now what the others did then, and eat the god that is still whole. He has friends abroad, in the Second Table, who very much agree, and who send him letters sealed in wax pressed with a fork. He fears being found out by Scant Hollis. Secret: he has eaten, twice, at Second Table banquets in Sated; it was Fatlands pork, nothing godly, and he enjoyed it so much he wept, and he has told no one. Meeting the PCs: he offers them generous work carrying letters, and offers it only once.

Mother Stint Avery, Keeper of the Pantry

Sixty-two, square, hard-handed, with a stone-mason’s forearms and a clerk’s ink-stained fingers. She wears an apron of oiled canvas and smells of sacking and mouse. She weighs out every ration in the Fast herself, on brass scales older than Wanting, and she has never once given anyone a grain extra. She knows there are four months of grain for six months of winter. She has already decided which villages: the furthest, the oldest, the ones with fewest children. She has not told Forbear Wend, because he will pray, and praying is a delay, and delay kills more. She is not cruel. She is the only person in the Fast who has done the arithmetic and not looked away from it, and that is a kind of hell. Secret: her own village, Avery Steading, is on the list. She has not told them. Meeting the PCs: she asks them to audit a Crumb-Runner’s tally, and they find the Company’s shortfall.

Abstain Rooke, called Abby

Eleven, bird-boned, curious, with a gap in her front teeth and a habit of asking why. Raised on the rules, she can recite them faster than anyone in her hamlet, and she has started leaving a crust on the windowsill at night, saved from her own three-quarter measure. Each morning it has been replaced with something better: a corner of white bread, a ripe plum, a sugared almond, a little honey-cake wrapped in a leaf. She has eaten none of it. She hides it under a loose floor-stone. The pile is getting large, and it does not rot, and it smells wonderful through the stone at night. She is not afraid. She thinks of it as a pen-friend. Her mother does not know; her mother is on Stint Avery’s list. Meeting the PCs: Abby asks them, very seriously, if it counts as accepting if you are only keeping it for someone else.

Brother Hallow Crust, the Seated

He has sat at a table on the valley road for forty years, eating air with a silver fork. He was a stout man; now he is a draped coat with a head on it, the cheeks hollowed to the teeth, the eyes sunk into blue pits, the hair gone to a few white strands. He is perfectly happy and perfectly sane. He describes each course in detail, in a voice like dry leaves: the mutton with caper sauce, the eel pie, the syllabub with nutmeg grated over. He asks after your family. He remembers your answers. He cannot remember his own wife’s name, but he remembers every dish he has been served since 601. People who listen too long pull out a chair. Secret: he was a Tablebreaker, and sat down deliberately, to see if he could get up. He has been meaning to, all forty years. Meeting the PCs: on the Long Table road; he calls them by name.

The syllabub tonight is very fine, with nutmeg grated over. You ought to have some. Do you know, I can’t think of my wife’s name. Isn’t the nutmeg lovely?
Brother Hallow Crust, the Seated

Dr. Mercy Thrane

A physician of starvation, forty-seven, gaunt and grey-eyed, with spectacles mended with wire and a satchel of scales, calipers, and notebooks. She measures the Unfed: arm circumference, the pinch of the skin, the colour of the gums, the slow pulse. She has written the only proper book on what hunger does to a body over a lifetime. She was the first to document the trade in Unfed bodies. She has traced her missing patients to surgeries in four countries, where blank blood and blank organs fetch a noble’s ransom: Unfed kidneys sewn into Laden matriarchs, Unfed eyes into lidless Vigil heirs, Unfed hearts for Sallowreach Unvacated who want to feel one beat that is not Ossel’s. She has a ledger of names and buyers. The trail leads to the Second Table. She fears she will not live to publish it. Meeting the PCs: she hires them to bring a body home.

The Blank-Organ Trade

Godsign does not live in Unfed flesh. A kidney, liver, eye, length of gut, or pint of blood taken from one of the Unfed is, so far as any surgeon can tell, wholly clean, and when it is sewn into a Godeater it is the one part of that body the god does not grow into. For a few months, or a few years, the High Cut buyer has one organ that is only theirs. Laden matriarchs buy Unfed stomachs to feel, for a season, what it is to be full. Lidless Eye-lines buy Unfed eyes that can close. The price for a whole pair of Unfed kidneys in Sated is about 6,000 lacks; a heart in Lastgate, twice that. The organs are taken from the living where possible, because the Unfed die very quickly of the surgery and the buyers want the organ warm. Poachers keep their captives alive, and fed, for exactly that reason. Then the godsign of the buyer slowly grows into the new organ, as ivy grows into a wall, and in a few years they need another.

The Trade, Itemised

The Blank trade is not a black market in the way Rim smugglers’ markets are. It is a luxury, and it behaves like one: discreet, referred, expensive, and very nearly respectable. It has surgeons of standing in four capitals, a vocabulary of polite words (an Unfed captive is a lodger, an organ is a refitting, a living Unfed kept for repeated cuttings is a keeping-room guest), and a clientele drawn almost entirely from the High Cuts, who have the money and the most god to escape. The best-known practitioner is Master Quillon Barr of Sated, a courteous, careful man who has read Dr. Mercy Thrane’s book on starvation with genuine admiration and keeps his lodgers alive between cuttings for years, in rooms with no west windows, warm, fed by tube, some of them in brine-tanks to the neck in his Lastgate house, where the cold of the fen keeps the cut flesh sweet. Several of his lodgers have begun, after years of it, to put on weight. Some of them have asked not to be taken home.

The prices below are those Dr. Thrane has recorded from bills of sale, the Red Ledger she keeps of her missing patients, and the confession of one poacher. They are what a buyer pays the surgeon. The poacher gets a tenth.

RefittingWanted byPrice (lacks)How long it stays clean
A pint of blank bloodAnyone dosing against their own Regrowth150 to 300A day in the body; a week of easier sleep
A blank eyeLidless Eye-lines of the Vigil3,000A season or two; the first blink is weeping joy
Both kidneys, from the livingLaden matriarchs; Sallowreach Unvacated6,000 to 9,000Two to five years
A blank stomachThe Gut-lines, to feel full once7,000A season; they eat until it bursts
A blank heartHand-lines who want one beat that is not Ossel’s12,000It beats for a year, then slows to Ossel’s time
A blank wombCaul-line women of Cradlewrack, for a child of no godNever quoted; paid in landOne birth, if any
A whole lodger, keptAny of the above, by subscription40,000 and a yearly feeAs long as the lodger lives

The trade’s dirtiest secret is the one Dr. Thrane has not yet been able to prove. Some of the buyers, she believes, are not trying to escape their gods at all. A man with a two-tined fork pinned inside his lapel has been buying children. They are not for refitting. A child of no god, raised from infancy in a closed house on nothing but one land’s god-meat, would grow into an empty vessel filled with a single god and nothing else: no inheritance, no dilution, six centuries of bloodline skipped in one generation. What would grow in such a body is a question the Second Table has apparently decided to answer by experiment. Dr. Thrane has three addresses and no proof. Kale Dragoman has been asked, once, to deliver to one of them, and refused three times, and the fourth asking was very well paid.

A receipt, on good Sated paper with a deckle edge, found by Dr. Mercy Thrane in a surgery’s waste-basket in 638. The client’s name has been inked out. The surgeon’s has not.

Received with thanks of the Honoured House of (inked out), the sum of eight thousand four hundred lacks, in platters, for: one refitting (renal, paired, warm), from a lodger of the Fast, female, about twenty-six years, of Brindle border stock, weighed on receipt at seven stone two pounds and brought by careful feeding to eight stone eleven before the procedure, at which weight the organs are at their best. Lodger did not survive refitting, as is usual with that stock, and has been returned to the supplier for disposal at no further charge. The Honoured House is reminded that refittings of this kind are not permanent, and that the god will find its way into the new tissue in two to five years, and that Master Barr will be pleased to keep the Honoured House’s name on his list for a further refitting at that time, at the same rate, supply permitting. Supply is presently good.

With every respect, Q. Barr.

They come in so thin. You have to be patient. You have to bring them up slowly, broth, then milk, or the heart gives. I learned that from a physician’s book. She’s very good.
Kale Dragoman, to a Company toll-clerk

Kale Dragoman, the Poacher

A Fatlander of thirty-five, broad, ruddy, and handsome in the Fatlands way, with heavy jowls, beautiful teeth, and a laugh that rolls. He smells of woodsmoke and roast fat, always, because he cooks. He hunts the Unfed for the Blank trade and takes them alive with net and cosh, and he feeds them well on the road: stews, roast fowl, soft white bread, honey, warm milk. He coaxes, he spoon-feeds, he holds their heads. Half his captives refuse and starve before they reach the buyers. The others eat, and weep, and arrive at the surgeries plump and healthy and full of self-loathing. That is the part his captives find hardest to forgive. He thinks he is kind. He is, by Fatlands lights. Meeting the PCs: across a campfire on the Rim, offering them supper. Three times.

Envoy Prudence Lowell

Fifty, thin as a lath, in a high-collared black coat buttoned to the throat, with a voice like a cold chisel. She is the Fast’s one ambassador, posted to a hired room above a chandler’s on the Rim Road, and her entire brief is to remind six nations that they are damned and her people are not. She attends every treaty-sitting and every Company congress, refuses every refreshment three times, and then reads aloud, in perfect Table-speech, the latest numbers of their Regrowth. She is very good at it. She has no friends. She has eaten alone, standing, facing a wall, in fourteen capitals. Secret: a Vigil envoy once offered her a fourth time, sincerely, and she very nearly accepted; she has dreamed of his face every night since. Meeting the PCs: she needs Unfed escorts, and she needs, though she would never say so, someone to talk to.

Scour, the Returned

A Reckoner of thirty, lean and fox-faced, sleeves always buttoned to the knuckle. He spent a year undercover in the Fatlands as a renderer’s labourer to scout a Gut-line house, and had to eat to keep his cover. He ate their meat for a year. He came home with godsign. Under his sleeves the skin of his forearms has gone soft, warm, and faintly loamy, like turned earth; there are fine pale threads in it, like root-hairs. He is hungry in a way no Unfed has ever been hungry: a hunger that has nothing to do with the belly. He hides it under his sleeves and volunteers for every raid, because on a raid he can carry his own food and refuse it, and because he wants to die doing something clean. Meeting the PCs: on a raid, when a PC sees him, alone, eating dirt from a Fatlands field.

Verger Sober Osmond

Seventy-nine, stooped, with soft white hair, a sweet vague smile, and a long black cassock gone green at the seams. He keeps the Empty Chair, the last temple of Orrum, alone. Every night he lays one place at the head of the long table, against all law, with the old temple plate: pewter platter, horn cup, a linen napkin folded into the shape of a bird. He lays nothing on it. Every morning the plate is clean, wiped, still faintly warm. He believes this is why the god has stayed gentle: someone has kept faith with it. He is not wrong. He fears dying, because no one will lay the place. Secret: for the past month the morning plate has not been clean. It has had a single crumb on it, as though someone had eaten and, being a well-mannered guest, left a little. Meeting the PCs: he asks one of them to stay and learn the duty.

Yield Hartsell, the Farmer

Seventy, wiry and bowlegged, brown as a nut, with the cracked thumbs and quiet humour of a woman who has spent fifty years doing something useless because someone should. She has planted the dead soil of her family’s ten acres every spring since she was twenty. This year one seed came up. She has built a fence around it and told no one, because she does not know who watered it. She sits up with it at night, with a lantern and a hayfork. Each morning the soil around the blade is wet, and there are no footprints, but the frost around the field is melted in a wide ring, as though something large had knelt there. She is more frightened than she has ever been, and happier. Meeting the PCs: she asks them to sit up with the wheat, and to see what comes, and not to hurt it.

Little Fain

An orphan of six, small and sturdy, with curly hair and dimpled hands: dimpled, in the Fast. Fain went missing for a week and came back plump, clean, rosy, and happy, with a ribbon in their hair and the smell of warm milk on their breath. Someone had said “Come in,” and Fain had. Fain will not say who cooked, only that they cried when it was time to go, and that there was a big kitchen and a fire and lots of chairs but most of them were empty. The Abstinent do not know what to do. Fain cannot be Seated; Fain got up. The other children follow Fain about. The adults will not touch Fain. Secret: Fain was not let go. Fain was sent, and Fain is supposed to bring someone back. Meeting the PCs: Fain takes a PC’s hand in the street and says, “You can come too.”

There was a big kitchen and lots of chairs and most of them were empty. They cried when I had to go. You can come too.
Little Fain

Marshal Keep Aldane

A heavy-boned man of fifty with a broken nose and an old crossbow wound in the thigh, commanding sixty Unfed spearmen at Brindle Cross. He holds the border against poachers coming in, and, lately, against pilgrims: starving Fatlanders who have heard that somewhere in the Fast there is a table where you finally feel full. He was trained to kill poachers. He was not trained for three hundred hungry people kneeling in the mud of the toll-road, begging him to let them in so they can sit down and die happy. He has turned back nine hundred. He has started to wonder why he is doing it, and what right an Unfed has to refuse anyone a meal. Meeting the PCs: he needs men; or he arrests them as poachers.

Brindle Cross Spearman Threat 2 · Flesh 12 · Guard 14 · Attack +5 (spear 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Osanna Blythe, the Pilgrim

A Fatlands woman of forty, enormous by Unfed standards and gaunt by her own, her skin hanging in folds from a body that has been ravenous every second of her life. Her eyes are bright, her voice is warm and rolling, and she laughs often, a great hungry laugh. She is leading three hundred like her into the Fast to find the Host and sit down. She knows what happens to the Seated. She thinks it sounds wonderful: to be full, finally, for decades, smiling, among friends. She has an Unfed name sewn on her coat, given her by a Tablebreaker who could not bring himself to stop her. Her pilgrims are dying on the road, and the Unfed do not feed them, because that would be hospitality. Meeting the PCs: she asks them for directions. She is very polite about it. She asks three times.

Meek Garrity, the Historian

A small, round-shouldered man of sixty-six, ink to the elbows, with thick spectacles, a voice barely above a whisper, and the long bloodless fingers of a lifelong copyist. He has spent forty years in the oldest records of the Pantry, and he has found the seating plan for Hallowboard: a slate, scratched in the old hand, listing the order in which the households of the heartland were to stand around the table on the night. It is dated. There was no refusal. The Unfed arrived on the tenth day, with knives. The table had already been cleared. Something had eaten first. Secret: the slate shows eight sides, and seven are allotted to households; the eighth has a word scratched beside it, and the word has been scraped away, and Garrity has spent a year with a lens trying to read the shadow of the chisel. Meeting the PCs: he needs the slate moved before the Abstinent burn it.

Welcome Ardent, the Steward

He walks a mile ahead of Orrum, laying the tables. He is tall and very thin and wears an old-fashioned steward’s coat of dark green, the cuffs immaculate, with a white apron over it and a ring of keys at his belt. His face is gentle, lined, and grey with an exhaustion so deep it has become a kind of serenity. His hands are warm, always, and smell of bread. He was the first of the Unfed ever to accept, on the eleventh morning, six hundred and forty years ago, and the only guest who was offered a position. He lays the cloths, sets out the plates, angles the chairs, and writes the place cards in whatever hand will be loved. He is polite, exhausted, and would like very much to be relieved. He has been laying an extra place lately, and he will not say for whom; when asked, he only says, We’re expecting one more.

We’re expecting one more.
Welcome Ardent, asked whom the extra place is for
Welcome Ardent — the Steward of the Host
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 6 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 5 · Caul 6
Cut & Refusalnone (in service; not of any blood) · Want 0 · Pangs 0, forever
SkillsPersuade 5, Rites 5, Craft 5, Instinct 4, Lore 4, Resolve 1
BodyFlesh 19 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Fray 10, steady, unbreaking
Attacksnone; he has never struck anyone and cannot
GiftsLay a Place (in one minute, he lays a table for any person he can see; it calls them by name, and they must make an Invitation check). The Fourth Offer (he alone may make a fourth offer, and it is sincere; an Unfed who refuses him a fourth time gains 3 Want and his deep gratitude). The Steward’s Keys (any door, gate, lock, or bricked hearth opens for him).
WantsTo be relieved. Someone must accept the position freely.
Dread3 (to see him at work); 4 (to read a place card in his hand)
SecretHe knows who the extra place is for. He has been told, by his master, that when that guest arrives, the Steward will be released, and everyone else will be served.
Orrum, the Host

Orrum has no stat block. It does not fight, cannot be harmed by any weapon known on the Table, and has never been seen clearly by anyone who returned whole. To see it at a distance (a tall shape stooping in a lit doorway) is a Dread 4 check. To see its face is Dread 5. It is warm, and always kind. If PCs approach it, it will offer them food three times, sincerely, in voices they love. It will never make the fourth offer. If they refuse three times and remain in its presence, it will weep, and the ground for a hundred yards will grow warm enough to raise blisters, and they must leave or be Seated by the heat. If they ask it a question, it will answer with a gesture: a long hand laid on the back of an empty chair.

New Faces

Scarce Odell, the Kin-Reader

A former under-clerk of the Cutwrights’ College in Sated, forty, dry and fastidious, with a squint from decades of tiny genealogical script. He is Unfed by birth, and was placed in the College as a boy by the Reckoners, to read. Now he is home, and he supplies the Reckoners with complete kin-trees so they can murder whole lines: not just the main house but married-out daughters, bastard sons, cousins at sea, infants placed with wet-nurses in other towns. He makes his lists like a careful tailor, measuring twice. He sleeps well. Secret: his trees include Unfed foundlings who carry High Cut blood without knowing, and he has started adding them, quietly. Meeting the PCs: he asks them to verify a name.

Withy Gaunt, Matron of the Lean House

A spare, kind-faced woman of fifty-eight with chapped hands and a soft voice, who keeps the Lean House where the omitted go to die. She does not feed them; that would be against the rule and, she believes, cruel, since it would only extend the waiting. She washes them. She changes the straw. She holds their hands and listens to them talk about food, as they all do at the end, in loving detail, for hours. She writes down every name in the Book of the Omitted, with the date they came and the date they stopped, and what they said last. Most last words are recipes. Secret: she has started reading the Book’s recipes aloud at night to the dying, and Orrum has started standing outside the door, listening. Meeting the PCs: a PC’s friend is in the Lean House.

Abide Kettering, the Sexton

A wiry, cheerful man of forty-five with a pickaxe on his shoulder and a cart he drives to the Lean House and back. He buries the omitted and the starved in the fields, face down, without markers, as is proper. Or he did. For six years he has been selling them, still warm, to Kale Dragoman’s men at a crossroads three miles west, and burying sacks of stones. The bodies of the dead are worth less than the living, but blank kidneys keep a few hours, and blank blood a day. He tells himself the dead do not need them. He has started to look at the Lean House’s residents with an eye to timing. Meeting the PCs: they see his cart at the crossroads, lamp lit, at the wrong hour.

Kettering’s Cart-Hands Threat 1 · Flesh 10 · Guard 12 · Attack +4 (shovel 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Factor Joss Mardle of the Rim Road Company

A smooth-shaven, prosperous Oathen-trained factor of fifty, in a good grey coat, who never says anything unqualified. He holds the Fast’s grain contract at Brindle Cross. He shorted the autumn deliveries on Company orders, diverting the grain north to buy oil for the Vigil’s lamps, at three times the price. The contract allows it, in a clause about “force of circumstance” he drafted himself. He knows exactly how many Unfed will starve. He has done the sum and filed it. Secret: the Company has instructed him to exercise its “first refusal” on the Unfed dead this winter, and he is ashamed enough to have delayed. Meeting the PCs: he offers them a contract.

Hollow Ann Pruett, the Card-Keeper

A spry, birdlike old woman of seventy-five with a bag over her shoulder, who walks the Fast collecting place cards from broken tables: over three hundred, kept in an oiled box, sorted by name. She has cards for people now Seated, people now dead, people who were never born in the Fast. She has cards with Rim names. She has three cards with the names of PCs, collected years ago. And she has one card that has no name on it at all, only a small, careful drawing of an empty chair, pushed in, square to the table. She found it at a table with eight chairs. She will not let anyone hold it. Meeting the PCs: she gives one of them their own card, and asks them to keep it, since it is theirs.

From Hollow Ann's Box: Place Cards Found

Every card is stiff cream stock, folded into a little tent, written in brown ink the colour of dried gravy, in a hand somebody loved. Roll when a PC finds a card at a laid table, in a pocket, under a door or in Hollow Ann’s box. A card with the PC’s own name on it is an Invitation check at Grim 18, as normal; these are what the card says.

d20The card reads
1The PC’s name, in their dead mother’s hand, and under it: Your favourite. I remembered.
2The PC’s childhood pet name, which no one living knows, in a grandmother’s careful copperplate.
3The name of a companion in the party, in the PC’s own handwriting.
4Kept warm for you. No name. The card is warm. It stays warm in a pocket for a week.
5The name of someone the PC killed, in that person’s hand, and under it: I’m not cross any more.
6The PC’s name spelled the way they spelled it at five, with the s backwards.
7A Rim name the PC has never heard. Three nights later they meet its owner on the Rim Road.
8The name of a Reckoner’s victim, a High Cut child, in a nursemaid’s round hand. Found in a Reckoner’s coat.
9The PC’s name and a seat number on the Long Table: mile, side, chair. The chair is empty when visited, and pulled out.
10Lenten, in Forbear Wend’s own hand as a young man. He has never written to her.
11Two names together, the PC’s and someone they have never admitted to loving.
12The PC’s name, in the hand of a sibling who is still alive, and who swears they did not write it.
13Steward, in Welcome Ardent’s hand. Lent Ashby’s card, or one like it.
14A Seated relative’s name, crossed out neatly, and the PC’s written underneath. To take her place.
15The PC’s name in a child’s hand, a child they have not had yet.
16Bounty. In Welcome Ardent’s own hand, which he swears he never wrote. He has looked for that name on every card for six hundred years.
17The name of every PC in the party, on one card, in one hand that each of them recognises as a different person’s.
18The name of a walker of Sallow Hatch, and under it: Thank you for ringing. You did ever so well.
19A card for a Godeater PC, which reads only the name of the god in their blood, spelled correctly, with great tenderness.
20No name. A careful drawing of an empty chair, pushed in, square to the table, its back to the lamp. Dread 3. Hollow Ann will want it, very badly, and will not say why.
She’s got my card. She won’t give it me. She says it isn’t time, and she’d know.
Tarry Moss, of Hollow Ann Pruett

Minor Folk and Foes

Reckoner Knife Threat 3 · Flesh 13 · Guard 16 · Attack +7 (black-iron knife 2; first strike on a sleeper is a Grace) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Tablebreaker Axe Threat 2 · Flesh 14 · Guard 14 · Attack +6 (axe 4) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Seated of the Long Table Threat 0 · Flesh 3 · Guard 8 · Attack none · Armor 0 · Dread 2 (Dread 3 when they all turn and look); each call by name forces an Invitation check at Routine 10

Fatlands Poacher Threat 2 · Flesh 13 · Guard 13 · Attack +5 (cosh 3, or net) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Fatlands Pilgrim Threat 1 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (fist 1) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (to hear them beg)

Playing the Unfed

Hunger is honest.
— Unfed proverb

You are the only person on the Table with nothing in your blood but blood. You have never tasted a god. You have also never, not once in your life, been full. You are proud, cold, thin, disciplined, and very, very hungry, and the warmest, kindest thing in the world is following you, laying tables.

Attribute bonus: +1 to any one attribute of your choice. (Most Unfed take Caul or Gut.)

Cut: 0. You cannot Partake. You have no Tooth, no Hunger track, no Regrowth, no Gifts, no Wants, and no Sop. Instead you have Want and Pangs.

Want: The Refusal Mechanic

The Godeaters have the god in them. You have the space where a god would be, and you have learned to use it. Want is a pool from 0 to 10 that measures how much you have refused, and how sharp the refusing has made you. The Unfed say the other peoples have many Wants and they have only one, and it is the size of everything. Start play with Want 3.

Earning Want.

  • Refuse an offer of real value (food, drink, shelter, rest, a gift, a kindness) in a scene where accepting would clearly help you: +1 Want. Once per scene. It must cost you something; the GM may ask for a Caul + Resolve roll (Routine 10) if the offer is sincere and you are Hollow or worse.
  • Refuse Orrum. Pass an Invitation check against a laid table, a “Come in,” a place card, or a Steward’s offer: +2 Want (+3 on a Grace).
  • End a day hungry. A day on half a ration or less: +1 Want. A day with nothing at all: +2 Want (and a Pang, below).
  • Say the Decline at a deathbed (a companion’s, or a Seated guest’s): +1 Want, and you gain 1 Fray.

Spending Want.

  • The Second No (1 Want): reroll one die of a Grace Roll you just made. Keep the new result, even if it is worse.
  • The Gnaw (2 Want): add a d6, the Empty Tooth, to any roll. This is the Unfed’s answer to Partaking. It adds no Hunger. If the Empty Tooth shows a 1, you gain 1 Pang: your body paid.
  • Nothing to Hold (2 Want): add +4 to resist any godsign effect aimed at you: a Closer’s touch, a Calling, a Sayer’s word, a blink-dream, a Fatlands meat-lure, a Cradlewrack door. Your blood is empty; there is nothing in you for the god to hold on to.
  • Clean Through (5 Want): ignore a godsign effect aimed at you entirely, once, as though it had never been made. Witnesses who carry godsign make a Dread 2 check: something in their blood flinched.
  • Steady (1 Want): add +2 to any Dread check about hunger, food, tables, or the Seated.

At Want 10: Hollow. You are perfectly empty, and Orrum notices. That night, a table is laid for you within sight of wherever you sleep, with your name on the card. You must make an Invitation check each hour until dawn. Want cannot rise above 10. Spend it down.

Invitation Checks

When Orrum offers (a laid table, a voice at a door, a smell of bread on the wind, a place card, a chair pulled out), roll Caul + Resolve against the offer’s strength.

OfferDifficulty
Smell of baking on the windRoutine 10
A laid table, seen from a roadHard 14
A voice saying “Come in”Grim 18
A place card with your name in a loved handGrim 18
A chair pulled out, within reach; TablenightDire 22

Add your Pangs to the Difficulty: the hungrier you are, the better it smells. On a success, you refuse; gain Want. On a failure, take one step toward the table and roll again next round at +2 Difficulty; companions may hold you (an opposed Gut + Brawl) or speak the Decline for you (their Tongue + Persuade as a bonus die, once). On a Lack, you sit. On double 1s, you thank the chair.

The Seating. A PC who sits is Seated, and is lost: they become a guest, smiling, eating air, and will waste for decades at the table. The player may play out the First Course for a scene: the food is real to them, the best they have ever eaten, and they will say so. They can be dragged away only to die. They can never be rescued. Lent Ashby got up; the GM may decide that one other person in history might. It will not be cheap, and Welcome Ardent will want something.

Pangs: Starvation

Every character in the Fast tracks Pangs, from 0 to 10.

  • A ration is a day’s adequate food (about 1 lack’s worth). A Pantry measure is half a ration.
  • A day on a full ration: −1 Pang. A day of real plenty (two rations, rest, warmth): −2 Pangs, but an Unfed must succeed at a Gut + Endure roll (Hard 14) or lose 1d6 Flesh to cramps, sweats, and the heart’s stutter, refeeding sickness.
  • A day on a Pantry measure: no change. Unfed live here.
  • A day on less than a Pantry measure: +1 Pang.
  • A day with nothing: +2 Pangs. (Non-Unfed: +2, and +1 more after the third consecutive day.)
PangsStateEffects
0–2PeckishNone for Unfed. Others: −1 Caul + Resolve vs food.
3–4Hollow−1 to Gut and Lung rolls. Smells of baking everywhere.
5–6Gaunt−2 Gut and Lung; −2 Flesh max; you dream of meals.
7–8Wasting−3 all Hand, Gut, Lung rolls; −4 Flesh max; +1 Fray daily.
9BrinkEach dawn, Gut + Endure (Grim 18) or suffer Ruin.
10StarvedYou die, unless something feeds you in the night.

The Unfed feel it differently. At Hollow the cold gets in, and the fingers go white and dead; at Gaunt the hair comes away in the comb and the gums bleed when you bite; at Wasting the heart thuds slow and heavy, the ankles swell, sores open on the hips where you lie, and the mind goes sharp and strange and full of food: you recite recipes you have never been taught. At Brink you stop feeling hungry. That is the worst sign, and every Unfed knows it.

Playing the Hunger

Pangs are a number on a sheet, and they should never feel like one. The Unfed live at Peckish and Hollow their whole lives, and a good Unfed player plays the hunger as a constant low weather inside the character: something that shapes every sentence without being mentioned in most of them.

  • The body. Your character is cold, always, and their fingers go white and dead in the wind. They bruise when someone grips their arm. They feel their own heartbeat slow and heavy when they lie down, and they listen to it. They stand to eat, facing a wall. They chew a mouthful forty times because it makes it last. They pick crumbs from their coat at the end of a day and eat them, and are ashamed, and do it anyway.
  • The mind. At Hollow and below, the mind fills with food. Not cravings, exactly; the Unfed are trained out of crave. Arithmetic. How many oats in a measure. How many measures to the Rim. How many days at this rate. Recipes, from nowhere, in a grandmother’s voice. Unfed PCs should be the ones in the party who know exactly what everyone has left to eat, to the mouthful, and say so.
  • The pride. Hunger is the one thing an Unfed has that no Godeater can buy, and they are proud of it the way a soldier is proud of a scar. Let your Unfed be insufferable about it. Let them watch a Fatlands companion eat with a kind of pitying fascination. Let them refuse the offered hand up a step three times, and take it on the fourth, and say nothing, and remember.
  • The cracks. Every Unfed PC should have one food they cannot stop thinking about: a smell from a Rim inn window at eight years old, a sugared almond a poacher once held to their lips, a plum on a sill. Write it on the sheet. The GM will use it. It will be on the plate.

When the Unfed Eat a God

An Unfed who eats the god-meat of another land (Fatlands crop or meat, Brinehollow brine, anything grown in a Godeater soil long enough to carry its god) has done what Tobias Wether and Scour did, and it cannot be undone.

  • They gain that land’s godsign. They become Cut 1 of that land’s line, at Regrowth 1 (the Taste), and gain the Tooth, a Hunger track, and that land’s Gifts, Wants, and Sop as their Regrowth rises.
  • They lose the Refusal. Want drops to 0 and can never again be earned. Orrum never again lays a place for them. That sounds like freedom. It is felt as being struck off a list.
  • The Empty Room (something worse). An Unfed body has no ancestral habit of the god, no six centuries of bloodline to dilute and slow it. The god moves into them as into an empty, well-kept house, and makes itself comfortable. Their Tooth bites back on a 1 or a 2. Each time their Hunger empties, their Regrowth rises by 2, not 1. And the meat in them is looking for a god to belong to: within a season they will hear its voice, in the voice of someone it was eaten with.
  • A second land’s meat. If a Returned eats the god-meat of a second land, roll on the Mangling table at once: two gods are fighting over the house.

The Unfed call them the Returned, never to their faces. Most hide it. Some go to the Lean House. Some go back over the Rim and eat, and eat, and are not seen again.

What You Carry

Every Unfed PC starts with a ration-cloth, a water flask, a wax tin, a small household axe, three days’ Pantry measures, a coat that is not warm enough, and a name chosen for refusal. They have no money worth counting: 2d6 lacks.

Background Concepts

  • Measure-Bearer. You carried the list to the hamlets, and you know whose names were missing. You have never forgiven yourself for not looking at it first.
  • Tablebreaker’s Rope-Holder. You have pulled your Breaker back from a chair a dozen times. Last week you didn’t pull fast enough.
  • Poacher’s Escapee. You were taken over the Rim, fed for a month, and broke loose before the surgeon came. You came home plump and ashamed, and nobody will stand next to you on Tablenight.
  • Kin of a Portion. Your great-grandmother walked out to the stones in 559 and has written to your family every Lack since. You were raised never to say the word. You have her card, and you have read it.
  • Notched Door. You grew up in a house with five notches in the frame, and the last is at the height of your sister’s heart. You do not visit the verge. You stand at the edge of town some evenings, and your neighbours fetch you in.
  • Returned Knife. You were a Reckoner who ate to keep a cover, as Scour did. The god in you is a season old. You have not told your band. You carry your own food on every raid, and refuse it, and the god in you laughs.
  • Lean House Survivor. You were omitted, and walked to the Lean House, and on the twenty-second day your name was read again (a clerk’s error, a forged chit, a kindness nobody owns). You came back with the borrowed cheeks and a recipe you cannot stop saying.
  • Pin-Setter. You set the pins on the Great Map. You know where the walkers are, and the Seated, and the god. You have noticed what the newest pins are making, and nobody has asked you.
  • Poacher’s Get. You were born on the Rim to a captive who was fed on the road and kept in a warm room with no west windows, and you were smuggled home to the Fast as an infant by a Crumb-Runner who will not say how. You are Unfed by blood. You were fed on Fatlands milk for your first year. You do not know what that means yet.

Names

  • Given names: Forbear, Abstain, Decline, Stint, Tarry, Nay, Spare, Lent, Wont, Want, Meagre, Scant, Yield, Keep, Abate, Withhold, Forswear, Fallow, Bare, Pinch, Sparing, Lean, Scarcity, Reft, Abide, Hesitate, Cease.
  • Old (shameful) given names: Welcome, Ardent, Mercy, Hallow, Blythe, Bounty, Cheer, Plenty, Supper, Kindle.
  • Surnames: Ashby, Hollis, Moss, Avery, Rooke, Bellamy, Garrity, Hartsell, Wend, Corliss, Marsh, Tolland, Osmond, Aldane, Odell, Kettering, Hume, Corve, Kell, Pruett, Fennick, Lammas, Brindle, Hatch.

Carrying Your Own in a Mixed Party

Most parties that cross the Fast include Godeaters, and most Unfed PCs will spend more of their lives on the Rim than in Wanting. A few customs make an Unfed easy to play alongside the others, and hard to play lightly.

  • Never feed, never be fed. An Unfed will not take food from a companion’s hand, and will not give their own. They may set food down, and walk away, and let a companion pick it up: food set down is not offered, it is only there. Unfed PCs who have spent long on the Rim learn to do this so naturally that their companions do not notice they are being fed.
  • Count the chairs. At any inn, any hall, any feast, the Unfed counts the places before sitting, and gets up if there is one too many. In 640 and after, on the Rim Road, they are getting up more and more often.
  • The question. An Unfed will, early, ask after the state of a companion’s blood, kindly, as a courtesy. A Godeater who answers honestly gains an Unfed friend for life, and that friend will keep the count of their Regrowth more carefully than the Cutwrights do, and will say so.
  • Godless blood. Unfed are the one people on the Table that godsign cannot grip, and parties quickly learn to put them between the danger and everyone else: in front of a Closer, at the edge of a Hush, in the doorway of a Sayer. The Unfed know this and are proud of it. They also know what they are worth to a poacher, and that every Godeater in the party, every one, is a body that could be bought with a pair of Unfed kidneys. Some Unfed PCs never quite stop doing that sum.

Why You Left Wanting

Every Unfed PC is on the road for a reason, and few of them are good ones. Choose, or roll a d10.

d10Why you left
1Your name was left off the list. You did not walk to the Lean House. You walked east instead, to the Rim, and you are still not sure which was braver.
2You were a Reckoner Carrier, and you looked away at the bedside, and they sent you home, and you could not stay home.
3A place card came for you in a hand you loved. You have kept moving ever since, and the tables keep getting closer.
4You are carrying a letter for Envoy Prudence Lowell, sealed, and you have been told not to stop until it reaches her. That was a season ago.
5You are looking for someone taken by poachers. You have a name, a date, and a crossroads three miles west of the Lean House.
6Your family took a Rim name. You are considered emigrated. You are spoken of in the past tense, to your face, by your mother.
7You are hunting a table: the one your father sat down at, which moved. The Hostwatch say it is on the Rim Road now.
8Dr. Mercy Thrane hired you to bring a body home. You found it. It was not dead.
9You said come in to a knock at your door in Wanting, half asleep, without thinking. Nobody in the Fast will cross your threshold again.
10You do not know. You woke one morning on the Rim Road with your lips glazed sweet and sticky, a week gone, and a napkin folded in your pocket.
Hungry is alive. That’s all it means. It doesn’t mean anything nicer than that.
a Lean House survivor, explaining the proverb to a Rim physician

Horrors of the Fast

For the GM

The Fast is the quietest chapter of the book. Nothing attacks. Everything offers. Run it slowly: golden afternoons, empty roads, the smell. Let the players be hungry. Track Pangs openly. Describe food constantly, lovingly, and never let them eat it. The horror of the Fast is that the god is good, the food is real, and the only thing between your players and perfect contentment is a rule their grandparents made up while starving to death. Let them doubt it.

d20Scene
1A farmhouse kitchen with the table laid for a family of six. Five plates are clean. The sixth has the PC’s name, and the food on it is still steaming.
2The Long Table at dusk. Three hundred Seated lift their forks together, chew together, swallow together. The sound is like a herd grazing.
3A mother in Wanting carries her child’s ration to the Lean House, where her husband lies omitted. She stands at the door, and does not go in, and eats it.
4A Seated girl of perhaps twenty has been at table so long her hair has grown into the cloth. She asks a PC to brush it.
5A Reckoner band comes home through Brindle Cross. One of them has a christening spoon in his pocket and does not know how it got there.
6A warm front crosses the camp at night. In the morning everyone’s lips are glazed, sweet, and sticky. Nobody remembers eating.
7An Unfed grave in an open field, with a little table beside it. The earth of the grave has been disturbed from inside. The chair is pulled out.
8Kale Dragoman’s camp: four Unfed captives, fat and clean, sitting by the fire with bowls of stew in their laps, weeping, unable to stop eating.
9A Starved Saint’s novice offers a PC a twist of cloth with honey-cake crumbs in it, and asks them to taste it and tell her if it is poison.
10A Seated man dragged from the Long Table by his son dies in the road in two minutes, all at once, his body collapsing like a dropped tent. He thanks the host.
11A child’s voice from a cottage door calls a PC by their childhood nickname, and says supper’s ready, and says Mam’s made your favourite.
12An empty Rim inn, every table laid, every chair pulled out except one at each table: pushed in, square, its back to the lamp.
13A pilgrim column on the road, dying. A Fatlands woman asks a PC to hold her up so she can smell it one more time.
14A Reckoner Knife in a Wanting alley, alone, sobbing into a baby’s knitted blanket, saying the Decline over and over.
15Abide Kettering’s cart at the western crossroads. A sack moves.
16The bricked hearth in a PC’s lodging is warm to the touch. Through the mortar comes the soft sound of a spoon in a pot.
17A table on a frozen pond. Under the ice, a family of the Seated, perfectly preserved, smiling up, forks raised.
18The Pantry, at midnight, with every door locked. Inside, the ledgers are laid out on a long cloth like place settings, open at the names of the omitted.
19Hallowboard on a still evening. On the eighth, unworn side, a single chair stands in the untrodden chalk, pushed in. There are no footprints near it.
20Orrum, at a distance, across a gold field: a tall shape in an open doorway, stooping, lamplight behind it, holding out one long arm. It is crying. It is holding the door for someone it is not looking at. (Dread 4.)
We have been saying no for six hundred and forty-one years. It has been saying please for exactly as long. One of us is going to stop.
[ Spare Tolland of the Hostwatch, to the Warden of the Map, Carving 641 ]
Chapter 10

Threads Between the Lands

Every land is certain that the cure is next door.
— Rim Road saying
The road goes round. So does everything on it.
— painted over the door of the Company inn at Saltlick Cross

The lands of the Table are not separate stories. They share a road, a coin, a grace and a doom, and the crises in each are beginning to touch. This chapter takes the open storylines that cross borders and lays them out as campaign threads: who is involved in each land, how the thread escalates if nobody interferes, what the Guests can see and do about it, what it will cost them, and how it might end. Most of the endings are bad. That is not a failure of imagination; it is the setting. A thread resolved well is a thread that ends one way rather than a worse way.

Each thread is written in stages. Advance a thread one stage whenever the Guests spend a season elsewhere, or whenever the GM wishes the world to feel the weight of the clock. Threads touch: the Sayer’s Sentence feeds the Deadwatch, the Blank Trade feeds the Second Table, the Low Water feeds Eight Chairs, and almost everything, sooner or later, feeds Eight Chairs.

Every thread opens with an in-world document that hints at it before anything is explained, offers Scenes the Guests Might Witness to stage in full, and closes with a What It Costs box: the price, in Fray, Hunger, coin and conscience, of touching it at all. Fifteen threads follow: the twelve of the first edition, deepened with what Seven Tables has since uncovered, and three new ones that the year 642 is about to pull tight.

Running Threads

Pick two or three threads to run in the background of a campaign and let the others exist only as rumors. Keep a simple track for each, Stage 1 to Stage 4, on a card the players never see. When a thread reaches Stage 4 it resolves, with or without the Guests, and the world changes. Guests who intervene can hold a thread at its current stage for a season, push it back one stage at great cost, or steer which ending it reaches. They cannot make it not have happened.

A useful habit: whenever a thread advances off-screen, put one physical sign of it in front of the Guests within the next session. A place card on an inn table. A candle that keens when the wind drops. The world should be seen to move before it is explained.

Nobody on the Rim says “if” any more. They say “when the road closes,” the way a farmer says “when the frost comes.”
Factor’s letter, Lampwick Halt, Carving 641

The Calendar of 642

Many of the people of the Table have clocks running toward a particular day in the coming year. The GM who wants the threads to pull together should know where those days fall. Nothing below must happen; all of it will, if nobody stands in the way.

The Deadwatch

The dead cannot be Counted. Think on it, Castellan. It is the only sum in the city that comes out clean.
Sabine Larch, to Envoy Dray

Summary. The Vigil cannot sleep and is running out of everything: beds, rouse, oil and time. Its Warden-Prime has sent Envoy Castellan Dray to Lastgate to buy the secret of Keeping from Regent Ansel Grue: if the Vigil’s citizens could be killed and kept upright, a city of the dead would never need to sleep. The flaw is geography. The Kept cannot leave Sallowreach, so the Vigil would have to move there. Dray has not written this down, because he knows Ilvane Stroud will say yes; and Stroud has already decided, without telling him, to leave the sixty thousand Counted behind on the Lid, unwatched. A dispatch from the clerk Bell Lisle, now on the Rim Road, will make them both tell the truth.

To C. Dray, Envoy, care of the Company post-house, Lastgate. Fourth letter of Carving. Burn after.

Castellan. A Counted sleeper cannot be relieved of the risk she poses except by being relieved of her bed; a citizen who dies awake in the fen poses no risk at all. I have struck forty names from the general rows this month and can strike no faster without being noticed. You could strike a hundred thousand and be thanked on the Stair. I do not ask you to love the arithmetic. I ask you to show me where in it the murder is. Tell the Regent the Lessening pays in rouse, promptly.

S.L.

The Players.

  • The Vigil: Envoy Castellan Dray; Warden-Prime Ilvane Stroud; Dr. Aldous Crane, whose dose curve gives the Vigil eleven years; Benedikt Lour, already drawing plans for the whole population; Sabine Larch, First of the Lessening, who writes to Dray every week because the dead cannot be Counted; Bell Lisle’s dispatch, somewhere between Lampwick Halt and Fogmouth.
  • Sallowreach: Regent Ansel Grue, tempted by a hundred thousand new taxable dead; Lady Corrow Vane, who would have to Close nobody and keep everyone; the Heirs, who see a new population of the never-dying arriving to sit on top of them forever; Tam Ruddock, who already knows how to move people across the Drop and will sign on with Dray in 642 for a fee that would let him stop.
  • The Rim: the Company, which would carry the migration and price it; Fogmouth, where the line is painted.
StageWhat Happens
1Dray negotiates in Lastgate. Small trials: Vigil volunteers are brought north, killed in Sallowreach, and kept. They do not sleep. It works. The Lessening quietly funds the volunteers’ passage.
2Bell Lisle’s dispatch arrives. Dray and Stroud confess by letter, and agree. The Watch votes in secret to relocate. Caravans of the Slope’s poor begin moving west under Company contract.
3The first mass Killing at Fogmouth: thousands of Vigil folk die north of the Drop and stand back up. The Heirs riot. The Mortuary Court demands a toll per head. Tam Ruddock buys a bigger notebook.
4Lastgate’s lower levels fill with sleepless dead foreigners. The Vigil’s lamps go out one district at a time as the city empties into the fen. The Counted lie on the Lid with nobody counting them.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Trial at Fogmouth. A Slope laundress named Ottie Fane, thirty, lidded, nine days without a full sleep, kneels on the north bank where the line is painted on the planks in Company red. She has asked to be drowned rather than cut, because she has heard the Kept feel their wounds. Two Fen Guard hold her under the black water. It takes longer than anyone wants. Her heels drum the boards; her fingers find Dray’s boot and close on it. Then the drumming stops, and the Guard lift her out, and the water runs out of her nose and her open mouth in a long brown sheet, and her chest does not move, and she sits up. She coughs up a palmful of fen-weed. She looks at Dray, and her eyes are bloodshot and wide and perfectly clear. I’m still tired, she says. I thought it would stop. It never does. That is a Dread 3 check.
  • The Lower Levels. A Guest sent to inspect the first Vigil lodgings in Lastgate’s flooded under-streets finds a long cellar where two hundred dead foreigners stand in rows because there is nowhere to lie down, all awake, all rotting at the speed of the fen, the soft ones at the ankles going green and slack where the water laps. Nobody talks. They count, under their breath, in the Vigil way. Their eyes follow the lamp.

What the Guests Can Do. Escort or sabotage the trial caravans. Expose to the Vigil’s poor what Keeping actually feels like (Kept bodies rot and feel it for centuries). Uncover the Court’s hidden reason for agreeing: the Court believes new dead without Hand-line blood may slow the Hushes. Steal Dray’s commission, which the Warden-Prime would rather die than see read aloud. Intercept, delay or deliver Bell Lisle’s dispatch; whoever carries it decides when the city’s two oldest friends stop lying.

Endings.

  • The Dead City: the Vigil moves north and becomes a district of Lastgate, a hundred thousand rotting, wakeful foreigners. The Dormitory is abandoned with its Counted inside, unguarded, and the lamps go out over sixty thousand beds.
  • The Broken Deal: the Heirs drag Dray to a Hush; the Vigil, betrayed, closes the Rim at Lampwick Halt; Sallowreach loses its rouse and oil, and Lastgate’s candle-makers turn to the only fuel left.
  • The Worst Arithmetic: a Vigil sleeper is brought north, unconscious, and killed in Sallowreach. They do not wake and do not die. They lie there, Kept and Counted at once, and the Dormitory’s number goes up by one.
What It Costs — The Deadwatch

Witnessing a trial Killing is Dread 3; witnessing a mass Killing at Fogmouth is Dread 4. A Guest who helps a volunteer die gains the volunteer’s gratitude, which is permanent and sleepless. Sabotaging a caravan earns the Lessening’s attention: within a season, the Guest’s name (or a loved one’s) appears on a list for the general rows. Siding with the Heirs closes the Vigil to the party; siding with Dray closes Lastgate’s upper levels.

The Host on the Road

Lack keep away. And if it won’t, set it a place.
said by Rim innkeepers since the tables began

Summary. For six centuries Orrum kept to the Fast. Now its tables have been found laid at crossroads in three other lands, and the seemers of the Vigil, the scavengers of Brinehollow and the pilgrims of the Fatlands have all seen the same tall figure laying a table. That figure is Welcome Ardent, the Host’s steward, walking a mile ahead of his god around the Rim. On fourteen walls in fourteen capitals, Envoy Prudence Lowell has made a small chalk stroke where she stood to eat facing the plaster, like a table seen edge on. In three of those capitals, someone has drawn eight short marks beneath it.

A place card, cream board, gilt edge, found at the crossroads of the Drove Road and the Rim, Plenty 641. The hand is beautiful and slightly unsteady.

Goodwife Hanna Spurling, of Stile Farm

Seated at the third place. The soup is barley with marrowbone; the bread was baked this morning, and there is butter. Please do not wait for the others. You have been hungry such a long time. You were always so polite about it.

(On the reverse, in the same hand, smaller:) I am sorry. I am so sorry. Do not sit. It is very good. Do not sit.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Welcome Ardent, polite and exhausted; Spare Tolland of the Hostwatch, mapping the warm ground; Decline Marsh and the Tablebreakers; Envoy Prudence Lowell and her chalk marks.
  • The Vigil: Mirela Sconce, who recorded eleven districts hallucinating a table being laid in the street.
  • The Fatlands: Osanna Blythe and her three hundred pilgrims, hungry every second of their lives, looking for a table where they will finally feel full.
  • Brinehollow: salvagers on the Uncovered who have found tables laid on the dry seabed with the plates still wet.
  • The Rim: the wardens at Saltlick Cross; every innkeeper who has seen a tall shape stoop to look in at the window.
StageWhat Happens
1Tables appear at Rim crossroads, one a season. Tablebreakers cross the Hem to smash them. Place cards bear the names of people who live nearby.
2Welcome Ardent is seen in person at a Rim inn. He asks, politely, whether anyone would take over his duties. The first non-Unfed sit down: a Fatlands family, a Vigil nudger, a Kept man a yard north of the Drop at Fogmouth, who now cannot leave the table or the fen.
3Orrum itself is seen on the Rim at night, stooping to look in at windows. Whole villages along the Fatlands border are found Seated. Osanna Blythe’s pilgrims find their table.
4Tables are laid in every capital on the same night, with a place card for every head of state. In each, one chair is left without a card.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Spurling Table. Hanna Spurling sat. So did her husband and two grown sons, at the places laid for them. The Guests find them nine days later: the table is still warm to the touch, the bread still steams when torn, and the four Spurlings are eating. Their cheeks have fallen in to the shape of the teeth beneath. Their wrists are rope. Their nails have grown long and curled against the spoons, and their lips are split and bleeding into the soup, and they are smiling, and they say you must try the butter. They do not want to be lifted. They scream, thin and high, if they are.
  • The Face at the Window. In a Company inn after midnight, the shutters on the road side darken one by one, left to right, as something very tall walks slowly past outside and stoops at each. At the last window it stops. The Guests hear it breathe once, like a bellows in an empty forge. In the morning the frost on the sill has melted in the shape of two great hands laid flat.

What the Guests Can Do. Track Ardent and talk to him (he is the only one of Orrum’s guests who can still get up, and he will answer questions honestly if he is not invited to sit). Smash tables, at the risk of finding their own names. Protect or stop the pilgrims. Discover that the cardless chair at each table faces away from the others.

Endings.

  • The Long Table Grows: the Seated spread along the Rim, a second endless table around the whole continent, happy, wasting, praising the food. Trade stops because the road is full of diners.
  • The Relief: a Guest accepts Ardent’s position. Ardent finally sits down and eats, and dies in moments, weeping with gratitude. The Guest now walks a mile ahead of the god forever, and knows exactly whom the tables are for.
  • The Unanswered Door: the tables stop, all at once. Orrum stands still at Hallowboard facing the eighth side. The Hostwatch reports that it has never looked so frightened.
What It Costs — The Host on the Road

Coming upon a Seated family is Dread 3. Smashing a table is a Hard Caul + Resolve roll; failure means the smasher eats one mouthful first, without meaning to, and gains 2 Hunger and the Want Sit Down (resist Hard 14 whenever offered food by a stranger) until the next Tablenight. A Guest who finds their own name on a card makes a Dread 4 check. Speaking with Ardent costs nothing but sleep: the night after, the Guest dreams of laying a table for someone who is late. Taking his position is the end of that Guest’s story as a player character.

Brine in the Rouse

Dry Jonah’s Tonic — Sea-Air in a Bottle — For the Chest, the Nerves, the Long Night. Do Not Exceed Three Drops.
label, Lowmark bottling, sold on the Slope at four lacks

Summary. Captain Jonah Skerry, called Dry Jonah, bottles what Brinehollowers cough up at bailing and sells it inland as tonic. It sells best in the Vigil, where the Slope dealer Rook Quarter-Bell cuts it into rouse because it is cheap and it works. The sleepless are now feeling the Calling, four hundred miles from any coast. Customers stay awake. They have also started walking west. On the coast, the Assay clerk Brenna Kelp has proved that the sea falls by nine hundred and twelve thousand barrels for every Tenanted soul returned from it, a figure the clerks call the Kelp. If a Vigil walker comes back Tenanted, the constant will have to count her. The ocean, it seems, does not mind which land its people come from.

From the private daybook of Dr. Aldous Crane, Apothecary-General. Not for the Watch.

Batch 41, Slope-street rouse, cut approx. one part in nine with coastal tonic (Skerry’s). Subject held awake 31 hours on a standard dose; control, 30. One hour. One hour is eleven thousand waking hours across the city per night. One hour is a year off the curve. Side effects: dry cough, salt crust at the lips by the second day, a tendency to stand at west-facing windows. Subject 6 asked me, very politely, what the water was like where I came from. I have not reported this batch. I have ordered forty barrels.

The Players.

  • Brinehollow: Dry Jonah, who has not bailed in years and is due to be Called before Tablenight; Tolly Brack, who knows by the color of bailing water who will be Called next; Brenna Kelp and her constant; the Netwatch, who are going to see Called strangers arrive from the east.
  • The Vigil: Rook Quarter-Bell; Dr. Aldous Crane, desperate for anything that stretches the dose; the Wakers; Inspector Hale Grimmer, whose blink-murders begin to cluster on the western edge of the city; Senna Vole, on her forty-first dive into the room.
  • The Rim: Lampwick Halt and Lowmark Spur, the two ends of the walk.
StageWhat Happens
1The Slope’s addicts stand at west windows. Dr. Crane notices that brine-cut rouse holds an hour longer and does not report it.
2Vigil citizens begin walking west across the plateau in their sleep-that-is-not-sleep, eyes open, straight lines. The Wakers net them at the city edge. Dry Jonah is Called from the deck of the Bess.
3Crane formulates brine into the official rouse. The whole Vigil now carries a little of the sea. Lines of walkers cross the Rim heading for a coast they have never seen.
4The first Vigil walkers reach the Uncovered and keep going, out toward the Trench. Some come back Tenanted: calm, courteous, rested. They are the first people in the Vigil in three centuries who sleep and wake again. The sea, by the Kelp, falls a little faster.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The West Window. A Slope tenement, fourth floor. Eleven people stand at a single west window, shoulder to shoulder, faces to the glass. Their breath has fogged it and then salted it, a white crust the shape of eleven mouths. One of them, a boy of seventeen, is coughing quietly and steadily; what comes up is grey, foaming and smells of a harbor at low tide, and in it are threads of something green and slick that moves a little on the floorboards before it stops. None of them turns around. One of them is humming a tune the Guests will hear again, if they ever stand on the cliff at Lowmark at Low Water.
  • The Net. A line of walkers crosses the plateau at dawn, spaced exactly apart, eyes open and dry. The Wakers string a net across the road. The walkers walk into it and keep walking, and the net creaks, and their faces press through the mesh until the cord cuts into the cheeks, and they do not stop pushing, and they do not cry out, and they bleed.

What the Guests Can Do. Trace the supply chain from bailing buckets in Lowmark to dealers on the Slope. Kill or bargain with Dry Jonah before the sea takes him. Shepherd walkers home or follow them to see where they go. Present the Watch with the choice: brine buys the Vigil years of wakefulness at the cost of the sea pulling on every citizen.

Endings.

  • The Walking City: the Vigil adopts brine-rouse openly and loses a tenth of its people a year to the west. The Watch calls it emigration.
  • The Tenanted Wardens: Tenanted Vigil-folk, rested and calm, are found to be immune to the Dormitory’s dream. The Watch begins appointing them to office, as Brinehollow did with its judges. Nobody asks whose eyes are looking out.
  • The Meeting of Waters: the Trench, the draining sea and the long dim room in the Vigil’s dream turn out to be closer than anyone thought. Senna Vole, on her forty-first dive, hears water.
What It Costs — Brine in the Rouse

A Guest who takes brine-cut rouse gains a single extra watch awake per dose but rolls Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) each dawn after: failure means a Called walk of an hour westward before waking, Lung + Athletics to stop safely. Three failures and the Guest hears the Calling permanently, as a Brinehollower does, wherever they stand. Netting walkers is Dread 2. Killing Dry Jonah makes an enemy of every coastal bottler and buys nothing: the tonic trade has six other captains. Telling the Vigil’s poor the truth starts a riot at the Bitterhouse in which the Wakers’ long needles are used freely.

The First to Eat

What grows in an Unfed body is not the god the body ate.
Odo Venn, private notes, never sent to Quire

Summary. Tobias Wether, a runaway raised on six centuries of refusal, crossed into the Fatlands and ate. The Reckoner called Scour spent a year undercover in the Fatlands, had to eat to keep his cover, and came home with godsign. Two Unfed bodies now carry a god that was never theirs, and the meat inside them seems to be looking for something. Tobias does not know that the drover Sal Trotter, who took him in, named him after the son she culled for a debt; or that the lead steer of her herd, branded with that son’s plot-number, hums her song a beat ahead of her. Wont Bellamy has guessed what Scour is, and has written to the Second Table that he may soon have “a dish of rare interest.”

College tasting-slip, Odo Venn’s hand, folded into a hymnal at Sated. The official copy, filed at Quire, reads “Subject W.: Ummer-line, trace, unremarkable.”

Subject W. Blood drawn from the thumb, tasted at room heat. First: Ummer, faint, the usual gravy and grass. Under it: nothing. Not absence, as with a Blank. A space. A room with the door left open. I held it on the tongue for the count of twelve and something on the far side of the space noticed me holding it. I have rinsed eleven times. I will not record this.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Scour, hiding his godsign under his sleeves and volunteering for every raid; Reckoner-Captain Scant Hollis; the Abstinent, for whom this is the worst possible news; Meek Garrity, whose research says the Unfed never refused at all; Wont Bellamy, with his letter.
  • The Fatlands: Tobias Wether; Sal Trotter and her humming steer; Corder Lank of the Thin, who is very interested in a man who came from emptiness into hunger; Brother Glut of the Second Helping, who sees a convert.
  • Cross-border: Odo Venn of the College, who wants to taste them; the Second Table, who want to know whether an Unfed stomach makes room for a god.
StageWhat Happens
1Tobias shows his first godsign. It is not purely Ummer’s: he dreams of a long dim room and closes doors behind him. Scour’s signs are similar.
2The College learns of them. Unfed blood with godsign is, by the ledgers, impossible. Odo Venn tastes Tobias and goes pale and does not report the flavor.
3Scour’s comrades find out. The Abstinent strike his name from the Pantry. He flees to the Rim, where the Second Table is waiting with an invitation.
4Tobias and Scour, kept apart, begin to show identical signs at the same hour. Neither carries any one god. Both are getting hungrier for the same thing, and when they meet, they set a table.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Doors. Tobias, lodged at an inn, cannot pass through a door without closing it behind him, then opening it, then closing it again from the other side, three times, his lips moving. If anyone stops him he goes grey and sweats and his stomach makes a long, low, hollow sound, like wind across the mouth of a jar. The door he did not get to close is found in the morning with the paint scored by fingernails on the inside, low down, where a crouching person would reach.
  • Under the Sleeves. Scour, in a Reckoner bunkhouse, unwinds his wrappings by a candle when he thinks he is alone. The godsign on his forearms is the marbling of good beef, fat laced through red, but in it, if a Guest looks closely, the fat has drawn itself into lines: a long rectangle, and eight small squares around it.

What the Guests Can Do. Protect them, hide them, study them or kill them. Bring Tobias back into the Fast and see what happens to the Lack around him. Learn, from Venn’s private notes, that what grows in an Unfed body is not the god the body ate.

Endings.

  • The Empty Vessel: the Second Table buys Scour and serves him, as a test. The diners all sleep badly afterward, and dream of a room where someone is laying a table.
  • The Lack Breaks: Tobias returns to the Fast and plants. The dead soil sprouts where he walks. The Abstinent call it a miracle and then realize what it means: the heartland can be fed if its people eat. Wont Bellamy wins the next vote.
  • Two Places Laid: in Lack 642, Tobias and Scour vanish from their guarded rooms on the same night. Two Orrum tables are found the next morning at the Rim, with their names on the cards, and the chairs pushed in.
What It Costs — The First to Eat

Hiding either man makes the Guests enemies of the Reckoners (who end lines) or of the Second Table (who end dinners), and usually both. Tasting their blood, as Venn did, needs Caul + Godsign (Grim 18) to learn anything and imposes a Dread 3 check whatever the result; on a Lack the taster gains the Derangement Open Doors (cannot bear a door left shut behind them). Killing them is murder of the gentlest people in the chapter, and their tables are laid anyway.

The Blank Trade

Price per pound, Unfed, dressed: forty lacks. Price per pound, Blank, living, any land: name your figure.
chalked inside a poacher’s lean-to, Fast border

Summary. Wren Hollowell in the Fatlands, Cassian Wry in Oathen and the entire population of the Fast are worth more in parts than whole. Blank blood, marrow and organs are believed to slow the Regrowth. Dr. Mercy Thrane of the Fast is following the buyers, and the trail leads to the Second Table. She carries a plank from a hidden surgery in Sated with A.T. scratched into it and believes it was a patient’s. It was her brother’s. Abide Thrane has lived for nine years in Master Quillon Barr’s brine-tanks, and has started to put on weight; and Barr has read Mercy’s book, admired it, and sent her a pair of spectacles.

Docket, Rim Road Company freight, Wanting Post to Sated. Found pasted inside a barrel lid.

Consignment 6612. Contents: PICKLED GOODS (BRINE), 4 barrels, sealed. Shipper: A. Kettering, sexton, by proxy. Receiver: K. Dragoman, for the account of a gentleman. Weight declared: 9 stone 4. Weight at Sated scales: 9 stone 4. Company does not open sealed freight. Clerk’s note in pencil, faint: one of them knocked.

The Players.

  • The Fast: Dr. Mercy Thrane; Marshal Keep Aldane, holding the border against poachers; Abide Kettering, the sexton who sells the omitted dead at Brindle Cross; Withy Gaunt, who once sold a baby there so that he would live; every Unfed child sent to fetch water at dusk.
  • The Fatlands: Kale Dragoman, poacher, plump and kind and smelling of woodsmoke, who is that baby grown and does not know it; Wren Hollowell, with a bounty on her weight that does not specify alive; Lord Chastain Loin, who wants a Blank set in aspic for the Second Table’s cellar; the Board of Plenty.
  • Oathen: Cassian Wry, the crown’s Blank spy, kept in luxury and never let out of sight; the Bench of Clauses, which has received an offer.
  • Cross-border: Master Quillon Barr and Lady Seraphine Dalgety of the Second Table; the Rim Road Company, whose wagons carry sealed brine-barrels it does not open.
StageWhat Happens
1Unfed disappearances double along the eastern border. Thrane finds a surgery in Sated with an Unfed man’s name scratched inside a cupboard.
2Wren Hollowell is taken. A Fatlands Gut-line matriarch is seen at the Weighing ten stone lighter and, for the first time in thirty years, not eating.
3Oathen’s Bench agrees, in a forty-page conditional, to lease Cassian Wry’s kidney to a foreign buyer. The surgery is scheduled at Treaty Stair.
4Thrane traces the trail to Barr’s surgery, and finds Abide, nine years a donor, fat and smiling, and the eighth course on a menu pinned to the wall, still blank.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Tanks. Barr’s cellar is warm and smells of vinegar, cloves and the inside of a cheek. Six copper tanks, lidded, each with a glass port at face height. In the third, Abide Thrane floats in green brine to the chin, his scalp shaved and seamed, plump, pink, the skin of his belly puckered with nine years of neat little scars like the stitching on a quilt. He opens his eyes at the lamp and smiles, and mouths a word through the glass. It is his sister’s name.
  • The Lean House. Kale Dragoman comes himself to collect a body. Withy Gaunt smells woodsmoke and turns. Kale nicks her hand to price an old woman in the straw, licks the drop, and tastes his own name in it. Kettering is in the doorway with the pickaxe.

What the Guests Can Do. Raid a surgery. Escort Wren out of the Fatlands, which will put every bounty-hunter in the south on their trail. Free Cassian Wry, who has been kept all his life and does not know how to live unwatched. Follow the money to the Company’s sealed barrels and make the Company choose between its neutrality and its conscience. If a Guest is a Blank, this thread is about them.

Endings.

  • The Market Holds: the trade goes on, and prices rise. The Fast begins to sell its own people to buy grain, and calls it Pantry policy.
  • The Exposed Table: the trail is published. In every capital, a few High Cuts are revealed to be carrying Unfed organs, and the Reckoners have a new list.
  • Room Made: Barr’s patients begin, one by one, to feel empty inside, in exactly the places where a Blank organ was sewn in. They become very hungry. They do not know for what.
What It Costs — The Blank Trade

Seeing Barr’s tanks is Dread 3; recognizing someone in them is Dread 4. Abide cannot survive outside the brine without a surgeon (Hand + Stitching, Dire 22, over a week) and if he survives, he weighs twice what the Fast can feed. A Blank Guest is worth 2,000 lacks living to any Second Table buyer, and every hireling the party takes on is a possible seller. Opening a sealed Company barrel breaks Company law: the party’s platters are refused at every inn for a year.

The Missing Hand

WANTED: a LEFT HAND, female, born in the Grace of 637 to a woman of Low Sett. Generous reward. No questions as to how.
bill posted on pang-houses along the Kest road

Summary. In a guarded barn in Cradlewrack, Dov Marrin and the Assemblers have fitted the Parts of four hundred families into one figure eleven feet long. They call her Herself. She has nine arms, forty-one eyes that wept last week, and two chest cavities: the left holds the heart of Dov’s own wife Liss, born to her as a Part at sixty; the right is empty. She breathes, and the lamps lean. She is missing a left hand and a voice. Hester Lowe bore a left hand and is hiding it. Juniper Dell was born saying half a sentence. The roof over Herself was paid for in Second Table coin by Lord Casimir Morwen, who sends the Barn everything his veiled wife delivers; one of the forty-one eyes is the Duchess’s. In Plenty 641 Herself turned her head toward the Sill.

From Dr. Lazar Voss’s sketchbook, the forty-third sheet. Copies sold to Lady Dalgety at three hundred lacks.

Count of major structures, Herself, as of Carving: arms 9. Eyes 41. Hearts 1, cavities 2. Spines: one complete, one partial (the partial is not human and not, I think, Vey’s: nine-jointed, grey, fits the Sallowreach finger exactly). Note: the right cavity is lined. It has been lined since before Liss’s heart went in. Somebody built a place for a second heart and has not yet been born.

The Players.

  • Cradlewrack: Dov Marrin; Hester Lowe, who will kill for the hand; Juniper Dell, called Firstword; Ambrose the Eldest Infant, who claims to remember being Vey’s left eye; Old Hinge at the Sill; Lord Casimir Morwen and his veiled Duchess; Dr. Lazar Voss of the Vigil, who has drawn the figure and counted more than two of several things.
  • Sallowreach: Marrow Jack, the part-thief, who has been buying Cradlewrack Parts on the Rim; Sister Tisane Halloway’s jar of grey hinged joints, which fit together.
  • The Rim: Petra Quick, who smuggled a Part across the border without knowing it.
StageWhat Happens
1The Assemblers hire outsiders to find the hand. Hester moves house every night. The hand has begun to point.
2Juniper Dell meets someone, somewhere, who says the other half of her sentence. Nobody hears it but them.
3The hand is taken, or given. Herself’s left arm is complete. She sits up. The pangs fall to seven days.
4Juniper is brought to the barn. She speaks her half and Herself speaks the other half. The Sill door swings fully open for the first time since the Gorging.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Hand in the Sack. Hester keeps it in a flour sack, in a basket, under a shawl. It is small, a woman’s, warm as a sleeping child, with a pink nail-bed and a crease of fat at the wrist where it ends in smooth closed skin. At night it crawls on its fingertips to the end of the sack and points, through the cloth, toward the Barn; turn the basket and within the hour it has turned back. Hester sings to it. She has bitten one of her own fingers to the bone so as to have something to bite when the singing does not work.
  • The Breathing Barn. Inside, a hundred lamps on poles, all leaning inward. Herself lies on straw that smells of a lambing-shed, sheep-fat and warm milk; her forty-one eyes are half-lidded and they move together. When she breathes, the Guests’ own breath falls into time with hers within three counts and cannot be made to fall out of it.

What the Guests Can Do. Protect Hester and the hand. Find the person with the other half of the sentence before the Assemblers do. Burn the barn (Herself will not burn easily; she will begin again out of the ashes). Learn from Dr. Voss’s drawing that the figure is not Vey alone: some of its Parts came from outside Cradlewrack, some belong to no god anyone has named, and the empty cavity was lined before anyone knew it would be needed.

Endings.

  • The Firstborn: Herself stands, walks to the Sill and goes through. Whatever was describing the view to Old Hinge comes back through the other way.
  • The Hand Withheld: Hester refuses to the last and is killed; the hand crawls away into the hills and is never found. Herself lies incomplete and breathing, and Cradlewrack’s pangs continue to shorten anyway. It was never the figure the land was in labor with.
  • The Sentence: the full sentence is spoken aloud once. Everyone who hears it understands exactly what is being born out of the ground, and when. Nobody who hears it can be persuaded to say it again.
What It Costs — The Missing Hand

Standing in the Barn is Dread 3; breathing in time with Herself for a full hour adds 1 Regrowth to any Cradlewracker present. Taking the hand from Hester by force is kin-slaying in everything but blood: the Attendance treats it as the murder of a child. Burning the Barn makes the Guests enemies of four hundred families who each gave something of their own body to it. Hearing the full Sentence is Dread 5.

The Sayer's Sentence
