What a Sayer says, is. What she has been writing on her wall for nine years, nobody has thought to read.
Grandam Cess of Knot Canyon

Summary. Every land with a failing cure has thought of the same thing: go to Oathen, and have Lady Imre Dath, the Sayer, say that it is fixed. What a Sayer says, is. Nobody knows what Tolm would make true if she did. The Bench of Clauses is debating, in forty-page conditionals, whether to take out her golden bit; and she has begun to write her own sentences. The one on her wall is already binding at Course strength. Each night she fails to finish it, it renews. It is waiting for a word. Meanwhile, Chief Clausewright Sorrin Vael swears in his sleep, and his wife has two years of it written down: a treaty between “the party who listens” and “the party who comes late to table,” granting the second party “a chair, and the first portion.”

Draft the Ninety-Second, Bench of Clauses, clause 211 of 418. Marginal hand: S. Vael.

211. That the Regrowth, as it is commonly called, in every land of the Table, shall cease and stand, PROVIDED that no person now living shall thereby be ended; AND PROVIDED that “cease” shall not be read to include the beating of hearts, the falling of rain, the growth of crops, the healing of wounds, or the bearing of children, being processes the Bench wishes to continue; AND PROVIDED

(margin): every proviso is a door. I can hear something trying the handles.

The Players.

  • Oathen: Lady Imre Dath; Sorrin Vael, Chief Clausewright, who would draft the sentence; Ket the Ninth, who must nod; Garl Tome, who made the gold bit, and whose daughter Merit has promised the king her first words, at Plenty, in the Hall of Conditions; Yusra Thole, Rainwarden, whose silence about the late rain is being noticed.
  • Every land: envoys from the Vigil (Let the Vigil sleep and wake), Brinehollow (Let the sea return), Sallowreach (Let the dead finish), the Fatlands (Let the hungry be full), Cradlewrack (Let nothing more be born wrong).
  • Cross-border: the Rim Road Company, which needs the Kept Rain kept; the Second Table, which wants a single sentence of its own: Let the second meal hold.
StageWhat Happens
1Envoys arrive in Tacit and bid. The Bench begins drafting. Lady Imre is caught with chalk and a wall full of her own sentences.
2An envoy, impatient, bribes a guard. Someone gets into the Gilded Cells with a question. The Sayer answers. A valley in Oathen changes overnight.
3The Bench agrees on a text, four hundred conditions long, to be spoken at the next unmuzzling. Every faction on the Table tries to alter one clause.
4The bit comes out. She speaks.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Changed Valley. A Fatlands envoy’s clerk got in, and asked whether his master’s valley would be fed. It is full, said the Sayer. The Guests ride into Low Sorrow the next morning. Every goat, every shepherd, every child in the valley is full: bellies drum-tight and shining, skin split in white stretch-marks from navel to ribs, and they are sitting very still in the grass, with the patience of people who cannot bend, and they are full of what, nobody can say. A shepherd’s lips are blue. He thanks the Guests. He says he has never been so content.
  • The Wall. Lady Imre’s cell is gilded and lamplit and the wall behind her bed is chalk to the ceiling, the same sentence ten thousand times, each one stopping at the same place, mid-word. The chalk on the last line is still wet with spit, because she had no water to wet it with. Her ears, all of them, turn toward the Guests.

What the Guests Can Do. Carry an envoy’s bid, or forge one. Guard the Cells or break into them. Edit the sentence, one clause at a time, through bribes, threats and Clausewrights. Read Lady Imre’s own wall, where she has written, over and over, a sentence she has never been allowed to say. Learn that nobody has ever once asked the Sayer what she wants.

Endings.

  • It Is Fixed: she says the Bench’s sentence. Every Regrowth stops dead where it stands. So does every other change, of any kind. See the Secrets chapter.
  • Her Own Sentence: she says what she has been writing. It is short. It is about her. The god in her gets what it wants.
  • The Slip: the sentence is spoken and does not take. A god’s word has slipped again, worse than the rain. Every oath in Oathen loosens by a hair, every Forsworn body in the Breakdowns begins, slowly, to heal, and every sworn contract on the Rim begins to fail.
What It Costs — The Sayer’s Sentence

Entering the Gilded Cells uninvited is a capital crime in Oathen, tried by the Bench and executed by the Breaking of the trespasser’s own oaths. Asking the Sayer a question is the Guest’s to regret: the GM decides what becomes true, and it is always true exactly. Altering a clause of the Bench’s draft needs Tongue + Clause (Dire 22) or a bribe of 2,000 lacks, and the GM notes which clause; it will matter. Reading the wall is Dread 3, and a Guest who reads it aloud finishes the sentence.

Eight Chairs

Seven pushed in, one pulled out. Same on the mud, same in the hill. Somebody’s late.
Cray Lobbett, in the Pickled Stair, drawing in spilled gin

Summary. Cray Lobbett found a stone table on the seabed of the Uncovered, older than the Gorging, with eight chairs, seven pushed in; the Passenger who rides Orrin Wake says Cray has three visits left before he sits. Hallowboard, at the center of the world, has eight sides. Grandfather Peat, a bog body hauled from the Sump, is the last witness to the Night of Seven Tables and says the god was smiling. Meek Garrity has found the seating plan for Hallowboard, and Sober Osmond a line in the Empty Chair rite about the one who comes late. In the Vigil, Aveline Morne has spoken in Bed One: There is someone at the door who has not been fed. Set another place. Someone is going to put these together. This is the thread that leads to the Secrets chapter, and it should be the spine of any long campaign.

Transcript, interview with the bog body called Grandfather Peat, Lastgate, by a hired translator of the Sump dialect. Paid by an unnamed College buyer.

Q. You were at the table that night.

A. At the bank. We were the bank. We stood.

Q. How many tables were there?

A. Seven tables. Eight sides to the hill. We laid the seven.

Q. And the god was smiling?

A. Ours was. Ours had seen him come.

Q. Seen who come?

A. (long silence; the translator notes the jaw working with no sound) Write down that I was smiling too. Write down that we were all so glad to be eating that nobody looked behind.

The Players.

  • Brinehollow: Cray Lobbett, who cannot stop going back; Hask Tarn, the only pilot who knows the ground; Ilse Marl, whose transcriptions of the Tenanted’s singing make a chart that now runs from the table toward the Headland; the Passenger, who wants a hand at the eighth place.
  • Sallowreach: Grandfather Peat; Old Bettany Shroud, whose forty thousand shelved dead all whisper the same word.
  • The Fast: Meek Garrity and his plan; Fallow Brindle; Verger Sober Osmond at the Empty Chair; Hollow Ann Pruett with a card on which someone has drawn an empty chair; Welcome Ardent.
  • The Vigil: Aveline Morne in Bed One; Matron Cecily Dorm, who writes down what her lips say.
  • Cross-border: Archprovost Hesper Lune of the College, reconstructing the chiseled figure; Envoy Prudence Lowell, who has asked that Garrity be left off the winter list, the first death she has ever asked for; the Second Table, who want the eighth line of their menu filled.
StageWhat Happens
1Garrity’s plan leaks. The Abstinent call it forgery. Lobbett tries to sell the table’s location again and finds a buyer who pays in Company platters.
2Someone brings a translator to Grandfather Peat. He describes the Night in full. He describes the bank behind the god, and what was on it.
3Rubbings from the seabed table are compared with Hallowboard and with Lune’s reconstruction. They match. The eighth chair on the seabed is the only one pulled out, and it faces the same way as the eighth side of Hallowboard.
4The word Bettany Shroud’s dead whisper is the older word for guest. It is said aloud, in full, by someone who has put it together. Everything that has been hiding hears it.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Table on the Mud. Three miles out on the Uncovered at dead low tide, through ground that sucks to the thigh and smells of rot and something sweet beneath it, like a pantry. The table is black basalt, crusted with barnacles everywhere but its top, which is clean, as if wiped. Seven chairs pushed in. The eighth pulled out a hand’s breadth, and in the silt of its seat, a hollow, the shape of someone recently risen. Cray Lobbett sits down on the mud beside it and touches the eighth square he has drawn on every wet surface for a year, over and over, and weeps without noise.
  • The Lofts Whisper. Old Bettany Shroud takes a Guest up to the fourth floor of Hall Two at night. Shelf on shelf of the Set-Aside, forty thousand dry mouths, and every one of them moving, and the sound of it is like wind in a field of barley, one word long, again, again. Close enough to a single mouth to hear it plainly is close enough to smell the leather of the lips.

What the Guests Can Do. Everything, and that is the danger. Dive to the table. Interrogate Peat. Steal Garrity’s papers, or keep him off the winter list. Sit at Bed One with the Matron’s pencil. Visit Hallowboard and count the sides. Each discovery should cost Fray. The right questions in the right order lead, inevitably, to the Secrets chapter’s answers, and the answers are not survivable in any comfortable sense.

Endings.

  • Counted: the chairs are counted aloud. It does not matter by whom. The eighth chair, on the seabed, at Hallowboard, at every inn on the Rim, turns from the wall to face the table.
  • The Silence Kept: the Guests destroy the evidence and kill or silence those who know. The world goes on not knowing for a few more years. The Guests do not get to.
  • The Place Card: at the end of a long investigation, a Guest finds a table laid for them, with a card in the Host’s handwriting, and a second card, in another hand, at the chair beside them.
What It Costs — Eight Chairs

Every major discovery is a Dread check, rising: the seabed table Dread 3, Peat’s full account Dread 3, the matching rubbings Dread 4, the word itself Dread 5. A Guest who Breaks on this thread gains the Derangement The Eighth Place (they must count the chairs in any room before sitting, and cannot sit if the count is even). Silencing Garrity makes the party murderers of a gentle old man for the sake of a Refusal that never happened. The GM should never let this thread be cheap.

The Second Table

Your attendance is requested at a supper of seven courses. Dress is grey. Knives are provided. The eighth course will be announced.
card, delivered by hand, Lastgate, Lack 641

Summary. In every capital, a few of the highest Cuts are sharpening knives for a meal they intend to eat twice. When the gods finish regrowing, they will eat them again, a few diners instead of a mob, and inherit another six centuries of grace. They are further along than anyone guesses. Prudence Lowell’s dispatches are copied at Wanting Post and sold to them, so that the Fast’s Register of Damnation has become their menu-calendar. Lord Casimir Morwen has sold them the date of the Dilation’s opening. Commodore Vell means to carry a carving party to the Trench. Lord Absalom Hethe has drawn up plans for a lead coffin. And Wont Bellamy, a heretic on the Fast’s own council, wants the Unfed to join them, starting with the one god that is still whole.

Bill of fare, practice supper, the cellar table at Marrable Hall. Found in a dead waiter’s apron.

I. A clear broth, of the Lofts. II. Eel, Brinemoss style, with a jelly of the Pickler’s making. III. Lark’s tongues in tear-salt. IV. A bread that remembers rain. V. Cheek of a Weighed man, slow-roasted, with his own fat. VI. Caul, Morwen house, in pastry. VII. A sorbet of brine, to cleanse. VIII. (left blank; a thumbprint in gravy at the margin)

The Players.

  • Every land: the Carvers: Lord Absalom Thrale (Grand Carver, Sallowreach); Lady Seraphine Dalgety (the Vigil); Master Quillon Barr (surgeon); and in every capital two or three Trenchermen of the highest Cut, among them Lord Absalom Hethe in Lastgate, Lord Evander Quell on the Vigil’s Stair, Commodore Vell in Brinehollow, Lord Casimir Morwen in Kest and Lord Chastain Loin, who took his own father’s heart to the cellar table to be admitted.
  • The Fast: Wont Bellamy, who argues the Refusal was only a postponement.
  • Cross-border: Lysander Coyle of the Company, selling them the price of the world; Silas Fenwright, whose stolen ledgers would tell them which gods are ripe.
StageWhat Happens
1Practice dinners. Guests of standing are invited to one. The dish is not named until afterward.
2The Table commissions its knives: eight, of grey bone, from a Sallowreach bone-carver who is found Closed afterward.
3Wont Bellamy carries a motion before the Abstinent: the Unfed should do now what the others did then. Orrum is seen, for the first time, standing still while the Hostwatch approaches, as if waiting.
4The Second Table gathers at Hallowboard on Tablenight, all of them, around the eight-sided table, with knives, and the Host lies down.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Fifth Course. Grey candles, grey linen, grey silk veils, each diner with a silver fork laid crosswise. The fifth course arrives under a dome. The meat is dark, fine-grained, glossy with its own fat, and it smells of pork and clove and, faintly, the lavender water the Weighed rub into their skin before the scales. Across the table, a Guest recognizes a signet ring, still on the bone of the finger, garnishing the dish like a sprig of parsley. Everyone eats. Everyone watches who does not.
  • Loin Served. On Tablenight 642, if no one intervenes, Lord Chastain Loin attends his last supper as the dish. He is beautifully dressed. He does not seem surprised.

What the Guests Can Do. Infiltrate a dinner and finish the plate. Expose a Carver. Steal a knife. Warn the Fast, which may not believe them. Cut the copying of Prudence Lowell’s dispatches at Wanting Post, and blind the Table to which land is ripest. Discover that the Head of the Table presides from an empty chair, and that nobody at the dinners has ever seen anyone sit in it.

Endings.

  • The Second Meal: they eat the Host. See the Secrets chapter for what this does. It is the worst thing anyone has ever done.
  • The Table Turned: the Guests expose the cult; the Reckoners and the Purgation do the rest. Every High Cut in the world is now suspect, and the Lancings begin on a scale not seen since Brookhythe.
  • Served: at the final dinner, the Carvers discover that they are not the diners. The empty chair is occupied.
What It Costs — The Second Table

Attending a practice dinner and keeping a polite face is Tongue + Deceive (Grim 18); refusing the course marks the Guest as an enemy at the table, and eating it is cannibalism (Feast, Hard 14, to keep it down; 1 Hunger; a Dread 2 check when the dish is named). Exposing a Carver in their own land is a duel with a High Cut and a house. The Second Table never forgets a guest who left early: from then on, every invitation the party receives may be one of theirs.

The Undying Flame

Burns a month to the inch. No smoke. Slight sound at night; not a fault.
Wick Tallow’s trade card, Lastgate

Summary. The Vigil has ninety days of oil. Lamplighter-General Garron Ashlock has a supplier who doubled his price and a standing order to tell no one. In Sallowreach, fires smolder for decades and nothing can finish, and Wick Tallow renders the unclaimed dead into candles that feel themselves burn and give a very steady light. A Sallowreach flame does not go out. The Vigil has noticed. What Ashlock does not know is that the Vigil has already begun to make its own: Rosamund Kell, a chandler of the Lamplighters’ Guild, has rendered one Counted sleeper taken from the general rows on a Lessening list, where the beds of families ten seasons behind on the Bed-Due are quietly marked. The lamp it fills stands in Ashlock’s own office. It does not flicker. It breathes, four times a minute.

Order, Lamplighters’ Guild to W. Tallow, Lastgate, by Company post, sealed.

Supply for the Lid, Lack quarter: tapers, long, 2,000; lamp-stubs, 6,000; bracket-candles, 800. Specification as before (adult, unclaimed, no Hand-line). The Guild notes complaints from Brazier Row concerning the sound. Please advise whether a quieter grade is available, e.g. from the very old, or those without tongues. Payment in rouse, at Fogmouth, as agreed. G.A.

The Players.

  • The Vigil: Garron Ashlock; Rosamund Kell; Benedikt Lour; the Lamplighters’ Guild; Sabine Larch, who supplies the general rows.
  • Sallowreach: Wick Tallow, the Chandler; Regent Ansel Grue, who would sell the unclaimed dead by the cartload; the Loft-Wardens, whose forty thousand shelved dead are also, technically, unclaimed.
  • The Fatlands: Mistress Brisket Annalow of the Renderers’ Union, who supplied the Vigil’s tallow and is being undercut; Quartermaster Ivo Stockpot, who has noticed what goes into the Vigil’s barrels and notches it in his ledger.
  • The Rim: the Company, which must decide whether candles of people are freight or Hush-toll.
StageWhat Happens
1Ashlock buys a crate of Tallow’s candles in secret. They burn for a month without shortening. He weeps with relief. Rosamund Kell’s breathing lamp is set on his desk.
2A contract is sworn in Oathen. Wagon trains of Kept-candles go east along the Rim. The Lofts begin to empty. Bettany Shroud reports her shelved dead are being taken in the night.
3The Vigil’s street-lamps are lit with people. Citizens can hear them at night, a faint high keening from every bracket. The Seeming begins to show faces in the flames. The general rows thin.
4A candle is carried out of Sallowreach and should, by the Rule, finish at the Drop. It does not. It keeps burning. Something has changed about what can end, and where.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Rendering Shed. Tallow’s yard on the Sinks: copper kettles the size of boats, a smell like a chapel’s candle-store crossed with a tannery in summer, sweet, thick and rancid, coating the back of the throat so that food tastes of it for days. A Kept woman is lowered by a hoist into the kettle, awake. She does not scream; Tallow’s people sever the jaw-tendons first, as a kindness to the workers. The fat rises in yellow curds. Her hand, sinking last, opens and closes once.
  • Brazier Row at Night. Every bracket on the street holds a candle, and every candle sings, very high, on one note, the way a wet finger sings on the rim of a glass, rising when the wind gusts against it. In the steady flames, if a Guest looks too long, there are faces, eyes squeezed shut, mouths open.

What the Guests Can Do. Guard or hijack a candle train. Speak to a candle (they can hear and, with care, be made to answer). Help Ashlock find another way, or help him justify this one. Bring the Loft-Wardens’ witnesses into it: the Set-Aside are aware, and they have opinions about being burned.

Endings.

  • Light Eternal: the Vigil lives in a permanent glow of its neighbors’ dead, and Sallowreach is paid in rouse and mirrors. Nobody in either city sleeps well.
  • The Lofts Rise: the Set-Aside, learning what is planned, refuse. Forty thousand dead begin to whisper the same word louder. The Loft-Wardens open the doors.
  • The Finished Light: the candles all go out at once, everywhere, on the night the first Hush opens in the Vigil, four hundred miles from Sallowreach. The Hushes are not bound to the fen anymore.
What It Costs — The Undying Flame

The rendering shed is Dread 3; Kell’s breathing lamp, once its source is known, is Dread 3. Speaking to a candle needs Caul + Rites (Hard 14) and costs the speaker a night’s sleep, during which they feel the wick. Hijacking a train makes the Vigil go dark faster: every season the Guests hold the Flame at Stage 1, one district of the Lid loses its lamps, and the Dormitory’s count rises by a few hundred. There is no version of this thread in which nobody burns.

The Slipping Seal

She’s the Company’s knot. Everything else is rope.
a Warden of Quillhouse, of Jessamy Quill

Summary. Oathen’s Kept Rain came three days late, and everyone believes a god’s promise slipped. Every Company contract, every platter, every bond of every Bonded Hand rests on the word of one notary, Jessamy Quill. If Tolm’s word can slip, so can hers, and the Company is secretly preparing a second notary. It does not know what it is pulling on: the knot at the center of Oathen. In 601 Quill swore that no other notary of the Rim should be sworn while she lives; Ona Fell, the Surety, stands for an anonymous principal who is Quill; Sorrin Vael drafted both oaths and the Company’s instruction, forty years apart, and has never laid them side by side. Swear the second notary and Quill’s oath breaks, the Breaking falls on Ona, and Ona has one default left. And the Rain did not slip. Rainwarden Yusra Thole’s Tally shows the god kept its word to the hour: Tolm’s year has grown three days longer. A heart beats slower when the body it drives grows larger.

Company circular, sealed, to all Spokes. Not to be read aloud within the borders of Oathen.

Re-swearing of Instruments. All contracts, bonds and platters of the Company sworn before Grace 641 are to be re-sworn before witness at the earliest convenience. Wording unchanged. Agents will not discuss the reason. Agents will not discuss the Rainwarden. Agents will note, on a separate sheet, any bonded person who has broken a term and shown no Breaking, with date, hour, and the weather. Agents will not discuss the second seal.

The Players.

  • Oathen: Jessamy Quill; Ona Fell, the Surety, one default from death; Sorrin Vael; Yusra Thole, Rainwarden, silent for a month, her pulse pausing for most of a minute; Ottoline Vant, whose miscut word broke a man; Grandam Cess of Knot Canyon, who frees the sworn and whom Ona hates.
  • The Rim: First Spoke Odalys Penhallow; Auditor-General Lysander Coyle; Reeve Calder Stokes, the Company auditor in Brinehollow who tasted salt this morning.
  • Everywhere: every government that has ever sworn a treaty in Oathen, which is every government.
StageWhat Happens
1A Bonded Hand steals from the Company and does not break. The wardens hang him anyway, quietly. The Company begins re-swearing contracts.
2Quill becomes ill. Her body shows marks that match no oath she has broken. The Company doubles her guard and readies its second notary.
3A treaty fails: two lands discover that a border sworn in Oathen two centuries ago no longer binds either side. War is spoken of, carefully.
4The second notary is sworn. Quill breaks; the Breaking falls on Ona Fell; Ona dies. Half the trade of the Table comes unbound in an afternoon. Every platter is worth its weight in bone and nothing more.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Thief Who Did Not Break. A Bonded Hand named Teague Orr pockets a platter at Wanting Post, and waits, white, for his fingers to go. They do not. He laughs. He cannot stop laughing; he walks out into the yard laughing and the wardens take him there, and the Guests watch the quiet hanging behind the stables, done with a wagon-chain, Company-fashion, because a man who can break his bond and live is worse for business than a thief.
  • Ona’s Default. The Surety’s chamber in Tacit, if Stage 4 arrives. Ona Fell at her desk, and the oath she stands for coming due all at once, in her body. The Guests hear her joints go first, a sound like knuckles cracked in a quiet church, one after another, wrists, elbows, shoulders, then the long bones, and she does not fall, because she is holding the edge of the desk, and she keeps holding it.

What the Guests Can Do. Protect Quill. Investigate why the Kept Rain was late; Yusra Thole knows and cannot lie, so she will not speak, but her Tally can be read. Find the Company’s second notary, and lay Vael’s three drafts side by side before anyone swears them. Carry the Company’s frantic re-swearing across the Rim. Discover that Odalys Penhallow is preparing for the Company to survive the lands, and what she means to feed the wagons.

Endings.

  • Unbound: the Rim dissolves into seven tolls and seven armies. Every land must now get what it needs from neighbors it finds obscene, without a neutral road in between, and it gets it by force.
  • The New Witness: the Company finds something else to swear by. It is listening, and it is not Tolm, and it is very glad to be asked.
  • The Last Wagons: Penhallow’s sealed wagons set out, carrying the Spokes and the archive, around and around the Rim, and the Company becomes a procession with no destination, lit at night, stopping at no inn.
What It Costs — The Slipping Seal

Reading Yusra’s Tally and understanding it is Eye + Reckoning (Grim 18) and a Dread 3 check; from then on the Guest knows the god is growing, and every Oathener they meet can ask them about it. Untying the knot without killing anyone requires all three of Quill, Ona and the Company to be re-sworn in one sitting before the Bench: a Dire Tongue + Clause roll by whoever drafts it, with each Lack on that roll costing one of the three their life. Anyone a Guest saves here is in their debt by oath, which, in Oathen, is not a figure of speech.

The Stolen Ledgers

Every line ends. The College only writes down where.
motto over the door of the Master Concordance, Quire

Summary. Silas Fenwright, a renegade Lineman of the Cutwrights’ College, walked out of Quire with three quires copied from the Master Concordance: the full lines of the highest houses of three lands, and the College’s graph of every Regrowth bending upward at the same moment after 600 A.G. Everyone wants them. Whoever holds the ledgers knows where each god is regrowing fastest, and who is next. In the north, Provost Carrion Sedge has already learned what it is to hold a dangerous ledger: his own map of the Hushes has a pinhole in it, and the pinhole is the Hall of Hands, and he has dated the next great Hush to Lack 642, give or take a season.

Page offered for sale at the Groaning Board, Plenty 641. The buyer was found before dawn with the page folded into his mouth.

House Dalgety, Eye-line. Cut 5 in the direct line since 402. Mean Regrowth of living members: 7.4. Rate since 600: doubled. Projected Seating of the head of house: within the decade. Projected rate after 641: see graph, sheet iv. (Annotation, Lune’s hand:) Every curve on sheet iv bends at the same place. Seven gods do not agree on a date unless something has given them one.

The Players.

  • The College: Archprovost Hesper Lune; Odo Venn; Provost Carrion Sedge.
  • Cross-border: the Purgation, who want a massacre list; the Second Table, who want a menu; the Reckoners, especially Deny Fallon, who wants a target roll.
  • Every land: noble houses who would pay anything to have their own line removed, and their rivals’ added.
StageWhat Happens
1Fenwright offers a single page for sale at the Groaning Board. The buyer is murdered before dawn.
2A Lancing in the Fatlands follows the ledger’s exact order of houses. A Reckoner raid in the Vigil follows the same page.
3The College’s graph is copied and nailed to toll-houses on the Rim. The Bait doctrine takes it as proof. Riots in three capitals.
4The third quire, the one Fenwright has not shown anyone, is opened. It is a list of every Blank born on the Table in two centuries, with their present whereabouts.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Lancing in Order. A Gut-line hall in the Fatlands, Purgation lancers at the door with the page in a leather sleeve. They take the household one by one in the ledger’s order, grandmother first, a long iron lance at the base of the throat, and the blood that comes out is thick, gravy-brown, sweet-smelling, and pools without spreading. The seventh name on the page is a girl of nine. The lancer looks at the page, and at her, and at the page. The Guests are in the room.
  • The Graph on the Toll-House. Seven lines in seven colors climbing a nailed sheet, all bending upward at the same year. Someone has drawn, in charcoal, an eighth line above them, flat, waiting. A crowd is reading it in silence.

What the Guests Can Do. Catch Fenwright, buy from him, or protect him. Return the quires to Quire, or not. Read them, which is a Grim Eye + Lore roll and a Dread 3 check; a Guest who succeeds learns their own line, and what it ends in. Track the Blank list before the Second Table does.

Endings.

  • The Lists Are Read: massacre and counter-massacre along family lines in every land. The Regrowth slows a little where the High Cuts are gone. The College records the numbers.
  • The Ledgers Burn: the Guests destroy the quires; the Master Concordance at Quire burns soon after, in a fire that no one admits setting. Nobody now knows where the gods are, which helps no one.
  • Your Own Line: the ledger shows that a Guest is closer to a Seating than they knew, by far. Every faction that holds a copy knows it too.
What It Costs — The Stolen Ledgers

Holding even a page makes the holder a target of four factions; the GM rolls a d6 each week the party carries one, and on a 1 someone comes for it. Reading one’s own line changes nothing in the blood and everything in the mind: Dread 4 if it ends in a Seating within the decade. Burning the quires is the only ending that saves the Blanks on the third list, and it blinds everyone, including those who might have used the graph to save a land. Returning them to Quire is a 30-day journey with every road watched.

The Low Water

The sea says dawn’s at the half-bell. Your chests say it’s now. I ring for the chests.
Finn Undertow, Tide-Bellman of Lowmark

Summary. A new thread. Every Brinehollower fills with the sea’s water at dawn and dusk, and for ten years that tide in the chest has drifted ahead of the tide on the Uncovered. Finn Undertow, who rings the Headland bell for the chests and not for the sea, has done the sum: the drift closes at the Low Water of Carving 642, when every Brinehollower will fill at the same moment. He does not know the drift follows the slow breathing of Ondine Vasht, the Dowager Below, in the cellars under Fathomhouse. That same night Ilse Marl’s chart of the Tenanted’s singing completes, and Dagna Hull’s Follow makes its trial descent toward the Trench with Commodore Vell and his knives aboard. Meanwhile Reeve Calder Stokes carries to Tacit the figure Brenna Kelp proved by buckets, the Kelp: the sea falls nine hundred and twelve thousand barrels for every soul returned to it. By the Company’s tolls, which had the figure first, Brinehollow has eight years and a season, and the Company will sell the price. The Drowned Bench has read Brenna’s copy. Justice Maren Oake wrote in its margin: The figure is correct. The constant will change.

Chalked on the inside of the Headland bell-house door, Lowmark. Each morning the old figure is rubbed out with a wet thumb and a new one written.

377. Chests ahead of the sea by 11 min. Mile Nine filled at the half-bell, all of it, one breath. Dowager’s house dark. 376. 12 min. A child on Mile Two filled in her sleep and did not wake for the bell; her mother says she was smiling. 375. 12 min. Rang early. Admiralty clerk again. Told him the sea is not the one that drowns in bed.

The Players.

  • Brinehollow: Finn Undertow and his count; Ondine Vasht, the Dowager Below, breathing; Ilse Marl and her chart; Dagna Hull, building a ship to come back, and Hollis Brine, sabotaging it with her own hammer because he heard Nerys Colm’s invitation and knows there is no coming back; Commodore Lysander Vell; Brenna Kelp and the Kelp; Justice Maren Oake; Father Ebb, holding a broken chain closed in his fist.
  • The Rim: Reeve Calder Stokes and his satchel; Auditor-General Lysander Coyle, who had the constant in 633.
  • Cross-border: the Second Table, for whom the Follow’s hold is a carving party; the Vigil’s brine-walkers, who will reach the coast at the season’s end; Cray Lobbett and the table on the mud, toward which, and away from which, Ilse’s chart runs.
StageWhat Happens
1Finn rings early and is reprimanded. Calder Stokes sets out for Tacit. Vell tries to buy Ilse’s pages and Brenna’s working. Whole Miles begin to fill on the same breath.
2The Number Twice: Brenna’s proof and Calder’s meet, or are made to. The Admiralty kills to keep one of them quiet. The figure is posted on a tide-post on Mile Fourteen and torn down by morning.
3The Company prices the coast in Tacit and sells the price. The Deepening prepares its largest procession. The Follow is floated; its air-bladder valve is fitted with a hand-lock on the inside.
4The Low Water of 642. Every chest on the Table fills at once, and breathes in time with the Dowager Below. The ring on the Uncovered walks. The Follow goes down. The constant changes.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Filling. In a crowded Lowmark tavern on a drift night, sixty people choke at the same instant, without warning, mid-word and mid-swallow. They go purple together, bent double together, and sixty mouths spill the same cold grey water onto the boards together, a sound like a slop-bucket emptied down a stair, and then they straighten and look at one another, and nobody speaks, and at the far end of the room a man who did not finish coughing in time is lying on his face in the wet. Anyone not of the coast in that room is suddenly alone.
  • The Hold. Below the Follow’s deck, behind a bulkhead Dagna never drew, Vell’s hold: hooks, salt-tubs, a rack of eight grey knives, and lead-lined boxes the size of a man’s torso, with drain-holes. It smells of cedar and fresh tar and, under that, a butcher’s back room. Chalked on the bulkhead, in a neat hand, First course.

What the Guests Can Do. Bring Finn’s count to the Admiralty, which does not want it, or to the Dowager Below, who may. Put Brenna and Calder in one cellar, the most dangerous meeting in Brinehollow, or keep them apart. Expose the Follow’s hold, which makes Dagna strike Vell; expose Hollis, which ruins her; or do nothing, and all three go down together. Read Maren Oake’s marginal note and ask the Drowned Bench what the constant will change to.

Endings.

  • The Coast in One Breath: the drift closes and does not open again. Brinehollow fills and empties as one body, forever, to the Dowager’s breathing, and when she is still, everyone is still. The Admiralty calls it discipline.
  • The First Course Delivered: the Follow reaches the bottom of the Trench, and Vell’s knives find what is reassembling there. The air-bladder rises without anyone aboard. Months later, Second Table diners in four capitals report a dish that tastes of being held.
  • The Constant Changes: at the Low Water, the ring walks inland, and the sea follows it, not as a wave but as a long, slow, calm return, through the people: every Tenanted soul on the coast begins, gently, to weep salt water, and does not stop, and the Uncovered goes dark and wet under the moon for the first time in six hundred years.
What It Costs — The Low Water

A non-Brinehollower in a room when the chests fill makes a Dread 2 check; a Brinehollower Guest on the night of Low Water makes a Grim Caul + Resolve roll or walks with the ring, and must be physically restrained (Gut + Labor, Hard 14, each minute for ten minutes). Bringing Brenna and Calder together marks every Guest present for the Admiralty’s quiet men and for the Company’s auditors. Sabotaging the Follow drowns its crew; saving its crew delivers its hold. Anyone who reads the Kelp and understands it takes a Dread 3 check and can never again watch a Tenanted bride walk up the steps without doing the sum.

Three, One, Three

There is someone at the door who has not been fed. Set another place.
the lips of Aveline Morne, Bed One, as transcribed by Matron Cecily Dorm

Summary. A new thread. In Carving 640, Queen Dowager Sibyl Aubrey of Cradlewrack, forty-three years pregnant with a King who has ruled from her womb since 601, felt him kick three times, then once, then three, and again, until dawn. Nobody had asked him anything. It has happened every night since. Absalom Gage, the bricklayer of Kest, feels the same pattern in his walls: the knock the highlands give a new brick, three, then the answer, then three again. Old Hinge hears it from the far side of the Sill, answered from the Queen’s chamber. In the Vigil, Corwin Half-Bell, the only man to turn around in the long room and come back, will not stand with his back to a door. In Oathen, between the beats of the new heart under the Gullet, there is a sound like a chair being drawn up to a table. The knocking comes from one place, and is heard in all of them.

A clapping game of the Kest hills, played by girls on the steps of the pang-houses. Collected by an Attendance midwife, Carving 641, who notes that she had never heard it before that year and that every parish knows it.

Knock three, knock one, knock three again,

Who’s on the step in the wind and the rain?

Knock three for the bread and one for the cup,

Three for the chair, and nobody get up.

Nobody answer and nobody tell,

Nobody open, and all will be well.

(At the last word the girls slap the step three times, then once, then three, and the one who is slowest must stand facing the door until the next pang.)

The Players.

  • Cradlewrack: Queen Dowager Sibyl Aubrey and the King Within, whose kick is law; Lord Chamberlain Eamon Seele, who reads him questions; Absalom Gage; Old Hinge at the Sill; Una Knocker, whose longest-bricked debtor has begun, at night, to tap back.
  • The Vigil: Corwin Half-Bell, who cannot bear an open door; Sister Vesper Null, who came back from the room on purpose, while the real Vesper stands at the back of it listening to the same knock; Aveline Morne in Bed One; Matron Cecily Dorm and her pencil.
  • Oathen: Yusra Thole, whose goatskin of Gullet sand beats once a minute against the ear.
  • The Fast: every Unfed household, which closes the door from the outside, opens it, and closes it from the inside, and has done so for six hundred years without anyone remembering why.
  • The Rim: every innkeeper on the road, who has begun to hear a knock at the third hour of the night on the door that faces the middle of the continent.
StageWhat Happens
1The King kicks the knock nightly. Gage’s new walls knock back. The clapping game spreads through the Kest hills in a single season.
2The knock is heard in the Vigil: doors in the Dormitory’s oldest rows, struck from the room side. Corwin will not enter the building. Rim innkeepers begin nailing their middle-facing doors shut.
3On a single night the knock is heard in every land at once, at the same hour. In the Fast, a hundred doors are found open in the morning, opened from the outside. Aveline speaks her sentence again, louder.
4Someone answers. The knock stops, everywhere, for a full night. In the morning the King has turned in the womb, and lies facing north, and Old Hinge reports that the far side of the Sill is quiet, the way a room is quiet after a guest has come in.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The Throne Room. The Queen Dowager, ninety, propped on a litter in a room of red silk, her belly vast and hard and blue-veined under a linen shift, the skin so stretched that it shines in the lamplight like a skinned grape. The Chamberlain reads a question. Nothing. Then, unprompted, the belly moves: a heel, or a fist, against the drum of her, from inside, three times. The courtiers do not breathe. Once. The Queen’s mouth opens without sound. Three. Somewhere below the floor, in the old walls, a brick answers.
  • The Oldest Rows. In the Dormitory at the third bell, on a night of Stage 2, a Guest sitting watch hears it: a knock, three, one, three, on the inside of a door at the end of a row where there is no door, only a whitewashed wall. Every sleeper in the row has turned their face toward the sound. Their eyes are closed. Their lips are wet.

What the Guests Can Do. Trace the knock from the Queen’s womb to Gage’s walls to the Sill to the Dormitory, and draw it on a map, and see that the lines meet. Ask the King, through the Chamberlain, where the knocking comes from; the answer, given by kick, is that it comes from the room with the table. Stop the clapping game. Bring Corwin and Vesper to Bed One at the same bell, where the rows will turn toward them and the knock may be heard from this side. Never, ever knock back.

Endings.

  • Nobody Answer: the Guests persuade every land to keep its doors shut and its mouths shut. The knock goes on, nightly, everywhere, forever, and a generation grows up that has never slept through a night without it. The Fast’s custom spreads to every land and nobody remembers why.
  • The King Delivered: the King is born at last, in the Throne Room, forty-four years late, a man-sized infant with an old man’s eyes, and his first act is to knock, three, one, three, on the floor of the world, from this side. Something on the other side is very pleased.
  • Someone Answers: the knock stops. Read the Secrets chapter, and decide who opened the door.
What It Costs — Three, One, Three

Sleeping a week within the Aubrey palace gives a Guest the knocking dream; each further week is a Dread 2 check. Hearing the knock in the Dormitory’s oldest rows is Dread 3. A Guest who knocks back gains the Derangement The Late Guest (they set an extra place at every meal, and become distressed and then violent if it is cleared) and the GM notes that the knock is one door nearer to them. Telling anyone in Cradlewrack that the King is answering, rather than speaking, is treason under the Royal Assent.

The Lead Coffin

You asked to be of use, dear boy. I have found you a use.
Lord Absalom Hethe, letter to the west wing of Glovehall

Summary. A new thread. The Second Table has a problem: a god that is regrowing is a god that moves, and the Gorging worked because the Providers held still. Lord Absalom Hethe, Hand of the Court and a Trencherman since 625, has solved it. Osric Vane, Lady Corrow Vane’s gentler brother, at the Brink and confined in Glovehall’s west wing since his bare hand finished a Fatlands factor in 628, can close anything: a candle, a fly, a conversation, a Kept man through a door. He cannot refuse a request framed as a duty, and he longs to be useful. A Vigil clockmaker has drawn him a coffin, lead-lined, its breathing-holes meshed with lead, to hold in what he does until the lid is opened before a god on a table. Osric leaves Glovehall in Grace 642, declared to the Company as wine.

Company freight docket, Fogmouth, Grace 642, draft. The clerk’s pencil note is in another hand.

Consignment: WINE, CLARET, one cask, coffin-form, lead-lined, Hethe cellars, for the account of a gentleman, to be carried east by the Rim to a destination to be given at Wanting Post. Weight: 14 stone. Handling: KEEP UPRIGHT. DO NOT OPEN. DO NOT SPEAK TO. (Pencil:) Flies dead for twenty paces round the dray. Carter’s lamp went out twice. Cask asked me very kindly whether I was well.

The Players.

  • Sallowreach: Lord Absalom Hethe; Osric Vane, and his lead mittens, and the Fatlander Pell Ambry, whose face he sees in every face; Lady Corrow Vane, who keeps her brother in the west wing because she loves him and because she is afraid; the Mortuary Court, whose Hushes are fed, in part, by what Osric’s presence does to the fen; Edda Thrush, the Hushwalker, who wants to see if Dunmere has moved.
  • The Rim: the Company, which carries what is declared; the carters, who will not take the dray twice.
  • The Fast: the Hostwatch, who would see the coffin come over the Hem; Orrum, who has been seen, in the Second Table thread, standing still as if waiting; Wont Bellamy, who will meet the dray at Wanting Post.
  • Cross-border: Lord Absalom Thrale, Grand Carver; Commodore Vell and Lord Casimir Morwen, each of whom would like the coffin to come to their land’s table first.
StageWhat Happens
1Hethe visits the west wing with letters and a request framed as duty. Osric agrees, and weeps, and thanks him. The coffin is built in a Lastgate cooper’s yard; the cooper’s hands go numb and stay numb.
2Grace 642: the coffin leaves Glovehall. The small Hush in the Glovehall orchard stops growing. Fogmouth watches the dray go and the flies drop around it.
3The dray moves east along the Rim. What leaks through the lead is enough: wherever it stops, fires gutter out, voices stop mid-word, and the sick die quietly in the night. Inns begin to refuse it. Sallowreach’s Hushes, meanwhile, slow.
4The coffin reaches its table. The lid is opened, in the presence of a god. The god is still.

Scenes the Guests Might Witness

  • The West Wing. A black double-barred door with a hatch. The sound goes first: footsteps soften, the flies stop, the lamp leans away. Then the voice, warm and educated: Hello? Is someone there? I promise to keep my eyes shut. Through the hatch, a gaunt man of fifty-four in a silk blindfold and lead mittens, whose bare wrists, where the mittens end, are grey and smooth as a church floor. He asks the Guests, very kindly, whether Lord Hethe’s errand is a good one. He so wants it to be.
  • The Stopped Inn. The Guests overnight at a Company inn where the cask is stabled. Nobody at dinner can finish a sentence. The hearth goes out three times and cannot be coaxed. The landlord’s old dog lies down by the stable door and does not get up. Upstairs, a drover who was mending from a cough is found at dawn finished, with his eyes open and his face smoothed of every line, grey and polished as a church step, and his daughter is screaming at the stable for someone to take the cask away.

What the Guests Can Do. Visit Osric and tell him the truth about Hethe’s use for him, which will break his heart and possibly the door. Hijack the dray; nobody can bring themselves to open the cask, and nobody should. Learn from the Glovehall gardeners what the Hushes do while Osric is gone, and decide whether a slowed fen is worth a held god. Follow the coffin to see whose table it reaches.

Endings.

  • The God Held Still: the lid opens at Hallowboard on Tablenight, and Orrum, which has been running around the Rim laying tables for a year, stops, and lies down, and the Second Table takes up its knives. See the Second Table thread, and the Secrets chapter.
  • Of Use: the Guests bring Osric home, or to somewhere better than home, and find him a duty worth his life: an hour a day at the Ferrying Post, mittens off, finishing by consent the Kept who petitioned for a Closing and could never pay. He does it gladly, for years, and the Mortuary Court, which sells Closings at four thousand lacks, never forgives the Guests.
  • The Lid Lifted Early: someone opens the cask on the road. Osric, blind, ungloved, terrified, takes off his blindfold to see who has come. Everything within a quarter-mile finishes: people, horses, fires, sounds, the road itself, which is found afterward smooth and grey as his wrists. Osric is found standing in the middle of it, alone, apologizing.
What It Costs — The Lead Coffin

Standing in the same room as Osric is Dread 3; seeing him unmittened is Dread 4, and his bare touch finishes anything. Each night spent near the dray, a Guest at Ruin must pass Gut + Endure (Grim 18) or finish quietly before dawn. Stopping it makes enemies of Hethe and the Second Table; telling Osric the truth gives Lady Corrow Vane cause to close whoever told him. Delivering him anywhere at all is choosing what he is for, which nobody has ever let him do.

Where the Threads Meet

No thread in this chapter is complete on its own. The Deadwatch draws on the Lessening’s lists, and the Lessening’s lists feed the Undying Flame. The Low Water carries the Second Table’s knives to the Trench, and the Lead Coffin carries their stillness to the Host. Brine in the Rouse fills the Vigil with the sea, and the sea’s constant is being sold in Tacit while Tacit’s god grows three days a year. The Missing Hand and Three, One, Three are the same labor heard from two ends. And all of them, followed far enough, lead to a long dim room, a table, and a chair that is not pushed in.

The GM need not tell the players this. They will notice. Let them notice in their own time, one knock, one place card, one empty chair at a time, and let the noticing cost them.

Seven tables, and seven peoples at them, and every one of us so glad to be eating that nobody looked behind.
[ Grandfather Peat, through a translator, Lastgate, 641 ]
Part Two
The Rules
How to make a person of the Table, how dice decide their fate, how the god in the blood is spent, how the mind breaks, and how violence is done.
Chapter 11

Making a Guest

Ask a child of the Table who she is, and she will tell you three things, in this order: where her people ate, what part they were given, and what she does to earn her bread. Only then, if you are still listening, will she tell you her name.
— Provost Carrion Sedge, Introductory Lectures in Cutwrighting

From the intake ledger of the Thimble Cross waystation, Rim Road Company, month of Carving, 641 A.G.

Name: Halloway Brisk. Origin: Fatlands (Low Tilth, says she; accent says Sated). Cut: Gut-line, common. Middling. Bites her nails to the quick and then keeps going. Trade: Renderer, Union card, lapsed. Carrying: three cleavers, a rendering hook, eleven lacks, a jar she will not open. Purpose of travel: “Going north.” Asked why: “Because something in the south has my name on it.”

Name: Tolly Fane. Origin: the Vigil. Eyes like two holes burned in paper. Cut: Eye-line, low. Has lids, uses them sparingly. Trade: Courier, sworn. Carrying: a sealed satchel, a pin-cushion of needles, rouse enough for nine days. Purpose of travel: Did not answer. Had fallen asleep standing up. Woke before we could catch her. Says she did not.

Name: Lettered Corse. Origin: Cradlewrack. Says he is four. Has a beard. Cut: Caul-line, common. Knocked on my counter before he spoke to me. Knocked on the ledger before I wrote in it. Trade: Foundling Companies, discharged. Carrying: a crossbow, a brick, a trowel, a needle and red thread, a list of women’s names, most crossed out. Purpose of travel: “Looking for my mother. Or my father. Whoever it was.”

Name: Wenn-something, of Oathen. Would not finish her own name; said the rest of it was owed. Cut: Tongue-line, common. Trade: Surety. Carrying: a ledger she keeps under her shirt, against the skin. Both little fingers bent backward. Smiled at me with her mouth shut. Purpose of travel: “If able, to Gristmoot. Barring weather.”

Name: None given. Origin: the Fast, by the look of him. Thin as a fence. Cut: None. Refused bread three times and took it on the fourth, very politely. Trade: Says “breaker.” Has an axe. Carrying: the axe. A place card, folded small, which he showed to nobody but which I saw when he paid. It had his name on it, in a good hand. Purpose of travel: “To find the table it came from.”

Clerk’s note in margin: Five travellers. Laid the common table for five. Came back from the cellar and there were six places. Have reported this. Have been told to stop reporting this.

Every player except the Carver makes one character, called a Guest. A Guest is a person of the Table: born in one of its seven lands, descended from a bloodline that ate some part of a god or refused to, trained in a trade, owing debts and loyalties, and carrying, in all but the rarest cases, a god that is slowly growing back inside them.

Character creation takes about an hour the first time. It works best done together, at the table, so that the Guests can be bound to each other before play begins. A group of strangers who meet at an inn is the oldest beginning there is, and on the Table it is also the most honest: the Rim Road is where everyone ends up.

Groups in a hurry can take one of the seven ready-made Guests at the end of this chapter, one from each land, and be playing in ten minutes. Groups with time to spare can roll on the Lifepath tables after Step Nine and let the dice tell them what their Guest ate, buried, betrayed and swore. Neither is required. Both are recommended at least once.

We ask the land first because the land doesn’t change. Names change. Trades change. The god you were born carrying is the one you’ll be buried carrying, if anyone bothers to bury you.
a Company intake clerk, explaining the ledger’s order

The Steps

  • Concept. Decide, roughly, who you want to play.
  • Land. Choose where you were born. This sets your signature attribute, your god, your Gifts and your Wants. Choose or roll a name and a face.
  • Cut. Choose your bloodline’s station: Blank, Scrapling, Common, Prime or High. This sets how much god is in you, where you start on the Regrowth, and what you own.
  • Attributes. Distribute points among Hand, Gut, Lung, Eye, Tongue and Caul.
  • Calling. Choose your trade. It gives you skills, a Calling talent, Standing, and starting gear.
  • Skills. Distribute skill points.
  • Knacks. Choose two Knacks: small, specific advantages.
  • Derived traits. Calculate Flesh, Guard, Hunger, Regrowth and Fray, and note your Gifts, Wants and Sop.
  • The Four Questions. Answer the Last Meal, the Oath on the Dead, Who Waits at Home, and What You Will Not Do. If you like, roll the Lifepath first and let it answer for you.
  • Gear and money. Spend your lacks at the Rim Market.

Step One: Concept

Start with a sentence. A Seamer from Lastgate who has stitched her own mother back together thirty times and is beginning to resent it. A Fatlands drover who walks herds of things that are not cattle and has stopped naming them. A Clausewright’s apprentice who said one careless word as a child and has spent twenty years keeping it. The best concepts carry a wound and a want, and a reason to be on the road.

Discuss concepts as a group. Guests should have a reason to travel together, or at least a reason not to kill each other. Good shared premises include: a Rim Road Company caravan crew; a Cutwrights’ College survey team; a band of pilgrims or refugees; a Purgation cell; the household staff of a dying noble; a Tablebreaker company; strangers stranded at the same inn when the snow comes down and turns out to be fat.

Step Two: Land

Choose the land of your birth. Each land is described at length in Part One; its chapter ends with a section called Playing a Lander, which you will need now. The land gives:

  • +1 to a signature attribute (applied after you distribute points, and the only way to start at 5).
  • Your god. If your Cut is 1 or higher, the god your ancestors ate is in your blood, and the land’s rules for the Regrowth apply to you wherever you go.
  • Gifts: powers you gain as the god grows back.
  • Wants: the compulsions that come with them.
  • The Sop: the act that quiets your god, at a price.
  • The Tooth: how your god shows itself when you call on it.
LandGod EatenSignatureThe Rule of the Land
SallowreachOssel, the Closing HandHandNothing dies. Everything rots.
The FatlandsUmmer, the LadenGutEverything is meat. Nobody is full.
BrinehollowDromm, the FathomLungThe sea is inside the people.
The VigilIss, the LiddedEyeWhoever sleeps never wakes.
CradlewrackVey, the OpeningCaulNothing is born right; too much is born.
OathenTolm, the WitnessTongueWords bind flesh.
The FastOrrum, the Host (refused)Any oneNever accept.

Exiles and the Rim-Born

A character born on the Rim Road, in a waystation or a caravan, still has a land: the land of the bloodline they descend from. The god goes where the blood goes. A Brinehollower born in a Sallowreach inn still bails at dawn. If your parents were of two lands, choose one; the other god is too weak in you to count, though the Carver may give you a single Taste of it as a quirk.

Half-and-halves are the saddest people on the Road. They get one god’s hunger and the other god’s manners, and neither land will bury them.
a waystation keeper at Saltmile

Names and Faces of the Seven Lands

Each land’s chapter gives a longer list of names. The tables below are for the moment at the table when somebody needs a Guest’s name, or a stranger’s, or a face to go with one, and nobody can think. Roll a d10 for each column separately, or read across a row for a ready-made person. The Look is what a stranger notices first.

The Fatlands
