The Carver has run three scenes: a warm room where the Bedded let Tolly sit on a floor that does not slope (the Warm Table); an evening when a girl Tolly’s age told her, gently, that her mother in the Dormitory is happy now (the Answer); a night when Tolly blinked, and a Bedded elder said, kindly, that she had been gone for almost a minute and that she had smiled (the Long Night).

Each time, the recruiter (Threat 3, +2 Weariness, +1 Rattled, +2 for a doctrine that matches her god) rolled against Tolly’s Caul 3 + Resolve 2. Tolly lost twice. Hold 2. Then the elder told her she had not blinked at all the night before: she had slept for a full count of ten, and come back, which nobody does. Sunniva rolled Eye + Reckoning, at −2 for the blink: she lost. One Doubt.

Ressa comes to the house the next morning and says: “You were asleep for one breath and Abate pinched you. I was there.” That is a companion confirming the memory; +2 on the next roll, and the Carver lets the Doubt stand at 1. But Sunniva says, quietly, that Tolly wants to go back to the meeting that night. Just to see. The Carver writes Hold 2, Doubt 1, and says nothing at all.

Investigation

Much of play on the Table is finding out: who took the hand, where the Called go, what the Cullmasters’ list is for, why the Hushes follow the Hand-lines. These rules make investigation fast, fair and unpleasant.

Clues Are Not Rolled For

The clue that keeps the story moving is never behind a roll. If a Guest looks in the right place with a sensible approach, they find it. Rolls decide how much more they find, how fast, and what it costs. A failed search does not hide the clue; it means the clue is found late, or loudly, or by the wrong person first, or that finding it costs Fray, Hunger, or a night. The Carver should plan each mystery as a chain of leads, each pointing to at least two others, so that no single failure stops the investigation.

The Senses of the Table

Every skill can investigate. Each finds different things.

SkillFinds
Eye + SearchPhysical traces: marks, objects, the door that was opened from the inside
Hand + StitchingWhat a body says: how it died, what was done to it, what it ate, how long ago
Eye + LoreHistory, doctrine, whose crest, which bloodline, what the old carving shows
Eye + ReckoningLedgers, tallies, clocks, the arithmetic that someone wanted hidden
Caul + InstinctPeople: who is lying, who is afraid, who already knew
Caul + GodsignGodsign traces: a closing, an opening, a Tenant’s passing, a binding
Eye + FeastTaste and smell: what meat, which poison, whose kitchen
Tongue + ClauseDocuments: what the contract really says, the Exit buried in an oath

Each Helping on an investigation roll buys one of: another clue, the meaning of a clue, time (half as long), or discretion (nobody knows you found it).

The Bill

Every investigation has a Bill: a clock, from 4 to 8 boxes, that fills as the Guests stumble. A box fills on every failed investigation roll, on every day that passes, and on every Lack (two boxes). When the Bill is paid in full, the thing being investigated happens: the next blink-murder, the dusk shift goes out, the Second Table dines, the witness is Set Aside. The Guests can see the Bill. The Carver should draw it.

Each Land Its Witness

Every land offers investigators a way of knowing that would be impossible anywhere else, and each comes at a price.

  • Sallowreach. Ask the victim. The dead are Kept, and can talk, if their jaw is on. They may lie, and they may not know who did it, and a Kept murder victim is Dread 2 to interview.
  • The Fatlands. Taste it. A Fatlander with Taste the Name learns the eater’s secrets from a mouthful of flesh, at the cost of Hunger and the horror of witnesses.
  • Brinehollow. The indoor tide returns what it takes. Search a cellar at the ebb, and the sea may give back a ring, a tooth, a letter. Ask a Tenanted judge, who will answer truthfully and in two voices.
  • The Vigil. The Seeming is evidence. If a street saw it, it is on the record, and the Seemer’s ledgers can be read. Whether it happened is a separate question.
  • Cradlewrack. The Tally records every birth of every kind. If something was born, it is written down, and the Tallyman knows the arithmetic does not close.
  • Oathen. Have the suspect repeat their promise aloud, and watch. Judge Thane Urrow needs no other evidence. Neither will you.
  • The Fast. Read the place cards. The Host knows every name, and spells them correctly.
Example of Play: The Missing Hands of Clench Row

In the Sinks of Lastgate, four Kept on Clench Row have woken without their hands. The Carver sets a Bill of 6: when it fills, Marrow Jack sells the hands to someone who is collecting a particular set. Her leads: the stumps (Stitching), the victims’ testimony (Instinct), a drop of cedar oil on the sill (Search), and a fence’s ledger in the Lower Pilings (Reckoning).

Halloway examines the stumps: Hand 4 + Stitching 1, Hard (14). She rolls 15. Success: they were taken with a fine saw, not a cleaver, by someone who knew where the wrist bones part. Ressa interviews the first victim, an old Kept woman named Hessa Coombe, Instinct against Routine (10) because she wants to talk: 19, two Helpings. Ressa learns that Hessa can feel her missing hand, right now, being washed, gently, in warm water; and (the second Helping) that the water smells of cedar and salt. The Carver lets the Helpings buy meaning: the cedar is Lastgate perfume, which marks the buyer as rich; the salt is Brinehollow brine, which the rich of the Vigil drink in their rouse.

Tolly searches the sill: 11, failure. One box of the Bill fills. She finds the drop of cedar oil anyway (it is the clue that moves the story), but she finds it late, after a neighbour has seen her and gone to tell someone. Four boxes left, and somebody in the Lower Pilings now knows the company’s faces.

In Lastgate the murdered testify at their own inquests. It has not raised the conviction rate. They are as bad at noticing things as the rest of us.
Justice Ever Lathe, through his clerk

Chases

When someone runs and someone follows, use a chase. A chase is fast, a series of opposed rolls around a track of Lead.

The Lead

The chase begins at a Lead of 2 (a close chase: the hunter saw them go) or 3 (a head start). Each round, the quarry and the hunter each roll Lung + Athletics on foot, Lung + Wayfaring mounted, on a cart, or across hard country, or Lung + Stealth if the quarry is trying to vanish rather than outrun. Whoever wins moves the Lead by 1 in their favour, plus 1 per Helping.

  • Lead 0: caught. The hunter is close enough to grab, strike or tackle. A fight begins, or the quarry surrenders.
  • Lead 6: lost. The quarry is gone, hidden, or out of reach; the hunter must find a new trail, which is an investigation.

A group chasing or fleeing rolls with its slowest member, unless it leaves them behind. That choice is the most important one in most chases, and it should be put to the players out loud.

Breath

A body can run hard for a number of rounds equal to Gut + Endure. After that, each round requires a Gut + Endure roll at Hard (14) or the runner suffers −2 to chase rolls, cumulative. Bloodied, Starving and Weary characters run out of breath at half the count. The Kept, the Tenanted and the Seated never tire. That should be terrifying.

Complications

Each round, the side that lost the previous roll may describe a complication, or the Carver rolls on the table below. A complication is a single roll for whoever reaches it: success keeps the pace, failure costs 1 Lead (and a Lack costs 2 and a fall, a wound, or a dropped thing). The Carver should always describe the place.

d10Chase complications
1A crowd: a market, a procession, a wake. Tongue + Intimidate to clear it, or Lung + Athletics to thread it.
2A climb: a wet piling, a cliff stair, a slope of loose red clay. Lung + Athletics, Hard (14).
3A door, barred. Gut + Labor to break it (Grim 18), or Hand + Filch to open it (Hard 14). In Cradlewrack it is already open.
4A drop: a cut-away pier, a crowning, a sunken storey. Lung + Athletics, Hard (14), or take 1d6 and lose 2 Lead.
5A hiding place: the quarry may switch to Stealth, opposed by the hunter’s Eye + Search.
6Something in the way that should not be: a Kept beggar, a laid table, a Counted sleepwalker. Dread check, Dread 1–2.
7Mud, fen, warm soil that gives underfoot. Lung + Wayfaring, Hard (14). A Fatlander standing still may root.
8The hue and cry: bystanders take a side. The side with the better reputation here gains 1 Lead.
9A narrow way: a plank, a ledge, a single-file canyon path. Only one can pass at a time; the quarry may block it behind them.
10The land itself: a Black Noon, a pressure day, a pang, a Yawn, an echo, the smell of bread on the wind. The Carver decides who it helps.
Example of Play: A Chase on the Mile

A Rim Road Company clerk the company needs to question bolts from them on the Mile at Lowmark at dusk. Lead 2. The clerk is Threat 1; Tolly (Lung 3, Athletics 2) gives chase, because she is fastest.

Round one: Tolly 15, clerk 9. Tolly wins by 6, one Helping: the Lead falls by 2, from 2 to 0. Caught. Sunniva wants him held, so the Carver calls for a grapple, Hand + Brawl against the clerk’s Guard of 11; Tolly rolls 10 and misses by one. She gets a fistful of his coat, and he tears out of it and keeps running. The Carver puts the Lead back to 1 and hands Sunniva the coat. There is a ledger in the inside pocket.

Round two: the clerk lost, so the Carver rolls a complication: 6, something in the way. A procession of the Deepening is walking down the pier toward the end of the Mile with lanterns, two hundred strong, singing, and the clerk is running straight into it. Dread 2. Tolly holds. The clerk does not stop at the procession. He joins it. He takes a lantern from the nearest hand and walks with them, and he is weeping, and he looks back at Tolly once over his shoulder with an expression of enormous relief.

Tolly can follow him into the procession, and the Carver tells her plainly that this is now a different scene: the procession has the Pull. Sunniva has the ledger. She lets him go, and the Carver lets that cost her 2 Fray, and the table is quiet for a while.

Health, Hunger, and the Body

Ordinary Hunger and Starvation

Every person needs about one day’s bread a day: one lack’s worth. Each day a character goes without food, they gain one level of Starving: −1 to all rolls per level, cumulative. At Starving 3, they cannot recover Flesh. At Starving 5, they lose 1 Flesh per day. A day of decent food removes one level. In the Fatlands, ordinary food never satisfies (see that chapter); in the Fast, nothing grows, and the Starving rules are the weather. Inside the Fast, use the Pangs track from that chapter in place of Starving levels; a character who leaves the Fast converts Pangs to Starving levels at half, rounding up.

Half rations (a Fast “Pantry measure,” a sailor’s biscuit and water) neither add nor remove a level. A character may go a number of days equal to Gut on half rations before they begin to gain a level every second day.

StarvingWhat the body does
1The stomach talks. Thoughts go to food every few minutes. Short temper.
2Cold hands and feet, though the day is warm. Dizziness on standing. Dreams of meals.
3The body begins to eat itself. Wounds will not close. The breath smells sweet and wrong.
4Hair comes away in the comb. Gums bleed. The mind goes sharp and strange; you recite recipes you were never taught.
5The ankles swell. Sores open where you lie. The heart thuds slow and heavy. You lose 1 Flesh a day.
6+You stop feeling hungry. That is the worst sign. Each dawn, Gut + Endure (Grim 18) or suffer Ruin.

Refeeding. A character at Starving 4 or more who eats a full meal must roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or lose 1d6 Flesh to cramps, sweats and the heart’s stutter. The Unfed know this as refeeding sickness, and so does every Crumb-Runner who has watched a rescued child die of the first good supper.

What will be eaten. Starving people eat leather, glue, bark, tallow candles, the wallpaper paste, the dog. At Starving 4, a character who has a person’s body within reach and nothing else must roll Caul + Resolve (Hard 14) to leave it uneaten; a Fatlander with The Long Pig rolls at Grim (18). Eating a person knowingly is Dread 3, as the Dread table says, and if it crosses What You Will Not Do, the Guest takes 5 Fray as well. On the Table this is not a rare horror. It is how half the lands remember the Lack.

The Arithmetic of the Lifeboat

The Uncovered is full of salvage crews who were stranded between tides, and the Admiralty records are full of what they did. If a company of Guests is starving together and there is not enough, the Carver should make them decide who eats, out loud, each day. Track rations openly. Every day that someone takes less so that another takes more, give the giver a Portion at the session’s end. The Table remembers who fed whom. So do the players.

Cold, Exhaustion and Sleeplessness

Each night without shelter in Lack, or without sleep, imposes −1 to all rolls (cumulative, up to −4) until the character rests. The Vigil has its own rules for sleeplessness, which are worse.

Poison

A poison has a Potency (the Difficulty to resist), an Onset, an Effect, and a Course (how many times the victim must resist before it is done). When poisoned, the victim rolls Gut + Endure against Potency at Onset and again at each step of the Course; each failure applies the Effect. A Seamer may give +2 by care (Hand + Stitching, Routine 10, the right purge or poultice). An Iron Stomach gives +2; a Fatlander’s Iron Belly lets them eat mild poisons as food. Detecting a poison by taste or smell is Eye + Feast, at the poison’s Potency. The Table’s poisons are as particular as its gods:

PoisonPotencyOnset / CourseEffect per failure
Widow’s Supper (Fatlands, in gravy)Hard 14an hour / 32 damage; the victim keeps eating
Grey Kiss (Sallowreach, from a Closer’s glove)Grim 18at once / 1the limb touched goes cold and dead for a day
Drowned Milk (Brinehollow, bottled bail-water gone bad)Hard 14a night / 3lungs fill: −2 Lung, then drowning
Long Sleep (Vigil, poppy and linen-water)Grim 18minutes / 2+3 Weariness; in the Vigil, often murder
Second Water (Cradlewrack, red spring-water)Hard 14a day / 4false labor, −2 to all, then 1d6 damage
Hushwort (Oathen, chewed)Routine 10minutes / 1the tongue goes numb; no speech, no oaths
Hearthsmoke (anywhere, rumoured from the Fast)Dire 22an evening / 1the victim smells bread and walks toward it
Mind the gravy. It is always the gravy.
Jem Crackle’s only published advice

Example: At a Board inn outside Sated, Abate Kell refuses the gravy three times and takes it on the fourth, out of courtesy, which is a mistake. It is Widow’s Supper. Halloway, across the table, tastes her own and rolls Eye + Feast against the poison’s Potency, Hard (14): 16. She knows it at once, and knocks Abate’s bowl into his lap, but he has eaten half. Onset is an hour. Abate rolls Gut 3 + Endure 3 against Hard (14) three times over the night, with Halloway’s care (+2, after a Routine Stitching roll of 12). He passes the first (17), fails the second (13): 2 damage, and he keeps eating the bread on the table though nobody offers it, which for an Unfed is a horror of its own, Dread 2. He passes the third. In the morning the innkeeper asks, politely, whether the gentleman enjoyed his supper, and Halloway answers him with her cleaver on the counter.

Disease

Disease moves slower than poison and further. A disease has a Virulence (the Difficulty to resist catching it, and to throw it off), an Interval (how often the sick roll), and Stages. On exposure, roll Gut + Endure against Virulence; failure means infection. Then, once per Interval, the sick roll again: two successes in a row throw it off; each failure advances a Stage; the last Stage is death, outside Sallowreach. A Seamer’s care each Interval gives +2.

DiseaseVirulenceIntervalStages
The Sweats (Rim Road inns)Hard 14dayfever (−1) / delirium (−2, Seeing) / Ruin
Weep-Fever (Sallowreach)Hard 14weekrash / weeping sores / never ends, never kills
Gut-Worm (Fatlands, field-meat)Routine 10weekhunger / wasting despite eating / the worm is longer than the gut
Brine-Lung (Brinehollow, foreigners)Hard 14daycough / bailing like a native / the Calling, at a stranger’s tide
Rouse-Heart (Vigil, years of dose)Grim 18seasonflutter / stutter / Ruin at the next second dose
Childbed Fever (Cradlewrack, any bearer)Grim 18dayheat / festering of the wound / Ruin; the wound will not close
Mouthrot (Oathen, under the bit)Routine 10weeksores / teeth lost / jaw (as the Mangling)
The Bloody Flux (anywhere starving)Hard 14daycramps (−1) / blood (−2, lose 1 Flesh) / Ruin

When a disease spreads through a community, add +1 Pall for each week of it.

Rot and Festering

Wounds left unstitched for a day may fester: roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or lose 1 Flesh per day and suffer −2 to all rolls until treated. In Sallowreach, festering never kills, and never stops.

A festering wound smells first: sweetish, then like cheese, then like the Sump. It goes red, then hot, then purple-black at the edges, and the red climbs the limb in streaks toward the heart. A festering wound treated within three days can be cleaned (Hand + Stitching, Hard 14; on a Lack, the Seamer opens something they should not have). After three days, the limb must come off: a Grim (18) Hand + Stitching roll, a Dread 2 check for everyone in the room, and the patient suffers Ruin as though they had taken a Severed Limb Mangling, but lives. A Seamer who takes the limb off cleanly may offer it to a buyer. Many do. In Lastgate, Nan Pickering pays by the pound.

Healing

  • First aid (Hand + Stitching, Routine 10, a few minutes, once per wound) restores 2 Flesh, +1 per Helping.
  • Rest: a full day of rest restores Gut in Flesh; a full day under a Seamer’s care restores double.
  • Injuries from the Mangling table heal according to their own entries, and some never heal.

Torture

Torture is in this book because it is on the Table: in the Jar Room’s interrogations, in the Cullmasters’ back offices, in Jack Tenterhook’s former career, in the cells of every Purgation raid that took a high-Cut prisoner and wanted the names. These rules describe what it costs and what it gets. They never describe how. The Carver should keep it off-page, or to a single sentence of aftermath, unless the whole table has agreed otherwise.

What It Gets

Each session of torture (an hour, a night) the torturer rolls Tongue + Intimidate opposed by the victim’s Caul + Resolve. The victim suffers 1d6 damage, ignoring Armor, whatever the result, and on a Lack by either side suffers an Injury from the Mangling table. If the torturer wins, the victim answers one question per Helping, plus one.

The answers are not necessarily true. The victim says what will make it stop. The Carver decides, privately, whether each answer is the truth, a lie, or the victim’s honest belief about what the torturer wants to hear. A torturer may roll Caul + Instinct against the victim’s Caul + Resolve to tell which, and even then, a person who has been broken may not know themselves. This is why the Bench of Clauses, which has a god for a lie-detector, does not torture, and why every other land does it anyway.

A Blank, a Kept, and a Sayer each suffer differently. The Kept feel everything and cannot be killed by it, which makes them the Table’s favourite victims and its least reliable witnesses. A Sayer’s answer becomes true. Do not torture a Sayer.

What It Costs

The torturer makes a Dread 2 check each session they continue. And every session, whatever the roll, the torturer marks one Stain. Stain never goes away.

StainWhat it does to the torturer
1Dreams. The victim’s voice in the dark, saying ordinary things.
2The Dread checks for torture stop being needed. This is not relief. Those who know you sense something: −2 to Persuade with friends.
3Who Waits at Home knows, without being told. They can no longer remove your Fray.
4You gain The Cold Plate (Table Two, number 7) if you did not have it.
5You are good at it. The Carver may make you an NPC: a person others hire.

Example: Halloway Brisk has the Cullmaster Varn Sweetbread’s assistant tied to a chair in a slaughterhouse in Sated, and the dusk shift goes out in two hours, and there is a child on the list. Dev says she is going to make him talk. The Carver says, out of character, “Okay. One sentence of it, then we cut. What does Halloway do with her hands?” Dev thinks, and says: “She takes off her apron, folds it, puts it on the block. She rolls up her sleeves. That’s all you see.” Tongue 2 + Intimidate 2 + 2d10 (14) = 18, against the assistant’s Threat 2 + 2d10 (9) = 11. One Helping: two answers. The assistant takes 4 damage, which happens off-page. He tells her which field, and he tells her the child’s name, which she already knew. Both true. Halloway makes her Dread 2 check (14 on the nose: 1 Fray) and marks Stain 1. That night she dreams of the assistant telling her, very calmly, about his mother’s garden. She will dream it for the rest of her life.

The difference between my old work and my new work is the tipping.
Jack Tenterhook, wake-valet. He is lying. It shows on him.

Downtime and Ruin

Between stories, time passes: a week, a season, the long dead months of Lack. Downtime is where wounds close, debts come due, and lives quietly come apart.

Downtime Actions

Each downtime period (usually a week to a month) each Guest chooses one action, two if the period is a season or more:

  • Mend. Rest under care. Heal all Flesh, and advance every healing Injury one step. Remove 1 Fray.
  • Work. Ply your Calling. Earn (Standing × 5) lacks for a week, or (Standing × 20) for a season, on a Routine (10) roll of the Calling’s best pair; each Helping adds 10%.
  • Tend. Go home to Who Waits at Home. Remove all Fray once per story, as the Fray rules say, if they are still themselves; the Carver tells you how they are.
  • Treat. Undergo treatment for a Derangement: one period of the months of care the rules require. Three periods and 10 Portions treat one Derangement.
  • Restitch. For the Kept, or for those keeping them: Seamer upkeep, as the Sallowreach chapter gives.
  • Pursue. Advance a long task: research, a ledger, a forty-page vow. One roll per week.
  • Petition. Seek Standing: a deed the Calling recognises, and the Portions to pay for it.
  • Carouse. A vice, as the Fray rules give: 1d6 Fray gone, a Gut + Endure roll against a habit, and lacks spent at the comfortable or lavish rate.
  • Keep Faith. Tend an Oath on the Dead: visit the grave, the niche, the shelf, the place they were taken. +2 to the next roll made in the oath’s name.

The Cost of Living

Every downtime period costs the cost of living for its length, at the Guest’s chosen rate: destitute 1, modest 3, comfortable 8, lavish 25+ lacks a day. A Guest who cannot pay drops a rate. A Guest who cannot pay the destitute rate begins to slide into Ruin.

Ruin of a Life

Ruin in combat is the collapse of a body. Ruin in downtime is the collapse of a life, and it is measured the same way, in steps that do not come back easily:

RuinWhat has happened
1Debt. You owe someone (the Company, a Surety, a fence) and they know where you sleep.
2Disgrace. Your Calling’s people have heard. −1 Standing.
3Destitution. You sleep in doorways or the Lofts’ porch; Starving rules apply on any bad week.
4Outlawry. A warrant, a bounty, a Forsworn mark, a Board debt sold to the Cullmasters.
5The list. Your name is on someone’s list: the dusk shift, the Dormitory overflow, the Blank trade, a Reckoner’s knife, the Second Table’s menu.

A Guest gains a step of Ruin for a downtime period they cannot pay for, for a public crime, for a broken contract or oath, or for the deeds of their enemies. They lose a step by paying down debts (Ruin × 50 lacks), by a great service to a power that can lift them, or by fleeing to another land and starting again at Ruin 1, which is what the Rim Road is for.

While You Were Away

At the end of each downtime period, the Carver rolls a d20 for one Guest’s Who Waits at Home.

d20While you were away
1–6They are well. They wrote. The letter is short and kind and asks when you are coming home.
7–8They are ill. Not badly, yet. They did not want to worry you.
9They have a new friend, very attentive, who belongs to one of the Table’s congregations.
10They are in debt, because of you: someone came asking, and they paid.
11They have been questioned by a Cutwright, a Waker, a Netwatch officer, a Bench clerk.
12Their Regrowth has risen. They describe the first tell in a letter, lightly, as a joke.
13A table was laid in their kitchen one morning. It had your name on a card. They burned it.
14Their village’s Pall has risen: roll it as Uneasy.
15They have taken in a stranger who is very like you.
16They have stopped writing.
17They have been taken: Reaped, Called, Counted, Set Aside, bricked, bound, poached. Not dead. Findable.
18They have done something terrible for your sake, and they are waiting to tell you.
19They have started to change toward the god. They are happy.
20They are well, and they have news, and it is good, and it is real. Let it be real.

Example: Between stories, a month passes. Ressa takes two actions: Mend (her Flesh returns, and the black bruise where the hookman’s boathook caught her ribs fades to yellow) and Tend, going home to Ama in Gannet Reach, which clears her Fray because Ama is still herself. Tolly Works as a courier (Standing 1: 5 lacks a week, 20 for the month) and spends it all on rouse. Abate cannot pay even the destitute rate in Lowmark and will not accept charity; he gains Ruin 1, a debt to a Company quartermaster who knows where he sleeps. The Carver rolls While You Were Away for Ressa: 13. A table was laid in Ama’s kitchen one morning, with Ressa’s name on the card. Ama burned it. She mentions it in passing, over herring, as though it were nothing, and her hands shake.

Nobody on the Table goes home. They go back, which is different, and they find out how different when they knock.
Cradlewrack saying, from a country where you must

Oaths on the Dead

Every Guest begins with an Oath on the Dead, and any character may swear another. To swear on the dead, you speak the full name of a dead person, ideally where they lie, and promise something in their name.

  • The Strength of the Dead: once per scene, when you act directly to keep the oath, add +2 to a roll.
  • Keeping: when you fulfil an oath on the dead, remove all Fray and gain 2 Portions.
  • Breaking: if you deliberately break the oath, the dead come to collect. Gain 3 Fray immediately and suffer a Visitation, chosen by the Carver and shaped by the land where you swore: in Sallowreach the dead person, Kept, finds you; in the Fatlands you taste them in every meal; in Brinehollow their voice calls you from the water; in the Vigil they wait for you in every blink; in Cradlewrack you bear something with their face; in Oathen your body breaks to match the promise; in the Fast a place card bearing their name appears at every table you pass.

Swearing on the dead is not a light thing anywhere, and the Table is full of people who swore too easily. Grave-oaths sworn on the desecrated dead, over a body that has been opened or eaten or robbed, are said to bind twice as hard.

The Swearing, Clarified

  • Where. An oath sworn where the dead one lies (at the grave, the niche, the Loft shelf, the wake-table, the shore where they walked in, the bed in the Dormitory) is the full oath. An oath sworn elsewhere works, but its Visitation is shaped by the land where the dead one lies, not where you stood.
  • How many. A Guest may carry several oaths on the dead. Each grants its own Strength, once per scene, only when acting for that oath. When two oaths conflict, keeping one may break the other. The dead do not arbitrate. That is the point.
  • Twice as hard. An oath sworn over the desecrated dead grants +2 Strength twice per scene instead of once. Keeping it removes all Fray and grants 3 Portions. Breaking it brings two Visitations, and the second one the Carver does not have to tell you about until it arrives.
  • Oathen. Within Oathen, oaths on the dead are also Weight 5 oaths under Tolm, with the Breaking, the Testifying and all the rest that the Oathen chapter gives. They break you twice: once in the body, once from the dead.
  • Deliberately. Only a deliberate breach brings a Visitation. A Guest who fails to keep an oath despite trying, who is prevented, who dies trying, is not forsworn. The dead are not unfair. They are only very patient.

Visitations

A Visitation is not a single event. It returns, at least once a session, until the Guest makes amends: swears a new oath on the same dead, at the same place, for something harder than the first, and keeps it. Each Visitation that lands calls for a Dread check at the rating shown, or the Carver’s judgment. Roll a d10 on the table for the land where the dead one lies, or choose.

Promise the living what you like. They forget.
fen proverb, the first half. The second half is never said aloud.

Sallowreach: The Kept Come Calling

d10Visitation (Dread)
1They find you. Kept, rotted to the degree time allows, standing at the foot of your bed, asking why. (3)
2A parcel arrives: one of their hands, wrapped, still gripping. It holds yours when you sleep. (2)
3Every candle you light is a Tallow candle, and it is them, and it feels itself burn. (2)
4Your own fingers go cold to the knuckle and will not warm. Things you touch end a little. (2)
5A Loft-Warden writes to say that the shelved dead have begun whispering your name in their sleep. (1)
6Flies follow you, a small front, and in their sound is their voice, finishing the sentence of your oath. (2)
7You hear them breathing in the next room. The dead in Sallowreach do not breathe. (2)
8A Seamer’s bill arrives for their restitching, made out in your name. Then another. Then another. (1)
9Your reflection’s mouth is stitched shut. (3)
10They forgive you, in writing, in their own hand, every week, and it is worse than anything. (3)

The Fatlands: The Taste of Them

d10Visitation (Dread)
1You taste them in every meal: their skin, their sweat, their mother’s cooking. (2)
2A field near the road has their birthmark, white in the marbling. (2)
3Bread you break is full of their hair. (2)
4You are invited to their wake. You are told you were already at it, and you ate well. (3)
5Your belly growls in their voice, saying the oath. Everyone at the table hears. (2)
6A root in your garden has their face, eyes shut, and grows a little every night. (2)
7Nothing you eat stays down except one dish: the last one they cooked. (1)
8Your Want of the Second Plate fixes on their kin. (3)
9The Cullmasters receive your name, in their handwriting. (2)
10A small warm hill rises in a field you pass, and it says your childhood name. (4)

Brinehollow: The Voice from the Water

d10Visitation (Dread)
1Their voice calls you from the water, any water: a washbasin, a puddle, your cup. (2)
2You cough up their wedding ring at the dawn bailing. (2)
3The indoor tide leaves their footprints on your cellar stairs, coming up. (2)
4At the morning count, their voice answers for you. (3)
5Your rope is cut in the night, neatly. You wake facing west. (2)
6A Tenanted stranger greets you with their manners and their pet name for you. (3)
7You taste salt in everything, and the salt tastes of their tears. (1)
8Your Want of The West fixes on the place they walked in. (3)
9A shell grows in the corner of your eye, small and living and theirs. (2)
10They come back out of the surf, kind, courteous, and they do not mention the oath at all. (4)

The Vigil: The One in the Blink

d10Visitation (Dread)
1They wait for you in every blink, standing in the long room, much closer than last time. (3)
2A shared Seeming: the street sees them walking beside you. It is entered in the record. (2)
3Your nudger pinches you awake with their fingers. (2)
4You lose a second, and come back holding something of theirs. (2)
5Every lamp you pass gutters as you pass it, all the way home. (1)
6The Matron writes their bed number on your door. (3)
7Their voice lulls you, every evening, humming a song from childhood. +1 Weariness a scene. (2)
8Your reflection’s eyes are closed. (2)
9You count them, in every crowd. The count is always one too many. (2)
10In the room, at the end, beside the eye, there is a bed with your name on it, turned down. (4)

Cradlewrack: What You Bear

d10Visitation (Dread)
1You bear something with their face. It is small. It is breathing. (4)
2False labor, every night, and you count the interval in their voice. (2)
3Every door you shut is found open, and on the far side, their footprints. (2)
4Their old wound opens on your body. (3)
5The Tally reads their name aloud among this week’s births. (3)
6A Part comes looking for you: their hand, or one like it. (2)
7Every knot you tie is undone by morning, and retied in the way they tied them. (1)
8A born-grown stranger walks out of the fog, finishing their last sentence. (3)
9Your oldest scar speaks in the night, and what it says is the oath. (2)
10A midwife comes to your door with the Second Opinion and asks, kindly, whether you should stay. (3)

Oathen: The Body Keeps the Word

d10Visitation (Dread)
1Your body breaks to match the promise (the Breaking table, at Weight 5), and the dead Testify. (4)
2Your voice comes back to you from every wall, a half-second late, in theirs. (2)
3You cannot say their name. Your jaw locks on it. (2)
4Your oath is found carved on the Ledger, in a hand nobody at the Ledger has. (2)
5Every promise you make for a month is heard by the god at +1 Weight. (2)
6Your Exits stop working: the god will not accept a condition from you. (2)
7The echo of the broken oath finds you in a gorge and repeats, and renews. (3)
8A Surety arrives, unasked, and says that the dead have hired her to stand for you. She is already breaking. (3)
9Your hands sign the oath in handtalk while you sleep. Fingers snap. (2)
10Their bones are in your bed at dawn, arranged lying beside you. (4)

The Fast: The Card at Every Table

d10Visitation (Dread)
1A place card bearing their name appears at every table you pass. (3)
2You smell their cooking on the wind, in a land where nobody cooks indoors. (2)
3A chair is pulled out for you, by an invisible hand, in their manner. (3)
4You hear them say “Come in,” from inside a house you know is empty. (3)
5Every ration you carry tastes of the meal you had together. (1)
6The Steward stops you on the road to say they are well, and asking for you. (3)
7You find their name on the Long Table’s seating, in the next empty place. (3)
8Your Pangs rise by 1 each night you do not speak their name. (1)
9You dream of sitting down. Every night. You are very happy in the dream. (2)
10A table is laid for two. Your card. Their card. Both chairs pulled out. (4)
Example of Play: The Oath and the Line

Ressa Weir swore at the start of play: On my brother Ferrin, who walked in: I will never again drag anyone back from the water. Her line: she will not put a rope on a living person. In the Tooth example earlier in this chapter, she roped a Called girl on the Mile and dragged her back.

The Carver stops play. “That’s deliberate,” she says, gently, out of character. “You knew the oath.” Maya agrees. Ressa crosses What You Will Not Do as well: 5 Fray. The oath breaks: 3 Fray. Ressa is at Fray 9, Fraying, and must write a new line she will not cross. Then the Visitation. Ferrin lies in Brinehollow, in the sea. The Carver rolls a d10: 4. At the morning count, his voice answers for you.

The next dawn, in Gannet Reach, the neighbours call Ressa’s name through the wall, and before she can open her mouth, a man’s voice answers from inside her room, cheerfully, coughing the way Ferrin coughed. “Here.” Dread 3. Ressa’s sister-in-law Ama, who has come to visit, is standing in the doorway, white as salt, holding Ferrin’s chain.

Ressa has saved a girl’s life. The oath does not care. The way to amends is a harder oath at the place where Ferrin walked in, and the Carver already knows what it will be.

Travel

The Rim Road is about 2,200 miles around. On foot a traveler makes about 20 miles a day on the road; by cart 25; by fast horse 40; by Company post-coach, changing horses at every waystation, 70. Waystations stand roughly every 15 to 25 miles, and a day’s walk off the road in any land is somewhere stranger.

Each day of travel through dangerous country, the Carver may roll on the land’s encounter table (see the bestiary), and one Guest may roll Lung + Wayfaring (Hard 14) to find a better route, avoid trouble, or make up time. Crossing into the Fast is a different matter entirely, and the rules for that are in its chapter.

Off the road, halve these speeds in fen, canyon, highland or the Uncovered, and halve them again in Lack. A Guest who fails the day’s Wayfaring roll with a Lack has led the company somewhere: the Carver rolls on the land’s Horrors table instead of its encounters. Travelling hungry, cold or sleepless brings the Body’s rules to bear each night, and the Rim Road is very long.

Twenty miles a day on the Rim. Everyone walks it eventually, the same direction, round and round. Nobody has ever found the end, because it is a ring. Some people take a long time to understand that.
waystation keeper at Thimble Cross

Light and Darkness

The Table is lit by tallow, oil, rushlight and the candles of the dead. Darkness imposes −2 to Search and to attacks; total darkness, −4. In the Vigil there is no darkness, by law, and that is a horror of its own.

A lantern lights about ten paces; a candle, three; a Tallow candle made from the dead, three, steadily, and it whimpers. Characters who can see in darkness (a Brinehollower in the Course, a lidless Vigilant’s memory of a room) ignore the penalty. Fighting in the dark has its own rules in Blood on the Cloth.

The Grace Roll in Brief
  • Roll: 2d10 + Attribute + Skill vs Routine 10, Hard 14, Grim 18, Dire 22, Impossible 26. Each full 4 over is a Helping.
  • Omens: doubles. Success is a Grace; failure a Lack. Double 1s always fail; double 10s always succeed.
  • Partake: add a Tooth (d6; two at Cut 3+). +1 Hunger, +1 per Tooth showing 1, +2 more on a Lack.
  • Hunger 10: Regrowth +1, Hunger to 0. Sop: −1d6 Hunger, and the habit grows.
  • Brink (Regrowth 10–11): Wheel checks; Ridden marks. Regrowth 12: the Seating.
  • Dread: Caul + Resolve vs 10/14/18/22/26. Fail: Fray = Dread. Pass: 1 Fray. Grace: none.
  • Fray 10: Break, Derangement, Fray to 3. Witnesses check Dread 2 for contagion.
  • The Pall: a community’s Fray, 0–20; each week, 2d10 + Steadiness vs 10 + Pall.
  • Hold: 0–5, built by methods; Doubt: 3 marks and the false memory wins.
  • Chases: Lead 0 caught, Lead 6 lost; opposed Lung rolls; complications.
  • Oaths on the Dead: +2 once a scene; keep it, clear Fray and gain 2 Portions; break it, 3 Fray and a Visitation until amends.
Chapter 13

Blood on the Cloth

There is no clean way to open a person. There are only quick ways and slow ways, and the slow ways are cheaper.
— Jem Crackle, the Cook’s Knife, to an apprentice

The Warden came at Halloway with a boathook, the long kind the Netwatch use for pulling the Called out of the surf, and she knew from the way he held it that he had pulled more people out of things than he had ever put into them. That was his mistake. He wanted to hook her, drag her, take her alive. She only wanted him to stop.

She let the hook go past her ear. It caught her coat at the shoulder and tore it, and she stepped inside the length of the pole, where it was no use to anyone, and put the cleaver into the meat where his neck met his collarbone. It went in with the sound a joint makes on the block: that wet, final chock of iron finding the gap in the bone. She felt it through the handle into her wrist. His breath came out of him in a long, surprised whistle, and something warm and copper-smelling ran over her knuckles and into her sleeve.

He sat down. He kept looking at her. He was trying to say something about his wife. She worked the blade free, the way you do, a little rock and a twist, and that was worse, because then the blood had somewhere to go.

She had butchered four thousand animals in her life. Her hands knew this. That was the part she would not be able to forget: how well her hands knew it.

Violence on the Table is fast, ugly and expensive. Fights are short. People who are hurt stay hurt. Guests who solve every problem with a blade will be dead, maimed, or something worse inside a few sessions, and they will deserve the stories told about them.

This chapter gives the rules for fighting: the round, the attack, the wound, the Mangling, and the long list of things people do to each other with hooks and cleavers in the dark. It ends with three fights played through from first blow to last, with the same company of Guests who walk through The Grace Roll: Ressa Weir, Halloway Brisk, Tolly Fane and Abate Kell.

Every fight on the Table ends the same way: somebody has to clean the floor. Ask yourself, before you start, whether it will be you.
Netwatch drill-sergeant

The Round

Combat is played in rounds of about three seconds. Each round, every combatant gets:

  • One action: an attack, a dash, a grapple, a first-aid attempt, a shouted plea, a Sop, a Partake-and-act, anything that takes real effort.
  • One move: a few steps, drawing a weapon, standing up, opening a door (in Cradlewrack it may already be open).

A character can give up their action for a second move. Talking a little is free.

Initiative

At the start of a fight, everyone rolls 1d10 + Lung + Eye. Act from highest to lowest. Ties go to the Guests. Those taken by surprise do not act in the first round. Initiative is rolled once for the whole fight, unless something dramatic resets it (a Hush opening, a pang, the lights going out in the Vigil).

Threat-rated adversaries roll 1d10 + Threat. A mob or a swarm acts once, on a single initiative. The Carver may roll once for a whole group of identical foes and have them act together; it is faster, and it makes them feel like a pack.

Surprise and Ambush

A fight that begins with one side unready begins with an ambush.

  • Setting it. The ambushers roll Lung + Stealth (or Threat); use the lowest roll among them, because one cough gives everyone away. The ambushed roll Eye + Search (or Threat); use the highest, because one sharp eye is enough. If the ambushers win, they get a surprise round: one full round before the ambushed act at all. If they win with a Helping or more, every attack in that round counts the target as unaware.
  • Unaware targets. An unaware target’s Guard is 10, flat: no Lung, no skill. Attacks from hiding on a Silent weapon gain +2, as that quality says. The Reckoner’s talent In Their Beds adds +4 damage against an unaware target. Sleeping targets are always unaware, and in the Vigil, a sleeping target is a crime scene.
  • Sensing it. A character who loses the ambush roll may still roll Caul + Instinct at Hard (14). On a success they act in the surprise round, last. A Light Sleeper cannot be surprised while asleep or resting, as the Knack says, and the Carver should honour it with glee.
  • A failed ambush. If the ambushed win, nobody is surprised; roll initiative as normal, and the ambushers are probably standing somewhere foolish.
The Reckoners say a Godeater dies in his bed or not at all. It isn’t a boast. It’s a method, and the method is patience.
Dr. Mercy Thrane, notes

Attacking

To attack, roll 2d10 + Hand + Blades (for edged weapons), Brawl (for fists, clubs, teeth, grapples) or Shooting (for anything thrown or loosed), against the target’s Guard.

  • Melee Guard = 10 + Lung + the best of Athletics, Blades or Brawl.
  • Ranged Guard = 10 + Lung + Athletics. Add +2 for partial cover, +4 for heavy cover. Firing into melee without hitting friends needs a Helping, or a friend is hit on a Lack.

If the attack total meets or beats the Guard, it hits.

Damage

Damage = weapon damage + 2 per Helping − the target’s Armor.

A hit that is reduced to 0 or less by Armor does no Flesh damage, but on a Grace it still inflicts a Mangling. Damage is subtracted from Flesh.

WeaponDamage
Fist, kick, bite1
Knife, awl, needle, sling2
Cleaver, hatchet, club, sickle, shortbow3
Sword, axe, spear, boathook, harpoon, crossbow4
Poleaxe, maul, greatcleaver, Tablebreaker’s axe5
Siege weapons, falling masonry, a Laden’s weight6+

Weapon qualities (Hooking, Ripping, Heavy, Reach, Silent, Brutal, and so on) are listed in the Rim Market.

Carver’s Advice: Saying What the Blade Did

Numbers kill people; words make it matter. After every hit, say one true thing about the wound before the next roll: where it went, what it sounded like, what it smelled like, what the hit person did with their face. Keep it to one sentence for ordinary damage. Save the paragraphs for Manglings and Grievous wounds, and for the first blood a Guest ever draws. If the table winces, you have said enough. If someone says the Grace, stop at once and describe nothing more than the number.

Grace and Lack in Combat

  • A Grace on an attack inflicts a Mangling in addition to its damage (roll on the table below). Grace attacks are where people lose eyes and fingers.
  • A Lack on an attack means the weapon sticks, breaks, flies from your hand, or hits someone you did not mean to hit; or you overextend and the target gets a free attack against you.
  • A Lack on a defense (when you are rolling to resist a grapple, or the Carver calls for a roll to dodge something unusual) means you fall, drop something, or take a Mangling yourself.

Other Actions

  • Grapple: Hand + Brawl vs Guard. On a hit, the target is held: they can only try to break free (opposed Gut + Labor or Lung + Athletics) or attack with a small weapon at −2. A holder can choke (1 damage per round, ignoring Armor), drag, pin or bite.
  • Disarm: attack at −2; on a hit, no damage, the target drops their weapon.
  • Shove or trip: Gut + Labor or Hand + Brawl vs Guard; the target falls or is pushed back. Standing up takes a move.
  • Aim: spend an action aiming to gain +2 on your next ranged attack.
  • Full Defense: spend your action defending: +4 Guard until your next turn.
  • Flee: move away. Anyone engaged with you gets a free attack unless you win an opposed Lung + Athletics roll.
  • Partake: you can Partake on any combat roll. Many Gifts are combat abilities.

More Maneuvers

The Table fights dirty, in kitchens and on piers and in the aisles of the Lofts. These maneuvers cover most of what people try. None of them stack with each other in the same action.

  • Charge. Move and attack in one action, if you have a run of at least five paces: +2 to the attack, and −2 to your Guard until your next turn. A Reach weapon set against you strikes first.
  • All Out. Throw yourself into the blow: +2 to attack and +1 damage, −4 Guard until your next turn. Renderers call it going through the joint.
  • Two Weapons. With a Light weapon in the off hand, make one extra attack at −4 against the same or an adjacent target. A Lack on either attack is a Lack on both.
  • Feint. Tongue + Deceive opposed by the target’s Caul + Instinct (or Threat). Win, and your next attack against them this round or next counts them as unaware (Guard 10). Lose, and they know your tricks: −2 to feint them again this fight.
  • Bind. Lock the enemy’s weapon with yours, or with a hook, or with your own forearm: Hand + Blades vs Guard. On a hit, neither of you may attack with those weapons until one breaks the bind (opposed Gut + Labor). Others may attack the bound one at +2.
  • Brace. Set a Reach weapon against a charge or a rush. The first enemy to close this round takes your attack before theirs, at +2.
  • Hold the Line. Two or more fighters shoulder to shoulder in a doorway, on a pier, in a canyon cut: each gains +2 Guard while the other stands. Mobs can only reach a held line with as many attackers as there are bodies across it (see Fighting Many).
  • Cover. Ready an action: name a target and a trigger (if he moves for the lamp). When the trigger happens, you act first.
  • Cast Into. Shove a held or prone enemy into something worse: a fire, a fen, the Sump, a crowning, a laid table, off the end of the Mile. Gut + Labor vs Guard (Guard 10 if held). The Carver decides what the worse thing does; it is usually more than a weapon would.
  • The Dead as Shield. Hold a body, or a Kept, between you and the blows: +2 Guard, and every hit that misses you by 2 or less hits the body. If the body is someone the enemy knew, they make a Dread check before they swing. If it is someone you knew, you make one when it is hit.
  • Rally. Shout, slap, needle or bully a companion back into the fight: Tongue + Intimidate (or Rites) vs Routine (10). Remove 1 Fray from them, or let them shake off a freeze from a Lack on a Dread check. Once per companion per fight.
  • Yield. Drop your weapon and beg. Roll Tongue + Persuade against Hard (14), or Grim (18) if you have killed one of theirs. Success means the enemy must make a choice, and most people on the Table, faced with a begging human being, do not strike. Failure means they will. The Carver should let NPCs Yield, often.
  • Drag. Pull a fallen ally out of reach: your move and your action, Gut + Labor vs Routine (10), or Hard (14) under attack. Enemies engaged with you get a free attack.
  • Kill the Light. Put out a lamp, a lantern, a candle in reach: an action, no roll unless someone protects it. See Fighting in the Dark.

Called Shots

A fighter may aim for a particular part of the body. A Called Shot takes a penalty to the attack. If it hits, it deals damage as normal, and if it scores at least one Helping, the attacker may choose the matching Mangling result instead of the extra damage from that Helping. A Grace on a Called Shot inflicts the chosen Mangling and rolls on the table for another.

TargetPenaltyWith a Helping, choose
Hand or weapon arm−2Knuckles; or the weapon drops
Leg or knee−2Hamstrung; or the target falls
Face or mouth−2Teeth; Jaw (with two Helpings)
Head−4Skull
Eye−4Eye
Throat−4Throat (with two Helpings); otherwise target cannot speak or shout for 1d6 rounds
Belly−2Gut-Stuck; Opened (with two Helpings)
A Kept’s joint−2Severed Hand or Severed Limb, for dismemberment

Armor still counts, and the Carver may rule that a helm or a gorget protects the part entirely. Called Shots against an unaware target take no penalty. That is what assassins are for.

Aim for the hand that holds the hook. A man without his hook is only a man on a pier, and most of them remember they have mothers.
Lieutenant Sable Reef, to recruits

Fighting in the Dark

The Table is lit by tallow and oil, and a great many of its fights happen after the lamp goes over.

  • Dim light (a single candle, moonlight on the Plate, fog-light in Sallowreach): −2 to attacks and to Search.
  • Darkness (the lamp is out, a cellar, a new moon licked clean): −4 to attacks and Search, and everyone’s Guard counts as though they had no skill bonus (10 + Lung only), because nobody can see a blow coming.
  • Finding a foe. In darkness, a character must know where an enemy is before attacking: Caul + Instinct or Eye + Search (with the darkness penalty) against the foe’s Lung + Stealth, as an opposed roll. On a loss they swing at where the enemy was. On a Lack, they hit a friend.
  • The lamp-bearer. Whoever holds the light is seen by everyone and sees little beyond its circle. Attacks against a lamp-bearer from outside the light ignore the darkness penalty. Attacks from the lamp-bearer into the dark suffer it in full.
  • What sees in the dark. A Brinehollower in the Course sees in total darkness. The Kept do not need to see to grasp, and they smell the living (−2 to Stealth against them for anyone not wearing vinegar or cedar). The Counted, the Seated and things born in Cradlewrack’s lower wards behave as though it were noon. A Guest who Partakes may ask the Carver whether their Tooth gives them any sense in the dark; the answer should be in their land’s idiom, and it should never be free.
  • In the Vigil. There is no darkness, by law. When the lamps go out in the Vigil, it is because someone wanted them out, and every Vigilant within sight makes a Dread 1 check, because the dark is the closest thing in their lives to the room.
Put out the light, and every man in the room becomes the size of his fear.
Lamplighters’ Guild saying

Fear in the Fight

A fight against horrors calls for a Dread check when the horror is first seen, not once per round. Seeing an ally Mangled is Dread 2. Killing someone for the first time is Dread 2 (Dread 3 for someone you knew, Dread 4 for kin).

A Guest who freezes, flees, screams or vomits on a Lack loses their next action, and the Carver should describe it. A Guest who reaches Fray 10 mid-fight Breaks at once, and their Break plays out during the fight; the contagion rules apply to everyone who sees it, friend and foe.

Morale

Most people on the Table do not want to die, and most of them are hungry, tired and paid badly. Threat-rated adversaries check morale when: their side has lost half its number; their leader falls, flees or Yields; they suffer a Mangling or see one; or a horror of Dread 2 or more appears on the field. The Carver rolls 2d10 + Threat against Hard (14). Failure means they break: they flee, Yield, or hold back and do nothing useful. A Lack means they turn on their own leader, or on whoever brought them here.

Some never check: the Kept, the Called, the Seated, the faithful in their rite, the starving at a table, anything Ridden by a god, and Reckoners within reach of a high Cut. Some always check at Grim (18): conscripts, debtors on the dusk shift, a mob without a preacher.

Flesh, Ruin and Death

Flesh = 8 + Gut + Endure. A Guest at half Flesh or less is Bloodied: −1 to all rolls.

When Flesh reaches 0, the character suffers Ruin: they take an Injury (roll on the Mangling table) and collapse. They can crawl, whisper, and do nothing else useful. They are Dying.

A Dying character who takes any further damage is dead. A Dying character who is not treated within (Gut) minutes must roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) every minute; failure means death. A successful first-aid roll stabilizes them at 1 Flesh.

In Sallowreach, nothing dies. A character who would die there becomes Kept: see that chapter. They keep their Injuries. They keep everything.

Damage below 0 does not carry over; Flesh stops at 0, and the next point of damage is the end. A Seamer’s Reseat (the Seamer Calling) may spare a Ruined character the Injury, but not the collapse. Ruin heals: a Ruined character who is stabilized and rests recovers Flesh as normal, and is up and walking, badly, at a quarter of their Flesh.

Damage on the Table, by the Numbers

An ordinary Guest has 10 to 14 Flesh. A knife does 2 to 6, a sword 4 to 8, a crossbow bolt at close range 4 to 10. Two or three solid blows will drop anyone. A Grace can end a fight at once. Armor matters enormously: boiled leather turns a knife into a bruise. The cheapest way to survive a fight is not to be in it. Carvers should let NPCs surrender, flee, bargain and beg, and they should do so often. On the Table, everybody is somebody’s kin.

The Mangling Table

Roll 1d20 when a Grace attack lands, or when a character suffers Ruin. Add +2 if the weapon is Brutal or the damage dealt was 8 or more. Every Mangling is also a Dread 2 horror for those who see it happen to someone they care about.

d20ManglingEffect
1–2Laid OpenA long shallow cut that unzips the skin and shows the yellow fat beneath. Bleeds freely: 1 damage per round until bound. Scar.
3KnucklesFingers broken or split to the bone. −2 to Hand rolls until healed (2 weeks). On a Lack later, one finger is lost.
4TeethA blow to the mouth: teeth spat out in pieces with the blood, lips torn. −2 to Tongue rolls for a week; permanent gaps.
5Rib-CrackYou hear it before you feel it: a green-stick crack, then the grinding. −2 to Lung rolls; every deep breath is a knife (4 weeks).
6HamstrungThe tendon behind the knee parts like a bowstring. Movement halved; cannot run. Without a Seamer’s Grim (18) repair, limp forever (−1 Lung).
7The EarTorn half off, hanging by a flap of gristle. −2 to hearing-based Search. Stitched back crooked, or lost.
8Gut-StuckA wound in the belly that lets out the smell of the bowel. Fever in 1d3 days unless treated (Grim 18 Stitching); −2 to all rolls while it festers.
9EyeThe eye is punctured, crushed, or hangs on its cord. Lost. −2 to Search and Shooting thereafter (−1 after a month of adjustment). Dread 2 to see.
10SkullThe scalp splits and the bone beneath dents like an egg. Stunned for 1d6 rounds; roll Gut + Endure (Hard 14) or lose memory of the last day.
11Broken ArmThe forearm bends between the wrist and elbow, where there is no joint. Unusable for 6 weeks; splint and pray.
12Broken LegThe shin snaps, perhaps through the skin, white and wet. Cannot stand. 8 weeks; a Lack in healing means a permanent limp.
13Severed FingersOne to three fingers gone, rolled away in the dirt. Permanent −1 Hand for fine tasks. Someone may pick them up.
14OpenedA deep wound across the abdomen. Loops of grey-pink bowel slide free and steam. Dying in (Gut) minutes unless held in and stitched (Grim 18). Survivors are weakened (−1 Gut) for a season.
15Severed HandOff at the wrist; the stump sprays in rhythm with the heart. Lose 2 Flesh per round until tied off. The hand twitches for a while afterward. In Sallowreach, much longer.
16JawThe jaw is broken, dislocated or torn half away: the tongue lolls in a ruin of teeth. Cannot speak clearly; can only take liquid. 6 weeks. (In Oathen, many count this as mercy.)
17ThroatA cut or crush to the throat. Blood in the windpipe; breathing is a gargle. Dying in (Gut) rounds unless treated (Dire 22). Survivors speak in a rasp forever.
18UnmannedA savage wound to the hip, groin or pelvis; the bone grates, the blood pools black. Cannot walk for 2 months; Gut −1 permanently. Dread 2.
19Severed LimbAn arm off at the elbow, a leg off at the knee: hacked through, the bone ends splintered and pale. Lose 3 Flesh per round until tied off. Ruin follows. A Seamer may reattach a limb from another body; it will not be quite yours.
20+ButcheredThe blow opens the body like a carcass on the hook: the chest split, the skull cloven, the head half off. The character dies at once, outside Sallowreach. Inside it, they continue, in that condition, indefinitely. Dread 3 to all who see.

Bleeding from several Manglings adds together. “Tied off” and “bound” mean a first-aid roll (Hand + Stitching, Routine 10) that stops the bleeding but restores no Flesh; a Ripping wound needs the same.

Chalked on the shutter of a back-alley Seamer in the Lower Pilings, Lastgate. Prices in lacks.

Cut stitched, plain: 1. With the good thread: 2. With the good thread and you don’t scream: 3, because you’ll have had the poppy.

Finger back on: 4. Your own finger: 4. Somebody else’s finger: 4, and we don’t ask, and you don’t.

Hand back on: 15. Hand from stock: 30. Left hands: ask. (No left hands this week.)

Ear: 2. Eye: we can’t, love, nobody can, but we’ll sew the lid so it looks restful. 1.

Bowel put back: 25, paid before. Bowel put back on the Living (foreigners, the Breathing): 60, paid before, no refunds, sit there.

Head: 40, and bring someone to hold it.

NO CREDIT. NO KEPT ON THE BENCH AFTER DARK UNLESS SEEN TO. NO MARROW JACK.

The Grievous Table

Some blows are worse than a Grace. A Grievous blow is any of the following:

  • A Grace on an attack that also scores two or more Helpings.
  • A Grace with a Heavy or Brutal weapon against a held, prone or unaware target.
  • The killing stroke of an execution that goes wrong (see Executions).
  • Being crushed by a Laden’s weight, falling from the end of the Mile, a pang bringing down a house, a Tablebreaker’s axe in a frenzy, or anything else the Carver judges to be more than a body can be asked to bear.

On a Grievous blow, roll 1d20 on this table instead of the Mangling table. Grievous wounds are Dread 3 for anyone who cares about the victim, and Dread 2 for everyone else who sees them. Most are permanent. Several are fatal outside Sallowreach, and inside it, they are simply what you will be from now on.

d20Grievous WoundEffect
1ScalpedA sheet of scalp peels from the brow back, hanging by a hinge of hair; blood sheets into the eyes. Blind with blood (−4 to attacks) until wiped (an action) and bound; −1 Tongue forever among those who flinch.
2DeglovedThe skin of the hand comes away like a wet glove, leaving the red-and-white mechanism working underneath. −4 Hand with that hand until healed (a season); it never feels warm again.
3KneecappedThe knee is smashed inward, the cap floating loose under the skin like a coin in a purse. Cannot stand without a crutch; −2 Lung forever.
4Face ClovenA blow across the face: the nose split to the bone, a cheek laid open so the back teeth show when the victim breathes. −2 Tongue forever except to Intimidate (+1). Dread 1 to strangers.
5Tongue TakenThe tongue is bitten or cut through; the front of it is somewhere on the floor. No speech ever again. In Oathen, the victim may no longer be bound by speech; Sister Verity Amn would say that is not true.
6Both EyesA slash or a thumb across both eyes. Blind. Dying of nothing, but blind. In the Vigil, some call this rest.
7Stove RibsThree or four ribs driven inward; a flail of chest that moves the wrong way when the victim breathes. Lose 1 Flesh per round until bound (Hard 14); −2 Lung and Gut until healed (3 months).
8Shoulder Wrenched OutThe arm is torn half from its socket, muscle and gristle parting; it hangs a hand’s length too low. Useless until a Seamer resets it (Grim 18); −1 Hand forever.
9Hip ShatteredThe pelvis breaks like a dropped plate. Cannot walk; Dying in (Gut) hours from the inside bleeding unless a Seamer opens and closes (Dire 22). Survivors never walk without a stick.
10SpineThe back is struck through or broken. Below the wound, nothing answers. The Carver and player decide where. Outside Sallowreach, permanent. Inside it, also permanent, for centuries.
11UnseamedThe belly opens end to end and the bowel slides out in a heavy coil, tangling the feet. Dying in (Gut) rounds unless gathered and stitched (Dire 22). Survivors lose 1 Gut and eat carefully forever.
12ArteryA cut in the thigh or the neck that does not bleed so much as empty. Lose 4 Flesh per round until clamped (Grim 18 Hand + Stitching, or a fist and a strong friend for one round at a time).
13Both HandsTwo hands off, or crushed to pulp, in one blow, raised to defend. Lose 3 Flesh per round until both are tied off. Ruin follows. Somebody will have to feed you.
14Leg Off at the HipHacked through high, where no tourniquet sits well. Lose 4 Flesh per round. Dying unless sealed with fire or a Grim (18) Stitching.
15Skull OpenedThe skull is broken open and the grey shows. Unconscious; roll Gut + Endure (Grim 18) each hour or die. Survivors lose 1 Eye permanently and gain a Derangement from Table One.
16Jaw Torn AwayThe lower jaw is gone, or hanging by a strip: tongue, throat and teeth exposed. Dying in (Gut) minutes from blood in the windpipe unless treated (Grim 18). Survivors wear a leather mask, in Oathen a gold one.
17GuttedThe blow reaches the organs: the liver split, a kidney opened, the bowel cut through. The wound stinks at once. Dying in (Gut) minutes; a Dire (22) Stitching saves them for a fever that kills on a failed Gut + Endure (Hard 14) in 1d3 days.
18CrushedPressed under a weight, a wheel, a fall: bones broken in a dozen places, the body flattened in a way that looks wrong even before the blood comes. Ruin, and dead unless in Sallowreach. Dread 3 to all.
19Head Half OffThe neck is cut through to the bone; the head lolls on a hinge of muscle. Dead outside Sallowreach. Inside it, the head must be held on with both hands until a Seamer comes, and it keeps talking. Dread 4 to see.
20Taken ApartThe body is opened and broken so completely that it is no longer one thing. Dead outside Sallowreach. Inside it, the pieces go on, separately, and some of them try to find each other. Dread 4.
There is a Fatlands word for a wound you can put your whole hand into. It is also the word for “welcome.”
Hob Gristle, apologising

Special Situations

Fighting the Kept

The Kept of Sallowreach cannot be killed. Reducing one to 0 Flesh drops it, and it goes on moving: crawling, biting, grasping with whatever is still attached. To stop a Kept enemy you must dismember it: each Mangling result of Severed Hand, Severed Limb or Butchered removes the use of that part. Burning helps; it does not finish. Hand-line touch and the Hushes are the only true ends.

This is the Unending ability given in Things That Eat and Are Eaten: a Kept at 0 Flesh is Undone for 1d6 rounds, then recovers 1d6 Flesh and resumes, unless it has been dismembered, sunk, Closed, or carried across the border. The two rules are one rule. Undone, it crawls and grasps at −4; recovered, it fights as before with whatever it has left.

Kept Enemies, Clarified

  • What a Kept feels. Everything. A Kept does not check morale, because it cannot die and knows it, but it feels every blow, and it may scream, beg or curse the whole time. A Kept that begs is Dread 2 to keep fighting.
  • Taking them apart. A Called Shot at a Kept’s joint (−2) with a Helping severs it (Severed Hand at the wrist, Severed Limb at the elbow or knee). A Kept with no working limbs is out of the fight; a Kept with its head off is out of the fight but not out of the conversation.
  • What the parts do. Severed parts of a Kept go on. Roll a d6 for each: 1–2 it lies twitching; 3–4 it crawls toward the nearest warm body (Threat 0, Flesh 3, Attack +2, damage 1, Grapple 10); 5 it goes back to its owner and tries to reattach; 6 it goes somewhere else, and the Carver writes down where.
  • Fire. A burning Kept takes 2 damage a round, does not stop, and spreads the fire to whatever it grasps. Fires in Sallowreach smoulder for decades. A Kept that has burned is Rot +2 and Dread 2 to see.
  • Vinegar and cedar. The Kept find the living by smell. A character doused in fen-vinegar or cedar perfume is −2 to be found by a Kept in the dark, and a character with Vinegar Kiss is ignored by Kept until they act.
  • Kept Guests. A Kept player character follows the same rules, with Rot as the Sallowreach chapter gives it. They are terrifying allies in a fight, and the Carver should make them pay for it in Rot.
Why You Do Not Fight in the Sinks

The Kept outnumber the breathing nine to one in Sallowreach, and every one of them feels every blow and cannot die of it. A brawl in a Lastgate tavern does not end; it goes on, in a smaller and sadder way, for decades, in the Lofts and the Jar Room and the back rooms of part-thieves. Captain Dace Morrow, whose army cannot lose a man, has a standing order that his soldiers are never to fight the Kept at all, only to restrain them. His soldiers are Kept. They know.

Fighting Many

Mobs, the Forsworn of the Breakdowns, a Reaping crowd, the Finishers walking in: treat a mob as one character with Flesh equal to 5 × its number, Threat equal to 1 + one per 5 members (max 5), and damage equal to its best weapon + 1 per 5 members. Each 5 Flesh lost drops one member. Mobs break and run when they lose half their number, unless they are faithful, starving or Called.

Clarifications. A mob attacks with Threat + 3 and has Guard 10 + Threat, Armor equal to what most of its members wear (usually 0). It acts on one initiative and makes one attack a round against each target in its reach. The mobs already written up in Things That Eat and Are Eaten (the Forsworn Mob, the Called Procession, the Two-Legged Cattle) use their own quick lines, which already account for all this; the formula here is for the mobs the Carver makes up on the night.

  • Width. A mob can only bring as many members to bear on a held line as there is room. In a doorway or on a pier, a mob attacks with Threat 1 + one per 5 members who can actually reach, however many are behind. This is why the Netwatch fight on the Mile and the Breakdowns’ slum-lanes are a yard wide.
  • Fire and fear. Fire, a crossbow volley, a horror of Dread 2+ or the fall of a preacher forces an immediate morale check, even before half are down.
  • Crush. A character caught in a moving mob without a weapon out, or knocked down in one, takes the mob’s damage each round, ignoring Armor, until they win an opposed Gut + Athletics roll to get out or up.
  • The Pall. A mob is a community at its worst. A mob that forms in a town adds +1 to the town’s Pall; a mob that kills adds +2. A mob that Guests disperse without bloodshed (by Yield, by Rally, by a Celebrant’s preaching) lowers the Pall by 1.

Fighting Gods

You cannot. A Seated god has no Flesh to take. The rules for what you can do instead are in Things That Eat and Are Eaten.

Executions, Torture and Murder

Not every killing is a fight. When a Guest kills a helpless person, no roll is needed for the act. The roll is afterward: a Dread check at Dread 2 (Dread 3 for someone who begged; Dread 4 for kin). Torture extracts information on an opposed roll of the torturer’s Tongue + Intimidate against the victim’s Caul + Resolve, but the Carver decides how true the answers are, and the torturer makes a Dread 2 check each session they continue. Jack Tenterhook of the Vigil says the difference between his work as a wake-valet and his old job is the tipping. He is lying, and it shows on him.

The full rules for torture, including the Stain it leaves on the torturer, are in The Grace Roll. Kin-slaying by your own hand is Dread 4 whatever the circumstances, and on the Table, where everyone is somebody’s kin, the Carver should ask before each killing whose cousin this was.

Executions

A lawful killing, done by the state, is still a killing. Each land does it its own way, and each way has its horror.

LandThe sentenceWhat witnesses see
SallowreachJarring: Kept forever in pieces, on a shelf in the Jar Room. Or Refusal: struck from the Closing ledger forever.The Seamers unpick the condemned while they watch. Dread 2.
The FatlandsMaking good: killed in the Renderers’ yards; the victim’s family has first cut.The family eating. Dread 3, Dread 1 to Fatlanders.
BrinehollowLoosing: sleep unanchored for a set number of nights, the Netwatch ordered not to intervene.An empty bed, a rope coiled neatly on it. Dread 2.
The VigilBedding, suspended since 590; now the Rattlehouse, waiting for a sentence that cannot be carried out.Faces at the Rattlehouse bars, awake. Dread 1.
CradlewrackThe Second Opinion, given to the born and, rarely, to the grown; or bricking in the Lying-In’s lower wards.A midwife wiping her knife on her apron. Dread 2.
OathenJude Crake’s visit: an hour of pleasant talk, a small promise, the Breaking.Nothing, until the sound. Dread 3.
The FastThe list: a name left off the Pantry roll.A queue at the byre beyond the Cold Yards. Dread 2, and it lasts weeks.

The executioner’s roll. When a Guest carries out a killing stroke with a blade on a helpless person (a beheading at a Rim Road gallows, a Reckoner’s knife in a sleeping lord, a mercy given on a battlefield), they roll Hand + Blades against Routine (10). On a success, it is done, quickly. On a failure, it is not done, and the Carver describes the moment; the executioner must strike again, and the condemned’s Dread rating for all present rises by 1. On a Lack, the blow is Grievous: roll on the Grievous table and keep going. A botched execution adds +1 Pall to any community that watched, and the executioner’s name is known.

Lord, let it be one stroke. Lord, let it be one stroke. Lord, let it be —
prayer said by Rim Road hangmen, in every land, to every god, and to none

Ritual Killing

Some killings are meant to buy something. The Second Helping offers the eaten to the god of feeding. The Cullmasters walk the dusk shift into the fields believing the Reaping can be steered. The Deepening walks the willing into the sea with lanterns. The Purgation burns high-Cut houses with the families inside to starve the god of its vessels. The Second Table rehearses. In a hundred villages, in the worst years, the elders draw lots.

A ritual killing is a killing performed as a rite: with words, with a place, with a method fixed by doctrine. It is led by one celebrant, who rolls Tongue + Rites against Hard (14), or Grim (18) if the victim resists or begs. Every participant and witness makes a Dread 3 check, as the Dread table gives, and those who take part willingly each mark one Stain, as the torture rules give. A ritual killing adds +2 to the Pall of any community that knows of it, whether or not it approved.

Then the celebrant rolls on the table below to see what the rite has bought. The Carver may choose instead, but should be honest with herself about which result the world would give.

We gave it my sister and the sea still went out. We gave it Hask’s boy and the sea still went out. Mother Limpet says the sea is not going out. She says it is going home, and we are the road.
Wreckwife, Lowmark
d10What the rite buys
1–5Nothing. The god was not listening, or was, and did not care. The field still Reaps. The sea still falls. The interval still shortens. The celebrant will say it worked.
6Nothing yet. A sign that something was heard: the wheat leans, the tide stirs, a door opens. The congregation will want another.
7A sop. Every participant with a Cut loses 1d6 Hunger, as if they had performed their Sop, and gains the god’s Want of that land for a day.
8The wrong thing. The god takes the offering, and something else besides: a participant’s Regrowth rises by 1, or the next Reaping takes the celebrant’s own child.
9A delay. The thing feared holds off for one Turn of the Pall, one pang, one Reaping, one night. Then it comes, as it was always going to.
10Attention. Something answers: a god’s attention, Dread 4, falls on the celebrant. The Carver decides what it wants from them now.

This table is the Table’s answer to sacrifice. The Long Grace contains no rite that saves a village, no offering that turns back a god, and no victim whose death was worth it. The demand is real; the giving is real; the grief is real; the bargain is not. Run every ritual killing knowing that, and let the Guests find it out.

The Worthless Sacrifice

In the last bad year in Low Tilth, the village drew lots among its children for the field, because the Cullmasters had taken all the debtors and the Reaping was still hungry, and a preacher of the Second Helping had come through on his way to Sated and said, smiling, that a gift freely given is sweeter. The lot fell on a cooper’s daughter. Her father walked her to the field himself, because nobody else would, and he said the grace over her, and came home alone.

The Reaping took eleven that Carving, the same as the year before. Pell Hogget wrote it in the Long Count, in the same column as all the others, with no mark to distinguish it. The cooper asked him to add a note. Pell said he did not know what the note would say. Neither did the cooper. He still asks, every Carving, and Pell still does not know.

Three Fights, Played Through

The three fights below are told the way they happen at the table, with every roll shown. They use the company from The Grace Roll. For quick reference:

Ressa Weir (Brinehollow, Nightwarden) Flesh 12 · Guard 17 · Attack +5 (Netwatch boathook 4, Hooking, Reach) · Armor 1 (oilskin) · Initiative 1d10 + 6 · Cut 2, one Tooth

Halloway Brisk (Fatlands, Renderer) Flesh 15 · Guard 16 · Attack +8 (cleaver 4 with Know the Cut, Ripping) · Armor 1 (hide coat) · Initiative 1d10 + 4 · Cut 2, one Tooth

Tolly Fane (the Vigil, Crumb-Runner) Flesh 10 · Guard 15 · Attack +3 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Initiative 1d10 + 7 · Stealth 4, Filch 2 · Cut 2, one Tooth

Abate Kell (the Fast, Tablebreaker) Flesh 14 · Guard 17 · Attack +7 (Tablebreaker’s axe 5, Brutal, Two-Handed) · Armor 1 (padded) · Initiative 1d10 + 5 · Unfed, Want 3

Fight One: The Hooks at Gannet Reach

Ambush, Hooking, a Called Shot, a Grace, and morale.

Gannet Reach has gone Uneasy (see Madness in the Community). An old man has denounced his daughter-in-law as Tenanted, and the company has hidden her. At midnight, walking back along the village’s short pier, they are waited for: four Netwatch hookmen under the pier-lamps, sent by a lieutenant who wants the woman, and the strangers who hid her.

Netwatch Hookman (4) Threat 2 · Flesh 12 · Guard 13 · Attack +5 (boathook 4, Hooking 14) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

The ambush. The hookmen are crouched among the bait-barrels. The Carver rolls Lung + Stealth for them as Threat 2, and takes the lowest: 13 + 2 = 15. The company rolls Eye + Search and takes the highest: Tolly, Eye 4 + Search 3, rolls 3 and 2 for 12. The hookmen win by 3: a surprise round, but with no Helping, the Guests are not unaware and keep their Guards. Ade asks whether Abate can feel it coming. The Carver allows Caul + Instinct at Hard (14): Abate has Caul 4, Instinct 2, and rolls 9, for 15. He acts in the surprise round, last.

Surprise round. Hookman A swings for Ressa: 8 + 7 + 5 = 20 against Guard 17. A hit, by 3: no Helping. The boathook’s iron beak takes her across the ribs: 4 damage, minus her oilskin’s 1. Ressa is at 9.

Hookman B goes for Halloway: 6 + 6 + 5 = 17 against Guard 16. A hit, and a pair: a Grace for the hookman. The Grace grants a Helping and a Mangling. He spends the Helping on Hooking, giving up its damage to drag her a pace toward the pier’s unrailed edge (Halloway may resist with Lung + Athletics at Hard 14; Dev rolls 9, and fails). The hook does 4, minus 1: Halloway is at 12. The Mangling: a d20 shows 7, The Ear. “The hook goes in behind your ear and comes out the front of it,” says the Carver, “and the ear goes with it, mostly. It’s hanging on a flap. You can feel it slapping your jaw when you move.” Ressa and Tolly, who care about her, make Dread 2 checks; both hold, and take 1 Fray.

Hookmen C and D both miss. Then Abate, last: his axe into Hookman D, 7 + 5 + 7 = 19 against Guard 13. One Helping, and the axe is Brutal, so the Helping adds +3: 5 + 3 − 1 = 7. Hookman D is at 5.

Round one. Initiative: Tolly 15, Ressa 12, Abate 10, the hookmen 9 (rolled once, for all), Halloway 7.

Tolly kicks the nearest pier-lamp off its post. It goes over the side and smashes forty feet down on the dry seabed. One lamp remains: dim light, −2 to attacks for everyone outside its circle. The hookmen are under it. The Carver rules that attacks against them ignore the dim light; theirs, out into the dark, suffer it.

Ressa knows how hookmen fight, because she taught half of them. She makes a Called Shot at Hookman A’s hands, −2: 9 + 6 + 5 − 2 = 18 against Guard 13. One Helping. She spends it on the Called Shot’s effect: the weapon drops. Her own boathook raps his knuckles and his hook goes clattering down between the boards and off the pier. The rest is damage: 4 − 1 = 3. A is at 9 and has no weapon. “Sergeant Weir,” he says. She does not answer.

Abate swings at Hookman D again: 6 + 3 + 7 = 16. A hit with no Helping: 5 − 1 = 4. D is at 1.

The hookmen. B tries to finish dragging Halloway off the edge: 4 + 2 + 5 − 2 (dim) = 9. A miss. C swings for Tolly: 9 + 8 + 5 − 2 = 20 against Guard 15. A hit with one Helping, which C spends on Hooking: Tolly is knocked flat. 4 damage: she is at 6.
