Merchants of the Table

Never buy from a merchant who says the grace first. He wants something.
— Rim Road advice

These dealers can be dropped into any market scene. Each has a specialty: items in that line are one step more available from them, and they will buy such goods at three-quarters of the listed price instead of half.

Mardy Haunch, Sausage-Wife of Gristmoot

Mardy Haunch Threat 3 · Flesh 14 · Guard 10 · Attack +3 (cleaver 3, Ripping) · Armor 1 (suet) · Dread 0

Stock: Fatlands meat, toothed bread, Chute barrels, marrow-brandy. She has the widest stall on the Rim and has never once stood up behind it. Everything she sells is settling. She buys tattooed casings at a premium and will not say who for; it is Hob Gristle, who is trying to give them back to their families.

Abelard Myrrh, Perfumer of the Lower Pilings

Abelard Myrrh (Kept) Threat 4 · Flesh 9 · Guard 9 · Attack +2 (awl 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Stock: cedar, vinegar, smoke-oils, Kept gauze, Seamer’s lacquer. His own nose rotted off in 340 A.G. and he blends entirely by memory, which is perfect. For 40 L he will make a scent from a dead person’s clothes that convinces any Kept who smells it that they are home and loved. The Court has asked him to stop selling it to the Lofts. He has not.

Nan Pickering, Limb-Broker

Nan Pickering Threat 3 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (shelving hook 3, Hooking) · Armor 1 · Dread 2 (her drying-racks)

Stock: Kept limbs, seamed parts, Thief’s Kept Hands, Seamer’s kits. She buys from Marrow Jack and sells to back-alley seamers in Lastgate’s undercity. Every limb on her racks is labelled with its owner’s name, because she is honest. Some of the owners come to visit. She charges them admission.

Mags Weir, Salvage Queen of the Uncovered

Mags Weir Threat 4 · Flesh 13 · Guard 12 · Attack +5 (harpoon 4, Hooking) · Armor 1 (oilskin) · Dread 0

Stock: wreck goods, salvage-tins, Netwatch gear, Dromm’s Ear-Stones, Tenanted brine. She sells from a beached hulk two miles out on dry seabed. Her newest salvage came from a wreck that sank before the Gorging: a crate of silverware in services of eight. She has sold seven settings. The eighth keeps coming back to the crate.

Lucan Spill, the Oilman

Lucan Spill Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (sword 4) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Stock: lamp oil by the cask, mirror-lanterns, lamp-flasks. He is the supplier who doubled the price to the Vigil, and Garron Ashlock would kill him if killing him would not stop the oil. His new oil burns brighter and smells of low tide. It is rendered on the Uncovered from things with too many ribs, and the lamps that burn it have begun to drip seawater.

Dovey Pinch, Pin-Seller of the Slope

Dovey Pinch Threat 3 · Flesh 9 · Guard 13 · Attack +4 (Waker’s needle 2, Waking) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: pins, pin-gloves, Waker’s needles, rouse-tabs, hired nudgers by the hour. Seventy, sharp-eyed and pricked all over, she sells pain as a convenience. Her needles are recovered from dead Wakers, and each still remembers the last person it kept awake; if you stick yourself with one, you see their face.

Tamsin Keyless, Lock-Pedlar

Tamsin Keyless Threat 3 · Flesh 10 · Guard 12 · Attack +3 (hatchet 3) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: locks, bolts, bricks, mortar, knocker’s rings, counterfeit Agnes Latch locks. Her copies hold for a night, sometimes two. She does not mention that they hold only from the outside, and that what she sells to frightened mothers in Kest is not a way to keep things out but a way to keep them in.

Ruth Ninefold, Name-Broker of Kest

Ruth Ninefold Threat 5 · Flesh 10 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: naming-rights, Tally extracts, Attendance birth-fees on credit, living Parts in jars. She owns the rights to name two hundred births. Several were taken to the Lying-In. One was bought from a clay-digger at the rim of the Dilation, and its year is up at the next pang.

Silas Amend, Paper-Broker of Tacit

Silas Amend Threat 5 · Flesh 9 · Guard 10 · Attack +3 (quill-knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: sworn notes at a discount, Surety introductions, spyglasses, wax tablets, the occasional Snapped Note. He speaks only in conditionals and watches issuers’ bodies from the opposite cliff. He has quietly bought every note ever sworn by a single senior Clausewright of the Bench, and intends to call them all on one morning.

Nay-Saying Hobb, the Declining Grocer

Hobb Threat 3 · Flesh 8 · Guard 11 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (his shelves)

Stock: ration-bread, Unfed greys, frost-markers, Tablebreaker’s wedges. Wanting’s only shop, run by an Unfed elder who declines every sale three times as custom requires. Sometimes he declines a fourth. His shelves are fuller than the Pantry’s, and he cannot say who restocks them overnight. He does not sell the bread that appears on the top shelf. He throws it into the wind.

Factor Orsolya Tare, Mistress of the Cure-House

Orsolya Tare Threat 5 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +3 (knife 2) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Stock: platters at par, new-minted lacks by the barrel, clipped coin bought by weight, First Lacks under the counter. She runs the Company’s mint at Saltbridge and smells of boiled bone. Last month a coin-cutter brought her a fresh-cured lack with letters in the grain, as though the bone had grown them. It was a name. She has had the batch held back (see A Lettered Lack), and the Renderers’ Union keeps asking where it went.

Mister Cutlery

Mister Cutlery Threat 6 · Flesh 13 · Guard 13 · Attack +6 (Clausewright’s quill-knife 2, Silent) · Armor 1 · Dread 1

Stock: relics and godflesh of every land, laid out on velvet in a silverware case. A soft-voiced man in a silk mask with a silver fork embroidered on it, he travels the Rim in a black coach and sells to nobles. He will buy back anything he sold at triple its price, provided the seller names exactly where it came from. He is cataloguing the gods for the Second Table, one portion at a time. There is one thing he will not buy at any price, and if it is offered to him he closes his case and leaves the market, and does not come back for a year.

Bought: cauls, teeth, hair, names, minutes, nails. Sold: the same, dearer. Asked: nothing.
a slate at the Dry Anchor, Brackwater Bridge

More Merchants of the Rim

Abner Wedge, Arms-Man of Foreign Row

Abner Wedge Threat 4 · Flesh 15 · Guard 12 · Attack +5 (axe 4, Brutal) · Armor 2 · Dread 0

Stock: crossbows, bolts, cleavers, warden’s maces, boiled leather, second-hand mail of uncertain provenance. A Gristmoot Fatlander broad as a door who eats brawn while he sells and offers it to every customer. He sells to anyone, including the quiet women in grey who buy six bolts at dawn, and he has started to feel bad about it, which in a Fatlander shows as a loss of appetite. He has lost eleven pounds. His neighbours are worried.

Gaspard Thimble, Seamer of Foreign Row

Gaspard Thimble Threat 4 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +4 (Seamer’s awl 2, Piercing) · Armor 2 (wire-coat) · Dread 1

Stock: thread, wire, lacquer, Seamer’s kits, matched fingers on a cork board. A living Seamer from Lastgate who keeps a booth at Gristmoot and another at Fogmouth. His boy, Kit, cries the stock in a voice that was stitched back wrong after it broke. Gaspard did it on purpose: Kit was sold to him for a debt of his father’s, and a boy whose voice nobody can understand cannot ask a customer for help. Kit has learned to write. He writes on the backs of the price-slates, very small.

Widow Prosper Gammage, Cure-Seller of Gristmoot

Prosper Gammage Threat 4 · Flesh 16 · Guard 9 · Attack +2 (ladle 1) · Armor 1 · Dread 0

Stock: “safe” food sworn untainted, charms against the Calling, Orrum crumbs (fake), Wren Hollowell’s hair (fake), cures for everything. The queen of Cure-Sellers’ Lane, enormous and motherly, she has never sold a true cure in her life and does not believe there is one. She swears on her mother’s bones that her stew is clean of the god. Her mother’s bones are in the stew. She is, technically, not lying, and she says the grace before every sale.

Yarrow Fitch, Money-Changer of the Weeping Post

Yarrow Fitch Threat 4 · Flesh 10 · Guard 11 · Attack +3 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: coin of every land changed at a crumb in the lack, coin-testers’ kits, shut-mouths for collectors, minutes of Closing bought cheap from the north. A thin wet man at the always-wet post between Cradlewrack and Fogmouth, with a crescent bitten into his front teeth and a reference pouch of Rim grains sewn inside his shirt. He can read the grain of a lack by tongue. He keeps the person-lacks in a separate purse and will not spend them; the purse is very heavy, and he has started to hear it at night.

Bettris Caulfield, Caul-Merchant of Knocking Gate

Bettris Caulfield Threat 3 · Flesh 11 · Guard 11 · Attack +3 (hooked knife 3, Ripping) · Armor 0 · Dread 1

Stock: birth-cauls by the crate, cauls sewn into coats, caul-poultices, knocker’s rings. She buys cauls from highland families at eight lacks and sells them at the Spur as proof against the Calling at thirty. They do not work. Lately the Caul-line houses sell to her too, and their cauls are larger, and warmer, and one in her current crate has begun, very slowly, to grow over her hand when she lifts it.

Sabine Lisle, Glass-Wife of Lampwick Halt

Sabine Lisle Threat 4 · Flesh 9 · Guard 13 · Attack +4 (dazzle-mirror; Waker’s needle 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: lenses, spectacles, mirror-lanterns, dazzle-mirrors, lid-lamps, rouse. A Vigil glass-wife who keeps the last stall before the plateau road and has not slept in thirty-one years. She grinds spectacles that let the sleepless see what is really in front of them for an hour, instead of the Seeming. The customers who buy them come back the next day to return them, and will not say what they saw.

Honor Pyle, Surety-Broker of Mumchance

Honor Pyle Threat 5 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +2 (knife 2) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 (her roster)

Stock: Sureties for hire to foreigners entering Oathen, by the day or the crossing; cards of safe phrases; quiet-drops; felt slippers. A Bondsman retired at forty with her jaw wired and both knees reversed, she now rents other people’s bodies to merchants who will certainly say something careless in the canyons. Her roster is chalked on a slate by the inn door, each name with a count of what they have left. She is good to her Sureties. She buries them at her own expense.

Forgo Ainsley, Chit-Dealer of Wanting Post

Forgo Ainsley Threat 3 · Flesh 8 · Guard 12 · Attack +2 (grain-sock cosh 2, Stunning) · Armor 0 · Dread 0

Stock: ration chits bought and sold, Unclaimed Chits (see Relics), Rim grain at the Company’s risk premium, Barrow-Hair Rope. An Unfed man who stands in the yard at Wanting Post every day of the Lack season, buying spare chits from families on the list and selling them to families off it, declining every price three times. He is spat on twice an hour. He has never kept a chit for himself, and he is so thin now that the Crumb-Runners have started leaving bread at his post. He throws it into the wind.

Tobiah Nethercott, Auctioneer Behind the Stockyards

Tobiah Nethercott Threat 5 · Flesh 13 · Guard 11 · Attack +4 (cudgel 3, Stunning) · Armor 1 · Dread 2 (his calm)

Stock: debts, bonds, manifests, terms of service, “lots.” A courteous, tidy Gristmoot man with a knotted rope to measure the distance from the road, a gavel of Fatlands bone, and one rule: no lot under age. He has kept it for twenty years and is proud of it. He believes this makes him a decent man. He has sold four thousand people, and he says the grace with every buyer, and he would like the Guests to know that he has never once been asked by a lot to stop.

Strange Encounters at Market

Roll a d20 whenever the Guests spend time in a Rim Road market, or when a shopping scene needs something under the clove.

d20Encounter
1A Fatlands child is selling teeth by the cupful, sorted by village. She knows which village each cup is.
2A Kept auctioneer in Lastgate is selling himself by the limb, to settle a debt from 300 A.G. The bidding is brisk.
3A coin a character spent an hour ago is back in their purse. It is greasy and smells of the fen.
4A Vigil customer blinks mid-haggle and comes back from the long room three stalls away, holding a knife, with no idea why.
5A Brinehollow stall-keeper stops to bail. The brine she coughs into the bucket is moving in a slow circle.
6An Oathener, asked the price, says “Too much” without thinking. His purse splits open at his belt.
7A drover herds Sal Trotter’s cattle through the market. One of them, passing, says a character’s name.
8Someone has set a table at the market cross: white cloth, warm bread, a chair pulled out. Two Tablebreakers are running towards it.
9A Cradlewrack pedlar’s crate has given birth. Nobody knows to what. It is under the cart.
10A Price-witness offers his services, then quietly declines to witness a character’s purchase, and will not say why.
11The Company’s toll-men are weighing every lack in the market. Clipped coin is confiscated, and so are three thumbs.
12A Netwatch patrol drags a Called man through the stalls on a hook. He thanks every merchant he passes, courteously, by name.
13A Seamer’s boy offers a character a finger “that matches yours exactly.” It does. Down to the scar.
14Wick Tallow’s candles on a stall all lean toward one shopper. The chandler’s man goes pale and closes the stall.
15A Reckoner is buying nothing, watching a Gut-line merchant’s stall. She has been there since dawn.
16A Wreckwife sells her Tenanted husband’s clothes. He is helping her fold them.
17A Purgation preacher hands out emetics and begs the crowd to throw up the god. Some do, on the spot. The Bailiff’s men arrive.
18A Fast pilgrim, starving, offers everything she owns for a single Orrum crumb. Someone has one.
19A Cutwright with calipers measures customers’ skulls for free, and quietly writes certain names in a separate book.
20A stall that was not there an hour ago sells only one thing: place cards, in a fine hand. The one on top has a character’s name on it. The stall-keeper is very tall, and stoops under the awning, and is warm.
Pay the toll. Keep the peace. Say the grace. And count your change, because some of it was somebody.
[ the three articles of the Rim, with the fourth that every market adds ]
Chapter 15

Things That Eat and Are Eaten

Everything on the Table is either sitting at it or lying on it. Learn which you are before the knives come out.
— Tablebreaker saying, Wanting

REPORT OF THE THIRD NIGHT WATCH, NETWATCH, LOWMARK PIER-SECTION FOURTEEN. Entered by Lt. Sable Reef. 9th of Carving, 641 A.G. For the Admiralty Clerk of Losses. Not for the Bench.

Weather: salt rain from the second bell, fog off the Uncovered from the third. Pressure rising. Two of my hookmen bled from the ears before midnight and were sent to bail.

At the fourth bell the count came up short in Ropewalk Row. Widow Carse called her neighbour’s name through the wall three times and got no answer, and then, she says, got an answer from the wrong side, from the floor. We broke the door. Bed empty, anchor-rope sawn through from underneath. Not cut. Sawn, as if by something with a very small and patient mouth. The cellar was full to the fourth stair with water that had no business being there at that hour and smelled of a harbour I have not smelled since I was a girl. Weed on the stairs, still moving. I wrote the time.

We took the shore road at the run. Found the Called at the end of the old breakwater, which ends now in nine miles of dry seabed, and which she was walking down as if the water were still there to receive her. Woman of forty, nightdress, barefoot, feet cut to ribbons on the shell and not caring. Hookman Dabb put the boathook through the back of her collar as taught and she did not fall. She kept walking and dragged him. A woman of nine stone dragged a man of fourteen stone forty yards on his knees across the shingle. When I got the second rope on her she turned her head and looked at me, and I am obliged to record that her face was perfectly calm and she was weeping out of her nose. Brine. A good deal of it.

We netted her and sat on her. She bailed in the net, unasked, a bucket and a half, and some of what came up was alive and went scuttling under the planking. Dabb stamped on two. He says the third had a face. Dabb has been on the Watch four years and I do not think he is a man for faces, so I have written it down.

At the fifth bell, while we were roping her for the cart, the Uncovered sang. I have heard it before. Everyone on the Watch has, and none of us mention it at muster. It comes up out of the dark where the sea used to be, low, a sound like a hull grinding on a bar, and it has a tune if you let it. Hookman Persey let it. He put his hook down very carefully, the way you put down something you mean to come back for, and he started walking west. We got the rope on him at the tideline and he fought us harder than the woman had. He was crying and saying he was sorry, he was so sorry, they had been waiting such a long time.

On the walk back we passed something standing upright in the mud about a furlong out. In the lamp it looked like a wreck’s keel with the ribs still on. It was not a keel. It had more ribs than a keel and they were opening and closing. We did not stop. I note for the Clerk that it was nearer the pier at the sixth bell than at the fifth, and that the Watch’s standing orders do not cover it, and request that they be made to.

Called recovered: two, one of them my own man. Called lost: none tonight. Injuries: Dabb, bitten on the ankle by something under the planks, wound weeping salt, he swears it is nothing. Persey sleeps roped in the guardhouse. When I looked in on him at dawn the bucket beside him was full to the brim and he had not coughed once.

I would like it entered that I am not asking what the Called are walking toward. I am asking how much longer we are meant to pretend we are the ones doing the pulling.

S. Reef, Lt.

The Table is not short of monsters. It is short of anything else. Every land ate a god, and every land is now host to the slow return of what it swallowed, and that return does not confine itself to the bloodlines of the nobility. It gets into the soil, the weather, the drowned, the sleeping, the unborn and the overheard. It makes things. Some of those things were people a week ago. Some were never people at all, and some are people still, and are the worst of the lot.

This chapter is the GM’s larder. It gives rules for running adversaries in the terms of the Grace Roll, then walks the seven lands one by one, presenting the horrors native to each with full statistics, a witness’s word, and the unpleasant detail that makes them worth meeting: what they smell like, what they sound like in the dark, and what they leave for the family to find. After the lands come the human adversaries, who outnumber the monsters and do more harm, among them cult-shepherds and patient questioners. Then come the rules for the god-ridden; the Seated Gods, the endings of campaigns, and why nobody should expect to win against one; the lairs; and random encounters for every land and the Rim Road between.

Every monster on the Table was somebody’s supper once, or somebody’s son. Usually both.
Hob Gristle, the Honest Butcher

Running Adversaries

Threat and the Quick Line

Most adversaries do not need a full stat block. A Netwatch hookman, a field of toothed wheat or a mob of the Forsworn can be run from a single quick line, which gives everything needed at the table: Threat, Flesh, Guard, Attack, Armor and Dread. Threat is a flat bonus the adversary adds to every 2d10 roll that is not an attack: a Search to find a hidden player character, a Stealth to creep up on the camp, a Resolve against a Hush-walker’s silence. Threat 1 is a frightened farmhand. Threat 3 is a trained professional. Threat 5 is the best in the land at their work. Threat 7 and above belongs to things that are no longer working at anything human.

Attack is the full bonus added to 2d10 against the target’s Guard. Damage follows the core rules: the listed weapon damage, plus 2 for each Helping (every full 4 points the roll beats Guard), minus the target’s Armor. Doubles on an adversary’s roll produce a Grace or a Lack exactly as for player characters, and the GM should describe both with relish. A Netwatch hook that rolls a Grace has hooked a player character’s collar and is dragging them. A Seated guest that rolls a Lack has knocked over the salt, and the whole table turns to look at who did it.

Full Stat Blocks

Important adversaries, monsters with Gifts and anything with a name receive a full stat block. These use the same six attributes as player characters (Hand, Gut, Lung, Eye, Tongue, Caul) and the same skills. Humans rarely exceed 5 in an attribute. Monsters, the Laden, the Tenanted and the deep Regrowth may run to 6, 8 or 10, and a Seated fragment of a god ignores the scale entirely. Flesh, Guard and Attack are calculated by the core formulas where the creature is anything like a body; where it is not (a field, a tide, an echo), the block says so and gives what is needed instead.

Dread Ratings

Every adversary carries a Dread rating from 0 to 5. The first time in a scene that a character perceives the thing clearly, they make a Dread check: Caul + Resolve against the difficulty the rating sets. Failure adds Fray equal to the rating; success adds 1; a Grace adds nothing. Many entries specify what, exactly, sets off the check, since a Tenanted judge in a courtroom is Dread 0 until her lower voice finishes her sentence before her upper one does.

DreadDifficultyTypical horror
0noneAn armed man, a thin dog, an honest threat
1Routine 10A Kept beggar, a toothed ear of wheat, a corpse
2Hard 14An Unstitched Kept, a Forsworn’s opened ribs, a blink-murder
3Grim 18The Sump-thing rising, a Tenanted loved one, a table set for you
4Dire 22A Laden hill speaking, a crowning opening, a god’s attention
5Impossible 26A Seating, the Host’s face, any Seated god

Some horrors carry a rising Dread, written as “Dread 2/4”. The first number applies on sight; the second applies when the thing does what it does (a Hush-walker’s silence reaching the character, a Seeming turning to look at the one who imagined it). Others carry Contagion: anyone who sees a character Break in the creature’s presence must make the Dread check again, and on failure takes on the same Derangement the Breaking character did. The Table’s madness travels best in crowds.

You don’t get used to it. You get used to the smell, and you mistake the one for the other.
a Seamer’s apprentice, Lastgate

Godsign-Powered Creatures

Anything with the god in it can Partake. Creatures with a Cut are listed with it, and with a Hunger track exactly like a player character’s. Before any roll, the GM may Partake for the creature, adding one Tooth (a d6) or, for Cut 3+, two Teeth. Each Partake adds 1 Hunger, and every Tooth that shows a 1 adds 1 more. When a creature’s Hunger reaches 10, it empties and the creature’s Regrowth rises by one. For a monster this is not bookkeeping. It is escalation: the Sump-thing pulls three more drowned bodies into itself and gains Flesh, the Laden hill’s mouth opens wider, the Waker gone mad stops blinking. Each entry describes what a Regrowth rise does to that creature. Players learn quickly that a monster which gambles on its Teeth is a monster that gets worse, and that sometimes the best tactic is to make it Partake.

Godsign creatures also have Sops. A creature that performs its Sop removes 1d6 Hunger, exactly as a player character does, and the Sop is always something the players would rather it did not do: close a child’s eyes, eat the farmhand, take one more of the Called. Interrupting a Sop in progress is often the only way to break a creature’s momentum.

Monster Special Abilities

The following abilities recur through the chapter. They are written in the core rules’ terms and can be lifted onto any creature the GM builds.

  • Unending. The creature does not die from Ruin. At 0 Flesh it is Undone: it stops acting for 1d6 rounds, then recovers 1d6 Flesh and resumes, unless it has been dismembered, sunk, Closed, or moved out of Sallowreach. Every Kept thing has this ability within Sallowreach’s borders.
  • Swarm. The creature is many. Blades and Brawl attacks deal only 1 damage regardless of Helpings; fire, smoke, flood and area effects deal double. A swarm reduced below half Flesh disperses and re-forms elsewhere next scene.
  • Hooking / Grapple (X). On a hit with one or more Helpings, the target is held. Escaping is a Gut + Athletics or Lung + Athletics roll against difficulty X. A held target cannot move and suffers −2 to all rolls.
  • Engulf. Against a held target, the creature’s next hit pulls the victim inside it. Engulfed characters take the creature’s damage automatically each round, ignoring Armor, and make a Dread check each round they remain.
  • Fray Aura (N). At the start of each round within the creature’s reach, every character must pass a Caul + Resolve roll against difficulty N or take 1 Fray. This is in addition to the first sight Dread check.
  • Pull (N). The creature calls. Characters with the relevant Cut must roll Caul + Resolve against difficulty N each round or spend their action moving toward it. Resisting is not free: every success adds 1 Hunger, because the god in the blood wants to go.
  • Rooted. The creature cannot move, but cannot be pushed, knocked down or held. It usually has enormous Flesh and a reach measured in fields.
  • Tide (N). The creature’s influence rises and falls. On the GM’s turn, roll a d10: on N or less it acts twice this round. Things in Brinehollow and the Vigil have this.
  • Binding. The creature’s words count. When it speaks a sentence about a character and that character fails a Tongue + Clause roll (difficulty set in the entry), the sentence becomes physically true. Found only in Oathen and in very bad places elsewhere.
  • Hosting. The creature offers. Any character who accepts anything it offers (food, a seat, shelter, “Come in”) must roll Caul + Resolve against the listed difficulty or stay. Refusing three times grants +2 to the roll; thanking it imposes −4.
  • Known Voice (N). The creature speaks in the voice of someone the listener loves, living or dead. Each time it does, the listener rolls Caul + Resolve against N or takes one step toward it, and a character who has sworn an Oath on the Dead in that person’s name rolls at −2.
  • Leftovers. Destroying the creature does not end it entirely. Some part (a hand, a face, a wick, a word) goes on, and the entry says what it does and who will pay to have it.
  • Riding. The creature is a god wearing a person. It uses the rules for the god-ridden (see The God-Ridden, later in this chapter), and the person inside it can sometimes be called back by name.
  • Armor (type). Some armor is not leather. Waxed flesh, bone lattice, compressed water and layered fat all count. Where an armor ignores a damage type (fat ignores blunt, water ignores blades), the entry says.
  • Helping Effects. Many creatures list what their Helpings do in place of or alongside extra damage. A Flyfront that scores two Helpings does not deal +4 damage. It gets into the mouth.
  • Grace and Lack Effects. Some entries list special results when the creature’s own roll comes up doubles, or when a character’s roll against it does. A character who rolls a Lack against a Hush-walker hears, for one awful second, nothing at all.

Putting Things Down

Killing is not the same in every land. Outside Sallowreach, a creature at 0 Flesh suffers Ruin and further damage kills it, as for any character. Inside Sallowreach nothing dies, and the only ways to finish anything are a Hand-line’s Closing touch, a Hush, or carrying the thing across the border, where it drops at once. Many creatures in this chapter have a Weakness or an End entry, which describes the one way the people of that land have found to stop them. Some of those Ends are worse than the monster. Some are not ends at all, only delays, and the entry will say so.

What Is Left

Most of the Table’s horrors are discovered after the fact. The players arrive at a cottage, a cellar, a furrow or a bed, and somebody has to look. The table below gives the remains the GM can set in front of them when a creature has been and gone, or when a victim’s family brings the party in to see. Each is a Dread check at the listed rating, and each is a clue: read with Eye + Search (Hard 14), it names the kind of thing that did it.

d12What the family foundDread
1A pair of shoes, laced, side by side, still warm inside; nothing else, not a hair1
2A bed with a body-shaped hollow, the sheets soaked with salt water that is still cold1
3The victim, laid out, eyes shut, hands folded; no wound, no rot, and no flies, ever2
4A face, flat as a mask, pressed into peat; the eyes in it still blinking3
5Every door, drawer, box and cupboard in the house standing open, and the body likewise3
6Bones, tidy, scraped white, stacked by length in the larder, each set with a napkin3
7A smooth patch of tilled soil the length of a man, warm, rising and falling2
8A man with his ribs folded inward, gently, as if the sea had leaned on him2
9A woman broken at every joint at once, two hundred breaks, and a contract by her hand3
10The victim alive, unharmed, smiling, and certain they have eaten the best meal of their life2
11A cradle with its blanket folded back, and in it something warm that is not the baby4
12Nothing at all; but everyone in the house remembers someone who was never born4
The GM’s Larder: Pacing Horror

Every creature in this chapter is built to be survivable at first sight. The Dread check, not the attack roll, is where most of them do their damage. Use that. Let the players see the Sump bubble in patterns for a full session before anything comes up.

The best monster fights on the Table end without a death and with a cost: a player character’s Hunger maxed out to win a single roll, a companion who Broke and is now certain their sister has been replaced, a field that now knows their name. Track those costs and bring them back.

When a creature’s Hunger fills and its Regrowth rises mid-fight, describe the change before you describe its next action. The moment of transformation is the scene.

Smell first, sound second, sight last. The players should know what is in the cellar a full minute before the lamp shows them.

Remember that every creature here began as a meal, a mourner, a farmer or a child. Somebody on the Table loved it. Somebody is still bringing it dinner. Put that person in the scene.

Sallowreach: What Will Not Finish

Every monster in the north began as a person or a thing that tried to end and was refused. They are not malicious, mostly. They are in pain, and they have been in pain for a very long time, and pain that long becomes a kind of weather. Remember that within Sallowreach all of these have Unending unless noted, and that nothing they do to a victim is ever finished either: the people they hurt are still somewhere, still feeling it, and some of them can be found.

May you finish. And if you can’t, may you at least be shelved somewhere dry.
Lastgate leave-taking among the poor

The Sump-Thing

Weighted sacks go into the Sump by the hundred each year: the Kept too far gone for stitching, the unclaimed, the inconvenient. The sacks rot. The weights do not. Over decades, in the black peat-water forty feet down, the bodies find each other. Rotting flesh that cannot finish rotting goes soft as dough, and soft things press together under the fen’s weight until there is no telling where one grandfather ends and the next begins. A Sump-thing is what happens when a few hundred of them agree to come up.

It surfaces first as bubbles in patterns: rings, then spirals, then the shape of a hand spread flat under the water. Then the smell, which is not the sweet Sallowreach rot but something older, sulphurous and vinegary, a pickle-jar opened after a century, with a bottom note of wet wool and the copper of old coins. Then the mound breaks the surface, a slick dark heap twenty feet across, hair and sackcloth and peat-tanned leather stretched over a lattice of knitted bone, and out of it, everywhere, faces. Pressed flat. Mouths working. Some still have the twine of their labels around their necks, the ink long run, a name and a date of shelving. The sound it makes is a choir of drowned people trying to say their names through a lungful of fen, which comes out as a long wet gargle with words in it.

It wants to be finished, and it has learned that it cannot be, so it has settled for company. It drags the living down. Victims are not eaten. They are added. The process takes a week in the dark, and boatmen who have dragged the Sump for a lost brother on the third day have brought up something that was half him and half the mound, joined at the hip and the cheek, still breathing through both mouths. A week later a new face surfaces in the mound, and it is still screaming, and it will scream for centuries. Families who lose someone to a Sump-thing sometimes row out to listen for them, and sometimes hear.

Tactics: it rises under boats and walkways, grapples with dozens of arms, and sinks. It is slow on land but can drag itself up a bank like a slug of wet meat, leaving a furrow of black slime that smokes faintly in the cold. It does not flee. It has nowhere else to be.

From the daybook of the Sump-punt Patience, Seamers’ Guild bounty boat. “Took up a face at the second bend, female, middle years, label reads ’Agnes — 409.’ It would not stop asking whether her daughter had been told. We told it yes. We had no idea. Bounty six hundred. Agnes is in the cold-box. She is still asking.”

Sump-Thing — the Many Drowned
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 9 · Lung 1 · Eye 2 · Tongue 0 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 (the scraps of a hundred Hand-line servants) · Regrowth 4 (the Appetite) · Hunger 3
SkillsBrawl 4, Endure 5, Stealth 4 (underwater only), Instinct 3
BodyFlesh 40 · Guard 12 · Armor 2 (peat-tanned hide; blades deal −1 more) · Threat 4
AttacksMany Hands +7 (3, Grapple 18; it can attack three targets a round); Draw Down against a held target +7 (Engulf: 3 per round, drowning)
AbilitiesUnending. Swarm-of-bodies: severed arms keep grabbing for 1d6 rounds. Fray Aura 14 when it surfaces. Known Voice 14: one face in the mound always belongs to someone a character has lost. Each character Engulfed for 3 rounds is Added and lost; their face appears next scene.
Regrowthwhen Hunger fills, it pulls 1d6 bodies from the bottom and gains 10 Flesh. At the Course its hands go grey and long and its grip begins to Close what it holds (each held round, a held character must pass Caul + Resolve 18 or lose 1 point of an attribute permanently, as some part of them finishes).
SopAdding a living person. Removes 1d6 Hunger.
Dread3 (when it surfaces); 4 (on recognizing a face in it)
EndIt cannot be killed. It can be cut apart and its pieces carried out of Sallowreach on the Rim Road, which takes a caravan, or lured into a Hush, which takes a sacrifice. The Seamers have a standing bounty of 600 lacks per recovered face.

Hush-Walkers

Edda Thrush walked out of Dunmere Hush. She was the first. She is not the last. A Hush-walker is a person who entered a Hush and did not finish, or a Kept body from inside a Hush that was somehow refused even there and stood up. They come out of the silence carrying it with them. A Hush-walker has no smell at all, which in Sallowreach is the most alarming thing about it: one notices a gap in the stink of the world, a person-shaped absence of rot, before one notices the person. Their skin is clean and pale and perfectly still, unrotted, every fly that lands on them dropping dead and unmoving. Their clothes do not stir in the wind. Their hair does not lift. They walk slowly. Their feet make no noise on boards. Their mouths move.

Within ten paces of one, sound stops. Not quiet: stopped. A scream comes out as breath. A drawn blade makes no ring. A heartbeat cannot be heard in one’s own ears, and this is what breaks people: the body insists the heart has stopped. Swallowing makes no sound, and people who have stood in the Silence report that they kept swallowing, over and over, to be sure the throat still worked. In that silence something is listening, the way Edda Thrush insists something listens through her. Victims who stay in the silence too long simply end. They sit down, close their eyes, and are properly, completely dead, with no rot afterward and no flies, and their families tend to envy them. They are found sitting upright in the road, faces calm, mouths a little open, as if they had heard the end of a song. Hush-walkers wander toward Hand-line estates. Nobody is sure if they are drawn there or sent.

My Da went into the quiet after her. He’s sitting by the Glovehall road with his eyes shut and his face clean. Six weeks now. Not a fly on him. I go and sit with him. It’s the best he’s ever looked.
a reed-cutter’s daughter, to the Heirs
Hush-Walker — the Silence That Got Up
AttributesHand 2 · Gut 4 · Lung 2 · Eye 4 · Tongue 0 · Caul 7
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 (Hand-line, by contact) · Regrowth 10 (the Brink) · Hunger 0 (it does not hunger; it does not Partake)
SkillsInstinct 5, Search 4, Resolve 6
BodyFlesh 14 · Guard 12 · Armor 0 · Threat 5
Attacksa slow, gentle touch +4 (Closes: target makes Caul + Resolve 18 or suffers Ruin at once and, outside of Sallowreach’s protection, dies)
AbilitiesThe Silence (10 paces): no sound; Tongue rolls impossible; Partaking costs double Hunger as the god in the blood strains toward the stillness. Each round in the Silence, Caul + Resolve 14 or take 1 Fray and lose the next action to listening. NOT Unending: a Hush-walker reduced to 0 Flesh lies down and is finished, and the ground under it becomes a Hush a yard across.
Dread2 on sight / 4 on entering the Silence
EndDamage it enough. The problem is getting near enough to do it, and the hole it leaves behind. Pim Sorrel’s touch makes them kneel.

The Flyfront

Flies are Sallowreach’s weather, and a Black Noon is its storm. A Flyfront is a mass of carrion-flies thick enough to put out lamps, rolling across the fen at walking pace with a sound like frying fat. It is not a creature in the ordinary sense, but it behaves as one: it hunts. Everything in Sallowreach rots and never finishes, so the flies never finish breeding, and the oldest fronts are centuries old, and have a direction. They come down on the living because the living are warm and wet and still have their soft parts. Within a minute a person is black with them, flies in the eyes, the ears, the nostrils, the throat, a thick crawling paste that has to be scraped off with a knife. The taste is the worst of it, survivors say: bitter, buttery, and moving. The Kept caught in a front come out the other side with their faces gone to lace, lips and eyelids eaten to a fringe, the teeth showing in a permanent grin. The living come out choking up maggots for a week, and some of them, in the second week, find eggs hatching in the corners of their eyes. Justice Ever Lathe’s colony is said to have come from a front, which raises questions about what fronts want.

The Black Noon came over the Sinks at the fourth bell and when it lifted my neighbour was sitting on his step with his hands in his lap, and the flies had taken his face off so neatly you could see where he’d been smiling.
a lamp-trimmer of the Sinks

Flyfront Threat 3 · Flesh 30 · Guard 15 · Attack +6 (crawl 1; every Helping instead adds 1 Fray as they get into the mouth) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 · Swarm; lamps within it go out; Eye rolls −4; fire, smoke and vinegar deal double; a character with two Helpings scored against them is Choked and can do nothing but cough next round.

The Unstitched

The Seamers’ Guild holds Sallowreach together with gut-thread, wire, lacquer and resin. When a Kept body’s stitching fails all at once, from neglect or a lapsed fee or a Seamers’ slowdown, what results is an Unstitched: a person who has come apart along every seam, held together only by habit and old tendon. They lurch. Their arms swing loose from shoulders that are only hooked on. Their jaws hang. Their bellies, sewn shut a dozen times, open like purses with every step and have to be held closed with both hands, so their arms are never free, so they use their teeth. The old thread trails from them in grey loops, and the wire, rusted, rings faintly against their bones as they walk, which is how the poor of the Sinks know one is coming up the stair. They smell of everything Sallowreach smells of, all at once, concentrated: sweet rot, sour lacquer, vinegar gone off, the rancid tallow the very poor use instead of resin. Most Unstitched are not violent, only desperate: they come at the living begging for thread, for a needle, for someone to hold their face on while they get the wire through. Some, after enough decades of it, have stopped asking. Marrow Jack’s victims are often Unstitched, and come looking for their parts.

Seamers’ Guild arrears notice, nailed to a door in the Sinks. “To the household of Marl, Ropewalk Stair. Restitching of your Kept, one Grandmother Marl, is now fourteen months in arrears. The Guild regrets that it can no longer be responsible for her shape. Please keep her indoors.”

Unstitched Kept Threat 1 · Flesh 12 · Guard 10 · Attack +4 (teeth and loose hands 2, Grapple 12) · Armor 0 · Dread 2 · Unending; any Helping against it severs a limb, which keeps fighting on its own (Threat 0, Flesh 3, Attack +2, 1).

The Undone Closer

The Hand-lines sell death by touch, and the touch grows. Osric Vane in his lead mittens is the famous case. An Undone Closer is the case nobody contained: a Hand-line noble deep in the Course whose mittens came off and who went out into the fen. The hands are the thing. Grey, cold, damp like the underside of a stone, the fingers lengthened to a span and a half and jointed nine and ten times, so that they fold and unfold like a spider settling. The nails are long and yellow and clean. The hands move independently of the face above them, which is often weeping, and which has usually not eaten in weeks, because the hands will not hold a spoon without closing what is in it. Everything the hands touch finishes: a candle gutters and will not relight, a conversation stops mid-word and cannot be restarted, a person sighs and slumps and is done. The Closer cannot stop touching. It is the Want, gone total. Victims are found laid out tidily, eyes shut, hands folded, and the village around them strangely silent, birdless, every door closed, every book shut, every pot lidded, every shutter latched. In one hamlet near Glovehall a Closer passed in the night and in the morning even the well had a lid on it that nobody had made. Hunting one is the Mortuary Court’s most secret duty, because every Undone Closer is a cousin.

She came to the door with her hands behind her back like a little girl hiding a present. She said, “I am so sorry. Please don’t look at me. Please close your eyes for me, it’s easier.”
a survivor of the Fenlow closing, who did not
The Undone Closer — a Hand-line Out of Its Mittens
AttributesHand 6 · Gut 3 · Lung 3 · Eye 2 · Tongue 2 · Caul 5
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Hand-line) · Regrowth 9 (the Course) · Hunger 7
SkillsBrawl 4, Stealth 3, Instinct 4, Rites 3
BodyFlesh 13 · Guard 17 · Armor 1 (fine ruined coat) · Threat 4
AttacksClosing Touch +10 plus Teeth (on a hit, target makes Caul + Resolve 18 or suffers Ruin and is Finished, truly dead even in Sallowreach; each Helping raises the difficulty by 2)
AbilitiesThe hands may act separately: two Closing Touch attacks a round. Closing the World: once a scene it may touch a door, lamp or voice and end it. Wants: must close every open eye it sees, even a friend’s, even its own child’s.
Regrowthwhen Hunger fills it reaches the Brink and its touch spreads; the ground it stands on begins to Hush. At 12 it becomes a Hush, and a village goes silent.
SopClosing a living thing. 1d6 Hunger.
Dread2 / 3 when the face speaks and apologizes
EndIt can be Closed by another Closer, which the Court prefers, or killed outside Sallowreach, which the Court cannot allow anyone to see. The hands, severed, live on in a box, and are worth a fortune.

The Tallow-Saint

Wick Tallow renders the unclaimed into candles that feel themselves burn. A Tallow-Saint is a candle that did not want to be one. Sometimes, when a great many candles made from one family are burned together in one room, the tallow remembers itself, runs, and gathers on the floor into a figure of soft yellow wax five feet high, faceless, wicked through its crown and burning. It smells of mutton fat and singed hair, and under that, faintly, of the person it was: a pipe-smoker’s tobacco, a laundress’s lye, a child’s milky breath. It drips as it walks, leaving a trail of puddles that harden into the shapes of footprints, then of hands. Its light is very steady. People in the room with one find they can read by it perfectly, and that the words on the page have changed into the names of the dead. It wants to be put out, and nothing put out stays out in Sallowreach. So it hunts for darkness and for breath to snuff it, and it presses its burning crown into the mouths of the living. Those it embraces are found glazed in a skin of wax, mouths stopped with it, every pore sealed, a perfect yellow cast of a person with the person still warm inside.

We bought a box of the cheap ones for the wake. Halfway through the night they all leaned the same way, toward Mother. I swear to you they were trying to look at her.
a widow of Lastgate

Tallow-Saint Threat 2 · Flesh 16 · Guard 11 · Attack +5 (burning embrace 3, Grapple 14; held targets take 2 fire each round) · Armor 2 (wax; blunt weapons deal only 1) · Dread 2 · Unending until its wick is pinched out (Hand + Filch 18 while Grappled with it); water hardens it for 2 rounds; dark Sallowreach rooms make it act twice. Leftovers: a pinched wick goes on smouldering for a year and is worth 40 lacks to the Finishers.

New Horror: The Whispering Aisle

The Lofts hold the Set-Aside: nine storeys of shelving, forty thousand Kept too far gone to stand, wrapped, labeled, shelved, and still aware. The whispering is audible from the street. Most of it is the murmur of any ward: complaints, prayers, the names of grandchildren. A Whispering Aisle is what an aisle becomes when it has not been visited in a generation. Nobody comes on feast days. Nobody reads. The shelved have only each other, and over the decades their whispering has fallen into step, the way the breathing of the Counted falls into step in the Vigil, until two hundred wrapped mouths are saying one thing at one time.

The air in such an aisle is close and sweet, the linen gone brown with seepage and stuck to the shelves, the bodies beneath sagged together until a shelf is one long lumpen bolt of stained cloth with heads in it. As a visitor walks the aisle, the heads turn and the whisper rises: read to us, said very sweetly. A visitor who stops to listen hears their own name in it, then the ends of their own sentences before they speak them, then the thing they have never told anyone. The wrapped hands come through the linen then, grey and soft as wet bread, and take hold, very gently, the way the old take the hand of a visitor, and do not let go.

Bettany Shroud keeps a list of the aisles that have begun to whisper in unison. Lately they all whisper the same word, and it is not read.

From Old Bettany Shroud’s night-book, the Lofts, sixth storey. “Aisle 6-Q: in unison again since Tablenight. Went in with the lamp and the Lives of the Glad Century. Read eleven pages. They were quiet. When I stopped they asked me to stay. When I said I could not, they told me the name of my mother’s first husband, which I had never known. I have it written below. I will not read it again.”

The Whispering Aisle — Two Hundred Who Want Company
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 6 · Lung 0 · Eye 5 · Tongue 6 · Caul 6
Cut & RegrowthCut 2 (two hundred common Kept) · Regrowth 5 (the Appetite) · Hunger 4
SkillsPersuade 5, Instinct 5, Lore 6 (everything ever said near them), Brawl 3
BodyFlesh 45 (it is an aisle) · Guard 8 · Armor 1 (shroud-crust; fire deals double) · Threat 5
AttacksVisiting Hands +6 (1, Grapple 16, against everyone in the aisle each round; a character held by three or more hands is pulled onto a shelf and is Engulfed, 1 per round, wrapped)
AbilitiesRooted. Fray Aura 14. The Whisper: once a round it speaks one secret about one character (Eye + Search or Caul + Instinct 18 to know whether it is true; it usually is); the character takes 1 Fray and every other character who hears it must decide whether to believe it. Contagion: a character who Breaks in the aisle gains The Voice at Table or The Watchers, and so does anyone who fails the following Dread check. Being Read To: a character who reads aloud to it for an hour holds it quiet and gains the answer to one question about the dead.
SopKeeping a visitor. A living person wrapped and shelved among them removes 1d6 Hunger; the Wardens find them a week later, alive, still being whispered to.
Dread2 / 3 when it speaks the thing never told
EndVisit them. An aisle read to each feast day for a year goes back to murmuring. Burning it, which the Heirs have proposed, would put two hundred screaming people on the street in the middle of the night, still burning, and still Kept.

New Horror: The Sewn Gentleman

Marrow Jack takes limbs from the Kept while they shelve or sleep and sells them to back-alley seamers. The buyers are rarely poor. A Sewn Gentleman is what that trade looks like at the top of the market: an Unvacated elder, rich enough to buy and old enough to have rotted, who has replaced himself part by part over two or three centuries until almost nothing of him is his own. A sailor’s forearms, a laundry-girl’s small chapped hands, a ploughman’s back wired at the shoulders, a singer’s throat, two eyes not quite the same colour behind tinted glass. He dresses beautifully, in high collars that hide the joins. He smells of cedar, pomade and the cloves the seamers pack into the seams, and beneath that, faintly and always, of other people’s sweat.

The parts remember. That is the horror and the hunt. Marrow Jack’s victims wake up able to feel what their missing hands are being used for, and the Sewn Gentleman’s original donors, Kept and shelved and Unstitched across the north, feel all of him: his dinners, his correspondence, his razor, his nights. They come looking. And when their owners come near, the parts move toward them: a hand clenching on the dinner-knife, a borrowed throat breaking into a fen ballad in a girl’s voice. The Gentleman fights to keep his purchases. He has receipts for all of them.

He shook my hand at the Hall of Closings and I knew it at once. I knew the scar on the thumb. I put that scar there, with a fish-knife, when my brother was nine.
a petitioner, to Provost Sedge
The Sewn Gentleman — Paid in Full
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 5 · Lung 3 · Eye 3 · Tongue 5 · Caul 4
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 (Hand-line, cadet branch; the hands, however, are Scrapling) · Regrowth 6 (the Appetite) · Hunger 5
SkillsClause 4, Persuade 4, Intimidate 3, Blades 3, Haggle 4, Endure 4
BodyFlesh 22 · Guard 15 · Armor 1 (wire beneath the coat) · Threat 4
Attacksa borrowed fist +7 (2, Grapple 14); sword-cane +7 (4); his lawyers (he will sue)
AbilitiesUnending. Many Owners: each round, roll a d6; on a 1 one of his parts rebels (he loses his action as a hand clutches his own throat, or a leg walks him toward the nearest donor). Donors Near: if any former owner of his parts is present, his attacks are at −2 and that donor may, as an action, call a part home (Caul + Resolve 14; the part tears free at the seam, the Gentleman takes 4 damage and loses the use of it). Receipts: within Sallowreach, it is lawful to own a bought part, and a Court Warden will defend him.
SopPurchasing a new part and having it sewn in while the donor watches. 1d6 Hunger.
Dread1 / 3 when a character recognizes a part
EndTake him to pieces and give the pieces back. What is left at the end, the Seamers say, is about the size of a cat, and mostly lacquer, and still talking.

The Fatlands: The Crop That Stands Up

In the Fatlands the monsters are agricultural. Nothing there is anything but crop, and that includes what eats the crop. Fatlands horrors are warm, wet, slow, enormous and hungry, and the smell that precedes most of them is gravy. What they leave behind is rarely a body. It is a better yield.

Thank you, Long Furrow. Thank you, Hogget’s Bottom. Thank you, Grandmother.
a Low Tilth grace, naming the fields

The Laden Hill with a Mouth

Many of the best fields in the south are somebody’s great-grandmother. Most Seated Laden are quiet hills, warm to the touch, generous with barley. Some keep a mouth. Old Mother Rind is benign, more or less. Not all are. A hungry hill is a low green mound a hundred paces across, its turf rising and falling with slow breath, and in its side, at about the height of a cart, a mouth: lips of soft red loam, a tongue the size of a ploughshare, and teeth that were once teeth and are now stones, old roots, and the skulls of what it has eaten, pushed out through the gums like new growth. Its breath is hot and smells of ripe silage and stomach, and on cold mornings it steams like a midden. Its gullet can be heard working from the lane, a slow wet peristalsis under the turf like a cow chewing cud in the next field. It speaks, in the voice of the woman it was, and it is polite, and it is very, very hungry. It wants to be fed by its family, as is right. When its family stops coming, it calls out to passersby by the names of grandchildren. The ground around it is soft for a long way. The roots under that ground move. What it eats is never seen again, except as apples: the hill’s fruit that autumn is heavier, and in the core of each, where the pips should be, is a small white knuckle.

Gran wants feeding Sundays. We take her the slops and the old dog and a song. Last Sunday she asked for my husband by name. She always did like him.
a farmwife of the Dowager road
The Hungry Hill — a Gut-Line Matriarch, Seated
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 10 · Lung 0 · Eye 3 · Tongue 4 · Caul 6
Cut & RegrowthCut 5 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 12 (Seated) · Hunger 8 (it never drops below 5)
SkillsPersuade 4, Intimidate 3, Lore 4 (family scandal), Instinct 4, Feast 6
BodyFlesh 60 · Guard 10 · Armor 3 (turf and loam; blades deal −1 more) · Threat 5
AttacksRoots +6 (2, Grapple 18, reach: the whole hill and twenty paces beyond); the Mouth +8 against a held target (6, and the target is drawn in: Engulf, 4 per round)
AbilitiesRooted. Soft Ground: Lung rolls on or near the hill are Hard at best. Kindred Voice: it calls a character by a loved one’s name (Known Voice 14). Advice: it knows every secret of its bloodline and trades them for meals.
Sopbeing fed a living person by kin. Removes 1d6 Hunger and the hill grows a new apple tree.
Dread3 / 4 when it speaks in a voice someone knows
EndStarve it, which takes a decade and turns its fields to fat-scum. Burn it, which takes a month and smells for a mile. Or salt it, which the Board considers murder of a voting member.

The Scarecrow of Low Tilth

Nobody put it up. It stands in the far field with its back to the village, and each Carving it is a few furrows closer. Last year someone saw it turn around. Pell Hogget’s tally does not attribute the Reaping in Low Tilth to the scarecrow, but he has noted that the missing were all last seen nearer its side of the field.

Up close it is a figure seven feet high, cross-armed on a stake that it does not need. Its coat is sacking. Its stuffing is not straw, though straw sticks out of it. Its head is a sack, tied at the neck, and the sack is damp, and it is warm, and if pressed it gives like a full stomach. Under the hat, where the face is painted, the paint is very old, and very good, and the face is smiling. The crows will not land on it, and the flies will not leave it. When it moves, it moves only while nobody in the field is looking at it, and then very fast, and the sound of that is a dry, rushing crackle like a scythe through tall wheat. The taken are not found. In the following spring, the stuffing in the scarecrow’s arms has new fingernails in it, and the seams of its coat have been let out, as if to fit.

From Pell Hogget’s Long Count, Low Tilth leaf, the margin. “Fitch girl, last seen west headland, dusk, 3rd Carving. Note: scarecrow was at the ninth furrow at noon. Was at the fourth by lamp-lighting. I did not see it move. Nobody ever sees it move. That is the whole of what I know and I have written it down.”

The Scarecrow of Low Tilth — Nobody Put It Up
AttributesHand 5 · Gut 6 · Lung 6 · Eye 4 · Tongue 0 · Caul 7
Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Gut-line, of a whole village) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 6
SkillsStealth 6, Instinct 5, Brawl 4, Athletics 4
BodyFlesh 26 · Guard 20 · Armor 2 (sacking and packed meat) · Threat 6
AttacksSacking Arms +9 (4, Grapple 20); the Gathering against a held target +9 (target is stuffed into its body; Engulf, 3 per round; after three rounds they are gone)
AbilitiesUnwatched: it may move only when no character is looking at it; it then moves up to 60 paces in a heartbeat. Characters can keep it still by watching (each must spend an action and pass Eye + Search 14 each round, made harder by dusk). Never Moves While Seen. At dusk in Carving it acts twice each round.
SopReaping a person at dusk. 1d6 Hunger.
Dread3 when it is found closer than it was / 4 when it is seen to have turned
EndBurn it on its stake by daylight with every eye in the village on it. What runs out of the ashes is fat, and it screams in many voices. Next Carving there is a scarecrow in the far field, and nobody put it up.

The Toothed Field

Wheat with teeth in the ear has been a superior strain since 204 A.G., by ruling of the Board. A toothed field in its late Plenty is tall as a man, gold and red, and every ear is a small jaw of white milk-teeth set in a husk that clicks open and shut in the wind. On a still day it is quiet. On a windy one, a toothed field sounds like a crowd chewing. Harvesters wear leather to the shoulder. Anyone who falls in a toothed field in late Plenty is in serious trouble: the ears turn toward warmth like flowers to the sun, and every ear takes a nip, and there are millions of ears. Victims come out lacework, bleeding from a thousand pinpricks, skin hanging in fine pink threads, and the wheat they fell in is the best of the crop that year, heavy and pink in the grain. The loaves from it are said to taste faintly of the person. Granny Cracknel says the teeth in a field that has fed well are adult teeth.

Never lie down in the wheat, never sleep in the stook, never bleed in the furrow, and never, ever whistle. They like a tune.
harvest-rhyme of the Bleeding Orchards road

Toothed Field (per acre) Threat 2 · Flesh 40 · Guard 8 · Attack +5 (nipping 1 to everyone inside; every Helping adds a Bleed of 1 per round until bound) · Armor 0 · Dread 1 / 2 when the ears turn · Swarm; Rooted; fire spreads through it at a run and it screams; Lung rolls inside are Hard.

Two-Legged Cattle

Sal Trotter walks herds to market that the buyers call cattle. They are heavy, docile, and pinkish-white, with broad flat faces and soft lowing voices. On the road, when nobody watches, they stand up. Upright they are the height of a tall man, bellies swinging, forelegs tucked like hands, and they walk easily and well. They do not talk. They hum, sometimes, a hymn with a tune most Fatlanders know from childhood. Some have scars where a brand would be, and the scars are in the shape of letters. Their dung smells of a human privy and their eyes are a clear, startled blue. Nobody in the Renderers’ Union will say where the bloodstock comes from, but the Reaping takes people every Carving and the herds are larger every spring. Most cattle are harmless. A herd that has been mistreated, or that smells its own kind in a slaughterhouse, becomes a stampede on two legs, and it knows how to open gates. Trampled drovers are found with their pockets turned out, as if something had been looking for a name.

I stopped naming them the year one of them answered to Agnes.
Sal Trotter, the Drover

Two-Legged Cattle (herd of 20) Threat 2 · Flesh 30 · Guard 11 · Attack +6 (trampling 4 to all in its path) · Armor 1 · Dread 1 / 3 when they stand up and one of them says a name · Swarm; a single beast is Flesh 14, Attack +4 (3), harmless unless cornered.

Rootkin

Tansy Lard dug up a root with her mother’s birthmark on it. She was not the first. Rootkin are what the Reaping leaves in the soil: swollen root vegetables the size of a sleeping child, pale and veined and warm, with features. Most are lumpen. Some are exact, down to the crow’s feet and the old pox scar. Their eyes are closed. Pulled up, they flinch and leak a pinkish sap that smells of the person they resemble, a sweat-and-soap smell that brings mourners to their knees in the furrow. Eaten, they are delicious and their eater dreams the dead person’s memories for a week. Left in the ground, they grow. A Rootkin bed left unharvested through a full year sends up shoots with hands on them, and those hands pull down whatever leans too close. The Cullmasters harvest Rootkin by night and sell them to the Renderers’ Union by weight.

Sixpence the pound for plain, two lacks for a face, ten for a face somebody’ll pay to have back.
prices chalked on a Renderers’ board at the Chute

Rootkin Bed Threat 1 · Flesh 20 · Guard 9 · Attack +5 (grasping shoots 2, Grapple 14, then dragged underground at 1 per round) · Armor 1 (soil) · Dread 2 / 3 when a character recognizes a face · Rooted; lifting one is a Hard Labor roll and a Dread check.

The Reaping

The Reaping is not a monster. That is the Board’s official position, and it is technically correct: no single thing takes the Fatlands’ missing. The land does. On dusk in Carving, out in the far fields, the soil softens. The furrows deepen, slowly, so slowly a farmhand will not notice until her boots are below the surface. The rows of wheat lean in. The air thickens with the smell of fresh bread and fat. The earth makes a sound, low and continuous, like a stomach in the next room. And then the ground opens, wetly, the way a mouth opens around a spoon, and closes again, and the furrow is smooth, and the crop in that furrow will be very good next year. Sometimes a hand stays above the soil until morning, still clutching a hoe.

Run the Reaping as a hazard with a clock. Each character in a far field at dusk in Carving rolls Lung + Wayfaring each round against a rising difficulty (Routine 10, then Hard, then Grim, then Dire). Failure means they are held to the ankle, then the knee, then the waist; a fourth failure and they are gone. Allies can pull them free with a Gut + Labor roll at the same difficulty. Partaking for the Fatlands’ Gut-line, ironically, helps: the ground recognizes kin and loosens its grip for a round, though it costs Hunger as always. A Cullmaster’s assigned workers are marked with a strip of red cloth at the wrist. The ground knows the cloth. Remove it, and the difficulty drops by 4.

The Reaping has Dread 3 the first time it is seen to take someone, and Dread 4 when a character realizes the field is breathing in time with them.

We don’t say taken. We say the field was hungry. We say she went into the bread. Then we eat the bread, because what else would you have us do.
a Low Tilth widow, to Pell Hogget

New Horror: The Uneaten

The Fatlands have no graves. The dead are served at the wake, by the family, with the best plates, and to be buried uneaten would be the deepest insult to a life. Sometimes a wake fails. The family is too small or too grief-struck; a Thin son refuses his portion. Something is left on the platter overnight. The leftovers are buried, quietly, in a corner of the field, and the family tells nobody. A season later, the Uneaten comes home.

It is what remained of the dead: the joints that were not carved, the ribs that were picked half clean, the head that nobody could bring themselves to serve, drawn back together by the soil into the rough shape of the person and clothed in turf and root-hair and a skin of yellow fat. Its face is half a face, the other half carved down to the cheekbone in neat slices. It smells of a cold kitchen the morning after a feast: congealed dripping, stale gravy, and under it, sweet and terrible, the meat itself. It comes to the family table at the hour of the evening meal, sits down in its old chair, and waits to be finished. It will not leave until every scrap of it is eaten by its own kin. If they refuse, it begins to serve itself to them, and they find they cannot refuse that.

Statement of Wakemother Pudding Hesk to the Low Tilth bailiff. “I told them, you eat your mother or she’ll come back for it. They wouldn’t hear. Thin, the son was, the Thin had got him. Three months later I’m passing the cottage at supper and there’s five at table and the door’s open and one of the five is the mother, what’s left, and the son’s crying with his mouth full.”

The Uneaten — the Leftovers Come Home

Cut & RegrowthCut 3 (Gut-line, family) · Regrowth 7 (the Course) · Hunger 9
SkillsBrawl 4, Endure 5, Feast 5, Intimidate 4, Instinct 3
BodyFlesh 24 · Guard 12 · Armor 2 (fat and turf; blunt weapons deal −1 more) · Threat 4
Attacksgnawed hands +7 (3, Grapple 16); Serving against a held kinsman +8 (the character must eat; Gut + Endure 18 to spit it out, otherwise gain 2 Hunger, 1 Regrowth Taint roll at Grim, and a Dread 3 check)
AbilitiesKin-Bound: it attacks only its own family and those who stand between it and them. Rooted Return: if destroyed but not eaten, it reforms in the field in 1d6 weeks. Table Manners: it does not act while grace is being said; a grace that thanks it by name holds it still for a round.
SopBeing eaten by kin. 1d6 Hunger for every mouthful, which is the end of it.
Dread2 on sight / 4 when a character recognizes the dead and is kin
EndFinish it. Everyone in the family must eat a share. The Second Helping offers to stand in as kin for a fee, and the Board pretends not to know.

New Horror: The Bottomless

The Appetite in the Fatlands is eating without choosing: soil, tallow, leather, hair. The sufferer cannot stop for conversation. The Bottomless is the Appetite with nothing left to stop it, a Fatlander in whom the Want has become the whole person, as the Undone Closer is in the north. Usually it is a Gut-line cadet who one day ate past the wall even the Fatlands keep. It roams the back kitchens, larders and middens of Sated at night, enormous, the skin of the belly split in pale stretch-tears that weep yellow lymph, the jaw unhinged a little lower each month so that it can take things whole. It eats candles and their holders, the boot-leather of the sleeping, the dog, with a steady joyless crunching, and through it it talks, in a mild educated voice, about how hungry it is and how sorry.

What it leaves is a kitchen stripped to the plaster: no crumbs, no rind, no rats, the pans licked bright, the table gnawed to a curve at one end, and sometimes a cook sitting very still in the corner, missing the hand she held out to calm it.

He ate the pudding, the cloth it was boiled in, the string, and then he looked at me like I was the next course, and he said, “Do forgive me, Mrs Haslet, I really cannot help it.”
a scullery maid of Sated
The Bottomless — No Word for Full

Cut & RegrowthCut 4 (Gut-line) · Regrowth 8 (the Course) · Hunger 8

Attacksbite +7 (3; on two Helpings it takes something off: a finger, an ear, a hand, roll a Mangling); bulk +6 (4, knockdown)
AbilitiesCannot Stop: it must spend its move each round eating whatever is in reach; offering it food buys a round of peace. Feasting Heals: eating anything restores 2 Flesh, a person restores 8. Gut-Dread: anyone who sees it eat a living thing makes a Dread 2 check.
SopEating until something inside tears. 1d6 Hunger.
Dread2
EndStarve it, which is treason. Or feed it until it roots: the Board has a cellar under Sated where three of the Bottomless lie on their backs in the dark, rooting through the flagstones, swelling, fed by chute, and the Chairman’s physician calls this care.

Brinehollow: What the Sea Left Behind

Brinehollow’s horrors are patient, heavy and courteous. They press. Many have Tide, and all of them smell of a harbour at low water: weed, salt, rot and cold iron. Their victims are rarely torn. They are found wrung, folded, drowned on dry floors, or not found at all, and the family keeps the bail-bucket by the door for a year in case.

It’s not the sea going out. It’s the sea coming in. Into us. You can hear it slosh when the children run.
a Lowmark bucket-seller

The Tenanted

A Tenanted is not hostile. That is what makes it so hard. It walks out of the surf weeks after its Calling, heavier, calm, with the same face and the same memories, and someone else looking out. It knows your name, your nickname, the way you take your tea. It is kinder than the person was. Its skin is cool and faintly grey, its hands are always damp, and its breath, if you are close enough, smells of deep water, a clean mineral cold. Its weight is wrong: floorboards creak under a slight Tenanted girl as if under a cart, and a Tenanted man who sits on a bed leaves a dent that holds water. It does not sweat; it weeps salt from the pores in warm rooms, and its pillow is crusted white each morning. When it is angered, which is rare, it does not raise its voice. It presses. The air in the room thickens, ears pop, windows bow, and a man who has crossed a Tenanted judge has been found with his ribs gently folded inward, as if the sea had leaned on him, his eyes pushed a little way out of his face and his mouth full of pink froth.

A Wreckwives’ advice-sheet, passed hand to hand on the Mile. “He will be gentle. Let him. Do not ask where he went. Do not wake him by shaking; he does not wake, he surfaces, and you do not want to be leaning over the bed when he does. Count the children every morning, aloud, and make him count them with you, and watch his mouth.”

The Tenanted — Someone Else Looking Out
AttributesHand 3 · Gut 6 · Lung 3 · Eye 4 · Tongue 3 · Caul 6
Cut & RegrowthCut 3 (Lung-line) · Regrowth 12 in part (the Tenant has the whole house) · Hunger 2
SkillsClause 3, Persuade 3, Instinct 5, Search 3, Brawl 3, Endure 4
BodyFlesh 18 · Guard 16 · Armor 2 (compressed flesh; blunt weapons deal −1 more) · Threat 4
Attacksa heavy hand +6 (3, Grapple 18); the Press +7 against everyone within 5 paces (2, ignoring Armor; ears bleed)
AbilitiesTide 3. Riding (it is a god wearing a person; see The God-Ridden). Fathom Weight: cannot be knocked down, lifted or pushed. Two Voices: when it speaks in both, every listener rolls Caul + Resolve 14 or takes 1 Fray and believes what it says for a scene. Wants nothing it will admit. Treat it as a person first.
Dread0 at a distance / 3 when a loved one recognizes what is behind the eyes
EndCut it and it bleeds seawater by the gallon, more than its body can hold. Drained dry it lies down, an empty skin. Somewhere in the Trench, it is said, the water it held goes on.

Ribwalkers

On the Uncovered, among the leather weed-forests and the wrecks standing upright, there are things with too many ribs. Salvagers call them Ribwalkers. A Ribwalker is a cage of long curved bones, thirty or forty pairs, opening and closing like a slow bellows, mounted on legs that might once have been the ribs of something else. There is no head. There is meat inside the cage, a grey sack that pulses, and there is usually a salvager’s boot or two, and buttons, and once a wedding band on a finger bone. They move toward water, any water, at a creaking stalk, with a sound like a ship’s timbers working in a swell, and they open their ribs wide over anything wet and alive and close them, and squeeze, and drink. The squeezed come out flat, dry as leather, with their bail-buckets still on their belts and their faces pressed into the shape of a scream that made no sound, because there was no breath left to make it. Some salvagers swear the Ribwalkers are what the Admiralty’s fallen sailors become. Hask Tarn will not say.

Keep your water-barrel a hundred paces from the camp and your bucket on your belt and never, never bail after dark. They smell it.
Uncovered salvage-rule, first of nine

Ribwalker Threat 3 · Flesh 22 · Guard 13 · Attack +7 (rib-cage closing 4, Grapple 18; held targets lose 2 Flesh per round as the water is pressed out of them) · Armor 3 (bone lattice) · Dread 2 / 3 when it closes on someone · Tide 4; drawn to a character who has just bailed.

The Dowager Below

Lady Ondine Vasht lives in the flooded cellars of the palace in Lowmark, and the cellars have had to be extended twice. She is far into the Course and has not been seen whole in years. What can be seen of her, through the black water by lamplight, is a vast grey shape folded into the vaults, skin like a drowned sail, hair that drifts across the floor of three cellars, and eyes the size of serving platters, dark and wide and wet, which open one at a time in different rooms. The cellars smell of cold stone, bladderwrack and a great animal’s breath, and the water is warmer than it should be, blood-warm near the walls where she lies against them. She is still a grandmother. She still has opinions about the prince’s marriage. She speaks through the water: the surface of every cistern in the palace trembles with her words. She would like her grandson to come down. She has been asking for years. The servants who go down to feed her return with less of their breath every time, and some do not return. The ones that come up again sometimes come up years later, through a palace drain, pale and swollen and polite, asking whether the Dowager is receiving.

Her ladyship takes the mutton on Tuesdays and a footman on the first of the month. That is not written down anywhere, and you will not write it down either.
the palace steward, to a new under-butler
Lady Ondine Vasht — the Dowager Below
AttributesHand 4 · Gut 9 · Lung 5 · Eye 5 · Tongue 5 · Caul 8
